SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p811/r5.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p811/r5.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p811/r5.claim: Hamd is praise, not necessarily for a blessing and possibly for deeds; shukr responds only to blessings and is enacted through gratitude.
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p811/r5.anchor: الشكر فلا يكون إلا على النعم

BURHAN:v3p284/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p284/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p284/r1.claim: The Fātiḥa has the usual order الحمد لله; in al-Jāthiya فلله الحمد answers the implied question of who deserves praise, like the question about today's dominion and its answer.
BURHAN:v3p284/r1.anchor: فتقدم الحمد في الأول جاء على الأصل والثاني على تقدير الجواب فكأنه قيل عند وقوع الأمر لمن الحمد

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.claim: Al-Harali maps al-Fatiha's verses to the seven letters: praise, lawful and forbidden, command and prohibition, clear and ambiguous, then the corresponding petitions; its opening gathers all seven.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r1.anchor: فالآية الأولى تشتمل على حرف الحمد السابع

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.claim: He offers two readings of the merciful names: universal mercy permits created benefits while specific mercy protects from harm; he says the nearer reading is general lordly beneficence and a special divine mercy directed to felicity.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28#s002/r2.anchor: وأما الرحيمية فطهرتهم من مضار أبدانهم ورجاسة نفوسهم ومجهلة قلوبهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r3.claim: The surah begins with praise so the second half of the Qur'an opens with الحمد لله, echoing the opening of the first half in al-Fātiḥa and the approximate start of the fourth quarter in Q 35:1.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p244/r3.anchor: وهي مفتتحة بالحمد حتى يكون افتتاح النصف الثاني من القرآن ب الحمد لله

BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.claim: The surah is Fatiha because it opens the codex, instruction, Qur'an recitation, prayer, speech, revelation, the aims of this life, and the gates of Paradise.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r1.anchor: لافتتاح المصاحف والتعليم وقراءة القرآن والصلاة بها وإما لأن الحمد فاتحة كل كلام

BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.claim: It is also a key to the Qur'an's treasures: knowledge of its meanings unlocks ambiguous passages and illuminates its verses.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r2.anchor: لأنها مفتاح كنوز لطائف الخطاب بانجلائها ينكشف جميع القرآن لأهل البيان

BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.claim: Fatiha is the Mother of the Qur'an because it gathers the Qur'an's purposes: affirming divinity and prophethood, and establishing decree and predestination.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r3.anchor: أربعة : إقرار بالألوهية والنبوة وإثبات القضاء والقدر

BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.claim: The opening praise and names of the Merciful indicate God's divinity.
BURSEVI:v1p2/r4.anchor: {الحمد لله رب العالمين * الرحمن الرحيم} يدل على الألوهية

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.claim: It is called the seven oft-repeated because it has seven verses, each can stand for seven Qur'anic portions, and reciting them is said to earn the whole Qur'an's reward or close seven gates of Hell.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r1.anchor: لأنها سبع آيات أو لأن كل آية منها تقوم مقام سبع من القرآن

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.claim: The name al-mathani is explained by repetition in prayer or each rak'a, intercession in each rak'a, or revelation twice, in Mecca and Medina.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r2.anchor: فلأنها تثنى في كل صلاة أو في كل ركعة بالنسبة إلى الأخرى

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.claim: Other names include the Prayer, Healing, Cure, Foundation, Sufficient, Complete, Praise, Supplication, Thanks, and Invocation surahs because their meanings occur in it.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r3.anchor: وسميت بسورة الصلاة وسورة الشفاء والشافية وأساس القرآن والكافية والوافية

BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.claim: It is called the Treasure surah because a report says the Opening is a treasure from God's Throne.
BURSEVI:v1p2#2/r4.anchor: وسورة الكنز لما يروى أن الله تعالى قال : "فاتحة الكتاب كنز من كنوز عرشي"

BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.claim: The five divine attributes unfold a sequence: God creates, nurtures with favors, conceals sin in mercy, forgives repentance, and finally judges.
BURSEVI:v1p6/r2.anchor: خلقتك فأنا إله ثم ربيتك بالنعم فأنا رب ثم عصيت فسترت عليك فأنا رحمن

BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.claim: Bursevi relays the Najmiyya interpretation that the self has four faculties, matched by four divine attributes that draw the servant toward God.
BURSEVI:v1p9/r4.anchor: فللنفس أربع صفات : أمارة ، ولوامة ، وملهمة ، ومطمئنة

QASHANI:1:2/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r1.claim: Praise in action and in the tongue of each thing’s state is the appearance of its perfections and attainment of its ends, a fitting opening tribute to its Lord.
QASHANI:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد بالفعل ولسان الحال هو ظهور الكمالات وحصول الغايات من الأشياء إذ هي أثنية فاتحة ومدح رائعة لموليها

QASHANI:1:2/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r2.claim: All beings praise and glorify God through their particular properties, orientation toward ends, and actualization of potential; their dependence on Him alone denies partners and deficiency and manifests His majesty and beauty. The Qur’an says every thing glorifies Him.

QASHANI:1:2/r3.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r3.claim: God is Lord of the worlds as origin, preserver, and manager of all; worlds means everything known to God, and the sound masculine plural reflects encompassing knowledge or predominance.

QASHANI:1:2/r4.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r4.claim: Divine provision includes general and particular good: outward blessings such as health and livelihood, and inward blessings such as knowledge and recognition.

QASHANI:1:2/r5.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r5.claim: God is owner at the final return and recompense; only the worshipped one to whom sovereignty returns can reward enduring blessing for perishable life, as servants shed acts and attributes and receive true existence after annihilation.
QASHANI:1:2/r5.anchor: وباعتبار منتهائيته التي هي معنى مالكية الأشياء في يوم الدين إذ لا يجزي في الحقيقة إلا المعبود الذي ينتهي إليه الملك

QASHANI:1:2/r6.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r6.claim: All praise belongs to God eternally according to His due, at beginning, end, and everything between; He is both praiser and praised, worshipper and worshipped, in detail and in unity.
QASHANI:1:2/r6.anchor: فله تعالى مطلق الحمد وماهيته أزلا وأبدا على حسب استحقاقه إياه بذاته باعتبار البداية والنهاية وما بينهما

QASHANI:1:2/r7.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
QASHANI:1:2/r7.claim: Seeing God’s attributes in His speech leads servants to address Him by worship and ask His aid, since they see no other object of worship or independent power; every motion becomes worship and love seeks His beauty everywhere.
QASHANI:1:2/r7.anchor: ولما تجلى في كلامه لعباده بصفاته

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r1.claim: Hamd is praise of the praised one by naming noble attributes and beautiful acts; the definite article denotes the whole, so every praise, whether for attribute or act, belongs to God.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r1.anchor: حقيقة الحمد الثناء على المحمود ، بذكر نعوته الجليلة وأفعاله الجميلة ، واللام ها هنا للجنس ، ومقتضاها

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r2.claim: God is praised for the manifestation of His sovereignty and thanked for the abundance of His beneficence.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r2.anchor: فله الحمد لظهور سلطانه ، وله الشكر لوفور إحسانه

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r3.claim: Praise is due to God's majesty and beauty, while thanks answer His abundant gifts and gracious favors.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r3.anchor: والحمد لله لاستحقاقه لجلاله وجماله ، والشكر لله لجزيل نواله وعزيز أفضاله

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r4.claim: God's self-praise is a perfection of His attributes and power; creatures praise Him for His beneficence, generosity, majesty, and beauty.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r4.anchor: فحمده سبحانه له هو من صفات كماله وحوله ، وحمد الخلق له على إنعامه وطوله

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r5.claim: Qushayri enumerates God's eternal existence, generosity, oneness, everlastingness, hearing, sight, decree, speech, might, mercy, and beauty as aspects of His exalted perfection.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r5.anchor: فله الوجود ( قدرة ) القديم ، وله الجود الكريم ، وله الثبوت الأحدي ، والكون الصمدي ،

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r6.claim: The passage expresses divine unity through paired identities: His being is His essence, eternity His endlessness, decree His destiny, majesty His beauty, and command and anger are inseparable from their counterparts.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r6.anchor: رداؤه ، وعلاؤه سناؤه ، ومجده عزه ، وكونه ذاته ، وأزله أبده ، وقدمه سرمده ، وحقه

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r7.claim: Knowing that His friends long to praise Him but cannot do justice to His glory, God praises Himself in the Fatiha; hearing God's praise of Himself revives and honors their secrets.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r7.anchor: علم الحق سبحانه وتعالى شدة إرادة أوليائه بحمده وثنائه ، وعجزهم عن القيام بحق مدحه على مقتضى عزه

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r8.claim: On hearing God's self-praise, the Prophet recognized that restraint was fitting and said he could not enumerate God's praise, for God is as He praised Himself.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r8.anchor: لما سمع حمده لنفسه ، ومدحه سبحانه لحقه ، علم النبي أن تقاصر اللسان أليق به في هذه

QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r9.claim: Those at one level praise God for gifts that benefit or avert harm, but recognize only a portion of His kindness and favors.
QUSHAYRI:v1p9/r9.anchor: وتتفاوت طبقات الحامدين لتباينهم في أحوالهم ؛ فطائفة حمدوه على ما نالوا من إنعامه وإكرامه من نوعي صفة

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r1.claim: One group praises God for the subtle wonders disclosed to their hearts, hidden kindness in their innermost selves, and sudden inspirations of His encounters.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r1.anchor: وطائفة حمدوه على ما لاح لقلوبهم من عجائب لطائفه ، وأودع سرائرهم من مكنونات بره ، وكاشف أسرارهم

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r2.claim: Another group praises Him while witnessing the eternal attributes and does not turn from majesty and generosity to count blessings; praising majesty differs from thanking for favors.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r2.anchor: وقوم حمدوه عند شهود ما كاشفهم به من صفات القدم ، ولم يردوا من ملاحظة العز والكرم إلى

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r3.claim: A further group is consumed by divine unity: God speaks through them, from Himself and toward Himself, while outwardly they remain in differentiation and inwardly are held by the gathering of union.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r3.anchor: وقوم حمدوه مستهلكين عنهم فيما استنطقوا من عبارات تحميده ، بما اصطلم أسرارهم من حقائق توحيده ، فهم

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r4.claim: The name Lord means master; “the worlds” includes every creature, rational and inanimate, whose entities God owns and whose forms and dwellings He brings into being.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r4.anchor: الرب هو السيد ، والعالمون جميع المخلوقات ، واختصاص هذا الجمع بلفظ العالمين لاشتماله على العقلاء والجمادات فهو

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r5.claim: Lord also means nurturer: He supports worshippers' souls, guides seekers' hearts, unifies knowers' spirits, provides for bodies, and lets spirits witness generosity.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r5.anchor: ويدل اسم الرب أيضا على تربية الخلق ، فهو مرب نفوس العابدين بالتأييد ومرب قلوب الطالبين بالتسديد ،

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r6.claim: Lord also means one who sets affairs right: He cares for ascetics, suffices worshippers, and gives knowers His ancient care, leading some to contentment, others to longing, and others to readiness for meeting Him.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r6.anchor: فهو مصلح أمور الزاهدين بجميل رعايته ، ومصلح أمور العابدين بحسن كفايته ، ومصلح أمور الواجدين بقديم عنايته

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r7.claim: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim derive from mercy, an eternal attribute meaning the will of blessing; as emphatic forms they do not differ for those who verify spiritual realities.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r7.anchor: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة ، والرحمة صفة أزلية وهي إرادة النعمة وهما اسمان موضوعان للمبالغة ولا فضل بينهما

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r8.speaker: قيل
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r8.claim: An alternative view makes al-Rahman more emphatic and complete; only God is called al-Rahman absolutely, while al-Rahim can describe others.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r8.anchor: وقيل الرحمن أشد مبالغة وأتم في الإفادة ، وغير الحق سبحانه لا يسمى بالرحمن على الإطلاق ، والرحيم

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r9.claim: The servant recognizes God as al-Rahman through His mercy; without that mercy no one would know Him by this name.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r9.anchor: وبرحمته عرف العبد أنه الرحمن ، ولولا رحمته لما عرف أحد أنه الرحمن

QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r10.claim: If mercy is the will of blessing or blessing itself, blessings differ in rank: some benefit bodies and outward life, others spirits and inner life.
QUSHAYRI:v1p10/r10.anchor: وإذا كانت الرحمة إرادة النعمة ، أو نفس النعمة كما هي عند قوم فالنعم في أنفسها مختلفة ،

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r1.claim: On the view that distinguishes the names, al-Rahman has a specific name but broad meaning, giving everyone outward comfort, while al-Rahim has a broad name but specific meaning, giving believers inward life.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r1.anchor: وعلى طريقة من فرق بينهما فالرحمن خاص الاسم عام المعنى ، والرحيم عام الاسم خاص المعنى ؛ فلأنه

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r2.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r2.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r2.claim: The paired names are also read as outward refreshment from al-Rahman and inward illumination from al-Rahim.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r2.anchor: فالرحمن بما روح ، والرحيم بما لوح ؛ فالترويح بالمبار ، والتلويح بالأنوار

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r3.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r3.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r3.claim: Al-Rahman discloses His manifestation, while al-Rahim gently takes charge of the servant.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r3.anchor: والرحمن بكشف تجليه والرحيم بلطف توليه

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r4.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r4.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r4.claim: Al-Rahman grants faith, while al-Rahim bestows recognition; another pairing assigns recognition to al-Rahman and forgiveness to al-Rahim.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r4.anchor: والرحمن بما أولى من الإيمان والرحيم بما أسدى من العرفان ، والرحمن بما أعطى من العرفان والرحيم بما

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r5.claim: Further distinctions pair al-Rahman with granting forgiveness and al-Rahim with bestowing divine satisfaction, then pair them with veiling and the bliss of vision.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r5.anchor: بل الرحمن بما ينعم به من الغفران والرحيم بما يمن به من الرضوان ، بل الرحمن بما يكتم

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r6.claim: Al-Rahman enables spiritual practice, while al-Rahim brings realization; practice belongs to seekers and realized communion to those who have found.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r6.anchor: بل الرحمن بما يوفق ، والرحيم بما تحقق ، والتوفيق للمعاملات ، والتحقيق للمواصلات ، فالمعاملات للقاصدين ،

QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r7.claim: Al-Rahman makes things for the servants through gracious care, and al-Rahim wards things off through gracious solicitude.
QUSHAYRI:v1p11/r7.anchor: والرحمن بما يصنع لهم والرحيم بما يدفع عنهم ؛ فالصنع بجميل الرعاية والدفع بحسن العناية

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r1.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r1.claim: Praise is thanks to God for the favor of teaching people how to praise Him.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r1.anchor: قال ابن عطاء : معناه الشكر لله إذا كان منه الامتنان على تعليمنا إياه

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r2.claim: The phrase means that no one praises God except God Himself.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r2.anchor: وقيل معنى الحمد لله أي : لا حمدا لله إلا الله

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r3.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r3.claim: God is praised for all His attributes and states.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r3.anchor: وقيل الحمد لله أي : أنت المحمود لجميع صفاتك وأحوالك

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r4.speaker: الواسطي
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r4.claim: People praise at three levels: ordinary habit, gratitude for pleasure, and recognition that God did not leave them to sever blessings from witnessing His due.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r4.anchor: قال الواسطي : الناس في الحمد على ثلاث درجات

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r5.speaker: جعفر الصادق
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r5.claim: True praise knows God through oneness, sovereignty, and permanence, signified by the letters of hamd.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r5.anchor: وذكر عن جعفر الصادق في قوله ' الحمد لله ' فقال : من حمده

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r6.speaker: الجنيد
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r6.claim: Junayd tells a speaker to complete praise with Lord of the worlds; created beings leave no trace when joined to the Eternal.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r6.anchor: وقال رجل بين يدي الجنيد رحمه الله : الحمد لله فقال لأتمها

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r7.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r7.speaker: عطاء
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r7.claim: Praise expresses believers' affirmation of oneness, monotheists' affirmation of singularity, and knowers' recognition of God's rightful lordship and majesty.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r7.anchor: وذكر عن عطاء أو غيره أنه قال : الحمد لله إقرار المؤمنين

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r8.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r8.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r8.claim: Believers praise through the Fatiha, seekers through secluded remembrance, and knowers through longing and intimacy.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r8.anchor: وقيل الحمد : هو الثناء لله فثناء المؤمنين في قراءة فاتحة الكتاب

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r9.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r9.speaker: الحسين
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r9.claim: No blessing is better than praise; God is the praised, the servant the praiser, and praise is the state that connects to the seeker.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r9.anchor: وقال الحسين : ما من نعمة إلا والحمد أفضل منها

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r10.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r10.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r10.claim: God praised Himself for the worlds before their creation, knowing they could not fulfill His praise.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r10.anchor: وقيل أيضا : الحمد لله رب العالمين عن العالمين قبل العالمين

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r11.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r11.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r11.claim: Calling the worlds His subjects and adding them to Himself is mercy for them.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r11.anchor: وقيل هذا رحمة للعالمين بإضافته إياهم إليه أنه ربهم

SULAMI:v1p33#3/r12.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r12.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r12.claim: Praise is due in both ease and hardship, while thanks is due only for blessings.
SULAMI:v1p33#3/r12.anchor: وقيل في الحمد لله رب العالمين : إن الحمد يكون على السراء والضراء

SULAMI:v1p34/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r1.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r1.claim: Praise comes from being immersed in blessing, whereas thanksgiving seeks an increase.
SULAMI:v1p34/r1.anchor: وقيل : الحمد لله يكون لاستغراق الحامد في النعمة والشكر لاستزاده

SULAMI:v1p34/r2.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r2.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r2.claim: The phrase is the worlds' own utterance of praise.
SULAMI:v1p34/r2.anchor: وقيل في قوله : الحمد لله رب العالمين أي منطق العالمين لحمده

SULAMI:v1p34/r3.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r3.speaker: ابن عطاء
SULAMI:v1p34/r3.claim: God nurtures knowers with certainty, believers with patience and sincerity, seekers with honesty and loyalty, and knowers' hearts with reflection and insight.
SULAMI:v1p34/r3.anchor: وذكر عن ابن عطاء في قوله الحمد لله رب العالمين أي : مربى أفضل العارفين

SULAMI:v1p34/r4.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r4.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r4.claim: God created and nurtured the worlds through mercy so they could glorify Him; He praised Himself in eternity without cause, while creaturely praise is mixed with motives.
SULAMI:v1p34/r4.anchor: وقيل : رب العالمين أي هو الذي برأ العالمين بين رحمته الرحمن الرحيم

SULAMI:v1p34/r5.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r5.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r5.claim: God alone inspires the worlds to praise Him.
SULAMI:v1p34/r5.anchor: وقيل رب العالمين ، أي : ملهم العالمين بحمده وحده

SULAMI:v1p34/r6.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r6.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r6.claim: Knowing servants cannot adequately praise God, so He praised Himself in eternity and relieved them of an impossible burden; even the Messenger admits he cannot enumerate His praise.
SULAMI:v1p34/r6.anchor: ألا ترى سيد المرسلين كيف أظهر العجز بقوله ' لا أحصي ثناء عليك أنت كما أثنيت على نفسك '

SULAMI:v1p34/r7.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r7.speaker: بعضهم
SULAMI:v1p34/r7.claim: God's self-praise accounts for abundant blessings and human inability, lifting the burden of seeing the benefaction from servants.
SULAMI:v1p34/r7.anchor: وحمد نفسه بالأزل لما علم من كثرة نعمه على عباده وعجزهم عن القيام

SULAMI:v1p34/r8.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v1p34/r8.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
SULAMI:v1p34/r8.claim: Jafar explains the letters of hamd through God's oneness, gentleness, prior self-praise, majesty, and Islam, whose abode and greeting are peace.
SULAMI:v1p34/r8.anchor: وسئل جعفر بن محمد عن قوله : الحمد لله رب العالمين قال : معناه الشكر لله

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas calls praise of God a word of gratitude; when a servant says it, God says that His servant has thanked Him.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r1.anchor: عن يوسف بن مهران قال : قال ابن عباس : الحمد لله كلمة الشكر ، واذا قال العبد

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas describes al-hamd as thanking God, appealing to Him, and acknowledging His blessings and beneficence.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r2.anchor: عن الضحاك ، عن ابن عباس : الحمد لله هو الشكر لله ، الاستجداء لله ، والاقرار له بنعمه

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r3.speaker: كعب
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r3.claim: Ka'b says al-hamd is praise of God.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r3.anchor: عن السلولي عن كعب قال : الحمد لله ثناء على الله

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r4.speaker: الضحاك
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak calls praise the mantle of the All-Merciful.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r4.anchor: عن يحيى بن عبد الرحمن - يعني أبا بسطام - عن الضحاك قال : الحمد رداء الرحمن

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r5.speaker: علي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r5.claim: In one transmitted account, Ali answers Umar that al-hamd is a word God approved for Himself.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r5.anchor: عن ابن أبي مليكة عن ابن عباس ، قال : قال عمر : قد علمنا سبحان الله ، ولا اله الا الله ، فما الحمد لله ؟ فقال علي : كلمة رضيها الله لنفسه

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r6.speaker: علي
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r6.claim: A variant report has Umar ask what Subhan Allah means; Ali says it is a word God loves, approves, and wishes people to say.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r6.anchor: فقال فيه : قال عمر لعلي رضي الله عنهما واصحابه عنده : لا اله الا الله ، والحمد لله ، والله اكبر ، قد عرفناها ، فما سبحان الله ؟ فقال علي

IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r7.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says Gabriel told Muhammad that Lord of the worlds means God owns all creation: the heavens, earths, their inhabitants, and all between them, known and unknown.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p26#2/r7.anchor: عن الضحاك ، عن ابن عباس قال : ثم قال جبريل عليه السلام : قال الحمد لله رب العالمين ، قال : يا محمد ، له الخلق كله

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r1.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r1.claim: Abu al-Aliya says the worlds include humans and jinn and either eighteen thousand or fourteen thousand angelic worlds on earth, created for worship and distributed among its four corners.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r1.anchor: عن الربيع بن انس ، عن أبي العالية : رب العالمين . قال : الانس عالم ، والجن عالم ، وما سوى ذلك ثمانية عشر الف عالم

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r2.speaker: تبيع
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r2.claim: Tabi' says the worlds are a thousand communities: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r2.anchor: عن معتب بن سمى ، عن تبيع ، في قوله : رب العالمين ، قال : العالمين الف امة ، فستمائة في البحر

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r3.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r3.claim: Qatada glosses the worlds as whatever God described among His creation.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r3.anchor: عن مطر الوراق ، عن قتادة في قول الله : رب العالمين قال : ما وصف من خلقه

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas restricts the worlds to jinn and humans.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r4.anchor: عن ابن عباس ، في قولهرب العالمين قال : الجن والانس

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r5.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r5.speaker: author
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r5.claim: The source notes that a similar view is attributed to Ali through an unreliable chain.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r5.anchor: وروى عن علي بن أبي طالب باسناد لا يعتمد عليه مثله

IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r6.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r6.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v1p27/r6.claim: Mujahid is also reported to restrict the worlds to jinn and humans.

IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.claim: In a sacred report, God says that when the worshipper says praise belongs to God, the servant has praised Him, and when he says the two mercy names, he has extolled Him.
IBNABIHATIM:v1p28/r1.anchor: قال رسول لله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يقول الله : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي ، فاذا قال الحمد لله رب العالمين ، قال : مدحني عبدي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.claim: He reads the sura's annexation to Fatihat al-Kitab as descriptive: it means a sura characterized as the Book's opening, with no separate title needed.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r1.anchor: إضافة السورة إلى فاتحة الكتاب من إضافة الموصوف إلى الصفة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.claim: By contrast, Fatihat al-Kitab is a true annexation: al-Kitab here means the remainder of the Book apart from the sura called the Opening.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r2.anchor: إضافة فاتحة إلى الكتاب فإضافة حقيقية باعتبار أن المراد من الكتاب بقيته

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.claim: The names Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitab are established in the Sunna; “mother” denotes a thing's origin and source.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r3.anchor: وأما تسميتها أم القرآن وأم الكتاب فقد ثبتت في السنة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.claim: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says Abu Sa'id al-Khudri recited Umm al-Qur'an over a person suffering from a sting as a healing prayer.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r4.anchor: أن أبا سعيد الخدري رقى ملدوغا فجعل يقرأ عليه بأم القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.speaker: النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.claim: A sound hadith calls a prayer without Umm al-Qur'an deficient.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r5.anchor: كل صلاة لم يقرأ فيها بأم القرآن فهي خداج

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.claim: One explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it begins and opens the Qur'an, making it like its origin.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r6.anchor: أنها مبدؤه ومفتتحه فكأنها أصله ومنشؤه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.claim: A second explanation is that the sura gathers the Qur'an's three main aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r7.anchor: تشتمل محتوياتها على أنواع مقاصد القرآن وهي ثلاثة أنواع

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.claim: The opening praise gathers God's praised attributes, declares His uniqueness in divinity, and affirms resurrection and recompense.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r8.anchor: الثناء على الله ثناء جامعا لوصفه بجميع المحامد وتنزيهه عن جميع النقائص

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.claim: The sura's three aims together represent the Qur'an's original purposes, while its remaining material elaborates them.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r11.anchor: فهذه هي أنواع مقاصد القرآن كله ، وغيرها تكملات لها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.claim: He also supports the sura's comprehensiveness by citing the sound report that al-Ikhlas counts as a third of the Qur'an because all its wording praises God.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p132#2/r12.anchor: وقد يؤيد هذا الوجه بما ورد في الصحيح في : { قل هو الله أحد }

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.claim: A third explanation of Umm al-Qur'an is that it contains the Qur'an's theoretical wisdom and practical rulings, including theology, prophecy, admonition, worship, transactions, morals, and law.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r1.anchor: تشتمل معانيها على جملة معاني القرآن من الحكم النظرية والأحكام العملية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r2.claim: Al-hamdu lillah implies all attributes of perfection that entitle God to exclusive praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r2.anchor: يشمل سائر صفات الكمال التي استحق الله لأجلها حصر الحمد له تعالى

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r3.claim: Rabb al-alamin encompasses God's acts and creative attributes for those who affirm such attributes.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r3.anchor: يشمل سائر صفات الأفعال والتكوين عند من أثبتها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.claim: Taken explicitly and by implication, the sura gives a general outline of the Qur'an's aims and prompts readers to seek their fuller detail as able.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r11.anchor: يحصل من معاني الفاتحة تصريحا وتضمنا علم إجمالي بما حواه القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.claim: Requiring al-Fatiha in every rak'ah preserves recollection of the Qur'an's purposes contained within it.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p133/r12.anchor: فرضت قراءة الفاتحة في كل ركعة من الصلاة حرصا على التذكر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r1.speaker: النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r1.claim: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla says the Prophet identified al-Hamdu lillah as the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an given to him.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r1.anchor: عن أبي سعيد ابن المعلى ( أن رسول الله قال : { الحمد لله رب العالمين } هي السبع المثاني

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r2.claim: The sura has seven verses by agreement among reciters and commentators, with a few dissenting counts.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r2.anchor: أنها سبع آيات باتفاق القراء والمفسرين

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r3.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r3.claim: Hasan al-Basri counts the sura as eight verses.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r3.anchor: الحسن البصري فقال : هي ثمان آيات

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r4.speaker: الحسين الجعفي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r4.claim: Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counts it as six verses; an unspecified view counts nine, which requires excluding the basmala, while counting it in seven merges two verses.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r4.anchor: إلا الحسين الجعفي فقال : هي ست آيات

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r5.claim: Mathani is a plural of muthanna, with alternative vocalized or lightened forms; al-Jurjani notes that each can also be feminine.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r5.anchor: مفاعل جمع مثنى بضم الميم وتشديد النون

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r6.claim: Al-Kashshaf explains the name as referring to verses repeated in each rak'ah; this is also said to be transmitted from Umar.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r6.anchor: أن تلك الآيات تثنى في كل ركعة كذا في ( الكشاف )

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r7.claim: Ibn Ashur accepts the explanation tied to each rak'ah because al-Fatiha is joined to another sura in every rak'ah.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r7.anchor: لأن معناه أنها تضم إليها السورة في كل ركعة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r8.claim: Another account connects the name to the early form of prayer: prayers were first prescribed as two rak'ahs, travel prayer remained so, and residence prayer was lengthened; an opposite account is also mentioned.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r8.anchor: أن الصلوات فرضت ركعتين ثم أقرت صلاة السفر وأطيلت صلاة الحضر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r9.claim: A further view takes mathani to mean repeated in prayer, citing Arabic use of the dual for repeated action.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r9.anchor: لأنها تثنى في الصلاة أي تكرر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r10.claim: On this reading, mathani in al-Fatiha resembles the repeated narratives and themes in the Qur'an called mathani in al-Zumar.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r10.anchor: وعليه فيكون المراد بالمثاني هنا مثل المراد بالمثاني في قوله تعالى : { كتابا متشابها مثاني }

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r11.claim: The claim that al-Fatiha was named for being revealed once in Mecca and again in Medina is very remote: repetition of revelation is not accepted, and the sura is agreed to be Meccan.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p134/r11.anchor: وهذا قول بعيد جدا وتكرر النزول لا يعتبر قائله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.speaker: النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.claim: A hadith in both Sahihs from Abu Hurayra has God divide prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each portion of al-Fatiha and granting the servant's request.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r10.anchor: قسمت الصلاة نصفين بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.claim: The verse division differs by region: Medinans exclude the basmala and count “those You favored” as a verse; Meccans and Kufans include the basmala and combine that phrase with its verse; Hasan counts both separately.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p135/r11.anchor: فعند أهل المدينة لا تعد البسملة آية وتعد : { أنعمت عليهم } آية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r1.claim: Ibn Ashur says sound Sunna contains no evidence that the basmala is a verse at the beginnings of Qur'anic suras, and presents six proofs.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r1.anchor: فلا نجد في صحيح السنة ما يشهد بأن البسملة آية من أوائل سور القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r2.claim: The first proof is Malik's report from Abu Hurayra: God's division of prayer begins with al-Hamdu lillah, without mentioning the basmala; prayer here means recitation in prayer.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r2.anchor: والمراد في الصلاة القراءة في الصلاة ووجه الدليل منه أنه لم يذكر بسم الله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r3.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r3.claim: In the second proof, Ubayy ibn Ka'b recites the celebrated sura from al-Hamdu lillah to its end when asked how he opens prayer, without reciting the basmala.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r3.anchor: قال أبي فقرأت { الحمد لله رب العالمين } حتى أتيت على آخرها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r4.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r4.claim: Anas reports in Muslim and other collections that the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar began recitation with al-Hamdu lillah and did not mention the basmala at either end.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r4.anchor: لا يذكرون ( بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ) ، لا في أول قراءة ولا في آخرها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r5.speaker: عائشة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r5.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the takbir and began recitation with al-Hamdu lillah.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r5.anchor: كان رسول الله يستفتح الصلاة بالتكبير والقراءة بالحمد الله رب العالمين

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r6.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r6.claim: Ibn Mughaffal says he prayed with the Prophet and the first three caliphs but never heard them say the basmala, and directs worshippers to recite al-Hamdu lillah.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r6.anchor: فلم أسمع أحدا منهم يقول : ( بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ) ، إذا أنت صليت فقل { الحمد لله رب العالمين }

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r7.claim: The decisive sixth proof is Medina's continuous practice: across generations, its mosque did not recite the basmala aloud in congregational prayers, making the practice mutawatir evidence that it is not part of the sura.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p140/r7.anchor: فإن المسجد النبوي من وقت نزول الوحي إلى زمن مالك صلى فيه رسول الله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.speaker: البيضاوي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.claim: Al-Baydawi explains pairing God's proper name with al-Rahman and al-Rahim as invoking His entitlement to assistance and mercy: al-Rahman signals the gifts involved in righteous action, with al-Rahim explained later.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p150/r5.anchor: ثم يذكر وصف الرحمن إشارة إلى أن الاستعانة على الأعمال الصالحة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.claim: Important guidance requires preparing listeners, stirring their attention, and removing stubbornness, false assumptions, and satanic impulses that block learning.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r1.anchor: ما بقي يخالجها العناد والبهتان ، وتخامر رشدها نزغات الشيطان

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r9.claim: The sura also teaches gratitude by crowning supplication with praise of the giver of intellect and guidance; opening important speech with praise is therefore Qur'anic practice.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r9.anchor: أن يقدروا النعمة حق قدرها بشكر المنعم بها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.claim: As a Qur'anic preface, al-Fatiha models an Arabic literary opening that improves understanding and attentive reception.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p152/r10.anchor: وهذا الأسلوب له شأن عظيم في صناعة الأدب العربي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha models four rules for introductions: keep them brief, foreshadow the subject, use concise comprehensive wording, and begin with praise of God.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r1.anchor: وقد رسم أسلوب الفاتحة للمنشئين ثلاث قواعد للمقدمة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r2.claim: A short introduction avoids tiring listeners while they await the main subject; the sura's brevity also explains placing it before longer chapters.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r2.anchor: ومن هذا يظهر وجه وضعها قبل السور الطوال مع أنها سورة قصيرة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r3.claim: A prologue should display rhetorical aptness by signaling the purpose, preparing listeners either to receive its details or to assess and complete them, and showing the speaker's command of the subject.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r3.anchor: أن تشير إلى الغرض المقصود وهو ما يسمى براعة الاستهلال

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r4.claim: A prologue should also be made of concise, comprehensive expressions and should open by praising God.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r4.anchor: أن تكون المقدمة من جوامع الكلم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.claim: Because the Qur'an guides people and reforms both worldly and future life, listeners must prepare by removing stubbornness, error, and low impulses before receiving its wisdom.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r5.anchor: فلا مناص لها قبل استقبال تلك الحكمة والنظر من الاتسام بميسم الفضيلة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.claim: These aims help explain why al-Fatiha is called Umm al-Qur'an.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p153/r10.anchor: ولأجل هذا سميت هاته السورة أم القرآن

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r1.claim: God placed praise before the supplication, following Arabic eloquence in which requests to great people begin with commendation.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r1.anchor: أن يفتتحوا خطابهم إياهم وطلبتهم بالثناء والذكر الجميل

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r2.speaker: أمية ابن أبي الصلت
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r2.claim: Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt's praise of Abd Allah ibn Jud'an says the addressee's modesty and praise can make a request unnecessary.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r2.anchor: إذا أثنى عليك المرء يوما كفاه عن تعرضه الثناء

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r3.claim: Opening weighty speech with praise became Qur'anic practice; Muslims call an important speech without such an opening “cut off,” following a hadith from Abu Hurayra.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r3.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه بالحمد لله أو بالحمد فهو أقطع

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r4.claim: Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan's Basra sermon was nicknamed al-Batra because it did not begin with praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r4.anchor: وقد لقبت خطبة زياد ابن أبي سفيان التي خطبها بالبصرة بالبتراء

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r5.claim: Hamd is praise for a chosen beautiful quality, whether an action such as generosity or another quality such as courage; thana' is its broader genus.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r5.anchor: و ( الحمد ) هو الثناء على الجميل أي الوصف الجميل الاختياري

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r6.claim: Ibn al-Qatta' and others wrongly infer from a hadith that thana' can praise or blame; the negative usage is verbal symmetry and hints that one should praise a Muslim or stay silent.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r6.anchor: وإنما هو مجاز دعت إليه المشاكلة اللفظية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r7.claim: Natha' with an initial n is the term used for good or bad mention, especially bad mention.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p154/r7.anchor: وأما الذي يستعمل في الخير والشر فهو النثاء بتقديم النون

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r1.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r1.claim: The majority hold that madh is broader than hamd because it can concern voluntary or involuntary qualities.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r1.anchor: فذهب الجمهور إلى أن المدح أعم من الحمد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls hamd and madh “siblings”; Ibn Ashur rejects the interpretation that he means only a remote derivational relationship and reads him as calling them synonymous.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r2.anchor: والذي عليه المحققون من شراح ( الكشاف ) أنه أراد من الأخوة هنا الترادف

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r3.speaker: السيد الشريف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r3.claim: Al-Sayyid al-Sharif takes al-Zamakhshari to mean that both words remain restricted to chosen beautiful qualities, supported by his discussion of praise for beauty and noble character at 49:7.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r3.anchor: وعلى الأول حمله السيد الشريف وهو ظاهر كلام سعد الدين

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r4.claim: Ibn Ashur notes that reliable scholars of rhetoric restrict praise to core virtues such as eloquence, courage, justice, and chastity, even where people praise attractive appearance.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r4.anchor: قصر المدح على النعت بأمهات الخير وهي كالفصاحة والشجاعة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r5.speaker: عبد الحكيم السلكوتي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r5.claim: Abd al-Hakim al-Salkuti takes the two terms as synonymous without a voluntary-quality restriction, but Ibn Ashur presents this as an assumption or report rather than a preference.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p155/r5.anchor: حمله المحقق عبد الحكيم السلكوتي في ( حواشي التفسير )

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r1.claim: A difficulty for defining hamd by voluntary qualities is that it would exclude God's essential attributes such as knowledge and power; proponents offer several answers.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r1.anchor: من أن مذهبهم يستلزم أن لا يحمد الله تعالى على صفاته

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r2.claim: One answer treats God's sublime attributes as voluntary because their possessor is independent; another says their voluntary effects make them equivalent to voluntary qualities.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r2.anchor: بأن تلك الصفات العلية نزلت منزلة الاختيارية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r3.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r3.claim: A third answer reads “voluntary” as describing the praised agent, not the particular attribute for which praise is given.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r3.anchor: أن المراد بالاختيارية أن يكون المحمود فاعلا بالاختيار

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r4.claim: Ibn Ashur says the voluntary condition only excludes traits that are not perfections in human beings; God's necessary eternal attributes are perfections, so no workaround is needed.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r4.anchor: عدم الاختيار في صفات الله تعالى زيادة في الكمال

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r5.claim: Language can express transcendent realities only through the closest available terms from familiar human meanings.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r5.anchor: عبر لهم عنها بأقصى ما يقربها من كلامهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r6.claim: Al-hamdu is nominative in all transmitted readings; its predicate is lillah, while an underlying analysis treats hamd as an accusative verbal noun replacing an omitted verb meaning “we praise God.”
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156/r6.anchor: ( الحمد ) مرفوع بالابتداء في جميع القراءات المروية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r1.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r1.claim: Sibawayh explains conventional verbal nouns such as “beware” or “thanks” as accusatives governed by verbs suppressed from use, and distinguishes supplicatory formulas from other expressions.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r1.anchor: وإنما جلبناه هنا لأنه أفصح كلام عن أطوار هذا المصدر في كلام العرب واستعمالهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r2.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r2.claim: For hamdan or shukran, an understood verb such as “I praise” is omitted because the source itself stands in its place, as in the established supplicatory formulas.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r2.anchor: فإنما ينتصب هذا على إضمار الفعل كأنك قلت أحمد الله حمدا

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r3.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r3.claim: Sibawayh says some such source expressions can be made nominative topics, as in al-hamdu lillah; the definite form favors this declarative use.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r3.anchor: هذا باب يختار فيه أن تكون المصادر مبتدأة مبنيا عليها ما بعدها

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r4.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r4.claim: Not every source phrase permits the nominative pattern; Sibawayh says expressions such as al-saqyu laka or al-raʿyu laka are not licensed.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r4.anchor: وليس كل حرف ( أي تركيب ) يصنع به ذاك

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r5.claim: Ibn Ashur cites Sibawayh to explain the Arabic stages of this verbal noun construction and the rationale for the nominative al-hamdu lillah.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p156#2/r5.anchor: لأنه أفصح كلام عن أطوار هذا المصدر في كلام العرب

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r1.claim: Raising hamd creates a nominal sentence for permanence, generic al for comprehensive praise, and fronting for emphasis; these effects are unavailable in the ordinary accusative construction.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r1.anchor: والعدول عن النصب هنا إلى الرفع ليتأتى لهم الدلالة على الدوام والثبات

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r2.claim: Accusative hamd can take al in the Tamim reading, but an implicit “I praise” limits praise to the speaker and “we praise” to believers or monotheists; generic hamd instead includes every praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r2.anchor: فالتعريف حينئذ لا يكون دالا على عموم المحامد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r3.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r3.claim: Sibawayh's distinction is that nominative hamd reports praise from the speaker and all creatures, while accusative hamd reports the speaker's praise alone.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r3.anchor: إن الذي يرفع الحمد يخبر أن الحمد منه ومن جميع الخلق

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r4.claim: Ibn Ashur says the nominative definite wording is most eloquent, conveys enduring and comprehensive praise, and cites al-Kashshaf's comparison with Abraham's greeting at 51:25.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p157/r4.anchor: إن العدول عن النصب إلى الرفع للدلالة على ثبات المعنى واستقراره

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r1.claim: Praise precedes God's name because this occasion is the beginning of Qur'anic revelation, the great blessing that brings success in both worlds and evokes the Revealer's beautiful attributes.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r1.anchor: قدم الحمد لأن المقام هنا مقام الحمد إذ هو ابتداء أولى النعم بالحمد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r2.claim: Situational importance can warrant foregrounding praise despite God's name being inherently more important; rhetoric follows the occasion and highlights what might otherwise go unnoticed.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r2.anchor: الأهمية العارضة تقدم على الأهمية الأصلية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r3.claim: Hamd can be fronted deliberately even though it is the grammatical subject, since Arabic eloquent usage offers both al-hamdu lillah and lillah al-hamd.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p158/r3.anchor: للبلغاء صيغتين متعارفتين في حمد الله تعالى

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r1.claim: The al in al-hamd is generic: because the verbal noun stands in place of an action, the definite form presents the kind of praise as familiar and makes it prominent, rather than identifying one instance.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r1.anchor: والتعريف فيه بالألف واللام تعريف الجنس

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r2.claim: Although the generic article is not itself exhaustive, its combination with the lām of divine specification implies that every instance of praise belongs to God; the restriction is rhetorical and emphatic.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p159/r2.anchor: والاستغراق الذي توهمه كثير من الناس وهم منهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r1.claim: The lām in lillah can indicate rhetorical specification or strengthen the relation of the verbal-noun subject to its predicate; specification remains conveyed by the definiteness of both parts.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r1.anchor: يجوز أن يكون للاختصاص على أنه اختصاص ادعائي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r2.claim: To decide whether al-hamdu lillah is report or performance, Ibn Ashur first explains that Arabic can turn statements into speech acts, as with sale formulas and words of praise or hope.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r2.anchor: أن الإنشاء قد يحصل بنقل المركب من الخبرية إلى الإنشاء

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r3.claim: One camp treats the sentence as a plain report: reporting that God has praise acknowledges His beautiful qualities, and some say the speaker is included among those praising Him.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r4.claim: Other report-only explanations say the speaker's own praise follows conventionally from the statement or that its literal content serves an intended implication, though this can make the speaker's praise secondary.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r4.anchor: وأجيب أيضا بأن كون المتكلم حامدا قد يحصل بالالتزام من الخبر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r5.claim: He explains the indirect reading as analogous to saying “long sword-belt” to convey tall stature: a literal expression can serve an intended implication.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p160/r5.anchor: ونظيره قولهم طويل النجاد والمراد طول القامة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r1.claim: A second view treats the line as an informative sentence deliberately used to perform praise, as a report can enact sorrow in “I bore her as a female” at 3:36.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r1.anchor: أريد منه الإنشاء مع اعتبار الخبرية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r2.claim: A separate view says the sentence is a pure performative transferred from reporting, like formulas for contracts and praise; the original report sense remains possible with contextual support.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r2.anchor: المذهب الثاني أن جملة { الحمد لله } إنشاء محض لا إشعار له بالخبرية

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r3.claim: Ibn Ashur's conclusion is that al-hamdu lillah reports praise while functioning as its performance; declarative form adds permanence, comprehensiveness, exclusivity, and emphasis.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r3.anchor: والحق الذي لا محيد عنه أن الحمد لله خبر مستعمل في الإنشاء

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r4.claim: He says these effects cannot be achieved through a purely performative wording such as hamdan lillah or ahmadu Allah hamdan.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p161/r4.anchor: وشيء من ذلك لا يمكن حصوله بصيغة إنشاء نحو حمدا لله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r1.speaker: ذي الرمة
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r1.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's line about a flame says that it produced gratitude to its Creator, showing Arabs could describe praise or thanks as something brought into being.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r1.anchor: ولما جرت في الجزل جريا كأنه سنا الفجر

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r2.claim: Allah is the proper name of the necessarily existent divine essence, the one deserving every praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r2.anchor: والله هو اسم الذاتت الواجبب الوجود المستحق لجميع المحامد

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r3.claim: Ibn Ashur derives Allah from al-ilah, a common noun for deity; its root may mean worship or states such as bewilderment, stillness, fear, or ardor, all associated with submission and reverence.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r3.anchor: وأصل هذا الاسم الإلاه بالتعريف وهو تعريف إلاه الذي هو اسم جنس للمعبود

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r4.claim: The form is faʿal with passive meaning, like kitab; Arabs applied it to their objects of worship and pluralized it as alihah, easing the second hamza into a long vowel.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r4.anchor: فهو فعال بكسر الفاء بمعنى مفعول مثل كتاب

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r5.claim: He conjectures that the name was established before Arab idolatry as the unique true deity, becoming a proper name by exclusive reference rather than predominance; it then marked the Creator as uniquely deserving worship.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r5.anchor: فكان أصل وضعه دالا على انفراده بالألوهية إذ لا إلاه غيره

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r6.claim: Ibn Ashur finds no evidence that Arabs used the definite singular al-ilah for an idol; they used a possessive phrase, often rabb, or a plural, and a conquest report speaks of idols in the Kaaba.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r6.anchor: وإننا لم نقف على أن العرب أطلقوا الإلاه معرفا باللام مفردا على أحد أصنامهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r7.claim: He says frequent use led Arabs to drop the hamza in al-ilah when referring to God, as in al-nas from al-unas, though they retained it in some speech.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p162/r7.anchor: فحذفوا الهمزة من الإلاه لكثرة استعمال هذا اللفظ

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r1.claim: The divine name became a unique proper form whose article is treated as part of the word, as the vocative يا الله shows; its formation has no parallel among ordinary names.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r1.anchor: هذه الطريقة في العلمية التي عرضت لاسم الجلالة لا نظير لها في الأعلام

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r2.claim: Al-Kashshaf's derivation of Allah from al-ilah is well supported: the poet's fixed expression معاذ الإلاه shows speakers treated al-ilah as the name's source, with variation only in the form's letters.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p163/r2.anchor: علمنا أنهم يعتبرون الإلاه أصلا للفظ الله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r1.claim: A poet's use of لاه and fixed expressions such as لله أبوك support treating لاه as a shortened form of Allah.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r1.anchor: لاه أبوك لأن هذا مما لزم حالة واحدة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r2.speaker: الجوهري عن سيبويه
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r2.claim: One proposed origin is لاه, a verbal noun meaning that God is hidden, with the definite article added to suggest the original sense.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r2.anchor: أن أصله لاه مصدر لاه يليه ليها إذا احتجب

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r3.claim: Another proposal derives the name from ولاه, meaning one overcome by bewilderment; its initial wāw became hamza and the hamza was later dropped.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r3.anchor: أن أصله ولاه بالواو فعال بمعنى مفعول من وله

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r4.claim: A further proposal takes the divine name from Syriac لاها, adapted by dropping its final alif and adding Arabic ال.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r4.anchor: أن أصله ( لاها ) بالسريانية علم له تعالى

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r5.speaker: الزجاج
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r5.claim: Al-Zajjaj, with the view also attributed to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, holds that Allah was coined directly as God's name rather than derived from أله.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r5.anchor: وقد قال بهذا جمع منهم الزجاج ونسب إلى الخليل وسيبويه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r6.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r6.claim: Al-Kashshaf says all Arabs pronounce the divine lām emphatically, and their agreement shows the practice was inherited.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r6.anchor: وعلى ذلك ( أي التفخيم ) العرب كلهم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r7.claim: The verse puts الحمد before لله because praise for revelation and Islam frames the opening recitation; contextual importance can precede God's intrinsic priority, while praising Him still attends to His affairs.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p165/r7.anchor: فكان المقام للاهتمام به اعتبارا لأهمية الحمد العارضة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r1.speaker: التلمساني
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r1.claim: Al-Tilimsani reports a group of scholars who refrain from explaining the divine name out of reverence and because discussion requires scriptural permission; Ibn Ashur calls this an astonishing opinion.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r1.anchor: القول بأن اسم الجلالة يمسك عن الكلام في معناه نعظيما وإجلالا

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r2.claim: رب العالمين apposes God's name: praise first recognizes His intrinsic worth, then this description adds His descriptive worthiness for praise.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r2.anchor: وصف لاسم الجلالة فإنه بعد أن أسند الحمد لاسم ذاته تعالى

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r3.claim: The four descriptions that follow signal that each attribute also merits praise and distinguish God from the idols, objects, and elements other peoples worship.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r3.anchor: وقد أجرى عليه أربعة أوصاف هي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r4.claim: رب may be a verbal noun or an adjective from upbringing, meaning one who nurtures and directs; tarbiya gradually brings something to its perfection. It may also derive from ownership, with an intensive or rare adjectival form.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166/r4.anchor: والرب إما مصدر وإما صفة مشبهة على وزن فعل من ربه يربه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r1.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers deriving رب from nurturing and directing: it suits God's governance and gradual completion of creatures, and avoids redundancy with ملك يوم الدين; one could answer that the worlds here mean only this world.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r1.anchor: والأظهر أنه مشتق من ربه بمعنى رباه وساسه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r2.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r2.claim: Al-Kashshaf limits رب here to master or king, allowing either a verbal noun or adjective, because the word most commonly carries those meanings.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r2.anchor: إلا أن قرينة المقام قد تصرف عن حمل اللفظ على أكثر موارده

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r3.claim: The claim that Arabs reserved رب for God is false: they used it for human rulers and masters, idols, and particular possessions; الربّة was a name for al-ʿUzza and أرباب is plural.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p166#2/r3.anchor: أما إطلاقه على كل من آلهتهم فلا مرية فيه

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r1.claim: Quranic expressions about Joseph's master and the rival lords show that رب can refer to someone besides God; the term remained available in Arabic usage.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r2.claim: The hadith discouraging a person from calling a human master ربي is an etiquette rule to prevent suspected association; possessive phrases such as رب الدار remain permissible.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r2.anchor: وهو نهي كراهة للتأديب ولذلك خص النهي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r3.claim: عالم names a class of beings, perhaps because each class marks itself out or enables knowledge of its maker; the form suggests an instrument, and its rational plural gives rational beings precedence over other classes.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r3.anchor: لأن كل جنس له تميز عن غيره فهو له علامة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r4.speaker: التفتزاني
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r4.claim: Al-Taftazani defines عالم as knowledgeable beings or any species by which the Creator is known, not a singular name for everything besides God; Ibn Ashur endorses this as accurate Arabic usage.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p167/r4.anchor: العالم اسم لذوي العلم ولكل جنس يعلم به الخالق

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r1.claim: The article in العالمين is exhaustive because the context supplies neither an external nor mental referent; it therefore covers every relevant species and, by implication, its individuals.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r1.anchor: تمحض التعريف للاستغراق لجميع الأفراد دفعا للتحكم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r2.claim: The plural العالمين makes exhaustive scope explicit and removes a possible generic or familiar reading; Ibn Ashur rejects the claim among al-Sakkaki's followers that an exhaustive singular is broader than an exhaustive plural.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p168/r2.anchor: بطل ما شاع عند متابعي السكاكي من قولهم استغراق المفرد أشمل

TUSTARI:1:2/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:1:2/r1.claim: Praise means gratitude, which means obedience; obedience is God's guardianship, completed only by disavowing everything besides Him.
TUSTARI:1:2/r1.anchor: معنى: { الحمد لله } [2] الشكر لله، فالشكر لله هو الطاعة لله، والطاعة لله هي الولاية

TUSTARI:1:2/r2.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
TUSTARI:1:2/r2.claim: The Lord of the worlds is creation's master, nurturer, caretaker, reformer, and governor, acting by prior knowledge, will, command, and decree; none is their lord but Him.
TUSTARI:1:2/r2.anchor: سيد الخلق المربي لهم، والقائم بأمرهم، المصلح المدبر لهم قبل كونهم،

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r12.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r12.claim: Anas reports that saying “Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds” earns thirty good deeds above other speech.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r12.anchor: وروى أنس بن مالك أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «الحمد لله رب العالمين فضل ثلاثين حسنة على سائر الكلام

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r13.speaker: رسول الله
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r13.claim: Another report assigns twenty good deeds to the declaration of God's oneness and thirty to al-hamdu.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r13.anchor: ومن قال الحمد لله رب العالمين كتبت له ثلاثون حسنة

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r14.claim: For a believer seeking reward, al-hamdu combines praise with the oneness already implicit in it; in their doctrinal role against disbelief, however, the declaration of oneness is superior, as the Prophet says it is the best utterance.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p65/r14.anchor: ففي قوله توحيد وحمد، وفي قول لا إله إلا الله توحيد فقط. فأما إذا أخذا بموضعهما من شرع الملة

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r1.claim: Al-hamd is complete praise, with the definite article covering the whole class of praise; it is broader than thanks, which responds to a favor, while praise may simply describe qualities.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r1.anchor: الحمد معناه الثناء الكامل، والألف واللام فيه لاستغراق الجنس من المحامد، وهو أعم من الشكر

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r2.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r2.claim: Al-Tabari treats praise and thanks as synonyms; the author rejects this as unsatisfactory.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r2.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أن الحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد، وذلك غير مرضي

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r3.speaker: بعض الناس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r3.claim: Some distinguish thanks as praise for God's acts and favors, and praise as praise of his attributes; the author finds this more accurate than synonymy.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r3.anchor: وحكي عن بعض الناس أنه قال: «الشكر ثناء على الله بأفعاله وأنعامه، والحمد ثناء بأوصافه

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r4.claim: Al-Tabari's evidence “praise to God, in thanks” actually limits praise to praise for a favor and therefore argues against synonymy.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r4.anchor: واستدل الطبري على أنهما بمعنى بصحة قولك الحمد لله شكرا. وهو في الحقيقة دليل على خلاف ما ذهب إليه

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r5.speaker: القراء السبعة وجمهور الناس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r5.claim: The seven canonical readers and most people pronounce the dal of al-hamdu with nominative case.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r5.anchor: وأجمع السبعة وجمهور الناس على رفع الدال من «الحمد لله

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r6.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r6.claim: Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba reportedly read the dal with fatḥ, implying an omitted verb.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r6.anchor: وروي عن سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج «الحمد لله» بفتح الدال وهذا على إضمار فعل

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r7.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r7.claim: Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn ʿAli reportedly read the dal with kasra by assimilating its vowel to the following word.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r7.anchor: وروي عن الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي: «الحمد لله» ، بكسر الدال على إتباع الأول الثاني

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r8.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r8.claim: Ibn Abi ʿAbla reportedly reads both dal and lam with ḍamma, assimilating the second to the first.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66/r8.anchor: وروي عن ابن أبي عبلة: «الحمد لله» ، بضم الدال واللام، على اتباع الثاني والأول

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r1.claim: The continuation completes the implied command: worshippers are told to say “Praise be to God.”

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r2.claim: The same implied-command reading continues with “Say, You alone”; the author notes that Arabic often omits words clear from context.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r2.anchor: وعلى هذا يجيء «قولوا إياك» قال: وهذا من حذف العرب ما يدل ظاهر الكلام عليه

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r3.claim: The poet demonstrates ellipsis: when asked whom they had dug for, the answer “a vizier” means a vizier is the person buried.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r3.anchor:
فقال السائلون لمن حفرتم ... فقال القائلون لهم وزير
المعنى المحفور له وزير، فحذف لدلالة ظاهر الكلام

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r4.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r4.claim: Some read Rabb in the accusative as a form of praise.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r5.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r5.claim: Others take accusative Rabb as direct address, parallel to the implied address in “You alone.”
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r5.anchor: وقال بعضهم: «هو على النداء، وعليه يجيء إياك

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r6.claim: Rabb can mean the worshipped deity, master or owner, the one who manages and repairs affairs, or king; its absolute, unrestricted sense as Lord of lords belongs to God alone.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r6.anchor: والرب في اللغة: المعبود، والسيد المالك، والقائم بالأمور المصلح لما يفسد منها، والملك

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r7.speaker: غاوي بن عبد العزى
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r7.claim: Ghawy ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza's line uses Rabb for the one worshipped; Rabb of all in the unrestricted sense is God.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r7.anchor: أرب يبول الثعلبان برأسه ... لقد هان من بالت عليه الثعالب

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r8.speaker: لبيد
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r8.claim: Labid's line uses Rabb for a master or chief who oversees affairs.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r8.anchor: وأهلكن يوما رب كندة وابنه ... ورب معد بين خبت وعرعر

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r9.speaker: النابغة
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r9.claim: Al-Nabigha uses Rabb in the sense of king in his line about reaching al-Nuʿman.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r9.anchor: تخب إلى النعمان حتى تناله ... فدى لك من رب طريفي وتالدي

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r10.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r10.claim: The phrase adīm marbūb means repaired leather, showing Rabb as the one who sets something right; al-Farazdaq supplies poetic evidence.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r10.anchor: ومن معنى الإصلاح قولهم: أديم مربوب، أي مصلح، قال الشاعر الفرزدق

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r11.speaker: صفوان بن أمية
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r11.claim: Safwan ibn Umayya's saying about being governed by a Qurayshi rather than a Hawazini uses the verb rabbani for rule or mastery.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r11.anchor: لأن يربني رجل من قريش خير من أن يربني رجل من هوازن

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r12.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas likewise uses Rabb for being ruled when discussing ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r12.anchor: وإن كان لا بد لأن يربني رجل من بني عمي أحب إلي من أن يربني غيرهم

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r13.claim: Al-ʿAlqama's line shows Rabb as the master to whom another's household or property has passed.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r13.anchor: وكنت امرأ أفضت إليك ربابتي ... ومن قبل ربتني فضعت ربوب

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r14.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r14.claim: Al-Zajjaj derives ʿālam from knowledge or a sign because the world points to its maker; ʿālamīn encompasses all beings besides God, including human and jinn realms.
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p66#2/r14.anchor: ولفظة العالم جمع لا واحد له من لفظه وهو مأخوذ من العلم والعلامة لأنه يدل على موجده

AKHFASH:v1p7/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p7/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p7/r1.claim: In words beginning with the added alif-lām, the alif drops in connected speech and is always fatḥa when starting; the two letters function together like qad or bal.
AKHFASH:v1p7/r1.anchor: كل اسم في أوله ألف ولام زائدتان فالالف تذهب اذا اتصلت بكلام قبلها

AKHFASH:v1p7/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p7/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p7/r2.claim: The alif-lām is recognized as added because another alif-lām cannot be prefixed to words such as al-ḥamd, al-ʿālamīn, alladhī, and Allāh.
AKHFASH:v1p7/r2.anchor: لا تستطيع أن تدخل عليهن الفا ولاما أخريين

AKHFASH:v1p7/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p7/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p7/r3.claim: A preceding interrogative alif preserves and lengthens the article alif to distinguish a question from a statement; only a few Arabs leave it unlengthened.
AKHFASH:v1p7/r3.anchor: وانما مدت في الاستفهام ليفرق بين الاستفهام والخبر

AKHFASH:v1p7/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p7/r4.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p7/r4.claim: With an interrogative alif before aṣṭafā or aftarā, the interrogative is open and the following hamzat waṣl drops.
AKHFASH:v1p7/r4.anchor: الالفات مفتوحة مقطوعة، لأنها ألف استفهام

AKHFASH:v1p8/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p8/r1.claim: An initial alif is hamzat qaṭʿ when another article can be added, as with al-ilāh, alwāḥ, ilhām, and ilqāʾ.
