AKHFASH:v1p8/r1.anchor: فالالف من ذلك مقطوعة تكون في الاستئناف على حالها في الاتصال

AKHFASH:v1p8/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p8/r2.claim: The alif in ilā is also cut, but it is not an added article: ilā is a preposition rather than a noun, and its alif is kasra rather than fatḥa.
AKHFASH:v1p8/r2.anchor: لأنها ليست باسم، وانما تدخل الالف واللام على الاسم

AKHFASH:v1p8/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p8/r3.claim: Al-ḥamdu is nominative as a subject begun without a preceding governing verb; the beginning raises subject and predicate, an explanation al-Akhfash says is more analogical.
AKHFASH:v1p8/r3.anchor: والابتداء هو الذي رفع الخبر في قول بعضهم

AKHFASH:v1p8/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r4.speaker: بعضهم
AKHFASH:v1p8/r4.claim: Some grammarians say that the beginning raises both the subject and the predicate.

AKHFASH:v1p8/r5.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r5.speaker: بعضهم
AKHFASH:v1p8/r5.claim: Other grammarians say that the predicate raises the subject; al-Akhfash accepts both accounts but prefers the first as more analogical.

AKHFASH:v1p8/r6.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r6.speaker: بعض العرب
AKHFASH:v1p8/r6.claim: Some Arabs put al-ḥamdu in the accusative as a verbal noun in place of the verb, equivalent to saying a praise to God or I praise with praise.
AKHFASH:v1p8/r6.anchor: وذلك ان اصل الكلام عنده على قوله

AKHFASH:v1p8/r7.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p8/r7.speaker: بعض العرب
AKHFASH:v1p8/r7.claim: Some Arabs give al-ḥamdu a fixed kasra by treating it like indeclinable nouns; before and after are likewise fixed unless annexed, as the cited Qurʾanic examples show.
AKHFASH:v1p8/r7.anchor: فكسره، وذلك أنه جعله بمنزلة الأسماء

AKHFASH:v1p12/r1.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r1.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r1.claim: Al-Akhfash cites a rajaz couplet about every living being meeting death and every pair ending in separation, then says this usage is scarcely known; the witnessed word is ithnayn.
AKHFASH:v1p12/r1.anchor: يا نفس صبرا كل حي لاق

AKHFASH:v1p12/r2.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r2.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r2.claim: The lām makes li-llāh genitive, and rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm is also genitive as an attribute of Allāh.

AKHFASH:v1p12/r3.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r3.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r3.claim: The open nūn in the sound masculine plural is an added marker that disappears in the singular; its fatḥa distinguishes it from the dual's always-kasra nūn.
AKHFASH:v1p12/r3.anchor: وأما فتح نون {العالمين} فانها نون جماعة

AKHFASH:v1p12/r4.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r4.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r4.claim: Sound masculine plurals use wāw for nominative and yāʾ for accusative and genitive, while the dual uses alif for nominative and yāʾ for the other two cases.

AKHFASH:v1p12/r5.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r5.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r5.claim: The plural nūn falls in annexation like the dual nūn; unlike the root nūn in broken plurals such as shayāṭīn, dahāqīn, and masākīn, which remains.
AKHFASH:v1p12/r5.anchor: وهذه النون تسقط في الاضافة كما تسقط نون الاثنين

AKHFASH:v1p12/r6.author: al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ
AKHFASH:v1p12/r6.speaker: author
AKHFASH:v1p12/r6.claim: Al-ladhīna has an added open nūn because it disappears in singular alladhī; the text also cites the nominative form alladhūn.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r1.claim: Al-ḥamd is nominative as the subject and lillāh its predicate: praise is established and belongs to God.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r1.anchor: رفع بالابتداء و ﴿ لله ﴾ الخبر والمعنى الحمد ثابت لله

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r2.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r2.claim: Most readers pronounce the lām of lillāh with kasra; Ibn ʿAbla uses ḍamma, a dialect of some Rabīʿa according to al-Farrāʾ.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r2.anchor: والجمهور على كسر لام لله وضمها ابن عبلة قال الفراء هي لغة بعض بني ربيعة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r3.speaker: ابن السميفع
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r3.claim: Ibn al-Sumayfa reads al-ḥamda with fatḥa on dāl and kasra on lām.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r3.anchor: وقرأ ابن السميفع الحمد بنصب الدال لله بكسر اللام

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r4.speaker: أبو نهيك
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r4.claim: Abū Nuhayk reads both dāl and lām in al-ḥamd lillāh with kasra.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r4.anchor: وقرأ أبو نهيك بكسر الدال واللام جميعا

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r5.claim: Praise and gratitude overlap, but praise may be offered initially whereas gratitude is only in response to a blessing.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r5.anchor: الحمد قد يقع ابتداء للثناء والشكر لا يكون إلا في مقابلة النعمة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r6.speaker: قيل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r6.claim: Another grammatical account takes the wording as a declarative form whose intended force is a command: say, “Praise belongs to God.”
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r6.anchor: وقيل لفظه لفظ الخبر ومعناه الأمر فتقيدره قولوا الحمد

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r7.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r7.claim: Ibn Qutayba defines praise as commending a person's inherent virtues, while gratitude is praise for a favor or kindness received.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r7.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة الحمد الثناء على الرجل بما فيه من كرم أو حسب أو شجاعة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r8.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r8.claim: Ibn Qutayba notes that ḥamd can stand for shukr, as in praising someone for a kindness, just as one thanks him for courage.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r8.anchor: وقد يوضع الحمد موضع الشكر فيقال حمدته على معروفه عندي

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r9.claim: Rabb means owner; for a created being the title is used only in a construct phrase such as owner of the house or servant.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r9.anchor: فأما الرب فهو المالك ولا يذكر هذا الاسم في حق المخلوق إلا بالاضافة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r10.speaker: قيل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r10.claim: A second etymology derives rabb from nurturing or cultivation.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r11.speaker: أبو منصور اللغوي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r11.claim: Abū Manṣūr says rabba ṣanīʿatahu means to complete and improve one's craft; he cites poetry for the verb rabb.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r11.anchor: قال شيخنا أبو منصور اللغوي يقال رب فلان صنيعته يربها ربا إذا أتمها وأصلحها

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r12.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r12.claim: Rabb has three uses: owner, one who sets something right, and an obeyed master; the last is illustrated by Joseph 12:41.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r12.anchor: والرب يقال على ثلاثة أوجه أحدها المالك يقال رب الدار والثاني المصلح

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r13.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r13.claim: Most readers put rabb in the genitive; Abū al-Ghāliya, Ibn al-Sumayfa, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read it in the accusative; several others use nominative.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r13.anchor: والجمهور على خفض باء رب وقرأ أبو الغاليه وابن السميفع وعيسى ابن عمر بنصبها

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r14.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r14.claim: These readers pronounce the bāʾ of rabb in the nominative.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r14.anchor: وقرأ أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني برفعها

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r15.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r15.speaker: أهل العربية
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r15.claim: For Arab grammarians, ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam and names all created beings from beginning to end; people also call their present age a world.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r15.anchor: فأما العالمين فجمع عالم وهو عند أهل العربية اسم للخلق من مبدئهم إلى منتهاهم

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r16.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r16.speaker: الحطيئة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r16.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's line uses al-ʿālamīn for people of the present age, as evidence for that usage.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r16.anchor: فقال الحطيئة تنحي فاجلسي مني بعيدا أراح الله منك العالمينا

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r17.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r17.speaker: أهل النظر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r17.claim: The speculative theologians use ʿālam for the created cosmos as a whole: the celestial sphere, heavens, earth, and what lies between.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p10#2/r17.anchor: فأما أهل النظر فالعلم عندهم اسم يقع على الكون الكلي المحدث من فلك وسماء وأرض

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r1.speaker: أهل النظر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r1.claim: The derivation of ʿālam from ʿalāma, “sign,” supports the speculative theologians' view: the world is named as a sign pointing to its Creator.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r1.anchor: والثاني أنه من العلامة وهو يقوي قول أهل النظر فكأنه إنما سمي عندهم بذلك لانه دال على خالقه

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r2.speaker: الضحاك عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r2.claim: One reported interpretation takes “the worlds” to mean all creation: heavens and earths, what they contain, and what lies between them.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r2.anchor: أحدهما الخلق كله السموات والارضون وما فيهن وما بينهن رواه الضحاك عن ابن عباس

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r3.speaker: أبو صالح عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r3.claim: Another report interprets the worlds as every living creature that moves on the surface of the earth.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r3.anchor: الثاني كل ذي روح دب على وجه الأرض رواه أبو صالح عن ابن عباس

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r4.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد ومقاتل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r4.claim: A third interpretation identifies the worlds as jinn and humans; it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and held by Mujāhid and Muqātil.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r4.anchor: والثالث أنهم الجن والإنس روي ايضا عن ابن عباس وبه قال مجاهد ومقاتل

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r5.speaker: ابن عباس، واختاره ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r5.claim: A fourth view includes jinn, humans, and angels; it is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās and chosen by Ibn Qutayba.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r5.anchor: والرابع أنهم الجن والإنس والملائكة نقل عن ابن عباس أيضا واختاره ابن قتبية

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r6.claim: A fifth interpretation, also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, says the worlds here are the angels.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p12/r6.anchor: والخامس أنهم الملائكة وهو مروي عن ابن عباس أيضا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r44.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r44.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r44.claim: In the divine hadith, “prayer” means recitation, as in 17:110; because the Fatiha details the division, its recitation is a major pillar of prayer.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r44.anchor: أي : بقراءتك كما جاء مصرحًا به في الصحيح

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r45.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r45.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r45.claim: “Qur'an of dawn” in 17:78 means the dawn prayer, as the sound reports say angels of night and day witness it; scholars agree prayer requires recitation.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r45.anchor: والمراد صلاة الفجر ، كما جاء مصرحا به في الصحيحين

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r1.speaker: القراء السبعة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r1.claim: The seven canonical readers vocalize the dāl of al-ḥamdu with ḍamma, making al-ḥamdu a subject and li-llāhi its predicate.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r1.anchor: القراء السبعة على ضم الدال من قوله : { الحمد لله } وهو مبتدأ وخبر .

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r2.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r2.claim: Sufyan ibn Uyaynah and Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj read al-ḥamda with fatḥa as an implied verbal object.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r2.anchor: وروي عن سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج أنهما قالا

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r3.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r3.claim: Ibn Abi Abla reads both dāl and lām with ḍamma by assimilating the second vowel to the first; Ibn Kathir calls the reading anomalous.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r3.anchor: بضم الدال واللام إتباعا للثاني الأول وله شواهد لكنه شاذ

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r4.speaker: الحسن وزيد بن علي
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r4.claim: Al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read the dāl with kasra by assimilating the first vowel to the second.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r5.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r5.claim: Ibn Jarir explains praise as exclusive thanks to God for countless blessings, including faculties for worship, worldly provision, and guidance toward lasting bliss despite no prior entitlement.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r6.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r6.claim: Ibn Jarir says the phrase is God's praise of Himself and implicitly commands His servants to say it too.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r6.anchor: وفي ضمنه أمر عباده أن يثنوا عليه

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r7.speaker: ابن جرير
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r7.claim: Ibn Jarir reports a distinction that praise names God's beautiful attributes while thanks praises His favors, then argues Arabic speakers use both words interchangeably.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r8.speaker: جعفر الصادق وابن عطاء
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r8.claim: The Sufi authorities Ja'far al-Sadiq and Ibn Ata are reported to hold that praise and thanks are equivalent.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r8.anchor: نقل السلمي هذا المذهب أنهما سواء عن جعفر الصادق وابن عطاء من الصوفية

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the expression used by every grateful person.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r10.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r10.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r10.claim: Ibn Kathir questions Ibn Jarir's equation: praise is verbal commendation for necessary or bestowed qualities, while thanks applies only to bestowed qualities and may be inward, spoken, or enacted.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r10.anchor: أن الحمد هو الثناء بالقول على المحمود

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r11.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r11.claim: Ibn Kathir resolves the scope dispute by saying praise covers more kinds of objects but is speech-only, whereas thanks uses more kinds of means but concerns bestowed qualities alone.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r12.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r12.speaker: الجوهري
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r12.claim: Al-Jawhari defines praise as the opposite of blame, says taḥmīd is more emphatic than ḥamd, and regards ḥamd as broader than thanks.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r13.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r13.speaker: الجوهري
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r13.claim: Al-Jawhari defines thanks as praising a benefactor for what he bestowed and says using the preposition li- is more eloquent.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r13.anchor: هو الثناء على المحسن بما أولاكه من المعروف

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r14.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r14.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r14.claim: Ibn Kathir distinguishes praise from eulogy: eulogy can concern living or dead people and even objects, precede or follow a favor, and address necessary or bestowed qualities.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r14.anchor: وأما المدح فهو أعم من الحمد

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r15.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r15.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r15.claim: When Umar asks what al-ḥamdu lillāh means after learning other formulas of glorification, Ali answers that it is a phrase God approves for Himself.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r15.anchor: فقال علي : كلمة رضيها الله لنفسه

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r16.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r16.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r16.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-ḥamdu lillāh is a word of thanks; when a servant says it, God says that His servant has thanked Him.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r16.anchor: قال ابن عباس : الحمد لله كلمة الشكر

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r17.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r17.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r17.claim: Ibn Abbas explains praise as thanks, humble submission, and acknowledgment of God's favors, guidance, and origination.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r17.anchor: هو الشكر لله والاستخذاء له ، والإقرار له بنعمه

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r18.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r18.speaker: كعب الأحبار
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r18.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says al-ḥamdu lillāh is God's praise.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r18.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : الحمد لله ثناء الله

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r19.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r19.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r19.claim: Al-Dahhak calls al-ḥamdu lillāh the cloak of the Most Merciful and notes that a hadith has come with a similar meaning.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r19.anchor: وقال الضحاك : الحمد لله رداء الرحمن

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r20.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r20.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r20.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says that whoever says al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn has thanked God, who then increases him.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r20.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r21.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r21.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r21.claim: The Companion al-Aswad ibn Sari asks to recite praises of his Lord, and the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r21.anchor: ألا أنشدك محامد حمدت بها ربي

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r22.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r22.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r22.claim: The Prophet says the best remembrance is lā ilāha illā Allāh and the best supplication is al-ḥamdu lillāh; al-Tirmidhi grades this report ḥasan gharīb.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r22.anchor: أفضل الذكر لا إله إلا الله

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r23.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r23.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r23.claim: Anas reports that when a servant praises God for a blessing, the reward for that praise is better than the blessing received.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r23.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال : قال رسول الله

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r24.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r24.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r24.claim: Al-Qurtubi transmits a report that praising God would be better than possessing the whole world; he explains that the enduring reward for praise exceeds transient worldly enjoyment.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r25.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r25.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r25.claim: Ibn Umar reports that angels cannot calculate the full reward for a servant's praise fitting God's majesty, so God tells them to record it as said until He rewards him.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r25.anchor: فعضلت بالملكين فلم يدريا كيف يكتبانها

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r26.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r26.speaker: طائفة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r26.claim: A group holds that al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn is better than lā ilāha illā Allāh because it combines praise with monotheism.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r26.anchor: قول العبد : الحمد لله رب العالمين

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r27.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r27.speaker: آخرون
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r27.claim: Others hold that lā ilāha illā Allāh is superior because it distinguishes faith from unbelief and is the formula people must profess; reports also call it the best remembrance.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r28.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r28.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r28.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamdu encompasses every kind and form of praise as belonging to God, as expressed in a transmitted prayer.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r28.anchor: في الحمد لاستغراق جميع أجناس الحمد

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r29.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r29.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r29.claim: Rabb means owner and disposer, and in Arabic also master or one who manages something toward its good; each meaning applies to God.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r30.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r30.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r30.claim: The unqualified title al-Rabb is used only for God; for other possessors it must be annexed, and some say al-Rabb is the greatest name.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r31.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r31.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r31.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, encompassing every created being besides God; created kinds in heavens, earth, land, and sea are worlds, as is each generation.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r31.anchor: كل موجود سوى الله عز وجل

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r32.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r32.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r32.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the worlds as all creation belonging to God: heavens, earths, their inhabitants and everything between them, known and unknown.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r32.anchor: الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r33.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r33.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وعكرمة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r33.claim: Ibn Abbas, through Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah, and other early authorities interpret the worlds as jinn and humans; Ibn Abi Hatim's chain is said to be unreliable.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r33.anchor: عن ابن عباس : رب الجن والإنس

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r34.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r34.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r34.claim: Al-Qurtubi supports the interpretation of the worlds as jinn and humans by citing the description of the Qur'an as a warning to the worlds.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r35.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r35.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r35.claim: Al-Farra and Abu Ubayda restrict the term worlds to rational beings—humans, jinn, angels, and devils—and exclude animals.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r36.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r36.speaker: زيد بن أسلم وأبو عمرو بن العلاء
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r36.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Amr ibn al-Ala define worlds as everything with a spirit that receives provision.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r37.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r37.speaker: مروان بن محمد بن مروان بن الحكم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r37.claim: Ibn Asakir reports Marwan's claim that God created seventeen thousand worlds, with the inhabitants of the heavens and earth forming one and God alone knowing the rest.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r37.anchor: في ترجمة مروان بن محمد بن مروان بن الحكم

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r38.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r38.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r38.claim: Qatadah says each kind or species is a world.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r38.anchor: وقال قتادة : رب العالمين ، كل صنف

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r39.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r39.speaker: أبو العالية
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r39.claim: Abu al-Aliyah says humans and jinn are worlds and reports uncertainty between fourteen and eighteen thousand other angelic worlds on earth, in groups worshipping God.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r39.anchor: عن أبي العالية في قوله تعالى

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r40.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r40.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r40.claim: Ibn Kathir calls Abu al-Aliyah's extraordinary numerical report strange and says such a claim requires sound evidence.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r40.anchor: وهذا كلام غريب يحتاج مثله إلى دليل صحيح

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r41.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r41.speaker: تبيع الحميري
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r41.claim: Tubyay al-Himyari says the worlds comprise one thousand nations, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r41.anchor: عن تبيع ، يعني الحميري ، في قوله

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r42.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r42.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r42.claim: A similar count of one thousand worlds, divided into six hundred sea and four hundred land worlds, is also attributed to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r42.anchor: وحكي مثله عن سعيد بن المسيب

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r43.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r43.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r43.claim: A report through Jabir tells how locusts became scarce under Umar, then attributes to the Prophet a saying that there are one thousand nations and locusts are the first to perish; Ibn Kathir says Muhammad ibn Isa is weak.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r43.anchor: سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقول

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r44.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r44.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r44.claim: Al-Baghawi reports Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's view that God has one thousand worlds, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r44.anchor: وحكى البغوي عن سعيد بن المسيب أنه قال

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r45.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r45.speaker: وهب بن منبه
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r45.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has eighteen thousand worlds and this world is one of them.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r46.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r46.speaker: مقاتل
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r46.claim: Muqatil says there are eighty thousand worlds.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r47.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r47.speaker: كعب الأحبار
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r47.claim: Ka'b al-Ahbar says that no one knows the number of worlds except God.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r47.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : لا يعلم عدد العوالم

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r48.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r48.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r48.claim: Al-Qurtubi reports from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that God has forty thousand worlds and the inhabited east-to-west world is only one.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r48.anchor: حكى القرطبي عن أبي سعيد الخدري

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r49.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r49.speaker: الزجاج
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r49.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines a world as everything God created in this life and the next.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r49.anchor: العالم كل ما خلق الله في الدنيا والآخرة

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r50.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r50.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r50.claim: Al-Qurtubi prefers a comprehensive meaning encompassing all worlds, citing Pharaoh's question and God's identification of the Lord of the worlds as Lord of heavens, earth, and what is between them.

IBNKATHIR:1:2/r51.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r51.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r51.claim: Ibn Kathir says ʿālam derives from ʿalāmah, a sign, because every created thing points to its Maker, Creator, and oneness; he cites a poem by Ibn al-Mu'tazz.
IBNKATHIR:1:2/r51.anchor: لأنه علم دال على وجود خالقه وصانعه ووحدانيته

IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.speaker: الله تعالى
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.claim: In a divine report, God divides the prayer between Himself and His servant, responds to each recited section, calls 1:5 shared between them, and grants the servant's request.
IBNKATHIR:1:5/r11.anchor: قال : هذا بيني وبين عبدي ولعبدي ما سأل

FARRA:v1p1#2/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r6.speaker: القراء
FARRA:v1p1#2/r6.claim: Reciters agree on reading al-ḥamdu in the nominative.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r6.anchor:
الرحمن الرحيم
قوله تعالى: الحمد لله ... (2)
اجتمع القراء على رفع «الحمد»

FARRA:v1p3/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r1.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p3/r1.claim: Bedouin speech has several variants for al-ḥamd li-llāh, including a form that raises both the dāl and lām.
FARRA:v1p3/r1.anchor: ومنهم من يقول: «الحمد لله» . ومنهم من يقول: «الحمد لله» فيرفع الدال واللام.

FARRA:v1p3/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p3/r2.claim: Accusative al-ḥamda is possible because ḥamd is a verbal noun that can be replaced by a verb, as in “strike the necks.”
FARRA:v1p3/r2.anchor: «الحمد» ليس باسم إنما هو مصدر يجوز لقائله أن يقول: أحمد الله، فإذا صلح مكان المصدر (فعل أو يفعل) جاز فيه النصب

FARRA:v1p3/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p3/r3.claim: The same verbal-noun construction appears in “I seek refuge in God” and in Arabic expressions equivalent to “may God water you” or “care for you.”
FARRA:v1p3/r3.anchor: «معاذ الله أن نأخذ إلا من وجدنا متاعنا عنده» يصلح أن تقول في مثله من الكلام: نعوذ بالله.

FARRA:v1p3/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p3/r4.claim: Some lower the dāl in al-ḥamd because the frequent phrase has become one word and mixed short vowels are heavy; they analogize to ibil.
FARRA:v1p3/r4.anchor: وأما من خفض الدال من «الحمد» فإنه قال: هذه كلمة كثرت على ألسن العرب حتى صارت كالاسم الواحد

FARRA:v1p3/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r5.speaker: بعضهم
FARRA:v1p3/r5.claim: Those who raise the lām match the common Arabic pattern with two ḍammas, as in al-ḥilm and al-ʿuqab.
FARRA:v1p3/r5.anchor: وأما الذين رفعوا اللام فإنهم أرادوا المثال الأكثر من أسماء العرب الذي يجتمع فيه الضمتان

FARRA:v1p3/r6.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r6.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p3/r6.claim: Frequent phrases can be reanalyzed as one word: bi-abī becomes bābā; Abū Tharwān’s verse attests the resulting vocative form.
FARRA:v1p3/r6.anchor: إنما هو «بأبي» الياء من المتكلم ليست من الأب فلما كثر بهما الكلام توهموا أنهما حرف واحد

FARRA:v1p3/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p3/r7.speaker: أبو ثروان
FARRA:v1p3/r7.claim: Abū Tharwān’s poem uses “yā bībā” as evidence for the contracted phrase.
FARRA:v1p3/r7.anchor:
أنشدني أبو ثروان:
قال الجواري ما ذهبت مذهبا ... وعبنني ولم أكن معيبا

JISHUMI:v1p205/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r7.claim: The standard reading has ḥamd with a nominative dāl and li-llāh with kasra on lām; al-Ḥasan reads dāl with kasra, while Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAbla reads both letters with ḍamma by vowel-following.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r7.anchor: القراءة الظاهرة برفع الدال (لله) بكسر اللام، وعن الحسن أنه قرأ بكسر الدال

JISHUMI:v1p205/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r8.speaker: الفراء
JISHUMI:v1p205/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ allows kasra on the dāl or ḍamma on the lām by vowel-following, but most grammarians reject it as destroying inflection and because following across words is weak; only widely transmitted readings are valid.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r8.anchor: وعن الفراء جواز كسر الدال على الإتباع، وجواز ضم اللام على الإتباع

JISHUMI:v1p205/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r9.speaker: زيد بن علي
JISHUMI:v1p205/r9.claim: A nominative-style report from Zayd b. ʿAlī on the bāʾ of rabb is only proof of grammatical possibility, not a canonical reading.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r9.anchor: وروي عن زيد بن علي نصب الباء، ويحمل على أنه بين جوازه، لا أنه قراءة

JISHUMI:v1p205/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r10.claim: All reciters agree on kasra for the bāʾ in rabb.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r10.anchor: وأجمع القراء على كسر الباء في (رب)

JISHUMI:v1p205/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r11.claim: Ḥamd, praise, and gratitude are near-synonyms, but praise may answer to blessing or other good, whereas gratitude is only for a blessing; their opposites are blame and ingratitude respectively.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r11.anchor: وبين الحمد والشكر فرق؛ لأن نقيض الحمد الذم، ونقيض الشكر الكفر

JISHUMI:v1p205/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r12.claim: Another gloss defines praise and gratitude as acknowledging a benefactor’s blessings while believing in His greatness; gratitude is primarily of the heart, and may be required verbally when denial is suspected.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r12.anchor: وقيل: معنى الحمد والشكر: الاعتراف بنعم المنعم مع اعتقاد بعظمته

JISHUMI:v1p205/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r13.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r13.claim: Ḥamd fundamentally means describing someone with what is beautiful; it is a verbal noun with no dual or plural.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r13.anchor: وأصل الحمد: الوصف بالجميل، والحمد مصدر لا يثنى ولا يجمع

JISHUMI:v1p205/r14.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r14.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r14.claim: Rabb can mean master, owner, or nurturer/reformer, from the idea of upbringing.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r14.anchor: والرب: السيد، والرب: المالك، والرب: المربي المصلح

JISHUMI:v1p205/r15.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r15.speaker: ابن عباس وأبي علي
JISHUMI:v1p205/r15.claim: Al-ʿālamīn may derive from knowledge, from a sign of its maker, or denote the rational kinds—angels, jinn, and humans—according to Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū ʿAlī.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r15.anchor: والعالمين: واحدها عالم، وقيل: اشتقاقه من العلم؛ لأنه اسم يقع على ما يعلم

JISHUMI:v1p205/r16.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r16.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p205/r16.claim: Other explanations make al-ʿālamīn the people of each age or everything contained by the celestial sphere; it has no singular from the same word-form, like qawm and rahṭ.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r16.anchor: وقيل: أهل كل زمان عالم، وقيل: هو اسم لما حواه الفلك

JISHUMI:v1p206/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r1.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r1.claim: Al-ḥamd is chosen instead of al-shukr because praise applies to blessings and other things: God is praised both for favors and for His good acts and lofty attributes.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r1.anchor: لأن الحمد يكون على نعمة وغير نعمة، فنحن نحمده على نعمته علينا

JISHUMI:v1p206/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r2.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r2.claim: The clause al-ḥamdu li-llāh is formally a statement with the force of a command to praise God; one estimate supplies “say,” making it accusative.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r2.anchor: الحمد لله خبر ومعناه الأمر، كأنه قال: احمدوا الله

JISHUMI:v1p206/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r3.claim: Alternatively, “I say: praise belongs to God” allows nominative by treating praise as an initial subject; Arabic also permits accusative by supplying “make the praise for God.”
JISHUMI:v1p206/r3.anchor: وقيل: أقول: الحمد لله، فعلى هذا يحتمل الرفع بتقدير ابتدائي الحمد

JISHUMI:v1p206/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r4.claim: Rabb is kasra as an adjective of God, though accusative or nominative is also possible for praise.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r4.anchor: وكسر رب، لأنه جعل صفة لله تعالى، ولو نصب أو رفع جاز على المدح

JISHUMI:v1p206/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r5.claim: The article in al-ḥamd is generic: all praise and thanks belong to God because all blessings come from Him.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r5.anchor: والألف واللام للجنس، يعني كل الحمد لله؛ لأن النعم كلها منه

JISHUMI:v1p206/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r6.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn means either master and owner of creation or their originator and nurturer.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r6.anchor: قيل: سيد الخلق ومالكهم، وقيل: منشئهم ومربيهم

JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.claim: Al-Raḥmān gives the blessings of worldly life and religion; al-Raḥīm has expansive mercy, and the whole praise belongs to the One who creates, owns, blesses, and deserves worship.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r7.anchor: المنعم بنعم الدنيا والدين. الرحيم: واسع الرحمة

JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.claim: Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.anchor: قيل: لأن الأول ليس من السورة

JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.speaker: علي بن عيسى
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.

JISHUMI:v1p206/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r10.claim: The verse makes praise and gratitude for God’s blessings obligatory and teaches worshippers how to praise Him.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r10.anchor: الآية تدل على وجوب الحمد لله، والشكر على نعمه، وفيه تعليم منه لعباده

JISHUMI:v1p206/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r11.claim: A person fulfills the duty of gratitude by doing what is within his capacity; gratitude encompasses past and future blessings, which are known collectively, so it is owed collectively.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r11.anchor: إذا أتى بما في وسعه فقد أدى حق الشكر، ولأن شكره يتناول النعم الماضية والآتية

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r1.claim: Hamd and madh both mean praising what is beautiful, whether a blessing or another merit; thanks, however, is only for a favor and uses heart, tongue, and limbs.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r1.anchor: الحمد والمدح أخوان وهو الثناء والنداء على الجميل من نعمة وغيرها

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r2.claim: A prophetic report calls praise the head of gratitude and says no servant thanks God without praising Him; al-Zamakhshari grades it weak.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r2.anchor: الحمد رأس الشكر ما شكر الله عبد لم يحمده

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r3.claim: Praise is the head of thanks because speaking of a blessing and praising its giver makes it more apparent than hidden belief or ambiguous bodily acts.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r3.anchor: لأن ذكر النعمة باللسان والثناء على موليها أشيع لها وأدل على مكانها من الاعتقاد وآداب الجوارح

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r4.claim: Hamd is the opposite of blame and thanks the opposite of ingratitude; hamd is nominative as a subject with lillah as predicate, while some read it accusative with an implied verb.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r4.anchor: والحمد نقيضه الذم والشكر نقيضه الكفران

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r5.claim: Using the nominative instead of an accusative verbal noun signals a stable, lasting meaning; he compares the construction with Abraham's raised response of peace.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51#2/r5.anchor: والعدل بها عن النصب إلى الرفع على الابتداء للدلالة على ثبات المعنى واستقراره

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r1.claim: Abraham's nominative response of peace indicates a more abiding greeting than the greeting he received, which was accusative.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r1.anchor: رفع السلام الثاني للدلالة على ان إبراهيم عليه السلام حياهم بتحية أحسن من تحيتهم

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r2.claim: The phrase means that we praise God with praise; the next verse explains how, by saying that we worship Him alone.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r2.anchor: لأنه بيان لحمدهم له كأنه قيل كيف تحمدون

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r3.claim: The definite article identifies the recognized kind of praise; those who take it as exhaustive of every possible praise are mistaken.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r3.anchor: هو نحو التعريف في أرسلها العراك وهو تعريف الجنس

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r4.speaker: الحسن البصري
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p52/r4.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri reads al-hamdu with kasra on the dāl, assimilated to the following lām.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r1.claim: Ibrahim ibn Abi Abla reads the lām of lillah with ḍamma by assimilation to the preceding dāl.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r1.anchor: بضم اللام لاتباعها الدال والذي جسرهما

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r2.claim: He prefers Ibrahim's reading because it makes the inflectional ending follow the stronger grammatical inflection, unlike al-Hasan's reading.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r2.anchor: وأشف القراءتين قراءة إبراهيم حيث جعل الحركة البنائية تابعة للاعرابية التي هي أقوى بخلاف قراءة الحسن

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r3.claim: Rabb means owner; it can also be an intensive source used as an epithet, and unqualified Rabb is reserved for God while other uses require a possessive phrase.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r3.anchor: الرب المالك ومنه قول صفوان لأبي سفيان لأن يربني رجل من قريش أحب الي من ان يربني رجل من هوازن

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r4.speaker: زيد بن علي
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r4.claim: The segment introduces Zayd ibn Ali reading rabb al-alamin as praise; the grammatical form and rationale continue in the next segment.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53/r4.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله عنهما

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r1.claim: Rabb al-alamin may be accusative as praise, or governed by the omitted verb implied in praising God.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r1.anchor: بالنصب على المدح وقيل بما دل عليه الحمد لله كأنه قيل نحمد الله رب العالمين

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r2.claim: Al-alamin means beings with knowledge, namely angels, humans, and jinn; another view includes all created bodies and accidents through which the Creator is known.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r2.anchor: العالم اسم لذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين وقيل كل ما علم به الخالق من الأجسام والأعراض

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r3.claim: The plural al-alamin encompasses every genus included by the word, and its rational masculine plural form is licensed by its implication of knowledge.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p53#2/r3.anchor: ساغ ذلك لمعنى الوصفية فيه وهي الدلالة على معنى العلم

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55/r4.claim: God's lordship, ownership, universal beneficence, and final authority show that none but He deserves praise and thanks.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p55/r4.anchor: هذه الأوصاف التى أجريت على الله سبحانه من كونه ربا مالكا للعالمين لا يخرج منهم شيء من ملكوته وربوبيته

MAJAZ:v1p21/r6.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r6.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r6.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn means the created beings, and the singular of ʿālamīn is ʿālam; Labīd’s line witnesses the plural.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r6.anchor: «رب العالمين» (1) أي المخلوقين، قال لبيد بن ربيعة: ما إن رأيت ولا سمعت بمثلهم فى العالمينا

MAJAZ:v1p21/r7.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p21/r7.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p21/r7.claim: Al-ʿAjjāj’s line uses ʿālam in the singular, supporting the stated singular form.
MAJAZ:v1p21/r7.anchor: وواحدهم عالم، وقال العجاج: فخندف هامة هذا العالم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r1.claim: Hamd praises a person for fine attributes and acts, while shukr praises for a blessing; every thanks is praise but not every praise is thanks, so God may praise Himself but not thank Himself.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r2.claim: Hamd is deserved only for a good act, while madh may concern an act or a non-act; thus God may be praised for knowledge and power but not hamd for these essential attributes, while creation and provision merit both.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r3.claim: One derivation of Rabb is owner, as in the owner of a house.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r3.anchor: أنه مشتق من المالك , كما يقال رب

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r4.claim: Another derives Rabb from master; in 12:41 the word refers to a person's master.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r5.claim: A third meaning of Rabb is manager, as scholars are called rabbaniyyun for managing people through knowledge.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r5.anchor: منه قول الله عز وجل : { والربانيون والأحبار } وهم العلماء

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r6.claim: A fourth derivation is from nurturing or raising, as in the word for a wife's daughter raised in the household.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r6.anchor: الرب مشتق من التربية , ومنه قوله تعالى

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r7.claim: Calling God Rabb as owner or master describes an essential attribute; calling Him Rabb as manager and nurturer describes action.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r7.anchor: لأنه مالك أو سيد , فذلك صفة من صفات ذاته

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r8.claim: With the definite article al-Rabb is exclusive to God; without it the word is shared by God and creatures.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r8.anchor: اختص الله تعالى به , دون عباده , وإن حذفتا

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r9.claim: ʿĀlamīn is a plural with no singular of the same form, like raht and qawm; people of each era form an ʿālam.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r9.anchor: لا واحد له من لفظه , مثل : رهط وقوم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r10.speaker: العجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r10.claim: The cited line using ʿālam witnesses the word's poetic use.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p53/r10.anchor: وأهل كل زمان عالم قال العجاج :

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r1.claim: He defines the worlds as rational beings: angels, humans, and jinn.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r1.anchor: من الملائكة , والإنس , والجن , وهذا قول ابن عباس

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r2.claim: A second interpretation makes the worlds this world and all that it contains.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r3.speaker: أبو إسحاق الزجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r3.claim: He defines the worlds as everything God created in this world and the next.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r4.claim: If ʿālam means rational beings, the word derives from knowledge.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r4.anchor: أنه مشتق من العلم , وهذا تأويل من جعل

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r5.claim: If ʿālam means every creature, the word derives from sign because creation points to its Creator.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p54/r5.anchor: لأنه دلالة على خالقه , وهذا تأويل من جعل

MUQATIL:1:1-4/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r1.claim: Muqātil glosses praise of God as gratitude or thanks to God.

MUQATIL:1:1-4/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r2.claim: The Lord of the worlds means jinn and humans, as in the description of the Qur'an as a warning to all worlds.
MUQATIL:1:1-4/r2.anchor: يعنى الجن والإنس، مثل قوله: ليكون للعالمين نذيرا

MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the Prophet related that God divided this sūra between Himself and the servant: praise is thanks, the two mercy names are praise, the King verse is glorification, and the rest belongs to the servant; seeking help is God's special acknowledgment of the servant's plea.
MUQATIL:1:5-7/r8.anchor: عن أبى هريرة، أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.claim: The report begins God's response when the servant says “Praise belongs to God,” which indicates the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha; if it is outside al-Fatiha, consensus excludes it from other surahs too.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.anchor: فالابتداء بقوله الحمد لله دليل على أن التسمية ليست من الفاتحة

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r1.claim: Al-hamd is beautiful praise given preferentially; syntactically it is a nominative subject with an implied predicate such as “due” or “established,” while a reading with an implicit verb makes it an accusative verbal noun.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r1.anchor: الوصف الجميل على جهة التفضيل وهو رفع بالابتداء وأصله النصب

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r2.claim: The shift from accusative to nominative indicates that praise is settled and enduring.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r2.anchor: والعدول عن النصب إلى الرفع للدلالة على ثبات المعنى واستقراره

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r3.claim: Hamd and madḥ may both mean praising what is beautiful, whether a favor or an inherent quality; shukr is specifically for a favor and uses heart, tongue, and limbs, whereas hamd is praise by tongue alone.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r3.anchor: وأما الشكر فعلى النعمة خاصة وهو بالقلب واللسان والجوارح

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r4.claim: The cited poet says favors elicited three forms of gratitude: hand, tongue, and the veiled heart.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r4.anchor: قال أفادتكم النعماء منى ثلاثة يدى ولسانى والضمير المحجبا

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r5.claim: A report calls praise the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God without praising Him; verbal mention spreads notice of a favor more than inward belief or ambiguous bodily acts.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r5.anchor: ومنه الحديث الحمد رأس الشكر ما شكر الله عبد لم يحمده

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r6.claim: An alternative distinction makes madḥ praise inherent perfections, such as power and knowledge, and shukr praise for benefactions; hamd covers both.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r6.anchor: وقيل المدح ثناء على ما هو له من أوصاف الكمال ككونه باقيا قادرا عالما

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r7.claim: The definite article in al-hamd is exhaustive according to the author's school, against the Mu'tazila; joining it to Allah's proper name gathers every perfection and rests on the doctrine of created acts.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r7.anchor: والألف واللام فيه للاستغراق عندنا خلافا للمعتزلة ولذا قرن باسم الله لأنه اسم ذات

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r8.claim: Rabb means owner or master; the source cites Safwan telling Abu Sufyan that being ruled by a Quraysh man is preferable to being ruled by a Hawazin man, and allows “rabb” as an intensive verbal noun.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r8.anchor: ومنه قول صفوان لأبي سفيان لأن يربنى رجل من قريش أحب إلى من أن يربنى رجل من هوازن

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r9.speaker: الواسطى
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r9.claim: Al-Wasiti explains Rabb as creator at the beginning, sustainer through nourishment, and forgiver at the end, and calls it God's greatest name.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r10.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r10.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r10.claim: Rabb is used without qualification only for God; human use requires a restriction, as in the cited accounts of Joseph.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r10.anchor: ولم يطلقوا الرب إلا في الله وحده وهو فى العبد مع التقيد إنه ربى أحسن مثواى

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r11.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r11.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r11.claim: Al-ʿālamīn denotes what makes the Creator known—bodies, substances, and accidents—or every existent apart from God; its sound masculine plural reflects a descriptive quality associated with rational beings.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6#2/r11.anchor: والعالم هو ما علم به الخالق من الأجسام والجواهر والأعراض أوكل موجود سوى الله تعالى

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r1.claim: Abu Hurayra and Abu Saʿid report that when a servant says “Praise belongs to God,” God affirms the servant and says the praise belongs to Him.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r1.anchor: إذا قال العبد الحمد لله قال صدق عبدي الحمد لي

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r2.claim: Anas reports that God is pleased when a servant praises Him after eating a meal or drinking.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r2.anchor: إن الله ليرضى عن العبد أن يأكل الأكلة فيحمده عليها

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r3.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r3.claim: Hasan says that no blessing is better than saying “Praise belongs to God.”
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r3.anchor: ما من نعمة إلا والحمد لله أفضل منها

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r4.claim: Anas reports that praising God for a blessing is met with a gift greater than what the servant received.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r4.anchor: ما أنعم الله على عبد نعمة فقال الحمد لله إلا كان الذي أعطاه أفضل مما أخذ

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r5.claim: A report from Anas says that if someone owned the whole world and then said alhamdulillah, the praise would be better than it.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r5.anchor: لو أن الدنيا كلها بحذافيرها بيد رجل من أمتي ثم قال الحمد لله

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r6.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the enduring word is better because the world perishes, while praise remains among the righteous deeds; both world and praise ultimately come from God.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r6.anchor: لأن الدنيا فانية والكلمة باقية، هي من الباقيات الصالحات قال الله تعالى:

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r7.claim: A variant says the gift was greater than what was received; this treats praise as the servant’s gift and the world as God’s, though both are from God, who enriches with the world and honors with praise in the afterlife.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r7.anchor: فصير الكلمة إعطاء من العبد، والدنيا أخذا من الله فهذا في التدبير.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r8.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that angels could not record a servant’s praise “as befits” God’s majesty, so God told them to write it as spoken and reward him when they meet.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2/r8.anchor: يا رب لك الحمد كما ينبغي لجلال وجهك وعظيم سلطانك

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.claim: The expressions for a matter becoming difficult or blocked explain the report’s wording about the two angels; either verb form may be used without the extra yāʾ.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.anchor: أعضل الأمر: اشتد واستغلق والمعضلات بتشديد الضاد: الشدائد.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.claim: Abu Malik al-Ashʿari reports that purification is half of faith, praise fills the balance, and glorification with praise fills the space between heaven and earth.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.anchor: الطهور شطر الإيمان والحمد لله تملأ الميزان وسبحان الله والحمد لله

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.claim: One group prefers alhamdulillah because it combines praise with the monotheism expressed by “There is no god but God.”
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.anchor: في ضمنه التوحيد الذي هو لا إله إلا الله ففي قوله توحيد وحمد

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.speaker: طائفة من العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.claim: Another group prefers “There is no god but God” because it repels unbelief and shirk and is the profession for which people are fought.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.anchor: لا إله إلا الله أفضل لأنها تدفع الكفر والإشراك، وعليها يقاتل الخلق

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya chooses the monotheistic formula, citing the report that it is the best utterance of the Prophet and earlier prophets.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.anchor: أفضل ما قلت أنا والنبيون من قبلي لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.claim: Muslims agree God is praised for all blessings; since faith is a blessing and belongs among all created things, faith is God’s act and creation, against the Qadariyya.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.anchor: أجمع المسلمون على أن الله محمود على سائر نعمه، وأن مما أنعم الله به الإيمان فدل

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.claim: Hamd means complete praise; the definite article encompasses every kind of praise, all of which God deserves for His beautiful names and exalted attributes.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.anchor: الحمد في كلام العرب معناه الثناء الكامل والألف واللام لاستغراق الجنس

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r8.claim: A poet uses hamd in a small-number plural form; hamd is the opposite of blame, tahmid is more emphatic, and Muhammad names one rich in praiseworthy qualities.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#2/r8.anchor: فالحمد نقيض الذم، تقول: حمدت الرجل أحمده حمدا فهو حميد ومحمود

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r2.claim: The terms madhma and ahmada describe blame versus praise, finding something agreeable, and becoming worthy of praise; hamda can mean one who overpraises, while hamadat al-nar is its crackling.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r2.anchor: والمحمدة: خلاف المذمة. وأحمد الرجل: صار أمره إلى الحمد

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r3.claim: Al-Tabari and al-Mubarrad treat hamd and shukr as synonymous; al-Sulami also attributes this position to Jaʿfar al-Sadiq and Ibn ʿAtaʾ, who says praise is thanks for God teaching it.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r3.anchor: ذهب أبو جعفر الطبري وأبو العباس المبرد إلى أن الحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says “praise to God, in thanks” restricts praise to a blessing and therefore argues against equating praise and gratitude.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r4.anchor: إنما خصصت به الحمد لأنه على نعمة من النعم

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r5.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r5.claim: Some say gratitude is broader because it uses tongue, limbs, and heart, whereas praise is only verbal.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r5.anchor: إن الشكر أعم من الحمد لأنه باللسان وبالجوارح والقلب

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r6.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r6.claim: Others say praise is broader: it includes gratitude and commendation, can stand in place of gratitude, but gratitude cannot replace praise.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r6.anchor: وقيل: الحمد أعم، لأن فيه معنى الشكر ومعنى المدح، وهو أعم من الشكر

QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls praise the expression of every grateful person, citing Adam’s praise at a sneeze and praise by Noah, Abraham, David and Solomon, the Prophet, and Paradise’s people.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:1-7/r7.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال: الحمد لله كلمة كل شاكر، وإن آدم عليه السلام قال حين عطس: الحمد لله.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r1.claim: The Prophet admitted that he could not enumerate praise of God, illustrating the creature’s inability to fulfill God’s due praise.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r1.anchor: ألا ترى سيد المرسلين كيف أظهر العجز بقوله

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r2.claim: Other explanations say God praised Himself because servants cannot fully praise Him, or because abundant blessings exceed their capacity; divine praise removes the burden of gratitude.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r2.anchor: وقيل: لما علم سبحانه عجز عباده عن حمده، حمد نفسه لنفسه في الأزل

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r3.claim: Hamd praises the praised one’s attributes without prior favor, while shukr praises a benefactor for a favor; thus hamd is broader and fits the verse’s scope.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r3.anchor: قلت: الصحيح أن الحمد ثناء على الممدوح بصفاته من غير سبق إحسان، والشكر ثناء على المشكور بما أولى من الإحسان.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r4.claim: Hamd can mean satisfaction, as in saying one was pleased with someone or in the “praised station”; a Prophetic expression likewise means “I approve for you.”
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r4.anchor: ويذكر الحمد بمعنى الرضا يقال: بلوته فحمدته، أي رضيته.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r5.speaker: جعفر الصادق
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r5.claim: Jaʿfar al-Sadiq offers an esoteric reading of the letters of hamd: unity, dominion, and permanence; knowing these attributes is the reality of praising God.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r5.anchor: ويذكر عن جعفر الصادق في قوله «الحمد لله»: من حمده بصفاته كما وصف نفسه فقد حمد لأن الحمد حاء وميم ودال فالحاء من الوحدانية

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r6.speaker: شقيق بن إبراهيم
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r6.claim: Shafiq says gratitude requires recognizing the giver, accepting what is given, and not disobeying while one has strength.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r6.anchor: وقال شقيق بن إبراهيم في تفسير «الحمد لله» قال: هو على ثلاثة أوجه: أولها إذا أعطاك الله شيئا تعرف من أعطاك. والثاني أن ترضى بما أعطاك.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r7.claim: God praises Himself and opens His Book with praise, while scripture and the Prophet forbid human self-praise; human praise is compromised by motives, unlike God’s eternal self-praise.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r7.anchor: فمعنى «الحمد لله رب العالمين»: أي سبق الحمد مني لنفسي قبل أن يحمدني أحد من العالمين،

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r8.speaker: علماؤنا
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r8.claim: The scholars say an imperfect creature should not praise himself to attract benefits or ward off harms.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#3/r8.anchor: قال علماؤنا: فيستقبح من المخلوق الذي لم يعط الكمال أن يحمد نفسه ليستجلب لها المنافع

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r1.speaker: القراء السبعة
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r1.claim: The seven readers and most people read alhamdu with the dāl in the nominative; Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba report an accusative reading with an implied verb.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r1.anchor: وأجمع القراء السبعة وجمهور الناس على رفع الدال من «الحمد لله».

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r2.speaker: سيبويه
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r2.claim: Sibawayh says the nominative attributes praise to the speaker and all creation, while the accusative attributes it to the speaker alone.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r2.anchor: الذي يرفع الحمد يخبر أن الحمد منه ومن جميع الخلق لله

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r3.claim: Other grammarians take the phrase as an appeal for pardon and mercy, magnification, or a request rather than a plain report; another reading teaches people to say it.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r3.anchor: إنما يتكلم بهذا تعرضا لعفو الله ومغفرته وتعظيما له وتمجيدا

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r4.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r4.claim: Al-Tabari says God’s praise of Himself implicitly commands people to praise Him; Arabic can omit the understood imperative, as in the cited poem.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r4.anchor: فكأنه قال: قولوا الحمد لله وعلى هذا يجيء قولوا إياك.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r5.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r5.claim: Ibn Abi ʿAbla reads the dāl and lām with ḍamma for vowel harmony, a common Arabic tendency also illustrated by other readings and poetic examples.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#4/r5.anchor: وروي عن ابن أبي عبلة: «الحمد لله» بضم الدال واللام على إتباع الثاني الأول

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r1.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r1.claim: Hasan al-Basri and Zayd ibn ʿAli read the dāl with kasra by vowel assimilation.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r1.anchor: وروي عن الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي: «الحمد لله» بكسر الدال على إتباع الأول الثاني.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r2.claim: A poem’s “wayl ummiha” derives from “waylun li-ummiha”: the first lām was dropped and the hamza’s ḍamma shifted after kasra proved heavy.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r2.anchor: الأصل: ويل لأمها فحذفت اللام الأولى واستثقل ضم الهمزة بعد الكسرة فنقلها للام

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r3.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r3.claim: Rabb means owner; lexically it is a divine name, used of others only in a possessive construction, though pre-Islamic Arabs also used it for a king.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r3.anchor: وفي الصحاح: والرب اسم من أسماء الله تعالى، ولا يقال في غيره إلا بالإضافة

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r4.claim: Rabb can mean master, as in Joseph’s “your lord,” and the hadith that a slave woman gives birth to her mistress.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r5.speaker: الهروي
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r5.claim: Rabb also means one who repairs, manages, restores, or takes care of something; rabbani scholars are named for tending to scripture.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r5.anchor: قال الهروي وغيره: يقال لمن قام بإصلاح شيء وإتمامه: قد ربه يربه فهو رب له وراب

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r6.claim: A hadith asks whether someone has a blessing he tends for another, using rabbaha for tending and improving it.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r6.anchor:
" هل لك من نعمة تربها عليه "
أي تقوم بها وتصلحها.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r7.claim: Rabb can also mean the one worshipped; the cited poet mocks a fox worshipped after it soils an idol’s head.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r7.anchor: والرب: المعبود ومنه قول الشاعر: أرب يبول الثعلبان برأسه

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r8.claim: The verb has intensive forms and can mean raising a child; al-Nahhas records rabbahu, rabbabahu, and rabbatahu as forms.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r8.anchor: ويقال على التكثير: رباه ورببه وربته حكاه النحاس.

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r9.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r9.claim: Some consider Rabb God’s greatest name because supplicants frequently call upon Him by it and the name conveys the relation of care, mercy, and dependence.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r9.anchor: إن هذا الاسم هو اسم الله الأعظم لكثرة دعوة الداعين به

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r10.claim: Rabb may derive from nurture: God manages and raises creation; stepdaughters are called rabāʾib because a husband raises them, making Rabb an attribute of action, while owner or master is an attribute of essence.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r10.anchor: مشتق من التربية فالله سبحانه وتعالى مدبر لخلقه ومربيهم

QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r11.claim: With the definite article, Rabb belongs exclusively to God; without it, people may be called a household’s lord. God alone creates and provides, owns both owners and owned things, and cannot lose His dominion.
QURTUBI-FULL:1:2#5/r11.anchor: العاشرة: متى أدخلت الألف واللام على «رب» اختص الله تعالى به لأنها للعهد

NAHHAS:v1p169/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r1.speaker: البصريون
NAHHAS:v1p169/r1.claim: The Basrans parse al-ḥamdu as a nominative subject by inception.

NAHHAS:v1p169/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r2.speaker: الكسائي
NAHHAS:v1p169/r2.claim: Al-Kisa'i makes al-ḥamdu nominative through the pronoun implied in its predicate, treating the lām like a verb.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r2.anchor: وقال الكسائي ( الحمد ) رفع بالضمير الذي في الصفة والصفة اللام جعل اللام بمنزلة الفعل

NAHHAS:v1p169/r3.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r3.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v1p169/r3.claim: Al-Farrāʾ makes al-ḥamdu nominative by the grammatical position of the lām, treating the preposition like a noun that stands independently.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r3.anchor: وقال الفراء الحمد رفع بالمحل وهو اللام جعل اللام بمنزلة الاسم لأنها لا تقوم بنفسها

NAHHAS:v1p169/r4.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r4.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r4.claim: The grammarians use different labels for prepositions: al-Kisa'i says attributes, al-Farrāʾ loci, and Basrans adverbial containers.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r4.anchor: والكسائي يسمى حروف الخفض صفات والفراء يسميها محال والبصريون يسمونها ظروفا

NAHHAS:v1p169/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r5.speaker: ابن عيينة ورؤبة ابن العجاج
NAHHAS:v1p169/r5.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj read al-ḥamdu in the accusative as a verbal noun, a usage of Qays and al-Ḥārith ibn Samāma.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r5.anchor: وقرأ ابن عيينة ورؤبة ابن العجاج ( الحمد لله ) على المصدر وهي لغة قيس والحارث بن سامة

NAHHAS:v1p169/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r6.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r6.claim: The nominative is preferable in wording because a definite noun is being reported about, and in meaning because it includes the speaker's praise and everyone else's.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r6.anchor: والرفع أجود من جهة اللفظ والمعنى فأما اللفظ فلأنه اسم معرفة خبرت عنه

NAHHAS:v1p169/r7.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r7.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r7.claim: The accusative reading does not include the speaker's own praise in the same way.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r7.anchor: وإذا نصبت لم يعد حمد نفسك

NAHHAS:v1p169/r8.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r8.speaker: الفراء
NAHHAS:v1p169/r8.claim: Al-Farrāʾ transmits two further vocalized forms of al-ḥamdu lillāh.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r8.anchor: وحكى الفراء ( الحمد لله ) و ( الحمد لله ) قال أبو جعفر

NAHHAS:v1p169/r9.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r9.speaker: علي بن سليمان
NAHHAS:v1p169/r9.claim: ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān says neither of al-Farrāʾ's two forms is acceptable to Basran grammarians.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r9.anchor: وسمعت علي بن سليمان يقول لا يجوز من هذين شيء عند البصريين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r10.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r10.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r10.claim: The two forms are known dialects and transmitted readings, each with a grammatical rationale.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r10.anchor: قال أبو جعفر وهاتان لغتان معروفتان وقراءتان موجودتان في كل واحدة منهما علة

NAHHAS:v1p169/r11.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r11.speaker: الحسن
NAHHAS:v1p169/r11.claim: Al-Ḥasan is reported to read al-ḥamdu with the form preserved by Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh's transmission.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r11.anchor: عن الحسن أنه قرأ ( الحمد لله )

NAHHAS:v1p169/r12.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r12.speaker: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة
NAHHAS:v1p169/r12.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAblah reads al-ḥamdu with kasra, a dialect of some Rabīʿa tribes.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r12.anchor: وقرأ إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة ( الحمد لله ) وهذه لغة بعض بني ربيعة

NAHHAS:v1p169/r13.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r13.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r13.claim: Tamīm uses the kasra; the common word favors it because ḍamma is heavy before a following kasra, so vowels are harmonized for ease.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r13.anchor: والكسر لغة تميم فأما اللغة في الكسر فإن هذه اللفظة تكثر في كلام الناس والضم ثقيل

NAHHAS:v1p169/r14.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r14.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v1p169/r14.claim: Sībawayh treats the lām in lillāh as an added preposition whose underlying vowel is fatḥ; it is kasra with an overt noun to distinguish it from emphatic lām.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r14.anchor: وزعم سيبويه أن أصل اللام الفتح يدلك على ذلك أنك إذا أضمرت قلت الحمد لله

NAHHAS:v1p169/r15.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r15.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r15.claim: Rabb is genitive as an adjective of Allah; al-ʿālamīn is genitive by annexation, with its yāʾ marking the case.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r15.anchor: ( رب ) مخفوض على النعت لله ( العالمين ) خفض بالإضافة وعلامة الخفض الياء لأنها من جنس الكسرة

NAHHAS:v1p169/r16.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r16.speaker: سيبويه
NAHHAS:v1p169/r16.claim: Sībawayh says the nūn of al-ʿālamīn compensates for the loss of case vowel and tanwīn.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r16.anchor: والنون عند سيبويه كأنها عوض لما منع من الحركة والتنوين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r17.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r17.speaker: أبو العباس
NAHHAS:v1p169/r17.claim: Abū al-ʿAbbās says the nūn substitutes for tanwīn alone.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r17.anchor: والنون عند أبي العباس عوض من التنوين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r18.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r18.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v1p169/r18.claim: Abū Isḥāq says the nūn substitutes for the case vowel; its fatḥ distinguishes it from the dual nūn.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r18.anchor: وعند أبي إسحاق عوض من الحركة وفتحت فرقا بينها وبين نون الاثنين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r19.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r19.speaker: الكسائي
NAHHAS:v1p169/r19.claim: Al-Kisāʾī allows rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as a circumstantial expression, like rabb and god as praise.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r19.anchor: وقال الكسائي يجوز ( رب العالمين ) كما تقول الحمد لله ربا وإلها أي على الحال

NAHHAS:v1p169/r20.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r20.speaker: أبو حاتم
NAHHAS:v1p169/r20.claim: Abū Ḥātim explains the accusative as an implied I praise Allah, Lord of the worlds.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r20.anchor: وقال أبو حاتم النصب بمعنى أحمد الله رب العالمين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r21.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r21.speaker: أبو إسحاق
NAHHAS:v1p169/r21.claim: Abū Isḥāq permits the accusative as an annexed vocative.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r21.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق يجوز النصب على النداء المضاف

NAHHAS:v1p169/r22.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r22.speaker: ابن كيسان
NAHHAS:v1p169/r22.claim: Ibn Kaysān rejects an annexed-vocative parse because it would split the utterance into two clauses, and instead parses the accusative as praise.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r22.anchor: يبعد النصب على النداء المضاف لأنه يصير كلامين ولكن نصبه على المدح

NAHHAS:v1p169/r23.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r23.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r23.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn may also be nominative, with an implied huwa: he is Lord of the worlds.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r23.anchor: ويجوز الرفع أي هو رب العالمين

NAHHAS:v1p169/r24.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p169/r24.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p169/r24.claim: The word rabb has extended forms rabbāhu, rabbahu, and rabbathu, developed through b-to-y and then y-to-t changes.
NAHHAS:v1p169/r24.anchor: يقال على التكثير رباه وربه وربته وشرحه أن الأصل رببه ثم تبدل من الباء ياء

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.speaker: رسول الله [ ص ]
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.claim: The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.anchor: لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.claim: The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.anchor: ما يشير إلى طرف من حكمة اختيارها للتكرار

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r1.claim: After invoking the Merciful God, the worshipper turns to praise Him and name His unrestricted lordship over all worlds.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r1.anchor: وعقب البدء باسم الله الرحمن الرحيم يجيء التوجه إلى الله بالحمد ووصفه بالربوبية المطلقة للعالمين

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r2.claim: Praising God wells up in a believer's heart at His mention: existence itself and ceaseless blessings call forth praise.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r2.anchor: والحمد لله هو الشعور الذي يفيض به قلب المؤمن بمجرد ذكره لله

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r3.claim: Praise begins and ends the Islamic worldview; the Qur'an says God alone is deity and that praise belongs to Him in this world and the next.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r3.anchor: ومن ثم كان الحمد لله ابتداء

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r4.speaker: رسول الله [ ص ]
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r4.claim: Ibn Umar reports that the Prophet described a servant's expansive praise, which two angels could not record; God ordered them to write it as spoken and promised reward when the servant meets Him.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r4.anchor: أن رسول الله [ ص ] حدثهم أن عبدا من عباد الله قال

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r5.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r5.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r5.claim: The phrase Lord of the worlds states a core creed: God's complete lordship extends across all creation.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r5.anchor: فالربوبية المطلقة الشاملة هي إحدى كليات العقيدة الإسلامية

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r6.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r6.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r6.claim: In Arabic, rabb can mean master or the one who manages, reforms, and nurtures; God continuously tends every creature rather than leaving the universe unattended.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r6.anchor: ويطلق في اللغة على السيد وعلى المتصرف للإصلاح والتربية

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r7.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r7.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r7.claim: Recognizing God's unrestricted lordship separates clear monotheism from beliefs that combine one creator with multiple powers governing life.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r7.anchor: والربوبية المطلقة هي مفرق الطريق بين وضوح التوحيد الكامل الشامل

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r8.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r8.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r8.claim: Some polytheists claimed they worshipped lesser patrons only to bring them nearer to God, while some People of the Book treated their rabbis and monks as lords.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r8.anchor: اتخذوا أحبارهم ورهبانهم أربابا من دون الله

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r9.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r9.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r9.claim: Making God Lord of all worlds points away from a chaotic crowd of competing lords toward one sovereign, bringing order, certainty, and confidence in His constant care.

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r10.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r10.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r10.claim: Quṭb contrasts Islam's continuing divine care with Aristotle's alleged view that God creates the cosmos and then ignores it as beneath His attention.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r10.anchor: لا كما كان أرقى تصور فلسفي لأرسطو مثلا يقول بأن الله أوجد هذا الكون ثم لم يعد يهتم به

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r11.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r11.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r11.claim: Human conscience could not settle questions of the cosmos, the self, and life before it reached clear certainty about God, His attributes, and His relation to creation.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r11.anchor: ولم يكن مستطاعا أن يستقر الضمير البشري على قرار

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r12.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r12.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r12.claim: Islam therefore concentrated on freeing creed from every ambiguity through pure, comprehensive monotheism and an unambiguous account of God's absolute lordship.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r12.anchor: ومن ثم كان التوحيد الكامل الخالص المجرد الشامل

QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r13.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r13.speaker: author
