QUTB-ZILAL:1:2/r13.claim: Comparing Islam's simple, coherent account of God with the inherited tangle of beliefs reveals this creed as mercy for heart and mind.

QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.speaker: رسول الله
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.claim: Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن رسول الله [ ص ] :  "  يقول الله تعالى : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.claim: Many names indicate the honor of the named; Fātiḥat al-Kitāb is so called because it opens codices, teaching, recitation, and prayer, or because praise opens speech, or because it was the first sura sent down.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r1.anchor: اعلم أن هذه السورة لها أسماء كثيرة وكثرة الأسماء تدل على شرف المسمى

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.claim: It is called Sūrat al-Ḥamd because its opening word is praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r2.anchor: والثاني : سورة الحمد والسبب فيه أن أولها لفظ الحمد

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.claim: It is called the Mother of the Qur’an because its verses encompass the Qur’an’s four central aims: theology, resurrection, prophethood, and divine decree.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r3.anchor: أن أم الشيء أصله والمقصود من كل القرآن تقرير أمور أربعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.claim: A second reason for calling it the Mother of the Book is that all revelation comprises praise, worshipful service, and requests for unveiling; the sura includes each in that order.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r4.anchor: أن حاصل جميع الكتب الإلهية يرجع إلى أمور ثلاثة

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.claim: A third reason is that all knowledge concerns either divine lordship or human servitude: the opening praises God’s mastery, while the remainder shows the servant’s dependence on His aid and guidance.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r5.anchor: معرفة عزة الربوبية أو معرفة ذلة العبودية

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.claim: A fourth reason is that the sura gathers theology, religious duties, and spiritual purification: praise and lordship establish divine existence and attributes, worship presents duties, and guidance seeks unveiling.
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r6.anchor: أن العلوم البشرية إما علم ذات الله وصفاته وأفعاله وهو علم الأصول وإما علم أحكام الله تعالى وتكاليفه وهو علم الفروع

RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p144/r7.claim: In the mystical reading, guidance brings light to the heart, the blessed become polished mirrors reflecting sanctity, and the final plea seeks protection from desire and doubt.

RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r1.claim: The phrase al-ḥamdu lillāh raises questions about God’s existence and right to praise; Rabb al-ʿālamīn answers the first, while al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, and Mālik yawm al-dīn answer the second.

RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r2.claim: Knowledge of God’s existence is theoretical, not immediate; the world of heavens, earth, seas, minerals, plants, and animals needs a governing, originating, nurturing, and sustaining cause.
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r2.anchor: هذا العالم المحسوس بما فيه من السموات والأرضين والجبال والبحار والمعادن والنبات والحيوان محتاج إلى مدبر

RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r3.claim: Al-ʿālamīn includes everything besides God, which depends on Him for existence and continuance; every indivisible particle and individual accident proves the wise, powerful God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r3.anchor: أن العالمين إشارة إلى كل ما سوى الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r4.claim: Rāzī prefers Rabb al-ʿālamīn to Creator of the worlds because sustaining creatures after their beginning is disputed, and the phrase stresses their dependence on God at every moment.
RAZI-FULL:v1p149/r4.anchor: أنه لا يستغني عنه لا في حال حدوثه ولا في حال بقائه

RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r1.claim: As the Mother of the Qur’an, the Fātiḥa is the source from which other suras branch; every being besides God is evidence of His divinity.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r1.anchor: هذه السورة مسماة بأم القرآن فوجب كونها كالأصل والمعدن وأن يكون غيرها كالجداول المتشعبة منه

RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r2.claim: Al-Anʿām’s praise for creating the heavens, earth, darkness, and light is one subset of Rabb al-ʿālamīn; dependence on God for preservation entails dependence for origination.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r2.anchor: لأن لفظ العالم يتناول كل ما سوى الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r3.claim: Al-Kahf’s praise for the revealed Book concerns spiritual nurture through knowledge and unveiling, one kind of the Fātiḥa’s universal nurturing.

RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r4.claim: Saba’s statement that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to God is another subset within the universal lordship named in the Fātiḥa.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r4.anchor: الأشياء الحاصلة في السماوات والأرض له

RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r5.claim: Fāṭir describes bringing the heavens and earth into existence, distinct from creation as determination yet also included within Rabb al-ʿālamīn.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150/r5.anchor: والخلق هو التقدير والمذكور في هذه السورة كونه فاطرا لها ومحدثا لذواتها

RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r1.claim: Razi reads Lord of the worlds as an argument for the ancient God's existence; the created lights, darkness, and angels are kinds within that all-encompassing world-order.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r1.anchor: وهذه أسرار عجيبة ولطائف عالية ؛ إلا أنها بأسرها تجري مجرى الأنواع الداخلة تحت البحر الأعظم المذكور

RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r2.claim: Because worlds include everything besides God, including space and time, their Lord created them and existed before them; this proves His transcendence beyond place, direction, and spatial extension.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r2.anchor: ﴿ رب العالمين ﴾ يدل على كونه ربا للمكان والزمان وخالقا لهما وموجدا لهما

RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r3.claim: The same lordship excludes indwelling: the creator precedes every created locus and therefore never depends on a place, against Christians and adherents of indwelling.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r3.anchor: هذه الآية تدل على أن إله العالم ليس موجبا بالذات بل هو فاعل مختار

RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r4.claim: Deserving praise shows God acts by choice, not by necessity: fire and ice are not praised for natural effects, while changing effects prove a voluntary, powerful agent.
RAZI-FULL:v1p150#2/r4.anchor: فلما حكم بكونه مستحقا للحمد والثناء ثبت أنه فاعل بالاختيار

RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r1.claim: The world's evident order and its fitness for human interests show that its maker knows; praise thus implies God's existence, transcendence from place and indwelling, and utmost power, knowledge, and wisdom.
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r1.anchor: كان الإحكام والإتقان ظاهرين في العالم الأعلى والعالم الأسفل وفاعل الفعل المحكم المتقن يجب أن يكون عالما

RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.claim: The sequence Lord of the worlds, Merciful, Compassionate, Master of Judgment is, in Razi's view, a rationally unsurpassable ordering of God's attributes.
RAZI-FULL:v1p151/r3.anchor: مرتب ترتيبا لا يمكن في العقل وجود كلام أكمل وأفضل منه

RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.claim: Although the world contains evil, good predominates: health over illness, satiety over hunger, and ease and joy over painful states.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r1.anchor: الشر وإن كان كثيرا إلا أن الخير أكثر والمرض وإن كان كثيرا إلا أن الصحة أكثر منه

RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r2.claim: Changing states arise after nonexistence and therefore point to a capable creator; a necessary-by-nature cause would produce effects eternally without change.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r2.anchor: حدوث الأثر بعد عدمه يدل على وجود مؤثر قادر

RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.claim: Since beneficial ease and safety predominate, the agent is merciful and beneficent and deserves praise; these familiar facts make the reason for praising God apparent to every rational person.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153/r3.anchor: ومن كان غالب أفعاله راحة وخيرا وكرامة وسلامة كان رحيما محسنا

RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r1.claim: All worlds share the contingency, need, and change that make a person depend on God; their common cause of need establishes God's lordship over every creature and heaven.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r1.anchor: وهذه المعاني قائمة في كل العالمين فإنها محل الحركات والسكنات وأنواع التغيرات

RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r2.claim: The one able to create the immense worlds, Throne, heavens, and stars can destroy them and is independent of them.
RAZI-FULL:v1p153#2/r2.anchor: لا بد وأن يكون قادرا على إهلاكها ولا بد وأن يكون غنيا عنها

RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r3.claim: Because worldly benefits and protection from harm usually require visible causes, people love those causes, and repeated action and imitation make this attachment deeply rooted.
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r3.anchor: الأسباب الموجبة لحب الدنيا والمرغبة في التعلق بأسبابها كثيرة قوية شديدة جدا

RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r4.claim: Razi frames the needed reflection as asking whether a ruler's worldly sovereignty came from his own strength and wisdom.
RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r4.anchor: هذا الأمير المستولي على هذا العالم استولى على الدنيا بفرط قوته وكمال حكمته أم لا

RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r1.claim: A ruler may be weak and unintelligent, so his authority comes from the allotment of a wise determiner, not his own strength or wisdom.
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r1.anchor: ذلك الأمير ربما كان أكثر الناس عجزا وأقلهم عقلا

RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r2.claim: Recognizing the true cause detaches the heart from apparent means: every benefit comes from God and every harm is attributed to Him, so praise and requests belong to God alone.
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r2.anchor: كلما وصل إليه نفع وخير قال هو النافع وكلما وصل إليه شر ومكروه قال هو الضار

RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r3.claim: Reflection scales from the small world to the greater one: no condition in either world is ordered except by God's decree.
RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r3.anchor: ثم يترقى من العالم الصغير إلى العالم الكبير فيعلم أنه لا تنتظم حالة من أحوال العالم الأكبر إلا بتقدير الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r1.claim: Most scholars require recitation in prayer, while al-Asamm and al-Hasan b. Salih deny that recitation is obligatory.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r1.anchor: أجمع الأكثرون على أن القراءة واجبة في الصلاة وعن الأصم والحسن بن صالح أنها لا تجب

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r2.claim: The command to perform the dawn recitation in Quran 17:78 is a command to read and therefore makes recitation obligatory.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r2.anchor: والمراد بالقرآن : القراءة والتقدير : أقم قراءة الفجر وظاهر الأمر للوجوب

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r3.speaker: أبو الدرداء عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r3.claim: A man asked the Prophet whether prayer includes recitation; when the man concluded that it was obligatory, the Prophet approved him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r3.anchor: عن أبي الدرداء : أن رجلا سأل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال : أفي الصلاة قراءة

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r4.speaker: ابن مسعود عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r4.claim: In another report, the Prophet answers a question about reciting in prayer by asking whether there can be prayer without recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r4.anchor: الثالث : عن ابن مسعود أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سئل : أيقرأ في الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r5.speaker: الأصم
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r5.claim: Al-Asamm argues that the Prophet described prayer as things seen, whereas recitation is not visible and must therefore fall outside prayer; Razi answers that seeing with two objects means knowing.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r5.anchor:
حجة الأصم قوله - عليه الصلاة والسلام -
: صلوا كما رأيتموني أصلي جعل الصلاة من الأشياء المرئية والقراءة ليست بمرئية

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r6.claim: Al-Shafi'i and most scholars require al-Fatiha itself; omitting even one letter knowingly invalidates prayer, whereas Abu Hanifa says it is not required.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r6.anchor: قال الشافعي - رحمه الله - : قراءة الفاتحة واجبة في الصلاة فإن ترك منها حرفا واحدا

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r7.claim: The Prophet's lifelong practice of reciting al-Fatiha obligates imitation, supported by Quranic commands to follow him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r7.anchor: أنه - عليه الصلاة والسلام - واظب طول عمره على قراءة الفاتحة في الصلاة ؛ فوجب أن يجب علينا ذلك

RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r8.claim: Razi charges Abu Hanifa with inconsistency for requiring forehead wiping from one report while denying al-Fatiha's requirement despite its mass-transmitted practice.
RAZI-FULL:v1p156/r8.anchor: تمسك في وجوب مسح الناصية بخبر واحد وذلك ما رواه المغيرة بن شعبة

RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r1.claim: Because the established form of the Prophet's prayer included al-Fatiha, the command to establish prayer requires it; the command recurs over a hundred times in the Quran.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r1.anchor: والتي أتى بها الرسول - عليه الصلاة والسلام - هي الصلاة المشتملة على الفاتحة فيكون قوله : أقيموا الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r2.claim: The rightly guided caliphs consistently recited al-Fatiha; reports in both Sahihs say the Prophet, Abu Bakr, and Umar began recitation with al-Hamd, so their practice should be followed.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r2.anchor: روي في الصحيحين أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبا بكر وعمر رضي الله عنهما كانوا يستفتحون القراءة بالحمد لله رب العالمين

RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r3.claim: Razi criticizes Abu Hanifa for relying on Uthman's report in the fugitive-divorce issue despite contrary Companions and Quran, but not following all Companions' practice on al-Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r3.anchor: أنه تمسك في مسألة طلاق الفار بأثر عثمان مع أن عبد الرحمن وعبد الله بن الزبير كانا يخالفانه

RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r4.claim: Muslims everywhere recite al-Fatiha in prayer; even if some regard it as recommended rather than obligatory, abandoning the unanimous practice leaves the believers' path and incurs Quran 4:115's warning.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157/r4.anchor: فإنك لا ترى أحدا من المسلمين في المشرق والمغرب إلا ويقرأ الفاتحة في الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r1.claim: The prayer's two halves arise through the verses of al-Fatiha; since prayer entails this division and it entails this surah, al-Fatiha is necessary for valid prayer.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r1.anchor: الصلاة لا تنفك عن هذا التنصيف وهذا التنصيف لا يحصل إلا بسبب هذه السورة

RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r2.claim: Against the objection that the negation in no prayer except with al-Fatiha must mean incompleteness rather than invalidity, Razi cites a version explicitly denying prayer's occurrence for one who omits it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r2.anchor: الأول : أنه جاء في بعض الروايات : لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r3.claim: If al-Fatiha is a constituent of prayer, omitting it means the prayer's very essence does not exist, so the hadith's negation can remain literal.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r3.anchor: من اعتقد أن قراءة الفاتحة جزء من أجزاء ماهية الصلاة فعند عدم قراءة الفاتحة لا توجد ماهية الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r4.claim: If the hadith must be figurative, invalidity is nearer than mere incompleteness because a nonexistent act resembles an invalid act more than a valid but imperfect one; presumption, prohibition, and caution reinforce this reading.
RAZI-FULL:v1p157#2/r4.anchor: فكان حمل اللفظ على نفي الصحة أولى

RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r1.claim: The Prophet says a prayer without al-Fatiha is deficient and incomplete; Razi argues that a deficient performance does not discharge the continuing obligation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r1.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال : كل صلاة لم يقرا فيها بفاتحة الكتاب فهي خداج غير تمام

RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r2.claim: Razi compares Abu Hanifa's ruling that an Eid fast cannot make up Ramadan because it is incomplete and asks why the same reasoning does not invalidate prayer without al-Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r2.anchor: فلم لم يقل بمثل هذا الكلام في هذا المقام

RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r3.speaker: ابن المنذر عن أبي هريرة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r3.claim: Ibn al-Mundhir transmits from Abu Huraira that the Prophet said a prayer without al-Fatiha does not suffice.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r3.anchor: عن ابن المنذر أنه روى بإسناده عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : لا تجزىء صلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r4.speaker: رفاعة بن مالك عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r4.claim: A man who asks the Prophet to teach him prayer is told to face the qibla, say takbir, and recite al-Fatiha; Razi treats this imperative as obligation and recitation as part of prayer.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158/r4.anchor: روى رفاعة بن مالك أن رجلا دخل المسجد وصلى فلما فرغ من صلاته

RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r1.claim: The Prophet identifies al-Fatiha as a surah unmatched in the Torah, Gospel, or Psalms; the Companions' answer about what they recite in prayer indicates a known universal practice.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r1.anchor: روي أن النبي عليه الصلاة والسلام قال : ألا أخبركم بسورة ليس في التوراة ولا في الإنجيل ولا في الزبور مثلها

RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r2.claim: Razi argues that Quran 73:20 requires al-Fatiha: the options are al-Fatiha, another surah, or a choice; the latter two fail because another is not universally required and al-Fatiha is agreed better and more complete.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r2.anchor: فنقول : المراد بما تيسر من القرآن إما أن يكون هو الفاتحة أو غير الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r3.claim: Al-Fatiha is the recitation made accessible to all because every Muslim has it memorized, whereas other surahs may not be memorized by each person.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r3.anchor: لأن هذه السورة محفوظة لجميع المكلفين من المسلمين فهي متيسرة للكل

RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r4.claim: The original duty to pray remains until evidence shows discharge; al-Fatiha is superior and makes prayer more complete, so omitting it does not establish discharge.
RAZI-FULL:v1p158#2/r4.anchor: الأصل في الثابت البقاء خالفنا هذا الأصل عند الإتيان بها للصلاة المشتملة على قراءة الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r1.claim: Although belief in obligation may itself leave theoretical doubt, actual recitation creates no danger while omission creates fear of failing the duty; therefore action is the safer course.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r1.anchor: أما في العمل فإن القراءة لا توجب الخوف أما تركه فيفيد الخوف

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r2.claim: If prayers with and without al-Fatiha were both valid, habitual recitation would make other surahs abandoned; because the community agrees al-Fatiha is preferable, Razi concludes omission is invalid.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r2.anchor: لكنهم أجمعوا على أن الصلاة بهذه السورة أولى فثبت أن الصلاة بغير هذه السورة غير جائزة

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r3.claim: Just as bowing and prostration cannot be replaced, al-Fatiha cannot be replaced by another reading, with caution as the common rationale.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r3.anchor: أجمعنا على أنه لا يجوز إبدال الركوع والسجود بغيرهما فوجب أن لا يجوز إبدال قراءة الفاتحة بغيرها

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r4.claim: The duty to pray persists; neither Quran 73:20 nor analogy proves discharge without al-Fatiha, and ritual worship is a domain where analogy should be set aside.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r4.anchor: لأن التعبدات غالبة على الصلاة وفي مثل هذه الصورة يجب ترك القياس

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r5.claim: Since the Prophet recited al-Fatiha throughout his life, replacing it with another recitation is innovation and abandonment of the required prophetic example.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r5.anchor: فحينئذ تكون قراءة غير الفاتحة ابتداعا وتركا للاتباع وذلك حرام

RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r6.claim: Prayer without al-Fatiha loses an agreed extra virtue without compensation, which Razi regards as improper and therefore impermissible.
RAZI-FULL:v1p159/r6.anchor: الصلاة بدون الفاتحة توجب فوات الفضيلة الزائدة من غير جابر

RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r1.claim: Abu Huraira reports that the Prophet ordered him to announce that there is no prayer without recitation, even if by al-Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r1.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أنه قال : أمرني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن أخرج وأنادي : لا صلاة إلا بقراءة

RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r2.claim: Razi answers Quran 73:20 by the same three options: al-Fatiha itself, another passage, or a choice; the latter two fail, and al-Fatiha is accessible to all.
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r2.anchor: فنقول : المراد بما تيسر من القرآن : إما أن يكون هو الفاتحة أو غير الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r3.claim: Razi counters the opposing report with Abu Huraira's version no prayer except by al-Fatiha; if reports conflict, the stronger and safer view is his.
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r3.anchor: معارض بما نقل عن أبي هريرة أنه قال أمرني رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن أخرج وأنادي لا صلاة إلا بفاتحة الكتاب

RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r4.claim: Razi reports disagreement over the minimum recitation for Hanafis: Abu Hanifa accepts one verse, even isolated letters, while Abu Yusuf and Muhammad require three short verses or one long verse.
RAZI-FULL:v1p160/r4.anchor: فقال أبو حنيفة : إذا قرأ آية واحدة كفت مثل قوله آلم وحم والطور

RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.speaker: أم سلمة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.
RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2.anchor: روى الشافعي رضي الله عنه عن مسلم عن ابن جريج عن ابن أبي مليكة عن أم سلمة أنها قالت

RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.claim: In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2.anchor: فإذا قال العبد بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قال الله سبحانه مجدني عبدي وإذا قال الحمد لله رب العالمين

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r1.claim: Madḥ is broader than hamd: one may praise a living or inanimate thing such as a pearl, but cannot give it hamd.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r1.anchor: المدح قد يحصل للحي ولغير الحي

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r2.claim: Madḥ can precede or follow a benefaction, whereas hamd is only after beneficence.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r2.anchor: المدح قد يكون قبل الإحسان وقد يكون بعده

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r3.claim: Madḥ can be condemned, as in the warning to throw dust in flatterers’ faces, whereas hamd is generally commanded.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#2/r3.anchor: أما الحمد فإنه مأمور به مطلقا

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r1.claim: Madḥ denotes a general kind of excellence, while hamd denotes the specific virtue of benefaction; this completes the distinction that madḥ is broader.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r1.anchor: المدح عبارة عن القول الدال على كونه مختصا بنوع من أنواع الفضائل

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r2.claim: Hamd applies whether a benefaction reaches the speaker or someone else, while shukr is limited to a benefit received by the thankful person.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r2.anchor: الحمد يعم ما إذا وصل ذلك الإنعام إليك أو إلى غيرك

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r3.claim: Saying al-hamdu lillah rather than al-madhu lillah acknowledges God as a freely choosing agent, not a necessary emanation as philosophers claim.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r3.anchor: أن إله العالم ليس موجبا بالذات كما تقول الفلاسفة

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r4.claim: Al-hamdu lillah is better than ash-shukru lillah because it praises God for every benefit to the worlds, even one not received by the speaker; shukr is personal gratitude.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r4.anchor: كل إنعام صدر منه ووصل إلى غيره

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r5.speaker: المخالف
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r5.claim: One reported distinction says hamd thanks God for warding off calamity, while shukr thanks Him for gifts; an objection asks why the lesser benefit is named first.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r5.anchor: الحمد على ما دفع الله من البلاء والشكر على ما أعطى من النعماء

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r6.claim: Razi offers three answers: thanking for the lesser implies gratitude for the greater; warded-off harm is unbounded while gifts are finite; and preventing harm matters more than adding benefit.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r6.anchor: أنا شاكر لأدنى النعمتين فكيف لأعلاهما

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r7.claim: The formula says al-hamdu lillah rather than ahmadu Allah so it declares God worthy of praise before any creature praises Him, from eternity to eternity.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r7.anchor: كان محمودا قبل حمد الحامدين وقبل شكر الشاكرين

RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r8.claim: Al-hamdu lillah also means praise and thanks are God’s due and property, because His abundant favors make Him inherently deserving of them.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178#3/r8.anchor: الحمد والثناء حق لله وملكه فإنه تعالى هو المستحق للحمد

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r1.claim: Hamd praises beauty whether or not a favor was bestowed and is expressed only by the tongue; shukr is for a received favor and may be by heart, tongue, or limbs.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد: الثناء على الجميل سواء كان نعمة مسداة إلى أحد أم لا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r2.claim: A poem listing hand, tongue, and hidden conscience as three gifts illustrates that gratitude includes bodily action as well as speech.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r2.anchor:
وقال الشاعر:
34 أفادتكم النعماء مني ثلاثة
يدي ولساني والضمير المحجبا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r3.claim: Views range from treating hamd and shukr as synonymous, to making hamd absolutely broader, to distinguishing praise of attributes from thanks for acts.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r3.anchor: وقيل: الحمد هو الشكر بدليل قولهم: " الحمد لله شكرا ". وقيل: بينهما عموم/ وخصوص مطلق

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r4.claim: Tha'lab's derivation of hamd as a reversal of madh is unsound: both forms are equally common, and hamd applies to God where madh does not; a possible prohibition is acknowledged.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r4.anchor: وقيل: الحمد مقلوب من المدح، وليس بسديد وإن كان منقولا عن ثعلب

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r5.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r5.claim: Al-Raghib defines hamd as praise for excellence, narrower than madh but broader than shukr: every hamd is madh and every shukr is hamd, but not conversely.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r5.anchor: وقال الراغب: " الحمد لله الثناء [عليه] بالفضيلة، وهو أخص من المدح وأعم من الشكر

SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r6.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r6.claim: Al-Raghib says hamd can concern chosen and innate qualities, while shukr answers a favor; he also explains mahmud as praised, Muhammad as much-praised, and Ahmad as surpassing others in praise.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2/r6.anchor: الراغب: " الحمد لله الثناء [عليه] بالفضيلة، وهو أخص من المدح وأعم من الشكر، يقال فيما يكون من الإنسان باختياره وبما يكون منه وفيه بالتسخير،

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r1.claim: The article in al-hamd is analyzed as universal, generic, or referring to known praise; al-Zamakhshari chooses the generic reading.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r1.anchor: والألف واللام في " الحمد " قيل: للاستغراق وقيل: لتعريف الجنس، واختاره الزمخشري

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r2.claim: Al-Zamakhshari rejects the universal reading; the author infers that praise here is performed by the servant, who cannot produce every praise by himself and others.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r2.anchor: ومنع الزمخشري كونها للاستغراق، ولم يبين وجه ذلك

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r3.claim: Hamd is fundamentally a verbal noun and therefore normally has no dual or plural; Ibn al-A'rabi nevertheless reports an af'al plural with poetic evidence.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r3.anchor: والأصل فيه المصدرية فلذلك لا يثنى ولا يجمع، وحكى ابن الأعرابي جمعه على أفعل

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r4.claim: The common reading raises al-hamd as subject with a deleted nominal predicate, the preferred estimate, though a verb can also be supplied.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r4.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: " الحمد لله " برفع الدال وكسر لام الجر، ورفعه على الابتداء

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r5.claim: The author prefers a nominal estimate because it is mandatory in fa-idha and amma clauses; the relative clause al-ladhi fi al-dar instead requires a verb but is not structurally comparable.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r5.anchor: والدليل على اختيار القول الأول أن ذلك يتعين في بعض الصور

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r6.claim: A prepositional phrase or adverb functioning as clause predicate, relative clause, adjective, or circumstantial phrase has an omitted governor; a generic kā'in cannot be overt except in a poetic anomaly.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#2/r6.anchor: أن الجار والمجرور والظرف إذا وقعا صلة أو صفة أو حالا أو خبرا تعلقا بمحذوف

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r1.claim: The omitted governor can generally be a noun or verb, but relative clauses require a verb and the fa-idha and amma constructions require a noun; grammarians differ over the default elsewhere.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r1.anchor: ثم ذلك المحذوف يجوز تقديره باسم أو فعل إلا في الصلة فإنه يتعين أن يكون فعلا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r2.claim: A rare accusative al-hamda is parsed either as a verbal noun replacing I praise, or as an imperative-like source meaning say praise; al-Tabari favors the command interpretation, but the author prefers declarative force.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r2.anchor: وقرئ شاذا بنصب الدال من " الحمد " ، وفيه وجهان: أظهرهما أنه منصوب على المصدرية

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r3.claim: The accusative may alternatively be a direct object of recite or read, but the verbal-noun analysis is better because the wording itself supports it.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r3.anchor: والثاني: أنه منصوب على المفعول به أي اقرؤوا الحمد، أو اتلوا الحمد

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r4.claim: Raising al-hamd is stronger and more expressive of stable praise, while accusative signals renewal; Abraham's salām is better than the angels' salāman by the verse's instruction to answer more beautifully.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r4.anchor: وقراءة الرفع أمكن وأبلغ من قراءة النصب، لأن الرفع في باب المصادر

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r5.claim: On the accusative reading, li-llah is attached to an omitted explanatory verb such as I mean; source nouns do not normally govern this lām phrase, though it may strengthen a derivative verb.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#3/r5.anchor: على قراءة النصب يتعلق بمحذوف لا بالمصدر لأنها للبيان تقديره: أعني لله

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r1.claim: The kasra in a variant al-hamdi may be vowel harmony with the following lām, a Tamim and some Ghatafan dialect feature; another possibility is hidden nominative or accusative inflection.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r1.anchor: وقرئ أيضا بكسر الدال، ووجهه أنها حركة إتباع لكسرة لام الجر بعدها

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r2.claim: A variant with damma on the lām of li-llah follows the preceding dāl; al-Zamakhshari prefers harmony from inflection to building, citing a Qays dialect and Qur'anic murdifin.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r2.anchor: وقرئ أيضا: " لله " بضم لام الجر، قالوا: وهي إتباع لحركة الدال

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r3.claim: The lām in li-llah expresses entitlement here; other senses include ownership, transfer, kinship, cause, address, oath exclamation, clarification, result, location, endpoint, elevation, and augmentation.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#4/r3.anchor: ومعنى لام الجر هنا الاستحقاق، أي الحمد مستحق لله، ولها معان أخر

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r1.claim: The lām may be explanatory, resultative, locative meaning in, at, or after, terminative, or superposition; the source gives examples for each.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r1.anchor:
والتبيين نحو: قوله تعالى:
هيت لك
[يوسف: 23]، والصيرورة نحو قوله تعالى:
ليكون لهم عدوا وحزنا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r2.claim: The lām is regularly extra with a preposed complement of a verb or with a derivative governor, and elsewhere only irregularly.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r2.anchor:
وقد تزاد باطراد في معمول الفعل مقدما عليه كقوله تعالى:
إن كنتم للرؤيا تعبرون
[يوسف: 43] أو كان العامل فرعا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r3.claim: For raddafa lakum, some explain the lām by semantic inclusion and others regard it as extra.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#5/r3.anchor:
وأما قوله تعالى:
قل عسى أن يكون ردف لكم
[النمل: 72] فقيل: على التضمين. وقيل هي زائدة

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r1.claim: The common reading makes rabb genitive as an adjective or appositive to Allah; accusative allows an implied I praise, a detached praise, or vocative, with vocative weakest because it separates adjective from noun; nominative is detached predicate huwa rabb.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r1.anchor: وقراءة الجمهور مجرورا على النعت لله أو البدل منه، وقرئ منصوبا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r2.claim: Rabb can mean lord, owner, enduring, worshipped, or reformer; some add companion, supported by two poems, but here the author prefers owner and says no extra sense is needed; creator is another proposal.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r2.anchor:
قوله { رب العالمين }: الرب لغة: السيد والمالك والثابت والمعبود، ومنه:
42 أرب يبول الثعلبان برأسه
لقد هان من بالت عليه الثعالب
والمصلح

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r3.claim: One view treats rabb as an adjective, either fa'l or fa'il from rāb with a shortened long vowel; the author objects that bār and barr may simply be separate forms.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r3.anchor: فمنهم من قال: هو وصف ثم اختلف هؤلاء في وزنه، فقيل: هو على وزن فعل

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r4.claim: Others treat rabb as the verbal noun rabba yarubbu, meaning owned or governed, functioning as an agent noun like a just or fasting man.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r4.anchor:
ومنهم من قال: هو مصدر 



ربه يربه ربا أي ملكه

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r5.claim: Rabb is normally reserved for God unless annexed to a noun, though pre-Islamic Arabs used it without qualification for a human king, which the author calls unbelief.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r5.anchor:
ولا يطلق على غير الباري تعالى إلا بقيد إضافة، نحو قوله تعالى:
ارجع إلى ربك

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r6.speaker: الحارث بن حلزة
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r6.claim: Al-Harith ibn Hilliza's line calls a human king al-rabb without qualification, exemplifying pre-Islamic usage.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r6.anchor:
قال الحارث بن حلزة:
44 وهو الرب والشهيد على يو
م الحيارين والبلاء بلاء

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r7.claim: When a known noun is described by praise, blame, or compassion, its adjective may follow or detach with an implicit verb or subject; no explicit governor is allowed.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#6/r7.anchor: اعلم أن الموصوف إذا كان معلوما بدون صفته وكان الوصف مدحا، أو ذما أو ترحما

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r1.claim: With several such adjectives one may follow all, detach all, or mix them, but must follow first and detach later to avoid splitting adjective from noun.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r1.anchor: وإذا تكررت النعوت والحالة هذه كنت مخيرا بين ثلاثة أوجه

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r2.claim: Al-alamin is an annexed sound masculine plural in form but an ism-jam because its singular differs; it cannot be plural of alam if that covers all non-divine beings while al-alamin means rational beings only.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r2.anchor: والعالمين: خفض بالإضافة، علامة خفضه الياء لجريانه مجرى جمع المذكر السالم

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r3.claim: Sibawayh similarly says a'rab is not plural of arab because the former is narrower; an objection that al-alamin could mean only rational alam is answered by comparison with the unavailable form shay'un.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r3.anchor: وهذا نظير ما فعله سيبويه في أن " أعرابا " ليس جمعا

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r4.speaker: الراغب
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r4.claim: Al-Raghib transmits Ibn Abbas's explanation that al-alamin means angels, jinn, and humans, and says the word was formed as an instrument of knowing the Creator.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r4.anchor: ويؤيد هذا ما نقل الراغب عن ابن عباس أن

SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r5.claim: The author prefers al-Raghib's account that the sound plural includes all creation, with human usage prevailing when humans share the label.
SAMIN-DURR:1:2#7/r5.anchor: يطلق على العقلاء وغيرهم، وهو مخالف لما تقدم

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r1.claim: The declarative al-ḥamdu lillāh is preferable to ahmadu Allāh: it establishes praise as God’s right instead of reporting one speaker’s act.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r1.anchor: فثبت أن قوله الحمد لله أولى من قوله أحمد الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r2.claim: The lām in lillāh can signify fitting اختصاص, ownership, or power and dominion; each makes all praise belong to God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r2.anchor: اللام في قوله الحمد لله يحتمل وجوها كثيرة

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r3.claim: Al-ḥamdu lillāh has eight letters corresponding to Paradise’s eight gates; saying it with a pure heart merits those gates.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r3.anchor: الحمد لله ثمانية أحرف وأبواب الجنة ثمانية

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r4.claim: One grammatical view makes definite al-ḥamd refer to a prior known instance, or otherwise to all praise to avoid ambiguity.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r4.anchor: إن كان مسبوقا بمعهود سابق انصرف إليه وإلا يحمل على الاستغراق

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r5.claim: A second grammatical view says the definite noun denotes only the essence or nature of praise, not universal scope.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r5.anchor: أنه لا يفيد العموم إلا أنه يفيد الماهية والحقيقة فقط

RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r6.claim: On either grammatical analysis, the phrase denies that anyone besides God is independently entitled to praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p179/r6.anchor: فثبت على القولين أن قوله الحمد لله ينفي حصول الحمد لغير الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r1.speaker: Prophet
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r1.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that whoever does not thank people does not thank God; al-Rāzī answers that God is the true source of every human benefit.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r1.anchor: من لم يحمد الناس لم يحمد الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r2.claim: A human benefactor acts only because God creates the motive, the blessing, and the recipient’s capacity to benefit, so God is the true benefactor.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r2.anchor: كل من أنعم على غيره بإنعام فالمنعم في الحقيقة هو الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r3.claim: A giver who seeks reward, praise, repayment, or release from stinginess seeks compensation and is not the true benefactor; God gives from intrinsic fullness.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r3.anchor: كل من أنعم على الغير فإنه يطلب بذلك الإنعام عوضا

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r4.claim: Every blessing is a possible existent brought into being by God, directly or through means; therefore praise for blessing belongs to God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r4.anchor: كل نعمة فهي من الموجودات الممكنة الوجود

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r5.claim: A complete blessing requires benefit, freedom from harm, and security from loss, and only God supplies all three conditions.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r5.anchor: النعمة لا تكون كاملة إلا عند اجتماع أمور ثلاثة

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r6.claim: People cannot fully thank God because they cannot enumerate His countless blessings, as the Qur’an says.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r6.anchor: نعم الله على الإنسان كثيرة لا يقوى عقل الإنسان على الوقوف عليها

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r7.claim: The ability, motive, and freedom from obstacles needed for gratitude are themselves gifts, so thanking them would require endless further thanks.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r7.anchor: إذا زال عنه العوائق والحوائل فكل ذلك إنعام من الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r8.claim: Human conceptions of perfection never reach God’s greater perfection, so people cannot praise Him as He deserves.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r8.anchor: كل ما خطر ببال الإنسان من صفات الكمال والجلال فكمال الله وجلاله أعلى

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r9.speaker: الواسطي
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r9.claim: Al-Wāsiṭī calls gratitude shirk when a person imagines that his thanks can equal God’s blessings.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r9.anchor: وهذا معنى قول الواسطي الشكر شرك

RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r10.claim: Because full gratitude is beyond human capacity, the verse states that all praise belongs to God rather than commanding people to praise Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p180/r10.anchor: لم يقل احمدوا الله بل قال الحمد لله

RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r1.speaker: داود
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r1.claim: David asks how he can thank God when even the ability to thank depends on God’s gift; God says recognizing that incapacity is gratitude according to one’s capacity.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r1.anchor: يا رب كيف أشكرك وشكري لك لا يتم إلا بإنعامك علي

RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r2.speaker: Prophet
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r2.claim: A report says that when a blessed servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh, God tells the angels that the servant returned something priceless for an unvalued gift.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r2.anchor: إذا أنعم الله على عبده نعمة فيقول العبد الحمد لله

RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r3.claim: Al-ḥamdu lillāh encompasses every praise uttered or possible from all creatures, prophets, angels, saints, scholars, and future inhabitants of Paradise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182/r3.anchor: كل حمد أتى به أحد من الحامدين فهو لله

RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r1.claim: The report’s expanded wording contrasts one immeasurable blessing with the servant’s boundless thanks in saying al-ḥamdu lillāh.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r1.anchor: قد أعطيته نعمة واحدة لا قدر لها فأعطاني من الشكر ما لا حد له

RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r2.claim: Worldly blessings are finite, but the praise phrase is infinite; what remains after accounting for a finite blessing is endless, warranting eternal reward.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r2.anchor: غير المتناهي إذا سقط منه المتناهي بقي الباقي غير متناه

RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r3.claim: Existence is better than nonexistence, and every possible existent receives its existence from God; hence every creature receives His blessing and mercy.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r3.anchor: وجود كل شيء ما سوى الله تعالى فإنه حصل بإيجاد الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r4.claim: Praise precedes tasbīḥ because it includes transcendence and adds God’s beneficence, making Him beyond mere completeness.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r4.anchor: التحميد يدل على التسبيح دلالة التضمن

RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r5.claim: Rationally, beneficence requires knowing every need, power to meet it, and freedom from need; divine beneficence therefore presupposes perfection without deficiency.
RAZI-FULL:v1p182#2/r5.anchor: كونه محسنا لا يتم إلا بعد كونه منزها عن النقائص والآفات

RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r1.claim: Praise thanks God for past blessings and brings future increase, as promised in the Qur’an; it closes barriers and opens the way to knowledge of God, hence the name al-Fātiḥa.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r1.anchor: أما تعلقه بالماضي فهو أنه يقع شكرا على النعم المتقدمة

RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r2.speaker: السري السقطي
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r2.claim: Al-Sarī al-Saqaṭī spent thirty years seeking forgiveness for thanking God that his shop survived Baghdad’s fire while others’ homes and shops burned, since his happiness showed disregard for others.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r2.anchor: وقع الحريق في بغداد واحترقت الدكاكين والدور

RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r3.claim: The phrase should be reserved for the best blessings: religious benefits outrank worldly ones, inner acts outrank bodily acts, and seeing a worldly benefit as the giver’s gift is nobler than treating it merely as a benefit.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183/r3.anchor: نعم الدين أفضل من نعم الدنيا لوجوه كثيرة

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r1.claim: A report says Adam’s first words were al-ḥamdu lillāh after he sneezed; the people of Paradise end with the same praise, so the world begins and ends with it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r1.anchor: لما بلغ الروح إلى سرته عطس فقال الحمد لله رب العالمين

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r2.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects supplying an unspoken command ‘say’: the phrase is already a complete assertion that praise belongs to God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r2.anchor: قوله الحمد لله إخبار عن كون الحمد حقا له وملكا له

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r3.claim: The assertion makes God intrinsically deserving of praise through His essence and acts, whether people praise Him or not; what is essential exceeds what depends on another.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r3.anchor: يدل على كونه تعالى مستحقا للحمد بحسب ذاته وبحسب أفعاله

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r4.claim: Stating that praise is due, rather than directly commanding it, lets the obedient praise God while leaving the disobedient with a lesser offense than rejecting an order.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r4.anchor: فمن كان مطيعا حمده ومن كان عاصيا إثمه أقل

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r5.claim: The Jabriyya argue that if humans created faith, the human would deserve more praise for this noblest act than God; therefore God creates faith.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r5.anchor: لو كان الإيمان فعلا للعبد لكان استحقاق العبد للحمد أولى

RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r6.claim: The Jabriyya argue that Muslims praise God for the blessing of faith; if faith were a human act, praising God for it would wrongly credit Him with another’s act.
RAZI-FULL:v1p183#2/r6.anchor: أجمعت الأمة على قولهم الحمد لله على نعمة الإيمان

RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r1.claim: The Jabriyya argue that obligatory acts only avert blame and cannot earn praise, while voluntary grace would make God gain praise and thus be perfected by another.
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r1.anchor: أداء الواجبات فإنه لا يفيد استحقاق الحمد

RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r2.claim: They further argue that if God is praised intrinsically, no act causes that entitlement, so no duty, compensation, or reward is owed; if it is not intrinsic, God would depend on another.
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r2.anchor: استحقاقه الحمد والمدح إما أن يكون أمرا ثابتا له لذاته

RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r3.speaker: الجبرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r3.claim: The Jabriyya infer that faith too comes from God: all praise belongs to Him, praise follows blessing, and faith is the greatest blessing.
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r3.anchor: الإيمان أفضل النعم فوجب أن يكون الإيمان من الله

RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r4.speaker: الجبرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r4.claim: They argue that God’s self-praise, though blameworthy among people, shows divine acts cannot be judged by human standards and challenges Muʿtazilī principles.
RAZI-FULL:v1p184/r4.anchor: فلما بدأ كتابة بمدح النفس دل ذلك على أن حاله بخلاف حال الخلق

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r1.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r1.claim: The Muʿtazila say absolute praise is deserved by one whose acts contain no evil, rulings no injustice, and judgments no oppression; they reject the Jabriyya picture of God creating disbelief then punishing it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r1.anchor: المستحق للحمد على الإطلاق هو الذي لا قبيح في فعله

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r2.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r2.claim: They argue that if a servant deserves God’s praise, the servant must be capable of action, contrary to determinism; if God praises Himself, that is also invalid, so the phrase only works on their doctrine.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r2.anchor: إن كان الأول وجب كون العبد قادرا على الفعل

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r3.claim: Scholars disagree whether gratitude is owed by reason or only by revealed law; the latter cite the rule that punishment awaits a messenger and the removal of excuses by messengers.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r3.anchor: من الناس من قال : إنه ثابت بالسمع لقوله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r4.claim: Al-Rāzī argues that gratitude is due at all times, even before revelation: the verse makes praise God’s right without qualification and grounds it in His nurturing and mercy.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r4.anchor: يدل على ثبوت هذا الاستحقاق قبل مجيء الشرع

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r5.claim: True praise is any act expressing reverence for a benefactor: inward belief in perfection, spoken words of praise, or bodily deeds that express it; saying al-ḥamdu lillāh merely reports praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r5.anchor: حمد المنعم عبارة عن كل فعل يشعر بتعظيم المنعم

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r6.claim: One group says God cannot command praise: if it repays a blessing, the command makes generosity transactional; if not, it is needless toil imposed on another.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r6.anchor: ذلك التحميد إما أن يكون بناء على إنعام وصل إليهم

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r7.claim: The same group says praise is useless to a God complete in Himself and that punishing people eternally for omitting a useless act would not befit the generous Lord.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r7.anchor: الكامل لذاته يستحيل أن يستكمل بغيره

RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r8.claim: A second group calls praise bad manners: the tiny thanks cannot match immeasurable blessings, recalling blessings distracts from knowing the giver, and praise for benefits seems self-interested.
RAZI-FULL:v1p185/r8.anchor: الاشتغال بالشكر لا يتأتى إلا مع استحضار تلك النعم في القلب

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r1.claim: Only God is necessary in Himself; everything else is possible and is called the world because its existence points to God.
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r1.anchor: العالم كل موجود سوى الله وسبب تسمية هذا القسم بالعالم

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r2.claim: Possible existents divide into spatial bodies, attributes of bodies, and things neither; bodies include celestial spheres and scriptural entities, earthly elements and composites, while attributes comprise about forty genera.
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r2.anchor: كل ما سوى الله تعالى إما أن يكون متحيزا وإما أن يكون صفة للمتحيز

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r3.claim: The third class is spirits: lower spirits include good jinn and evil demons; higher ones are attached to celestial bodies or are holy, disembodied spirits.
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r3.anchor: فهو الأرواح وهي إما سفلية وإما علوية

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r4.claim: Since possible beings need God to bring them into existence and preserve them, He is their deity as creator and their Lord as sustainer.
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r4.anchor: هو الذي أخرجها من العدم إلى الوجود وهو رب العالمين

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r5.claim: Created nurturers seek their own profit, such as reward or praise, while God nurtures for the creatures’ benefit rather than His own.

RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p186/r6.claim: God’s nurturing does not diminish His store; unlike other givers, He gives from inexhaustible provision.

RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r1.speaker: Prophet
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r1.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that God loves those who persistently supplicate; no grading is stated.
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r1.anchor: إن الله تعالى يحب الملحين في الدعاء

RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r2.claim: God gives before being asked, nurturing a person as a fetus and protecting him before he can think or pray.
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r2.anchor: أما الحق تعالى فأنه يعطي قبل السؤال

RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r3.claim: Unlike human benefaction, God’s care never ends and reaches everyone.
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r3.anchor: والحق تعالى لا ينقطع إحسانه البتة

RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r4.claim: The four motives for honoring someone map onto the verse: intrinsic perfection, beneficence, hoped-for future good, and fear correspond respectively to God, Lord, Merciful, and Master of Judgment.
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r4.anchor: هذه الحالات هي الجهات الموجبة للتعظيم

RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r5.claim: Embryonic development forms distinct bones, cartilage, ligaments, vessels, and senses, displaying God’s care; He gives hearing through bone, sight through fat, and speech through flesh.
RAZI-FULL:v1p187/r5.anchor: فسبحان من أسمع بعظم وبصر بشحم وأنطق بلحم

RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r1.claim: A seed’s shoot and roots develop in opposite directions, then produce branches, flowers, fruit, food, oils, and medicines; fine roots draw nourishment even through hard soil.
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r1.anchor: الحكمة في كل هذه التدبيرات تحصيل ما يحتاج العبد إليه

RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r2.claim: God arranged night for rest and day for work, the sun and moon for timekeeping, stars for navigation, and earth and mountains for habitation; reflecting on nature reveals His providence.
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r2.anchor: خلق الليل ليكون سببا للراحة والسكون وخلق النهار ليكون سببا للمعاش

RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r3.claim: The sequence assigns praise to God, then names Him Lord of the worlds: Allah signifies necessary perfection, while Lord of the worlds shows that all else flows from His generosity, making Him beyond completeness.
RAZI-FULL:v1p188/r3.anchor: أن وجود كل ما سواه فائض عن تربيته وإحسانه وجوده

RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r1.claim: A Prophetic saying calls the human being God’s structure and curses whoever demolishes it; God guards people by night and day despite their sins.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r1.anchor: الآدمي بنيان الرب ملعون من هدم بنيان الرب

RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r2.speaker: القدرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r2.claim: The Qadariyya argue that God would not truly be Lord if He created a disbeliever’s unbelief and then punished him, or commanded faith while preventing it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r2.anchor: إنما يكون تعالى ربا للعالمين ومربيا لهم لو كان محسنا إليهم

RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r3.speaker: الجبرية
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r3.claim: The Jabriyya answer that faith is the greatest blessing, so if it comes from God He is the Lord and benefactor of all.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r3.anchor: لما كان الإيمان أعظم النعم وأجلها

RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r4.claim: Allah is nobler than Lord, although supplicants commonly call God ‘Lord’; al-Rāzī refers readers to his earlier discussion of the divine names.
RAZI-FULL:v1p189/r4.anchor: قولنا الله أشرف من قولنا رب

RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.claim: The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.anchor: فثبت أن هذه الآيات السبع دافعة لتلك الأخلاق القبيحة السبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r5.claim: “Lord of the worlds” signifies that God is one, owns all worlds, and is the only deity and object of worship.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r5.anchor: ليس في العالم إله سواه ولا معبود غيره

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.speaker: الله تعالى
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.claim: In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.anchor: فإذا قال العبد : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم يقول الله تعالى ذكرني عبدي

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.claim: Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.anchor: مدار الشرائع على رعاية مصالح الخلق

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.claim: Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.anchor: أن عند عدم قراءة الفاتحة وجب أن لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.claim: Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.claim: The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.anchor: أن الخلفاء الراشدين واظبوا على قراءتها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.claim: Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.anchor: أن جميع المسلمين شرقا وغربا لا يصلون إلا بقراءة الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.claim: The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.claim: The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.anchor: وظاهره الوجوب فكانت قراءة ما تيسر من القرآن واجبة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.claim: Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.anchor: أن قراءة الفاتحة أحوط فوجب المصير إليها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.claim: The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.anchor: وسابعها : أن الرسول عليه السلام واظب على قراءتها فوجب أن يكون العدول عنه محرما

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.claim: If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.anchor: ولا يلزم من الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الكامل الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الناقص

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.claim: Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.anchor: المقصود من الصلاة حصول ذكر القلب

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.claim: The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.anchor: أن هذا الخبر الذي رويناه يدل على أن عند فقدان الفاتحة لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r4.claim: The report that God says “my servant praised Me” shows that praise is higher than remembrance.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r4.anchor: هذا يدل على أن مقام الحمد أعلى من مقام الذكر

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r5.claim: Praise frames creation: the angels speak of it before Adam is created, and the inhabitants of Paradise end their invocation with it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r5.anchor: وآخر كلام يذكر بعد فناء العالم هو الحمد أيضا

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r6.claim: The mind cannot contemplate God's essence: one cannot conceive His true nature, and the Prophet instead directs people to contemplate creation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r6.anchor: تفكروا في الخلق ولا تفكروا في الخالق

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r7.claim: Contemplating creatures reveals more mercy, favor, and beneficence than evil, because good is essential and evil incidental; therefore praise and thanks predominate.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r7.anchor: أن الخير مطلوب بالذات والشر بالعرض

RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.claim: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.anchor: أن آيات الفاتحة سبع والأعمال المحسوسة أيضا في الصلاة سبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r2.claim: Praise corresponds to bowing: gratitude looks both to God and His gift, a middle state between turning away and absorption, as bowing lies between standing and prostration; abundant gifts also weigh the back down.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r2.anchor: والركوع حالة متوسطة بين القيام وبين السجود

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.claim: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.anchor: روح الأرواح ونور الأنوار هو الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.claim: Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.anchor: أما ما يتعلق بعالم الأرواح فله معراجان

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.claim: The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.anchor: ثم تترقى فتنتهي إلى الأرواح المقدسة عن التعلقات بالأجسام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.claim: The ascent continues through ever-higher spiritual ranks until God, the source of all good and mercy; thus the spirit-world is the unseen and God's presence the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.anchor: فثبت أن عالم الأرواح هو عالم الغيب وحضرة جلال الربوبية هي غيب الغيب

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.speaker: النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.claim: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.anchor: إن لله سبعين حجابا من النور لو كشفها لأحرقت سبحات وجهه كل ما أدرك البصر

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.claim: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.anchor: إن تحفة أمتك الصلاة وذلك لأنها جامعة بين المعراج الجسماني وبين المعراج الروحاني

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.claim: Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.anchor: فإنه إذا استحكمت المرافقة تعذرت المفارقة

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.claim: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.anchor: فاقطع نظرك عنهما بالكلية ووجه قلبك وروحك وسرك وعقلك وفهمك

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.claim: The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.anchor: ثم قل : سبحانك اللهم وبحمدك وفي هذا المقام تجلى لك نور سبحات الجلال

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.claim: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.anchor: لأن قوله تبارك إشارة إلى الدوام المنزه عن الإفناء والإعدام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.claim: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.anchor: أعلم وأعظم من أن تكون صفات جلاله ونعوت كماله محصورة في القدر المذكور

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.claim: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.anchor: كل صفات الجلال وسمات الكمال له لا لغيره

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.claim: Most scholars place al-Fātiḥah among the earliest sūrahs revealed in Makkah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.anchor: to have been revealed in Makkah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.claim: Mujāhid says al-Fātiḥah was revealed in Madinah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.anchor: According to Mujāhid (d. 104/722–23), one of the leading scholars among the second generation of Muslims, this sūrah was revealed in Madinah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.claim: Most scholars reject a Medinan origin because Muslims needed the sūrah to perform obligatory prayers.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.anchor: Most scholars claim that this is impossible, however, as the Muslims would not have been able to perform their required prayers without it

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.claim: Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.anchor: The primary meaning of al-Fātiḥah is “The Opening,” which indicates the sūrah’s function as “the opening of the Book”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.claim: The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.anchor: has been given the title Umm al-kitāb, “Mother of the Book,” a

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.claim: It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.anchor: It is also known as “The Mother of the Quran” (IK, Ṭ), a reference to its containing the meaning of the entire Quran

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.claim: Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87.

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.claim: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.anchor: is said to have healing powers for both body and soul

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
