STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.claim: The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.anchor: because it serves as a foundation

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.claim: As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.anchor: the Fātiḥah is recited at the beginning of each

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.claim: Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.anchor: In Shiite law one is allowed to recite the Fātiḥah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.claim: Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.anchor: It is also recited by Muslims on occasions as diverse as a funeral, a wedding, the birth of a child, the inauguration of an official event

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.claim: The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.anchor: the Prophet told a man that he would teach him the greatest sūrah; when asked what it was, the Prophet responded

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.speaker: God
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.claim: In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.anchor: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.claim: The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.anchor: the Fātiḥah is more than the confessional prayer of Muslims. It is a prayer that encapsulates all the metaphysical and eschatological realities

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.claim: Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.anchor: The Fātiḥah thus has a threefold structure: the first three verses deal with the nature of God, the middle verse deals with the relationship between God and human beings

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.claim: A report says nothing like the Fātiḥah was revealed in the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, or Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.anchor: In one the Prophet says, “By Him in Whose Hand lies my soul, in neither the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, nor the Quran was the like of it revealed”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.claim: One attribution says Satan was frightened when the Fātiḥah was revealed, among four events; others attribute the saying to the Prophet.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.anchor: attributed by some to Mujāhid (Q) and by

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.claim: The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.anchor: The exalted status of the Fātiḥah has resulted in numerous independent commentaries upon it, some numbering hundreds of pages

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.claim: A saying attributed to ʿAlī compresses the Quran into the Fātiḥah, the basmalah, its opening bāʾ, and the diacritical point beneath it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.anchor: a famous saying attributed to ʿAlī ibn AbīṬālib

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.claim: The point beneath bāʾ can symbolize the Divine Pen’s first drop of ink, which inscribed all archetypes on the Preserved Tablet before creation; thus basmalah marks both Quranic and cosmic beginnings.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.anchor:
This point can be understood to represent the first
drop of ink

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r1.claim: Al-ḥamd praises God for His qualities and thanks Him for worldly favors and next-world reward.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r1.anchor: Praise translates al-ḥamd, which indicates extolling the Praiseworthy

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r2.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r2.claim: The Prophet says that praising God, Lord of the worlds, constitutes thanks and brings increased bounty.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r2.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have said, “When you say, ‘Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds,’ you will have thanked God and He will increase your bounty”

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r3.claim: Thanks responds to what has already been received, while praise is more universal because it extols qualities prior to any gift.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r3.anchor: is given for what one has already received

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r4.claim: The definite form al-ḥamd indicates that all praise and gratitude belong to God.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r4.anchor: is rendered in the definite rather than the indefinite to indicate

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r5.claim: God praises Himself in the opening so humans can praise Him in divine speech, which He knows is more adequate than their own words.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r5.anchor: It is said that God has praised Himself in this opening address so that human beings can praise God in the speech of God

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r6.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r6.claim: The Prophet acknowledges that no one can enumerate praise due to God, who is as He praised Himself.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r6.anchor: the Prophet is reported to have addressed God

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r7.claim: Muslims use the basmalah to consecrate actions at their beginning and al-ḥamd to thank God upon completion; etiquette answers any inquiry about one’s condition with praise.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r7.anchor: whereas the basmalah is employed to consecrate a deed at its beginning, Praise be to God is employed to thank God for an act or event upon its completion

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r8.claim: Rabb denotes master, arranger, and possessor; of God it means peerless Master who orders affairs and owns creation.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r8.anchor: Lord renders rabb, which refers to a master

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r9.claim: Some relate rabb to cultivation: God is caretaker and trainer of things and of human souls, hearts, and spirits.

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r10.claim: Some take the worlds as four communities: humans, jinn, angels, and satans.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r10.anchor: Some say it refers to four communities: human beings, jinn, angels, and satans

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r11.claim: Others restrict the worlds to humans and jinn because only these communities need a warner, as in 25:1.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r11.anchor: others say it refers only to human beings and jinn, since the Prophet is referred to as a warner unto the worlds (25:1)

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r12.claim: Other interpretations include human generations, every species, or all levels from earth through the seven heavens.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r12.anchor: It may also refer to the different generations of human beings, to all of the species in creation

STUDYQURAN:1:2/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r13.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r13.claim: Some say the worlds are all existent things other than God; al-Rāzī adds that God can actualize infinitely many unknown universes, making Him Lord of all existence and space.
STUDYQURAN:1:2/r13.anchor: Thus some say that in the most universal sense the worlds refers to all existent things other than God

TAB-FULL:v1p136/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r1.claim: Al-ḥamd lillāh is gratitude and praise owed exclusively to God for countless blessings, including capacity for worship, provision, and guidance to lasting bliss.
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r1.anchor: دنياهم من الرزق وغذاهم به من نعيم العيش

TAB-FULL:v1p136/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains praise as gratitude, submission to God, and acknowledging His blessings, guidance, and originating gifts.
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r2.anchor: الحمد لله: هو الشكر، والاستخذاء لله، والإقرار بنعمته وهدايته وابتدائه

TAB-FULL:v1p136/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet says that saying “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude for which God gives an increase.
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r3.anchor: قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إذا قلت الحمد لله رب العالمين، فقد شكرت الله فزادك»

TAB-FULL:v1p136/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r4.speaker: كعب الأحبار
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r4.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār calls al-ḥamd praise of God; the narration does not specify whether he means praise for names and attributes or for blessings.
TAB-FULL:v1p136/r4.anchor: من قال الحمد لله فذلك ثناء على الله

TAB-FULL:v1p138/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r1.speaker: الأسود بن سريع
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r1.claim: A prophetic report says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, and that He praised Himself with “Praise belongs to God.”
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r1.anchor: ليس شيء أحب إليه الحمد من الله تعالى، ولذلك أثنى على نفسه فقال: الحمد لله

TAB-FULL:v1p138/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r2.claim: Arabic allows praise and thanks to overlap: the phrase “praise belongs to God, in thanks” works because each term can occupy the other’s place.
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r2.anchor: الحمد لله شكرا بالصحة. فقد تبين إذ كان ذلك عند جميعهم صحيحا

TAB-FULL:v1p138/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r3.claim: The definite article makes al-ḥamd signify all praise and complete gratitude belong to God; without it the wording would describe only this speaker’s praise.
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r3.anchor: أن دخولهما في الحمد منبئ على أن معناه: جميع المحامد والشكر الكامل لله

TAB-FULL:v1p138/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r4.claim: The inherited nominative reading al-ḥamdu preserves the intended universal claim; deliberately reading it accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment.
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r4.anchor: تتابعت قراءة القراء وعلماء الأمة على رفع الحمد

TAB-FULL:v1p138/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r5.claim: The whole passage is God’s speech: He first praises Himself, then teaches and obliges worshippers to say both the praise and “You alone we worship.”
TAB-FULL:v1p138/r5.anchor: فقال لهم: قولوا: الحمد لله رب العالمين وقولوا: إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين

TAB-FULL:v1p141/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r1.claim: Arabic regularly omits words recoverable from context, as in poetic answers and farewell formulas; a known meaning makes the unspoken expression unnecessary.
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r1.anchor: فكذلك ما حذف من قول الله تعالى ذكره: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2]

TAB-FULL:v1p141/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s report that Gabriel told Muhammad to say the praise confirms Ṭabarī’s implied command interpretation.
TAB-FULL:v1p141/r2.anchor: أن جبريل قال لمحمد: قل يا محمد: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2]

TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r1.claim: Rabb can mean an obeyed master; Labīd and al-Nābigha use it for the lords of Kindah and the speaker’s patron.
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r1.anchor: فالسيد المطاع فيها يدعى ربا، ومن ذلك قول لبيد بن ربيعة

TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r2.claim: Rabb can mean one who repairs or sets something right; al-Farazdaq’s unrepaired hide and ʿAlqama’s neglected affairs illustrate this sense.
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r2.anchor: والرجل المصلح للشيء يدعى ربا. ومنه قول الفرزدق بن غالب

TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r3.claim: Rabb can also mean owner; these lexical senses converge in God as incomparable sovereign, caretaker of creation, and possessor of command.
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r3.anchor: فربنا جل ثناؤه السيد الذي لا شبه له، ولا مثل في سؤدده، والمصلح أمر خلقه

TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Lord owns all creation—heavens, earths, their inhabitants, and what lies between—known and unknown, and resembles nothing.
TAB-FULL:v1p141#2/r4.anchor: يقول قل الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله، السموات كلهن

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r1.claim: ʿĀlamīn is a plural collective with no singular of the same form; ʿālam denotes a class of peoples, and each species or generation is its own world.
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r1.anchor: من كل صنف منها عالم ذلك القرن وذلك الزمان

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r2.claim: The poet al-ʿAjjāj calls his own generation “this world,” illustrating how a time’s people form a distinct ʿālam.

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r3.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes the worlds as all creation: the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and what is known or unknown.
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r3.anchor: عن الضحاك، عن ابن عباس: " {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r4.claim: Other reports from Ibn ʿAbbās define the worlds as jinn and humans; Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid report the same narrower gloss.
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r4.anchor: عن عكرمة، عن ابن عباس: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] : الجن والإنس

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r5.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r5.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says the worlds are jinn and humans, with a related report explaining each human and jinn community as a world of its own.
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r5.anchor: ابن آدم، والجن والإنس كل أمة منهم عالم على حدته

TAB-FULL:v1p145/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r6.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r6.claim: Mujāhid also interprets “Lord of the worlds” as referring to humans and jinn.
TAB-FULL:v1p145/r6.anchor: عن مجاهد: " {الحمد لله رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: الإنس والجن

TAB-FULL:v1p147/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r1.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r1.claim: Qatāda glosses the worlds as every distinct class or kind.
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r1.anchor: عن قتادة: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: كل صنف: عالم

TAB-FULL:v1p147/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r2.speaker: أبو العالية
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r2.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says humans and jinn are worlds, alongside either fourteen or eighteen thousand angelic worlds on earth, created to worship; he is uncertain which count.
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r2.anchor: الإنس عالم، والجن عالم، وما سوى ذلك ثمانية عشر ألف عالم، أو أربعة عشر ألف عالم

TAB-FULL:v1p147/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r3.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r3.claim: Ibn Jurayj gives the worlds as jinn and humans.
TAB-FULL:v1p147/r3.anchor: عن ابن جريج، في قوله: " {رب العالمين} [الفاتحة: 2] قال: الجن والإنس

TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.speaker: جماعة من أهل التأويل
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.claim: Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses.
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.anchor: أن ذلك من المؤخر الذي معناه التقديم، وإنما هو: الحمد لله الرحمن الرحيم رب العالمين

TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة عن رسول الله
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.claim: The Prophet reports God praises the servant’s recitation of praise, mercy, and sovereignty, then says the invocation from You alone we worship through the end belongs to the servant.
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.anchor: عن أبي هريرة، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " إذا قال العبد: {الحمد لله رب العالمين}

TAB-FULL:v1p203/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r3.claim: A parallel report from Abu Hurayra gives the same divine response to recitation but is explicitly transmitted without attribution to the Prophet.
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r3.anchor: عن أبي السائب، عن أبي هريرة، قال: " إذا قال العبد: الحمد لله، فذكر نحوه، ولم يرفعه

TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري عن رسول الله
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.claim: The Prophet says the prayer is divided between God and the servant: the opening praise, mercy, and judgment belong to God, and the remainder is the servant’s request.
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " قال الله عز وجل: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

TABATABAI:1:5#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r2.claim: Hamd praises voluntary excellence, while madh is broader and can praise non-voluntary qualities; the definite article here yields the same result whether generic or comprehensive.
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r2.anchor: الحمد على ما قيل هو الثناء على الجميل الاختياري والمدح أعم منه

TABATABAI:1:5#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r3.claim: Everything is God's creation, and He made every created thing good; creation and goodness therefore coincide in what He creates.
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r3.anchor: فلا خلق إلا وهو حسن جميل بإحسانه ولا حسن إلا وهو مخلوق له منسوب إليه

TABATABAI:1:5#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r4.claim: God creates and acts with knowledge and choice, not under compulsion; therefore every being is His voluntary beautiful act, and all genuine praise belongs to Him.
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r4.anchor: فما من شيء إلا وهو فعل جميل اختياري له

TABATABAI:1:5#2/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r5.claim: Since God is beautiful in names and acts and all praised beauty comes from Him, every true act of praise is rightfully His.
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r5.anchor: فقد بان أنه تعالى محمود على جميل أسمائه ومحمود على جميل أفعاله

TABATABAI:1:5#2/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r6.claim: The shift to direct address at the worship verse shows that the sura is speech placed on the servant's tongue, teaching how to praise and behave in servitude.
TABATABAI:1:5#2/r6.anchor: إن السورة من كلام العبد، وانه سبحانه في هذه السورة يلقن عبده حمد نفسه

TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r1.claim: God directly relates praise from selected prophets, Muhammad, and the purified inhabitants of Paradise; other creatures' praise is paired with glorification because they cannot encompass divine perfection.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r1.anchor: ولم يرد في كلامه تعالى ما يؤذن بحكاية الحمد عن غيره إلا ما حكاه عن عدة من أنبيائه المخلصين

TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r2.claim: Creatures cannot comprehend God's perfection; their praise would limit Him to their understanding, so they must first declare Him transcendent of what they delimit.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r2.anchor: فما وصفوه به فقد أحاطوا به وصار محدودا بحدودهم مقدرا بقدر نيلهم منه

TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r3.claim: God makes the praise and description of His sincerely purified servants His own.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#3/r3.anchor: فقد جعل حمدهم حمده ووصفهم وصفه حيث جعلهم مخلصين له

TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r1.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r1.claim: A report transmitted by both communities from the Prophet says no one can enumerate praise of God as fully as He praises Himself.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r1.anchor: لا أحصي ثناء عليك أنت كما أثنيت على نفسك

TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r2.claim: The opening الحمد لله is taught etiquette: a servant could not rightly utter this praise without God first teaching it and speaking on the servant's behalf.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r2.anchor: ما كان للعبد ان يقوله لو لا ان الله تعالى قاله نيابة وتعليما

TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r3.claim: Rabb means an owner who manages what is owned; human ownership is a conventional social relation, unlike real ownership grounded in dependence of existence.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r3.anchor: فالرب هو المالك الذي يدبر أمر مملوكه، ففيه معنى الملك

TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r4.claim: God alone has real ownership, which necessarily entails governance because whatever depends on Him for existence also depends on Him in its effects.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r4.anchor: فهو تعالى رب لما سواه لأن الرب هو المالك المدبر وهو تعالى كذلك

TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r5.claim: Alamin can mean all beings, kinds, or communities; because judgment concerns humans and jinn, the context most suitably means their communities.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#4/r5.anchor: فيكون المراد بالعالمين عوالم الإنس والجن وجماعاتهم

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r7.speaker: الصادق
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r7.claim: When al-Sadiq's father recovered a lost mule, he praised God only by saying الحمد لله and explained that every kind of praise is contained in that phrase.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r7.anchor: فما من حمد إلا وهو داخل فيها

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r8.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r8.speaker: علي
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r8.claim: Ali explains that God teaches servants general gratitude because His blessings cannot all be counted or known in detail; the author connects this to praise taught on the servant's behalf.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r8.anchor: لا يقدرون على معرفة جميعها بالتفصيل لأنها أكثر من أن تحصى أو تعرف

TABATABAI:1:5#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5#3/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5#3/r1.claim: Every effect and its perfections depend on their cause; since all causes end in God, all genuine beauty, praise, and thanks ultimately belong to Him.
TABATABAI:1:5#3/r1.anchor: فحقيقة كل ثناء وحمد تعود وتنتهى إليه تعالى، فالحمد لله رب العالمين

TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.claim: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests.
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.anchor: قسمت فاتحة الكتاب بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي، ولعبدي ما سأل

TABRISI:1:2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r1.claim: Readers agree on ḍamma in al-ḥamdu and kasra in lillāh; three noncanonical vowel combinations are also transmitted.
TABRISI:1:2/r1.anchor: أجمع القراء على ضم الدال من الحمد وكسر اللام من لله

TABRISI:1:2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r2.speaker: زيد بن علي
TABRISI:1:2/r2.claim: Zayd ibn Ali's fatḥa on the bā of rabb is understood as demonstrating that the form is possible, not as a recitation.
TABRISI:1:2/r2.anchor: وروي عن زيد بن علي فتح الباء ويحمل على أنه بين جوازه لا إنه قراءة

TABRISI:1:2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r3.claim: Praise, commendation, and gratitude are related: praise contrasts with blame and commendation with satire, while gratitude contrasts with ingratitude.
TABRISI:1:2/r3.anchor: الحمد والمدح والشكر متقاربة المعنى والفرق بين الحمد والشكر أن الحمد نقيض الذم كما أن المدح نقيض الهجاء

TABRISI:1:2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r4.claim: Praise need not respond to a favor, whereas gratitude is specifically for a favor; praise can nevertheless substitute for gratitude, as its use with shukran shows.
TABRISI:1:2/r4.anchor: إلا أن الحمد يوضع موضع الشكر ويقال: الحمد لله شكرا

TABRISI:1:2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r5.claim: Gratitude is acknowledging a blessing with reverence, rooted in the heart and also expressed by the tongue to deny a charge of ingratitude.
TABRISI:1:2/r5.anchor: فالشكر هو الاعتراف بالنعمة مع ضرب التعظيم ويكون بالقلب وهو الأصل ويكون أيضا باللسان

TABRISI:1:2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r6.claim: Madh is speech intentionally reporting the greatness of the person praised.
TABRISI:1:2/r6.anchor: وأما المدح فهو القول المنبئ عن عظم حال الممدوح مع القصد إليه

TABRISI:1:2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r7.claim: Rabb can mean an obeyed master, as Labid's verse calls the chief of Kinda its rabb.
TABRISI:1:2/r7.anchor:
السيد المطاع كقول لبيد:
وأهلكن قدما رب كندة وابنه

TABRISI:1:2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r8.speaker: النبي
TABRISI:1:2/r8.claim: The Prophet uses rabb to mean owner, asking a man whether he owns sheep or camels.
TABRISI:1:2/r8.anchor:
المالك نحو قول النبي لرجل:
" أرب غنم أم رب أبل

TABRISI:1:2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r9.speaker: أبو ذؤيب
TABRISI:1:2/r9.claim: Abu Dhu'ayb uses rabb in the sense of companion or owner of the dogs.
TABRISI:1:2/r9.anchor:
الصاحب نحو قول أبي ذؤيب:
قد ناله رب الكلاب

TABRISI:1:2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r10.claim: Rabb also means caretaker, cultivator, or reformer; it can be restricted in other compounds, though used absolutely it is reserved for God.
TABRISI:1:2/r10.anchor: ومنها المربب ومنها المصلح واشتقاقه من التربية يقال ربيته وربيته بمعنى

TABRISI:1:2/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r11.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r11.claim: Al-ʿālamīn has no singular of the same form and may derive from the mark by which creation points to its Maker, or from knowledge as what is known.
TABRISI:1:2/r11.anchor: العالمون جمع عالم والعالم جمع لا واحد له من لفظه كالنفر والجيش وغيرهما واشتقاقه من العلامة

TABRISI:1:2/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2/r12.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2/r12.claim: In ordinary usage the worlds can mean all created things, supported by Pharaoh's question about the Lord of the worlds and God's answer.
TABRISI:1:2/r12.anchor: وفي المتعارف بين الناس هو عبارة عن جميع المخلوقات وتدل عليه الآية

TABRISI:1:2#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة
TABRISI:1:2#2/r1.claim: Most commentators take each species and each generation of a species as a world, so al-ʿālamīn is plural across kinds and times.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r1.anchor: وقيل إنه اسم لكل صنف من الأصناف وأهل كل قرن من كل صنف يسمى عالما ولذلك جمع فقيل عالمون لعالم كل زمان وهذا قول أكثر المفسرين كابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير وقتادة

TABRISI:1:2#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#2/r2.claim: One view limits the worlds to rational beings: angels, jinn, and humans.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r2.anchor: وقيل العالم نوع ما يعقل وهم الملائكة والجن والإنس

TABRISI:1:2#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#2/r3.claim: Another view limits the worlds to jinn and humans, based on the warning to the worlds.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r3.anchor:
وقيل الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى:
ليكون للعالمين نذيرا

TABRISI:1:2#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#2/r4.claim: A further view limits the worlds to humans, based on the rebuke about approaching males among the worlds.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r4.anchor:
وقيل هم الإنس لقوله تعالى:
أتأتون الذكران من العالمين

TABRISI:1:2#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r5.speaker: الأخفش وأبو علي الفارسي
TABRISI:1:2#2/r5.claim: They parse al-ḥamdu as a nominative subject with an omitted predication such as is due or is established for God; the phrase lillah supplies its meaning.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r5.anchor: الحمد رفع بالابتداء والابتداء عالم معنوي غير ملفوظ به وهو خلو الاسم من العوامل اللفظية

TABRISI:1:2#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#2/r6.claim: The nominative reading is stronger and more laudatory than an accusative meaning I praise, because it makes praise due to God from all creation, not only the speaker.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r6.anchor: إلا أن الرفع بالحمد أقوى وأمدح لأن معناه الحمد وجب لله أو استقر لله وهذا يقتضي العموم لجميع الخلق

TABRISI:1:2#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#2/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#2/r7.claim: The transmitted broken and rounded vowel combinations arise by assimilation between the two words; many grammarians reject the assimilation because case vowels are not fixed.
TABRISI:1:2#2/r7.anchor: ومن كسر الدال واللام أتبع حركة الدال حركة اللام ومن ضمهما أتبع حركة اللام حركة الدال

TABRISI:1:2#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#3/r1.speaker: ابن جني
TABRISI:1:2#3/r1.claim: Ibn Jinni says kasra on ḥamd and ḍamma on lillah signal a close subject-predicate bond, making the two parts sound like one word.
TABRISI:1:2#3/r1.anchor: وقال أبو الفتح بن جني: في كسر الدال وضم اللام هنا دلالة على شدة ارتباط المبتدأ بالخبر

TABRISI:1:2#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#3/r2.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:1:2#3/r2.claim: The lām normally has fatḥa because it cannot begin with sukun; lām of possession and emphasis are distinguished, and attached pronouns restore its original opening vowel.
TABRISI:1:2#3/r2.anchor: وهذا كله قول سيبويه وجميع النحويين المحققين وليس من الحروف المبتدأ بها مما هو على حرف واحد حرف مكسور إلا الباء وحدها

TABRISI:1:2#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#3/r3.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:1:2#3/r3.claim: The kasra of lām in the jussive verb li-yafʿal distinguishes it from emphatic lām.
TABRISI:1:2#3/r3.anchor: وأما لام الجزم في ليفعل فإنما كسرت ليفرق بينها وبين لام التوكيد

TABRISI:1:2#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#3/r4.speaker: الأخفش
TABRISI:1:2#3/r4.claim: Al-Akhfash says rabb al-ʿālamīn is genitive as an adjective, with the adjectival relation itself governing the adjective, as shown by adjectives whose case differs from their head.
TABRISI:1:2#3/r4.anchor: { رب العالمين } مجرور على الصفة والعامل في الصفة عند أبي الحسن الأخفش كونه صفة

TABRISI:1:2#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#4/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#4/r1.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn may be accusative as praise or as an implied command to remember the Lord; a nominative praise reading is also possible, as poetry shows.
TABRISI:1:2#4/r1.anchor: ومن نصب رب العالمين فإنما ينصبه على المدح والثناء كأنه لما قال الحمد لله استدل بهذا اللفظ على أنه ذاكر لله

TABRISI:1:2#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#4/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#4/r2.claim: In al-ʿālamīn, yā is both the plural and case marker, while nūn replaces the singular's case vowel and is opened to distinguish it from the dual.
TABRISI:1:2#4/r2.anchor: والياء فيه علامة وحرف الإعراب وعلامة الجمع والنون هنا عوض عن الحركة في الواحد وإنما فتحت فرقا بينها وبين نون التثنية

TABRISI:1:2#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#4/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#4/r3.claim: Another account says the plural nūn is opened because kasra after waw or yā is heavy, like in sawfa and ayna.
TABRISI:1:2#4/r3.anchor: وقيل إنما فتحت نون الجمع وحقها الكسر لثقل الكسرة بعد الواو كما فتحت الفاء من سوف والنون من أين

TABRISI:1:2#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#4/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:2#4/r4.claim: All beautiful praise belongs to God, who deserves worship as the source of original blessings and the creator, nurturer, and reformer of creation; the verse teaches gratitude and praise.
TABRISI:1:2#4/r4.anchor: الأوصاف الجميلة والثناء الحسن كلها لله الذي تحق له العبادة لكونه قادرا على أصول النعم وفاعلا لها

TABRISI:1:2#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:2#4/r5.speaker: غيره من النحويين
TABRISI:1:2#4/r5.claim: Other grammarians hold that the same syntactic governor that governs the described noun also governs its adjective.
TABRISI:1:2#4/r5.anchor: وقال غيره من النحويين العامل في الموصوف هو العامل في الصفة

THALABI:v1p103/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p103/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p103/r4.claim: In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.
THALABI:v1p103/r4.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «يقول الله: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبادي نصفين

THALABI:v1p107/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p107/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p107/r3.claim: God praises Himself as a favor to creation; the declarative wording functions as a command meaning “say: praise belongs to God.”
THALABI:v1p107/r3.anchor: على نفسه، نعيما منه على خلقه. ولفظه خبر ومعناه أمر، تقريره: قولوا: الحمد لله

THALABI:v1p107/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p107/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p107/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-ḥamd as gratitude.
THALABI:v1p107/r4.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني: الشكر منه

THALABI:v1p107/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p107/r5.speaker: ابن الأنباري
THALABI:v1p107/r5.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says al-ḥamd is an inversion of al-madḥ, like the word-order reversals jabal/jalab and baḍḍ/ḍabb.
THALABI:v1p107/r5.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: هو مقلوب عن المدح

THALABI:v1p108/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r1.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p108/r1.claim: One distinction says praise concerns someone for what they are, while thanks concern what they do; praise can stand for thanks, but thanks cannot praise knowledge or forbearance.
THALABI:v1p108/r1.anchor: فالحمد: الثناء عليه بما هو به، والشكر: الثناء عليه بما هو منه

THALABI:v1p108/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p108/r2.claim: Because praise is broader than thanks, the verse praises God for His lofty attributes and beautiful names and for all His acts and kindness to creation.
THALABI:v1p108/r2.anchor: فمعنى الآية: الحمد لله على صفاته العليا وأسمائه الحسنى، وعلى جميع صنعه وإحسانه إلى خلقه

THALABI:v1p108/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r3.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p108/r3.claim: Another view makes praise verbal and thanks embodied in action, illustrated by commands to say praise and to work in gratitude.

THALABI:v1p108/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r4.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p108/r4.claim: Another distinction says praise is for blessings granted, while thanks is for what God has withheld.
THALABI:v1p108/r4.anchor: وقيل: الحمد لله على ما حبا وهو النعماء، والشكر على ما زوى وهو اللأواء

THALABI:v1p108/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r5.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p108/r5.claim: A further view assigns praise to outward blessings and thanks to hidden blessings.
THALABI:v1p108/r5.anchor: وقيل: الحمد لله على النعماء الظاهرة، والشكر على النعماء الباطنة

THALABI:v1p108/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p108/r6.claim: The Prophet calls praise the head of gratitude and says no servant thanks God without praising Him.
THALABI:v1p108/r6.anchor: حدثنا عبد الرزاق عن معمر عن قتادة عن عبد الله بن عمرو [بن العاص] قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «الحمد رأس الشكر

THALABI:v1p108/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p108/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p108/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says al-ḥamd is the word of gratitude spoken by the people of Paradise.
THALABI:v1p108/r7.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه سئل عن الحمد لله قال: كلمة شكر أهل الجنة

THALABI:v1p109/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r1.speaker: قراء العامة
THALABI:v1p109/r1.claim: The majority read al-ḥamdu with ḍamma on the dāl as a nominal subject whose predicate follows; another analysis fronts the predicate, meaning “to God belongs praise,” and another treats it as quotation.
THALABI:v1p109/r1.anchor: فقرأت العامة بضم الدال على الابتداء، وخبره فيما بعده

THALABI:v1p109/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r2.speaker: هارون بن موسى الأعور ورؤبة بن العجاج
THALABI:v1p109/r2.claim: Hārūn al-Aʿwar and Ruʾba read the dāl in the accusative, supplying “I praise praise,” since al-ḥamd is a verbal noun that is not dualized or pluralized.
THALABI:v1p109/r2.anchor: وقرأ هارون بن موسى الأعور ورؤبة بن العجاج بنصب الدال على الإضمار

THALABI:v1p109/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r3.speaker: الحسن البصري
THALABI:v1p109/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī reads the dāl with kasra by vowel assimilation.
THALABI:v1p109/r3.anchor: وقرأ الحسن البصري بكسر الدال، أتبع الكسرة

THALABI:v1p109/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r4.speaker: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة الشامي
THALABI:v1p109/r4.claim: Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla reads both dāl and lām with ḍamma, assimilating one ḍamma to the next.
THALABI:v1p109/r4.anchor: وقرأ إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة الشامي بضم الدال واللام

THALABI:v1p109/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r5.speaker: زيد بن علي
THALABI:v1p109/r5.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī reads rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise; Abū Saʿīd ibn Aws explains the reading as an implied “I praise the Lord of the worlds.”
THALABI:v1p109/r5.anchor: رب العالمين قرأ زيد بن علي: رب العالمين بالنصب على المدح

THALABI:v1p109/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r6.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p109/r6.claim: The usual genitive reading means creator, originator, owner, and manager of all creation.
THALABI:v1p109/r6.anchor: وقرأ الباقون رب العالمين بكسر الباء، أي خالق الخلق أجمعين ومبدئهم

THALABI:v1p109/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r7.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p109/r7.claim: Rabb can mean master or lord, as in Joseph’s use of rabb for one’s master; poetry calls leaders of tribes rabb.
THALABI:v1p109/r7.anchor: والرب بمعنى السيد، قال الله تعالى: اذكرني عند ربك أي سيدك

THALABI:v1p109/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p109/r8.claim: A Prophetic question uses rabb for an owner: “Are you owner of camels or owner of sheep?”; poetry likewise calls someone the owner of a bridge or herds.
THALABI:v1p109/r8.anchor: ويكون بمعنى المالك، قال النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: «أرب إبل أنت أم رب غنم؟»

THALABI:v1p109/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p109/r9.claim: Rabb can also mean companion, pasture or nourisher, and one who repairs something, each supported by Arabic poetry.
THALABI:v1p109/r9.anchor: ويكون بمعنى الصاحب، قال أبو ذؤيب

THALABI:v1p109/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r10.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
THALABI:v1p109/r10.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says rabb can mean staying in a place without moving, as in the usage rabb bi-l-makān.
THALABI:v1p109/r10.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل: الرب: اللبث من غير إثبات أحد

THALABI:v1p109/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p109/r11.speaker: أبو سعيد ابن أوس الأنصاري
THALABI:v1p109/r11.claim: Abū Saʿīd ibn Aws al-Anṣārī explains Zayd ibn ʿAlī’s accusative reading as an implied “I praise the Lord of the worlds.”
THALABI:v1p109/r11.anchor: وقال أبو سعيد ابن أوس الأنصاري: على معنى أحمد رب العالمين

THALABI:v1p110/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p110/r1.claim: The author prefers the sense of abiding because theologians agree God has always been Lord.
THALABI:v1p110/r1.anchor: وهو الاختيار لأن المتكلمين أجمعوا على أن الله لم يزل ربا

THALABI:v1p110/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r2.speaker: أبو بكر محمد بن موسى الواسطي
THALABI:v1p110/r2.claim: Al-Wāsiṭī defines the Lord as creator at the beginning, nourisher through sustenance, and forgiver at the end.
THALABI:v1p110/r2.anchor: فقال: هو الخالق ابتداء، والمربي غذاء، والغافر انتهاء

THALABI:v1p110/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p110/r3.claim: A creature cannot be called al-rabb with the definite article; only an annexed “lord of X” is allowed, since only God owns all and the article is universal.
THALABI:v1p110/r3.anchor: ولا يقال للمخلوق: هو الرب، معرفا بالألف واللام

THALABI:v1p110/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p110/r4.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is a plural of ʿālam without a singular of the same form, like anām, rahṭ, and jaysh.
THALABI:v1p110/r4.anchor: وأما العالمون فهم جمع عالم، ولا واحد له من لفظه

THALABI:v1p110/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r5.speaker: أبي بن كعب
THALABI:v1p110/r5.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s report says the worlds are angels, enumerating four groups of 4,500 and vast angelic hosts, including spirit beings whose praise reaches the Throne-bearers.
THALABI:v1p110/r5.anchor: عن أبي بن كعب قال: العالمون هم الملائكة، وهم ثمانية عشر ألف ملكا

THALABI:v1p110/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r6.speaker: أبو معاذ النحوي
THALABI:v1p110/r6.claim: Abū Muʿādh al-Naḥwī says the worlds are the children of Adam.
THALABI:v1p110/r6.anchor: وقال أبو معاذ [النحوي] : هم بنو آدم

THALABI:v1p110/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r7.speaker: أبو هيثم خالد بن يزيد، ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p110/r7.claim: Abū Haytham says the worlds are jinn and humans, citing “a warner to the worlds”; this interpretation is also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās by ʿAṭiyya and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.
THALABI:v1p110/r7.anchor: وقال أبو هيثم خالد بن يزيد: هم الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى: ليكون للعالمين نذيرا

THALABI:v1p110/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r8.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
THALABI:v1p110/r8.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the worlds are people, citing the address “Do you approach males among the worlds?”
THALABI:v1p110/r8.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل: العالمون: الناس، واحتج بقوله تعالى: أتأتون الذكران من العالمين

THALABI:v1p110/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p110/r9.speaker: العجاج
THALABI:v1p110/r9.claim: The poet al-ʿAjjāj gives a different interpretation of the worlds; the source does not spell it out here.

THALABI:v1p111/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r1.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
THALABI:v1p111/r1.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda say the worlds are four kinds of rational beings—angels, jinn, humans, and devils—excluding animals, and derive the term from knowledge.
THALABI:v1p111/r1.anchor: وقال الفراء وأبو عبيدة: هو عبارة عمن يعقل، وهم أربع أمم

THALABI:v1p111/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r2.speaker: عبد العزيز بن يحيى الكناني
THALABI:v1p111/r2.claim: ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Kinānī says the worlds are the purified among creation.
THALABI:v1p111/r2.anchor: وقال عبد العزيز بن يحيى الكناني: هم أهل التنزيه من الخلق

THALABI:v1p111/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r3.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد بن أسلم
THALABI:v1p111/r3.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says the worlds are those who receive sustenance.
THALABI:v1p111/r3.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن بن زيد ابن أسلم: هم المرتزقون

THALABI:v1p111/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r4.speaker: الخضر بن إسماعيل
THALABI:v1p111/r4.claim: Al-Khiḍr ibn Ismāʿīl treats al-ʿālamīn as a collective noun for a large multitude.
THALABI:v1p111/r4.anchor: وقال الخضر بن إسماعيل: هو اسم الجمع الكثير

THALABI:v1p111/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء، ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p111/r5.claim: Abū ʿAmr says the worlds are spiritual beings; the source links this with Ibn ʿAbbās’s gloss “every living thing that walks on earth.”
THALABI:v1p111/r5.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو بن العلاء: هم الروحانيون

THALABI:v1p111/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r6.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
THALABI:v1p111/r6.claim: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna says al-ʿālamīn is a collective plural for different kinds of things.
THALABI:v1p111/r6.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة: هو جمع للأشياء المختلفة

THALABI:v1p111/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r7.speaker: جعفر بن محمد الصادق
THALABI:v1p111/r7.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the worlds are the people of Paradise and the people of Hell.
THALABI:v1p111/r7.anchor: وقال جعفر بن محمد الصادق: «العالمون: أهل الجنة وأهل النار»

THALABI:v1p111/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r8.speaker: الحسن وقتادة ومجاهد
THALABI:v1p111/r8.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, and Mujāhid say the worlds comprise all created beings, citing Pharaoh’s question and God’s answer that He is Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them.
THALABI:v1p111/r8.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة ومجاهد: هو عبارة عن جميع المخلوقات

THALABI:v1p111/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r9.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p111/r9.claim: On the all-creatures interpretation, ʿālamīn derives from knowledge or sign, because creatures are visible and display the mark of their maker.
THALABI:v1p111/r9.anchor: واشتقاقه على هذا القول من (العلم) و (العلامة) لظهورهم ولظهور أثر الصنعة فيهم

THALABI:v1p111/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r10.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
THALABI:v1p111/r10.claim: Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib counts one thousand worlds, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
THALABI:v1p111/r10.anchor: فقال سعيد بن المسيب: لله ألف عالم منها ستمائة في البحر وأربعمائة في البر

THALABI:v1p111/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r11.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v1p111/r11.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk counts 420 worlds: 360 barefoot and unclothed, unaware of their Creator, and sixty that wear clothes.
THALABI:v1p111/r11.anchor: وقال الضحاك: فمنهم ثلاثمائة وستون عالما حفاة عراة

THALABI:v1p111/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r12.speaker: وهب
THALABI:v1p111/r12.claim: Wahb counts 18,000 worlds and likens the inhabited portion of this world amid wasteland to a tent in a desert.
THALABI:v1p111/r12.anchor: وقال وهب: لله تعالى ثمانية عشر ألف عالم

THALABI:v1p111/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r13.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
THALABI:v1p111/r13.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī counts 40,000 worlds, with the known world from east to west being only one.
THALABI:v1p111/r13.anchor: وقال أبو سعيد الخدري: إن لله أربعين ألف عالم

THALABI:v1p111/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r14.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
THALABI:v1p111/r14.claim: Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān counts 80,000 worlds, divided equally between land and sea.
THALABI:v1p111/r14.anchor: وقال أبو القاسم مقاتل بن حيان: العالمون ثمانون ألف عالم

THALABI:v1p111/r15.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r15.speaker: مقاتل بن سليمان
THALABI:v1p111/r15.claim: Muqātil ibn Sulaymān says fully explaining the worlds would require a thousand volumes of a thousand pages each.
THALABI:v1p111/r15.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن سليمان: لو فسرت العالمين، لاحتجت إلى ألف جلد

THALABI:v1p111/r16.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p111/r16.speaker: كعب الأحبار
THALABI:v1p111/r16.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says only God can count the worlds, citing the verse that none knows His hosts but He.
THALABI:v1p111/r16.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار: لا يحصي عدد العالمين إلا الله

ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r1.claim: “Worlds” covers every category of physical and spiritual existence.
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r1.anchor: the term "worlds" denotes all categories of existence both in the physical and the spiritual sense

ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r2.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r2.claim: Rabb combines rightful possession and authority with rearing, sustaining, and fostering something from its beginning to completion.
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r2.anchor: It comprises the ideas of having a just claim to the possession of anything

ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r3.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r3.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r3.claim: With the definite article, rabb is used in the Qur'an exclusively for God, sole sustainer of all creation and ultimate authority.
ASAD-NOTES:1:2#n2/r3.anchor: the designation rabb is applied, in the Qur'an, exclusively to God as the sole fosterer

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r1.claim: The opening fragment questions what thanks mean for a giver acting to obtain pleasure and answer compassion; its antecedent lies outside this segment.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r1.anchor: فأي معنى لشكر (¬3) من يعطي لاجتلاب لذته، ويجيب (¬4) داعي رأفته.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r2.speaker: أبو بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r2.claim: Abū Bakr suggests that God praises Himself at the start of Scripture to teach people praise and thanks, earning them greater reward through their recitation as a kindness to them.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r2.anchor: قال أبو بكر: ويحتمل أن يكون هذا ثناء أثنى به على نفسه، علم عباده في أول كتابه

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r3.speaker: أبو بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r3.claim: On this reading, an imperative is implicit: people are told to say al-ḥamdu lillāh, just as 39:3 implicitly means that the polytheists say they worship idols to bring them near God.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r3.anchor: فقال: {الحمد لله رب العالمين} أي قولوا: يا معشر الناس ما إذا قلتموه علت منزلتكم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r4.claim: Anyone who praises God thereby exposes himself to God's favor and reward.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r4.anchor: ثم إذا قال القائل: {الحمد لله} فقد (¬9) أثنى على الله تعالى، فيكون

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r5.speaker: بعض العلماء
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r5.claim: Asked how the best-formula hadith counts as supplication, a scholar answers that praise itself suffices: a servant need not state requests after praising God, just as a creature may be won by praise.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r5.anchor: أن بعض العلماء، سئل عن تفسير الحديث المروي: "أفضل الدعاء سبحان الله، والحمد لله،

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r6.speaker: أبو بكر
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r6.claim: Ḥamd is broader than shukr: thanks follow a prior favor and do not praise someone's inherent good qualities, whereas praise can precede a gift and commend qualities.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r6.anchor: وإنما اختير (الحمد) على الشكر للمبالغة والعموم، وذلك أن الشكر لا يكون

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r7.claim: A poet's indirect reference to praise as glorification and exaltation supports the breadth of ḥamd.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p466/r7.anchor: فترجم بالثناء (¬1) والتمجيد (¬2) عن الحمد، فدل هذا على عموم الحمد.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r1.claim: Rabb can derive from nurturing: al-Aṣmaʿī defines rabb al-ṣanīʿa as completing and improving a craft, and rabb al-skin as filling it with butter.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r1.anchor: قال الأصمعي: (رب فلان الصنيعة يربها ربا إذا أتمها وأصلحها)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r2.claim: Poetry about fat ripening in a skin and good deeds increasing supports the sense of completing and improving.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r2.anchor: فإن كنت مني أو تريدين صحبتي (¬5) ... فكوني له كالسمن (¬6) ربت له الأدم (¬7)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r3.claim: With the nurturing sense, God raises creatures and nourishes them through His blessings.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r3.anchor: فالمعنى (¬4) على هذا أنه يربي الخلق ويغذوهم (¬5) بما ينعم عليهم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r4.claim: Rabb can also mean owner: a person who owns a thing, or stands above someone as a master.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r4.anchor: الثاني: أن يكون الرب بمعنى المالك، يقال: رب الشيء إذا ملكه، ورببت (¬7) فلانا،

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r5.speaker: صفوان بن أمية
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r5.claim: Ṣafwān ibn Umayya uses rabb for a superior or master, preferring a Qurashī master to a Hawāzin one.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r5.anchor: ومنه قول صفوان بن أمية (¬9): لأن يربني رجل من قريش أحب إلي من أن يربني رجل من هوازن

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r6.claim: Anyone who owns something is its rabb; Arabic usage calls a person owner of a house or estate and includes the Prophet's question about owning camels or sheep.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r6.anchor: يقال: هو رب الدار ورب الضيعة (¬2)، وقال النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - لرجل

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r7.claim: The word rabb may mean master without literal ownership, as in 12:42 and al-Aʿshā's reference to the lord of Kindah; God is owner and master in truth.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r7.anchor: ثم (السيد) يسمى ربا وإن لم يكن مالكا على الحقيقة (¬6)، قال الله تعالى: {اذكرني عند ربك}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r8.speaker: some linguists
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r8.claim: Some linguists derive the owner sense from nurturing: an owner raises and brings up what he owns, while a master is an owner.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r8.anchor: وقال بعض أهل اللغة: المعنى الثاني راجع إلى الأول الذي هو بمعنى التربية

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r9.speaker: theologians
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r9.claim: Some theologians say rabb has eternally described God as an essential attribute and derive it as abiding, from rabb bi-al-makān, to remain in a place.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r9.anchor: فأما ما يذهب إليه المتكلمون أنه لم يزل ربا (¬2)، وأن هذا من صفة الذات

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r10.claim: The author rejects the theologians' proposed root as unattested to linguists: rabb does not mean remain, though arrabba can mean remain and could support their derivation.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p485/r10.anchor: وليس يصح رب (¬4) بمعنى: أقام (¬5)، وأرب بمعنى: أقام صحيح

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r1.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam on the faʿil pattern, and its derivation has two reported explanations.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r1.anchor: هو جمع (عالم) على وزن (فاعل) (¬1)، كما قالوا: خاتم (¬2)، وطابع، ودانق

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r2.claim: One derivation connects ʿālam with knowledge or signs: every creature is a sign pointing to its maker, and ordinary speech uses al-ʿālam to mean all created things.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r2.anchor: فمنهم من قال: اشتقاقه من (العلم) و (العلامة)، وذلك أن كل مخلوق دلالة وعلامة

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r3.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد وقتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r3.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda understand the worlds as all creatures, supported by Pharaoh's question and Moses' reply in 26:23–24.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r3.anchor: وهذا قول الحسن (¬6) ومجاهد وقتادة (¬7) في تفسير العالم: إنه جميع المخلوقات

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r4.claim: In Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's transmission, Ibn ʿAbbās says that when ʿālamīn derives from knowledge it means rational beings, namely jinn and humans.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r4.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية سعيد بن جبير: هم الجن والإنس

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r5.speaker: أبو الهيثم والأزهري
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r5.claim: Abū al-Haytham and al-Azharī choose the jinn-and-human interpretation, since 25:1 calls the Qur'an a warning to the worlds and Muḥammad warned those two groups.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r5.anchor: واختاره أبو الهيثم (¬2) والأزهري (¬3)، واحتجوا بقوله: {ليكون للعالمين نذيرا}

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r6.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل وأبو معاذ
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r6.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl and Abū Muʿādh say the worlds here are the children of Adam, citing 26:165.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r6.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل وأبو معاذ (¬5) النحوي: هم بنو آدم

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r7.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r7.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda define ʿālamīn as rational beings in four communities: angels, humans, jinn, and devils; beasts are not called a world.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r7.anchor: وقال الفراء (¬7) وأبو عبيدة: هو عبارة عما يعقل، وهو أربع أمم:

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r8.claim: The word can denote the people of a single era: God's favoring the Children of Israel above the worlds in 2:47 means their contemporaries.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r8.anchor: وقد ذكر الله تعالى {العالمين} وأراد به أهل عصر واحد،

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r9.claim: All rational-creature readings are compatible with the knowledge derivation; those who hold them say Moses answered Pharaoh with a clearer description to confound him, not with a lexical definition.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r9.anchor: إنه لم يشتغل بتفسير العالمين، وإنما أراد تعريفه على وجه أظهر من الأول

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r10.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r10.claim: Abū Isḥāq chooses the all-creatures derivation and equates Lord of the worlds with Lord of everything in 6:164.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p489/r10.anchor: وأبو إسحاق (¬5) اختار الطريقة الأولى، وقال: معنى العالمين: كل ما خلق الله.

WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r1.claim: Praise is acclaim for God and thanks to Him for His beneficence.
WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد لله هو الثناء لله والشكر له بإنعامه

WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:1:2/r2.claim: Lord of the worlds means owner of all created things.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r5.claim: Praise is laudation of God and thanks to Him for His beneficence.
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r5.anchor: هو الثناء لله، والشكر له بإنعامه.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:1-4/r6.claim: Lord of the worlds means the owner of all creatures.

ELMALILI:1:2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r1.claim: He renders the verse as praise belonging to the Lord of the worlds.

ELMALILI:1:2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r2.claim: The Quran has an exhaustive, subtle order among surahs, stories, verses, words, and letters; analyzing it involves innumerable sciences, beginning with grammar and rhetoric.
ELMALILI:1:2/r2.anchor: Kur’an’da sûreler, ekser sûrelerde kıssalar, kıssalarda âyetler, âyetlerde kelimât, kelimâtta hurûf

ELMALILI:1:2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r3.claim: Quranic rhetoric includes composition, context, implication, modes of expression, logic, wisdom, and the verbal and semantic beauties that secure fluency, force, balance, and inimitability.
ELMALILI:1:2/r3.anchor: Nazm-ı Kur’an’da terkîb, sibâk, siyâk, mantûk, mefhûm ve fehvâ, mutâbakat, tazammun ve iltizam ile ibâre, işâret, delâlet

ELMALILI:1:2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r4.claim: These relations combine linguistic convention, rational logic, and natural taste; translation loses much of the first and third and consequently affects logical signification too.
ELMALILI:1:2/r4.anchor: delâlet-i vaz‘iye ve lisâniye, delâlet-i akliye ve mantıkiye ve delâlet-i tabî‘iye ve zevkiye nâmıyla üç nevi delâletin muhassalası

ELMALILI:1:2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r5.claim: Because human power cannot detail every relation, he will sketch them in places and pause especially over al-Fatiha.
ELMALILI:1:2/r5.anchor: Bunun için biz bazı mevâki‘de bu münasebâtı icmâlen göstermeye çalışacağız. Çünkü tafsîline kudret-i beşer kâfi değildir

ELMALILI:1:2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r6.claim: Contextual relation may be backward or forward; if the basmala is part of al-Fatiha, backward context is irrelevant, while its relation to 96:1 belongs to revelation order and forward context.
ELMALILI:1:2/r6.anchor: Besmele Fâtiha’nın bir cüz’ü addolunduğuna göre birincisi mevzu‘-i bahis olamaz

ELMALILI:1:2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r7.claim: Nothing lies outside the basmala's attraction, so it relates generally to al-Fatiha as one recites, writes, praises, or begins the Quran in its name.
ELMALILI:1:2/r7.anchor: Besmele ile Fâtiha okuyorum, Fâtiha yazıyorum, hamd ediyorum, Kur’ân’a başlıyorum ilh… gibi

ELMALILI:1:2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r8.claim: Specifically, basmala and al-Fatiha are closely linked by cadence, wording, summary and explanation; al-Fatiha's gratitude answers the basmala's attraction of mercy.
ELMALILI:1:2/r8.anchor: besmeledeki câzibe-i rahmete Fâtiha’nın bir cevâb-ı şükrân olduğu ilk nazarda görülüyor

ELMALILI:1:2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r9.claim: Their structures correspond: the basmala has seven actual or implicit words, four independent words and three divine-name words; al-Fatiha has seven verses, four statements, and three complete pauses, with the middle tawhid verse linking two three-verse units.
ELMALILI:1:2/r9.anchor: Fâtiha yedi âyet, dört kelâm-ı müstakil, üç vakf-ı tâmdan mürekkeb bir kelâm-ı tâm nizamında bir sûre-i bedî‘adır

ELMALILI:1:2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r10.claim: The basmala names God and His attributes while leaving humanity implicit; saying it establishes the divine relation that lets al-Fatiha bring humans forth with gratitude into speech.
ELMALILI:1:2/r10.anchor: Orada اَللّٰه الرَّحْمٰن الرَّحِيم husustan umûma inbisat eden isim ve sıfâtı ile mezkûr iken biz ezelde olduğumuz gibi ef‘âlimizle beraber mahzuf ve muzmer idik

ELMALILI:1:2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r11.claim: Al-Fatiha begins in gratitude, places humans in the worlds under a hidden divine relation, renews the manifestation of mercy, and trains consciousness through truth and instruction until people recognize God and themselves.
ELMALILI:1:2/r11.anchor: Fâtiha bir şükran ile başlıyor ve bizi gıyâbî bir izâfet-i rabbâniye ile

ELMALILI:1:2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r12.claim: It then grants people speech to pledge exclusive worship and dependence, binding human will and the right to ask for guidance into an enduring covenant between God and humanity.
ELMALILI:1:2/r12.anchor: vahdâniyyet-i ilâhiyeye إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ diye bir ‘akd-i bey‘at yaptırmak üzere bize hakk-ı kelâm veriyor

ELMALILI:1:2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r13.claim: The hidden humanity of the basmala becomes a speaking subject in al-Fatiha, while God is present as interlocutor; the surah captures the full relation of life and existence.
ELMALILI:1:2/r13.anchor: ezeldeki ve besmeledeki bâtın, Fâtiha’da ve hâlde bir mütekellim-i zâhir oluyor

ELMALILI:1:2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2/r14.claim: A sacred hadith says al-Fatiha is divided equally between God and servant, with the servant entitled to what is asked; its opening praises and glorifies God, its middle is shared, and its ending is the servant's supplication.
ELMALILI:1:2/r14.anchor: Ben salât sûresi olan Fâtiha’yı Benim aramla kulum arasında yarı yarıya taksim ettim

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r1.claim: The community that reserves worship and appeal to God reflects a delegated divine trust and receives a share in creation; this supports communal consensus as a legally probative source.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r1.anchor: ümmetin icmâ‘ında da bir delâlet-i teşrî‘iye mevcut olabileceğini

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r2.claim: The relation between the basmala and Fatiha unfolds the primordial covenant between the eternal Lord and creation, inscribing a relation already present in human nature.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r2.anchor: besmele ile Fâtiha arasındaki sibâk-ı tenâsübün rûhu ezel ile lâyezâl beynindeki bu mu‘âdele nisbetinin inkişâfıdır

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r3.claim: Fatiha proceeds as instruction; the command to read in the name of the Lord is a key contextual sign of this teaching purpose.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r3.anchor: Fâtiha’nın bizzat kendisindeki sevki bir sevk-i ta’lîmdir

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r4.speaker: bazı müfessirîn
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r4.claim: Some exegetes posit an implicit command meaning say this at the start of Fatiha.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r4.anchor: bazı müfessirîn başta “böyle söyle” mealinde قل emrinin mukadder olduğunu

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r5.speaker: muhakkıkīn
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r5.claim: The discerning exegetes hold that the teaching is clear from the style itself, without supplying an omitted command.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r5.anchor: muhakkıkīn bu takdîre hâcet kalmaksızın sâde, siyâk-ı üslûbun bu ta‘lîmi iş‘âra kâfi olduğunda musırdırlar

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r6.claim: The opening three verses speak about God in the unseen; reflection makes God present to the worshipper, who can then turn to direct address and pledge worship and need.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r6.anchor: ma‘rifetullâha müte‘allik olan üç âyet tamâmen gāibâne

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r7.claim: The shift from unseen narration to direct address is an eloquent turn of address that compresses extensive meanings and contributes to the Qur’an’s inimitability.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r7.anchor: bir üslûb-i iltifâtın böyle tam makamında ve birçok cümlelere muhtaç mazmunları

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r8.claim: Fatiha’s successive clauses unfold the opening praise and return to alhamdu lillah; the surah is the root and comprehensive representative of the other Qur’anic surahs.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r8.anchor: Diğer süver-i Kur’an ile münasebâtı ise, Fâtiha; “Ümmü’l-Kur’ân”, “Ümmü’l-Kitâb”, “Esâs” isimlerinin

ELMALILI:1:2#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r9.claim: The basmala is the crown, the Qur’an a perfect body, Fatiha its head, and alhamdu lillah its face; mercy, guidance, worship, and divine unity express its spiritual life.
ELMALILI:1:2#2/r9.anchor: besmele bir taç, Kur’an bir vücûd-i ekmel, Fâtiha onun başı, ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ bu baştaki sîmâ

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r1.claim: Hamd is beautiful verbal praise that honors an agent for a voluntary benefaction or its source, goodness; it combines aspects of praise and gratitude and lacks a single Turkish equivalent.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r1.anchor: Hamd, ihtiyârî bir ihsâna veya onun mebde’i olan bir hüsne karşı inşirah ile sâhibine tâzim ifade eden bir zikr-i cemîldir

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r2.claim: Medh can praise living or inanimate things and can precede or follow a favor; hamd is directed to a choosing benefactor after a favor, though the benefit need not reach the praiser.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r2.anchor: medh, hayatı ve ihtiyârı olana da olmayana da yapılır

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r3.claim: Shukr responds in speech, action, or heart to a blessing actually received; spoken gratitude is also hamd and medh, while inward or bodily thanks need not be either.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r3.anchor: Şükürde ise bu da şarttır. Zira şükür gelmiş olan bir nimete kavlen veya fiilen veya kalben mün‘imini tâzim ile mukabele etmektir

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r4.claim: Every hamd is medh but not every medh is hamd; hamd is broader than gratitude in one respect and narrower in another, and unlike empty flattery both hamd and shukr affirm truth.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r4.anchor: Her hamd medhdir, lâkin her medh hamd değildir

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r5.claim: Hamd springs from justified hope or experienced enjoyment and leans toward the future, whereas shukr celebrates an accomplished gift and its received fulfillment.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r5.anchor: Hamd delile müstenid haklı bir ümidin neşvesiyle veyahut şükür gibi tahakkuk etmiş bir tenâ‘‘umun

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r6.speaker: Resûl-i Ekrem
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r6.claim: The Prophet commands that dust be thrown in the faces of professional eulogists, illustrating the moral danger of medh that can become flattery.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r6.anchor: Aleyhi’s-salâtü ve’s-selâm Efendimiz “Meddahların yüzlerine toprak saçınız

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r7.speaker: Resûl-i Ekrem
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r7.claim: The Prophet says that one who does not praise people does not praise God, making hamd generally commendable.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r7.anchor: Nâsa hamd etmeyen Allah’a da hamd etmez: مَنْ لَمْ يَحْمَدِ النَّاسَ لَمْ يَحْمَدِ اللّٰهَّٰ

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r8.claim: Gratitude is a distinctive mark of people of truth, yet only a few servants attain it.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r8.anchor: Şükür ise böyle erbâb-ı hakīkatin şi‘ârı olduğundan

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r9.speaker: Hazret-i Ömeru’l-Fârûk
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r9.claim: Umar’s remark that truth left him no friend conveys how difficult it is to remain faithful to truth.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r9.anchor: Nitekim fânî fi’l-hak olan Hazret-i Ömeru’l-Fârûk

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r10.speaker: Gustave Le Bon
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r10.claim: Le Bon and other thinkers conclude that imagination rules people more strongly than reality.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r10.anchor: Bunu mülâhaza eden bazı mütefekkirîn, ezcümle zamanımızda Fransız Gustave Le Bon

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r11.claim: Elmalılı rejects Le Bon’s conclusion: imagination affects people because it can represent reality, so reality remains the true source of its force.
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r11.anchor: Fakat bu doğru değildir. Çünkü hayalde görülen o hâkimiyet hakikati temsil edebilmesi haysiyetindendir

ELMALILI:1:2#3/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r12.speaker: Resûl-i Ekrem
ELMALILI:1:2#3/r12.claim: The Prophet calls hamd the head of gratitude and says that whoever fails to praise God has not thanked Him.

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r1.claim: Verbal expressions of reverence count as hamd; announcing a blessing is a moral virtue that praises its free agent and rightly rejoices in the happiness received.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r1.anchor: tahdîs-i nimet bir gurûr-ı temeddüh değil, nankörlüğü silen büyük bir fazilettir

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r2.claim: Human happiness depends on recognizing and tasting a blessing, not merely possessing it; the recipient’s expressed hamd lets the giver witness that the gift reached its fitting recipient.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r2.anchor: saadet tena‘‘umun kendisinde ve kemmiyetinde değil keyfiyetinde, yani zevki takdir edilip hissedilmesindedir

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r3.claim: Giving stands above receiving, so the station of the praised giver is the highest rank; the joy of this rank culminates in further hamd and increased gifts.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r3.anchor: makām-ı in‘âm, makām-ı tena‘‘umun fevkindedir. Binâen‘aleyh Makām-ı Mahmûdiyet ekmel-i merâtib ve aksâ-yı metâlibdir

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r4.claim: Hamd advances through four ranks: praising, being praised, uniting both, then receiving praise while praising.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r4.anchor: 1. Hâmidiyet, 2. Mahmûdiyet, 3. Hâmidiyet ve Mahmûdiyet, 4. Mahmûdiyet ve Hâmidiyet

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r5.claim: The final rank manifests the divine names Hamid, Mahmud, and Hamid together; the Prophet also bears the related names Ahmed and Muhammad.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r5.anchor: mahmûdiyet ve hâmidiyeti cem‘eden Hamîd, Mahmûd, Hâmid esmâ-i hüsnâsının tecellîsini

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r6.claim: The promised station of praise belongs especially to the Seal of the Prophets and is the station of the great intercession, where he receives the banner of praise.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r6.anchor: Makām-ı Mahmûd bilhassa Hâtemü’l-Enbiyâ Efendimiz’e mev‘ud olan ve onu hâmidiyetten mahmûdiyete terakki ettiren bir makām-ı a‘lâdır

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r7.claim: Through the Prophet’s intercession, the community gathered beneath the banner of praise shares in divine hamd, and the people of Paradise conclude their plea with this verse.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r7.anchor: ehl-i cennetin davalarının sonu da ٱلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ olacaktır

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r8.claim: Hamd’s fullest nature speaks through the Prophet’s Ahmediyyah and Muhammadiyyah; its ultimate reality belongs at its beginning and end to God alone.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r8.anchor: lafzen ve mânen mâhiyet-i hamd, bir Hakīkat-i Muhammediye’dir. Ve bu hakikatin evvel ve âhir Allah teâlâ’ya ihtisâsı

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r9.claim: The definite article in alhamd can express a known instance, totality, kind, or essence; because no particular hamd is presupposed, it here gathers the entire genus and all its ranks.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r9.anchor: Lisân-ı Arab’da ال ‘ahd-i ferd veya ‘ahd-i istiğrak veya ‘ahd-i cins ve hakikat ifade eden bir harf-i ta‘rîftir

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r10.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r10.claim: The lām in lillah denotes entitlement, particularity, and ownership; the whole genus and every form of hamd belongs to God.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r10.anchor: للّٰهّٰ da lâm, ihtisas, istihkak, milk mânalarında zâhirdir

ELMALILI:1:2#4/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r11.claim: Alhamdu lillah informs believers, implies reverent praise, and uses a timeless nominal sentence; the four following clauses explain it, making Fatiha one sentence in substance.
ELMALILI:1:2#4/r11.anchor: Fâtiha, bu tek cümle-i ismiyeden ibaret bir kelâmdır

ELMALILI:1:2#5/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:1:2#5/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:1:2#5/r1.claim: The sound plural al-alamin foregrounds rational beings; a concise Turkish rendering is difficult, but it means God alone is Lord of all realms and especially their rational inhabitants.
