ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r1.anchor: ورب مصدر وصف به على أحد وجوه الوصف بالمصدر، أو اسم فاعل حذفت ألفه

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r2.claim: Rabb is used absolutely for God, but for others only in a construct phrase such as the lord of the house.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r2.anchor: وأطلقوا الرب على الله وحده، وفي غيره قيد بالإضافة نحو رب الدار

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r3.claim: Although al-ʿālamīn is an irregular plural, Abū Ḥayyān favors the responsible creatures because a cited verse and Ḥafṣ's lām-kasra reading support that scope.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r3.anchor: والذي أختاره أنه ينطلق على المكلفين لقوله تعالى: إن في ذلك لآيات للعالمين

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r4.claim: God's lordship and mercy make Him worthy of praise; lordship as mastery or ownership is followed fittingly by mercy, which sustains servants' hope after failure.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r4.anchor: ومضمون الجملة والوصف أن من كان موصوفا بالربوبية والرحمة للمربوبين كان مستحقا للحمد

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r5.speaker: أبو العالية وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمرو
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r5.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ, and ʿĪsā ibn ʿAmr read raḥmān and raḥīm in the accusative, as detached epithets.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r5.anchor: ونصبهما أبو العالية وابن السميفع وعيسى بن عمرو

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r6.speaker: أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r6.claim: Abū Razīn, al-Rabīʿ ibn Khuthaym, and Abū ʿImrān al-Jūnī read both epithets in the nominative as detached clauses.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r6.anchor: ورفعهما أبو رزين العقيلي والربيع بن خيثم وأبو عمران الجوني

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r9.claim: Parsing rabb as apposition is weak because raḥmān and raḥīm intervene.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p35/r9.anchor: نصبه على البدل فضعيف للفصل بقوله الرحمن الرحيم

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r2.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamd intensifies praise by making it comprehensive.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r2.anchor: النوع الثاني: المبالغة في الثناء، وذلك لعموم أل في الحمد

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r3.claim: Some rhetoricians call “Praise be to God” a statement whose intended force is command, like “no doubt in it” meaning “do not doubt.”
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r3.anchor: النوع الثالث: تلوين الخطاب على قول بعضهم، فإنه ذكر أن الحمد لله صيغته صيغة الخبر،

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r4.claim: The lām in “to God” restricts all praise to Him, and the annexation “Master of the Day of Judgment” underscores His sole dominion when other dominions vanish.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r4.anchor: النوع الرابع: الاختصاص باللام التي في لله، إذ دلت على أن جميع المحامد مختصة به،

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r5.claim: The accusative reading of “al-ḥamd” involves ellipsis; grammarians differ over whether its omitted governing word repeats the noun or is another word.
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p53/r5.anchor: النوع الخامس: الحذف، وهو على قراءة من نصب الحمد ظاهر،

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r1.claim: Because the book opens with the basmala, a kind of praise, God follows it with comprehensive praise at the highest degree of perfection.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r1.anchor: ولما أفتتح سبحانه وتعالى كتابه بالبسملة وهي نوع من الحمد ناسب أن يردفها بالحمد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r2.claim: The phrase opens the Fātiḥa and also closes the final supplications, as in the verse describing the last prayer of Paradise’s inhabitants.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r2.anchor: وهو أول الفاتحة وآخر الدعوات الخاتمة كما قال تعالى ( وآخر دعواهم أن الحمد لله رب العالمين )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r3.claim: Hamd conventionally means verbal praise for what is beautiful, whether a virtue or benefaction; its realization involves a praiseworthy attribute, its ground, a praiser, the praised, and an expression of that quality.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r3.anchor: والحمد على المشهور هو الثناء باللسان على الجميل سواء تعلق بالفضائل أم بالفواضل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r4.speaker: الإمام الرازي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r4.claim: Al-Rāzī and other authorities allow the praised attribute to be positive or negative, transitive or not, and voluntary or involuntary; al-Dūrānī, Ṣadr al-Afāḍil, and Mullā Khusraw also affirm this.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r4.anchor: ولا فرق عند الإمام الرازي قدس سره بين كونه ثبوتيا أو سلبيا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r5.speaker: العلامة في شرح التهذيب
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r5.claim: An authority cited in Sharḥ al-Tahdhīb requires the praised attribute to be voluntary and adopts that condition; al-Ālūsī notes the parallel question about what praise is for.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r5.anchor: نقل عن عن البعض وجوب كونه إختياريا وأختاره كما في المحمود عليه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r6.claim: The praised ground is what the praise answers to and displays as the subject’s perfection; one thing can be both attribute and ground under different aspects, while the public view includes actions and qualities.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r6.anchor: الثاني ما يقع الثناء بإزائه ويقابله بمعنى أن المثنى عليه لما أتصف به

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r7.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r7.claim: The Imam appears to prefer a voluntary act as the ground of praise and to require that it arise from the praised person’s choice.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r7.anchor: ويفهم كلام الإمام إختيار الأول وأشترط أن يكون حصوله من المحمود بإختياره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r8.claim: Several answers address praise for God’s essential attributes: treat them as voluntary because the divine essence suffices for them, define choice as willing-agent attribution, or say they occur by choice in the sense that God acts if He wills.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p67/r8.anchor: وأجيب بأن الحمد عليها بتنزيلها منزلة الإختياري لكون ذاته كافية فيها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī challenges the philosophers’ appeal to conditional willing: if the contrary can occur, their account conflicts with their claim that the world necessarily proceeds eternally; if it cannot, will is only a name.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r1.anchor: فإن أريد بالدوام الدوام مع صحة وقوع النقيض فهو مخالف لما صرحوا به

ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r2.claim: Making divine attributes freely produced does not solve the issue: if power itself is produced by choice, it would precede itself, and the remaining proposed answers are unpersuasive.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r2.anchor: يبقى الإشكال في صفة القدرة ولا قدرة لدعوى صدورها بالإختيار

ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r3.claim: Some therefore do not require the praised ground to be voluntary, since it is what occasions praise; the verse about the Praised Station is cited as an example.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r3.anchor: لم يشترط بعضهم في المحمود عليه أن يكون إختياريا لأنه الباعث على الحمد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r5.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s preferred linguistic account restricts hamd to voluntary acts; praise for essential attributes is either linguistic by reference to their voluntary effects or conventional, while the cited examples use praise metaphorically for approval.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r5.anchor: والحق الحقيقي بالإتباع أن الحمد اللغوي لا يكون إلا على الأفعال الإختيارية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r6.claim: The third element is the praiser, who must exalt the praised in outward expression and inwardly; the next segment debates whether inward belief must match the praise.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p68/r6.anchor: ( والثالث ) وهو من يتحقق منه الحمد وشرطه أن يكون معظما بثنائه للمحمود ظاهرا وباطنا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r1.speaker: الدواني
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r1.claim: Al-Dawānī explains that praise without belief matching its content would become mockery, taking belief to mean the act of inward exaltation rather than propositional assent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r1.anchor: قال الدواني توجيه الشريف إشتراط التعظيمين بأنه إذا عرى عن مطابقة الإعتقاد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r2.claim: Al-Ālūsī answers that hamd can be performative, so correspondence to belief is inapplicable; ordinary speakers also use iʿtiqād to mean regard or esteem for someone.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r2.anchor: فإن الحمد قد يكون إنشائيا ولا معنى لمطابقة الإعتقاد فيه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r3.claim: He rejects two replies—that the speaker believes the attributed quality, or that the praise is figurative—because the first contradicts plain experience and the second often contradicts the facts.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r3.anchor: ( وأما الجواب ) بأن الواصف يعتقد الإتصاف وبأن المراد معان مجازية وإتصاف المنعوت بها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r4.claim: A statement’s not being believed does not prevent its literal or figurative use; deliberate falsehoods can serve emphasis, wit, testing, or imaginative purposes.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r4.anchor: لا يلزم من عدم إعتقاد المدلول أن لا يكون الكلام مستعملا فيه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r5.claim: The fourth element is the praised object; the fifth is an expression showing that it possesses praiseworthiness, conventionally assigned to the tongue.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r5.anchor: + ( الخامس ( وهو ذكر ما يدل على إتصاف المحمود بالمحمودية وقد اشتهر تقييده باللسان

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r6.claim: Tongue is the usual instrument, not an absolute condition: lip sounds without a tongue, or speech produced through another organ, still count as praise; the Qur’an says everything glorifies God’s praise.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r6.anchor: فلو فقد إنسان لسانه فأثنى بحروفه الشفوية أو خلق النطق في بعض جوارحه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r7.speaker: الأكثر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r7.claim: Most authorities interpret God praising Himself as reporting His entitlement to praise, commanding praise, speaking through servants, or figuratively displaying His perfect attributes; al-Sayyid favors the last explanation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69/r7.anchor: فذهب الأكثر إلى أنه إخبار بإستحقاق الحمد وأمر به أو مقول على ألسنة العباد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r1.speaker: الدواني
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r1.claim: Al-Dawānī objects that treating God’s praise as figurative conflicts with the orthodox affirmation of real divine speech, since saying and speech are equivalent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r1.anchor: وقال الدواني كون الحمد في حقه سبحانه مجازا بعيد عن قاعدة أهل الحق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r2.claim: The tongue restriction is either relative to heart and limbs or merely usual; hamd originally means displaying perfection, with speech its most familiar form and action potentially fuller.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r2.anchor: والمراد الأمر الذي مصدره اللسان غالبا أو هو قيد غالبي يسوغ الإستعمال فيه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r3.claim: Words often become conventionally narrow because one instance is common or other instances are unknown; this can obscure Qur’anic and Prophetic meanings that preserve original lexical breadth.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r3.anchor: وبذلك يفوت كثير من حقائق الكتاب والسنة فإن أكثرهما وارد على أصل اللغة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r4.claim: One distinction says hamd concerns voluntary acts of rational beings, while madḥ may concern voluntary or involuntary qualities and rational or non-rational subjects.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r4.anchor: أن الحمد يختص بالثناء على الفعل الإختياري لذوي العلم والمدح يكون في الإختياري وغيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r5.claim: Other distinctions reserve hamd for known perfection, certainty, and greater reverence, while madḥ may praise merely supposed or imperfect qualities and report beauty without love.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r5.anchor: أن الحمد يشترط صدوره عن علم لأظن وأن تكون الصفات المحمودة صفات كمال

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r6.claim: Hamd is also said to be both report and performative through love and reverence, unlike madḥ as bare report; one report says whoever does not praise people does not praise God, while another condemns flatterers.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r6.anchor: أن الحمد إخبار عن محاسن الغير مع المحبة والإجلال والمدح إخبار عن المحاسن

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī’s Kashshāf and Fāʾiq suggest hamd and madḥ are synonymous, defining hamd as praise and description with beauty; al-Ālūsī judges this likely but rejects it.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r7.anchor: ويشعر كلام الزمخشري في الكشاف والفائق بترادفهما

ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r8.claim: Al-Ālūsī holds that madḥ can praise involuntary qualities, unlike hamd; that distinction explains why God says al-hamdu lillāh, since God is a freely acting agent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p69#2/r8.anchor: فالحق الذي لا ينبغي العدول عنه أن المدح يكون على غير الإختياري

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r1.claim: Definitions distinguish gratitude as bodily deed versus hamd as speech, outward versus inward blessings, or tongue-only thanks for blessings; al-Rāghib’s account limits it to blessing.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r1.anchor: فهو ايضا مغاير للحمد إلا أن بعضهم خصه بالعمل والحمد بالقول

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r2.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r2.claim: Al-Ṭībī calls gratitude by speech, deeds, and heart the technical usage of legal theorists, who mean the obligatory worship of the benefactor; al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that linguistic gratitude is only verbal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r2.anchor: وقول الطيبي إن هذا عرف أهل الأصول فإنهم يقولون شكر المنعم واجب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r3.claim: Scripture applies gratitude to actions as well as speech: the Qur’an commands David’s household to act in gratitude.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r3.anchor: فإن ظاهر الكتاب والسنة إطلاق الشكر على غير اللسان قال تعالى ( أعملوا آل داؤد شكرا )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r4.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r4.claim: Al-Ṭabarānī reports that after the Prophet’s she-camel was stolen, he vowed to thank God if it returned; when it did, he said alhamdulillah, and the Companions awaited fasting or prayer, showing they understood gratitude as action.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r4.anchor: وروى الطبراني عن النواس بن سمعان أن ناقة رسول الله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم الجدعاء سرقت

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r5.speaker: صاحب التجريد
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r5.claim: Some add a fourth form, God thanking God, since only God can thank Him fully; a cited poem contrasts gratitude to people by heart, word, and deed with gratitude to God through His own thanking.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r5.anchor: وزاد بعضهم في أقسام الشكر رابعا وهو شكر الله تعالى بالله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r6.claim: Hamd and gratitude overlap in part, but hamd is stronger because it openly discloses blessing while ingratitude conceals it; verbal praise is clearer than hidden belief or deeds that may be habitual.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r6.anchor: بينه وبين الحمد عموم وخصوص من وجه والحمد أقوى شعبة لأن حقيقته إشاعة النعمة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r7.claim: Calling the state more eloquent than speech is a rhetorical claim: worshipful actions may be indistinguishable from ordinary habits, whereas verbal praise explicitly names God’s glory.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p70/r7.anchor: وكم فرق بين حمدت الله وشكرته ومجدته وعظمته وبين أفعال العبادة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r1.claim: Ibn ʿUmar transmits the saying that praise is gratitude’s head and that no servant thanks God without praising Him; al-Ālūsī notes its interrupted chain but says a supporting report strengthens it.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r1.anchor: قال صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم فيما رواه إبن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما الحمد رأس الشكر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r2.claim: Praise is like the head because speech makes meaning clearest, and the head is the most evident, elevated, and sustaining member; this may explain why God names praise first.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r2.anchor: حيث كان النطق يجلي كل مشتبه وكان الحمد أظهر الأنواع واشهرها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r3.claim: Other rationales say praise is a fitting beginning for the Lord and that praise exceeds thanks because it need not arise from a benefit received by the speaker.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r3.anchor: أو لأنه لو قال جل شأنه الشكر لله كان ثناء عليه تعالى بسبب إنعام وصل إلى ذلك القائل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r4.claim: Praise can concern withholding as well as giving and is thus unbounded, while gratitude answers a finite gift; averting harm is more urgent than gaining benefit, favoring praise first.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r4.anchor: ويمكن أن يقال إن الشكر على الإعطاء وهو متناه والحمد يكون على المنع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r5.claim: Praise has a narrower occasion but a broader object than gratitude; its inclusion may signal a sacred allusion, and tasbīḥ is omitted because praise already includes both negative and positive perfections.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r5.anchor: مورد الحمد في المشهور خاص ومتعلقه عام والشكر بالعكس

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r6.claim: Every tasbīḥ counts as praise, not vice versa: glorification negates deficiencies, whereas praise also affirms positive qualities, so its comprehensiveness suits the Qur’an; priority changes with context.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r6.anchor: كل تسبيح حمد وليس كل حمد تسبيحا لأن التسبيح يكون بالصفات السلبية فحسب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r7.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamdu is taken here to indicate the familiar genus of praise, illustrated by a line of Labīd about the wild asses and their she-asses.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71/r7.anchor: والتعريف هنا للجنس ومعناه الإشارة إلى ما يعرفه كل أحد من أن الحمد ما هو

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls comprehensive scope an imagined error and takes the article as genus; the ensuing debate addresses whether that reading protects the Muʿtazilī account of human acts.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r1.anchor: حتى قال والإستغراق الذي يتوهمه كثير من الناس وهم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r2.claim: One argument says Muʿtazilīs assign praise for human deeds to humans because they create their acts; the reply is that even good deeds depend on God’s power and enabling, so praise ultimately returns to Him.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r2.anchor: فإن أفعال العباد لما كانت مخلوقة لهم عند المعتزلة كانت المحامد عليها راجعة إليهم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r3.claim: Another defense treats genus in rhetorical context as the complete instance; a critic replies that comprehensive scope can likewise treat everything else as negligible, so neither reading avoids the theological difficulty unaided.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r3.anchor: وقيل أنه جعل الجنس في المقام الخطابي منصرفا إلى الكامل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r4.claim: A third argument derives genus from verbal nouns’ basic, non-comprehensive meaning; the reply is that surrounding indications can still make a verbal noun comprehensive.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r4.anchor: وقيل مبناه على أن المصادر نائبة مناب الأفعال

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r5.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that genus is the obvious common reading: in rhetorical settings a definite generic article commonly conveys comprehensiveness, especially when exclusive praise is at issue.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r5.anchor: ورد بأن المحلى بلام الجنس في المقامات الخطابية يتبادر منه الإستغراق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r6.claim: He prefers genus because its exclusivity follows directly from the wording and logically entails exclusivity of every instance, making the proof stronger than separately asserting total scope.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r6.anchor: فالحق أن سبب الإختيار هو أن إختصاص الجنس مستفاد من جوهر الكلام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r7.claim: He challenges the claim that genus exclusivity is immediately apparent: its inference is too subtle to be the obvious reading, and the manuscript ends while he disputes the argument’s rhetorical strength.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p71#2/r7.anchor: وفيه أن فهم إختصاص الجنس من جوهر الكلام يدل على سرعته

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī says treating genus as perfection and treating comprehensive praise as exhaustive both require interpretation; making everything else negligible adds an unnecessary step.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r1.anchor: على الثاني من أنه كما يجوز الحمل على الجنس بإعتبار الكمال على مذهبه يجوز الحمل على الإستغراق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r2.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r2.claim: One account answers how the speakers enact praise by joining verbal praise to bodily and inward worship and seeking aid.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r2.anchor: وقيل حاصل الجواب عن كيفية صدور تلك الحقيقة بتخصيص العبادة المشتملة على الحمد وغيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r3.claim: A grammatical rationale treats al-ḥamd as a verbal noun standing in for its verb, so it denotes the underlying reality and can be explained by the worship that follows.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r3.anchor: بل لأن الحمد مصدر ساد مسد الفعل وهو لا يدل إلا على الحقيقة فكذا ما ينوب منابه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r4.speaker: السعد
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r4.claim: Al-Ālūsī says treating You alone we worship as an explanation rests on the missing conjunction, but that reverses the proper relation between the opening and its continuation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r4.anchor: ولعل الذي دعاه إليه ترك العاطف فظن أنه لذلك لا يكون إلا بيانا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r5.claim: A further account makes worship the explanation of praise by combining verbal praise with bodily and inward devotion; al-Ālūsī says this does not require choosing genus over comprehensive scope.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r5.anchor: وقيل حاصل الجواب عن كيفية صدور تلك الحقيقة بتخصيص العبادة المشتملة على الحمد وغيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r6.claim: The sounder reading makes the first clause praise of God in the third person and the next a speaker’s self-report; the missing conjunction marks a change of state, not an explanation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r6.anchor: فالمحققون المحقون على تعميم الحمد وأن الفصل لأن الكلام الأول جار على المدح للغائب بسبب إستحقاقه كل الحمد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r7.claim: The following divine attributes imply that God deserves praise for them; since their scope is comprehensive, the praise should likewise be comprehensive, with God encompassing all names and worlds and mercy extending universally.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r7.anchor: وأيضا في تعقيب هذه الصفات للحمد إشعار بأن إستحقاقه له لإتصافه بها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r8.claim: Al-Ālūsī accepts genus, a generic instance, or comprehensive scope in principle, but this context calls for all praise: praise for every perfection ultimately belongs to God as its giver.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p72/r8.anchor: وأنا لو خليت وطبعي لا أمنع أن تكون أل للحقيقة من حيث هي

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r1.claim: In al-Taghābun, al-Zamakhsharī says the fronted phrases “His is the dominion” and “His is praise” signal their exclusivity; praise of others recognizes that God’s favor reached them through those people.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r1.anchor: فقال في قوله تعالى : ( له الملك وله الحمد ) قدم الظرفان ليدل بتقديمهما على معنى إختصاص الملك

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r2.claim: Even on the Muʿtazilī account, people’s praise does not displace God’s: He enables their acts and bestows the conditions, while their own agency merits a distinct, lesser praise.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r2.anchor: فإن من أصل المعتزلة أن نعمة الله تعالى جارية على يد العبد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r3.claim: Some read al-ḥamdu as true, complete praise alone belonging to God rather than all instances; al-Ālūsī says this meaning can be apt but rejects using it to evade comprehensive scope here.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r3.anchor: وقد يقال أيضا على أصله أن الحمد المستغرق لا يجوز أن يختص

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r4.claim: He rejects limiting the expression to “true complete praise” as an ad hoc escape from comprehensiveness, even when supported by a leading commentator, because rhetorical discourse often speaks through persuasive address.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r4.anchor: كلام لا أقبله وإن جل قائله ويعرف الرجال بالحق لا ألحق بالرجال

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r5.claim: Al-Ālūsī argues that comprehensiveness fits this passage’s total lordship, mercy, and continuing sovereignty; he contrasts it with another surah whose relevant details are absent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r5.anchor: ثم لما كان المقام مقتضيا لدقائق النعم وروافدها لم يكن تنزيل الحمد الغير الكامل منزلة العدم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r6.claim: The claim that exclusive genus praise is more comprehensive than exclusive individuals is reversible: if every individual is exclusively God’s, no instance remains outside the exclusive genus.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r6.anchor: فالإستلزام متعاكس على أن حقيقة الحمد يصدق عليها الحمد فهي فرد من أفراده

ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r7.claim: Rhetorical address is a divinely used mode even when a proof is available, because it affects hearts and benefits ordinary hearers; al-Ālūsī points to the command to invite with wisdom and good exhortation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p73/r7.anchor: ومن سنة الله تعالى التي لا تبديل لها إجراء الكلام على سبيل الخطابة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r1.speaker: أبو العباس المرسي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r1.claim: Al-Fākihī reports that Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mursī told Ibn al-Naḥḥās the article is referential: God praised Himself eternally on creatures’ behalf because they could not praise Him adequately.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r1.anchor: سمعت شيخنا أبا العباس المرسي يقول لإبن النحاس ما تقول في الألف واللام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r2.speaker: النبي ﷺ
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r2.claim: Al-Mursī appeals to the Prophet’s authentic supplication that people cannot enumerate God’s praise and that He is as He praised Himself.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r2.anchor: اللهم لا نحصي ثناء عليك أنت كما أثنيت على نفسك

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r3.speaker: بعض ساداتنا الصوفية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r3.claim: Some Sufi masters say “praise belongs to God” is like “might belongs to God”: God is both praiser and praised, and all things are His affairs, as the verse says creation and command belong to Him.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r3.anchor: وليس بالغريب عندهم أن الحمد لله على حد الكبرياء لله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r4.speaker: الماتريدي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r4.claim: Al-Māturīdī says God praised Himself to teach creatures; this is fitting because He deserves praise by His own essence and perfection.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r4.anchor: وعن إمامنا الماتريدي روح الله تعالى روحه أنه جعل هذا حمدا من الله تعالى لنفسه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r5.claim: The standard transmitted reading has al-ḥamdu nominative as the subject; Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Zayd b. ʿAlī assimilate the vowel of dāl to the following lām, while Ibrāhīm b. Abla and Bedouins do the reverse.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r5.anchor: وقرأ الحسن البصري وزيد بن علي الحمد لله بإتباع الدال اللام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r6.claim: The assimilation readings are anomalous; al-Zamakhsharī calls Ibrāhīm’s reading “more lucid,” while competing arguments favor each reading based on direction of assimilation and the relative strength of inflection and construction.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r6.anchor: وكأنه لتعارض الترجيح قال الزمخشري : وأشف القراءتين قراءة إبراهيم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r7.speaker: هارون بن موسى
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r7.claim: Hārūn b. Mūsā reads al-ḥamda in the accusative, like Arabs who use definite verbal nouns with an omitted verb; the implied “we praise” suits worship and seeking help better than royal “we.”
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r7.anchor: وقرأ هارون بن موسى الحمد لله بالنصب وعامة بني تميم وكثير من العرب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r8.speaker: الغزالي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r8.claim: Al-Ghazālī applies the plural-language explanation to the report that congregational prayer exceeds an individual prayer by twenty-seven degrees.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r8.anchor: وحمل الغزالي قدس سره حديث صلاة الجماعة تفضل صلاة الفذ بسبع وعشرين درجة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r9.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the nominative nominal sentence because, in context, it expresses established and continuing praise, whereas a verbal sentence ordinarily presents renewed action; permanence also depends on context, not form alone.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p74/r9.anchor: وأرفع آت قراءة الرفع لدلالة الجملة الأسمية على الثبوت والدوام بقرينة المقام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r1.claim: Some grammarians say verbal nouns are originally accusative because events require predication; the underlying verbal relation is normally expressed by a verb, making the noun-plus-verb construction seem redundant.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r1.anchor: أن أصل هذا المصدر النصب لأن المصادر إحداث متعلقة بمحالها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r2.claim: Al-Ālūsī opens a further question about whether “Praise belongs to God” is declarative or performative; most scholars call it declarative, following the apparent form.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p75/r2.anchor: أختلف في جملة الحمد هل هي إخبارية أم إنشائية فالذي عليه معظم العلماء أنها إخبارية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r1.speaker: الأكثر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r1.claim: The question is how a contingent human act of praise can be for God without inhering in Him; relation to an object does not entail inherence, as knowledge relates to its objects.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r1.anchor: وأجيب بأن المراد تعلق الحمد به تعالى ولا يلزم من التعلق القيام كتعلق العلم بالمعلومات

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r2.speaker: ابن الهمام
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r2.claim: Another interpretation parses al-ḥamd as a passive verbal noun meaning being praised; its form permits other readings, and some even take the lām as causal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r2.anchor: وقيل أن الحمد مصدر بناء المجهول فيكون الثابت له عز شأنه هو المحمودية وصيغة المصدر تحتمل ذلك وغيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r3.speaker: ابن الهمام
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r3.claim: Some interpreters propose forty-two possibilities for the phrase; a rare proposal makes its lām mean because of God.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r3.anchor: ولهذا جعل بعضهم في الحمد لله أوائل الكتب أثنين وأربعين إحتمالا وقيل وهو من الغرابة بمكان أن اللام للتعليل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r4.claim: Naming God by His essence avoids suggesting that entitlement to praise belongs only to one attribute; essential entitlement means no particular attribute is specified, not that praise lacks a beautiful ground.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r4.anchor: أنه أتى بإسم الذات في الحمد له لئلا يتوهم لو أقتصر على الصفة إختصاص إستحقاقه الحمد بوصف دون وصف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r5.speaker: الملا خسرو
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r5.claim: Entitlement by essence means entitlement without specifying a particular attribute; it does not mean God deserves praise apart from beautiful qualities.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r5.anchor: ومعنى الإستحقاق الذاتي ما لا يلاحظ معه خصوصية صفة حتى الجميع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r6.claim: Mystically, praise originating from God ranges across His hidden essence, absolute existence, manifestations, attributes, effects, and knowledge in general or detail.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r6.anchor: فإن وجد من الحق وصدر من الوجود المطلق فتارة يكون على الذات بإنفرادها ووحدتها وغيبتها في عماء هويتها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r7.claim: Mystical praise arising from creatures may concern God's essence, attributes, names, actions, mysteries, subtle workmanship, or hidden wisdom, according to each person's knowledge and understanding.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r7.anchor: وإن وجد من الخلق والوجود المقيد فتارة يكون على ذات الحق وتارة على صفاته وتارة على أسمائه ومرة على أفعاله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r8.claim: The question how servants’ created praise is “for” God is answered by distinguishing attachment from inherence, like knowledge attaching to its objects; another parses the noun as passive “being praised,” while a rare view makes the lām causal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r8.anchor: بأن المراد تعلق الحمد به تعالى ولا يلزم من التعلق القيام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r9.claim: Mentioning the divine proper name avoids implying that entitlement to praise belongs only to one attribute; the entitlement belongs to the essence without isolating it from its attributes.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r9.anchor: أنه أتى بإسم الذات في الحمد له لئلا يتوهم لو أقتصر على الصفة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r10.speaker: بعض ساداتنا الصوفية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r10.claim: A mystical account divides praise into praise originating from God and from creation: God’s praise concerns His essence, manifestations, attributes, and effects, while creatures praise His essence, names, actions, secrets, and wisdom according to their understanding.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r10.anchor: فإن وجد من الحق وصدر من الوجود المطلق فتارة يكون على الذات بإنفرادها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r11.claim: When all praise is considered together, it begins and ends in God: there is no praiser or praised one besides Him, and human understanding cannot encompass Him.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r11.anchor: وإذا أعتبر الجمع كان الكل منه وإليه ( وإن إلى ربك المنتهى )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r12.claim: Praise precedes the name “God” because the speaker is about to utter its meaning; the contextual need can outweigh the name’s greater intrinsic importance, unlike another verse whose arrangement has another purpose.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r12.anchor: وإنما قدم الحمد على الأسم الكريم لإقتضاء المقام مزيد إهتمام به

ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r13.claim: Rabb originally denotes nurturing: bringing a thing gradually to the perfection suited to its primordial capacity; the word’s derivation and grammatical form are debated.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p76/r13.anchor: والرب في الأصل مصدر بمعنى التربية وهي تبلغ الشيء إلى كماله بحسب إستعداده الأزلي

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r1.claim: Rabb is also used for creator, master, king, benefactor, reformer, worshiped one, and possessor; most commonly it means nurturing, which some treat as the literal sense because it comes first to mind.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r1.anchor: ويطلق أيضا على الخالق والسيد والملك والمنعم والمصلح والمعبود والصاحب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r2.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers derivation from nurturing and takes the other uses as metaphors, since they all involve care and Arabic principles favor metaphor over homonymy; al-Zamakhsharī instead chooses “owner.”
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r2.anchor: والأول أرجح لأن جميعها يوجد معنى التربية ووجود العلاقة أمارة المجاز

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r3.claim: He rejects “owner” here because “Owner of the Day of Judgment” would repeat the meaning, with no evident reason for placing al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm between them; nurturing better fits the context and signals divine beneficence, power, and wisdom.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r3.anchor: لأنه بعد تسليم أنه حقيقة في ذلك يؤدي إلى أن يكون مالك يوم الدين تكرارا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r4.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r4.claim: Al-Ṭībī favors simultaneously applying rabb to both meanings through their shared core, comparing it to an allusive expression that does not exclude its explicit sense.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r4.anchor: ما أختاره الطيبي من وجوب حمل الرب على كلا مفهوميه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r5.claim: Unqualified rabb is not widely used linguistically for anyone but God; in a construct or with a qualifier it can express limited lordship, though unrestricted human uses occur rarely.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r5.anchor: لا يطلق لغة على غيره تعالى إطلاقا مستفيضا إلا مقيدا بإضافة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r6.speaker: السيوطي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r6.claim: Al-Suyūṭī takes the prohibition on calling another “lord” as religious rather than linguistic; an old poem and al-Jawharī support him, while al-Shihāb allows non-owner senses with contextual indication.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r6.anchor: وأستظهر الإمام السيوطي أن المراد نفي إطلاقه على غيره تعالى شرعا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r7.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r7.claim: Al-Bukhārī and Muslim report from Abū Hurayra that one should not say “feed your lord” or “give your lord ablution”; instead one should say “my master” or “my patron.”
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r7.anchor: وروى الشيخان عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه لا يقل أحدكم أطعم ربك

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r8.claim: The human uses “return to your lord” and “he is my lord,” and Joseph’s brothers prostrating to him, are explained as licenses specific to that historical period.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r8.anchor: وأجابوا عن قول يوسف عليه السلام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r9.claim: Some say al-ʿālamīn is a plural restricted to rational beings; replies derive it from rational ʿālam after restriction, from grammatical predominance, or by treating knowledgeable signs as rational.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r9.anchor: وأعترض بأنه يعم العقلاء وغيرهم وعالمون خاص بالعقلاء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r10.claim: Another debate asks whether al-ʿālamīn is a regular plural, a collective noun, or a name for a totality; al-Ālūsī concludes it is a true plural because each member is itself called an ʿālam.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p77/r10.anchor: على أن للعالمين آحادا يسمى كل منها عالما

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r1.claim: ʿĀlam originally means a means of knowing, then came to denote what reveals the Creator: all that exists besides Him, substances and accidents, either as the whole or as each kind.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r1.anchor: والعالم كالخاتم أسم لما يعلم به وغلب فيما يعلم به الخالق تعالى شأنه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r2.claim: Although common usage applies ʿālam to the totality or to a kind, not ordinarily to an individual, its original sense can apply to every part, since every contingent thing witnesses its need for the necessary Creator.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r2.anchor: لتحقق الحاجة إلى المؤثر الواجب لذاته في الكل

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r3.claim: Every created thing, great or small, present or absent, is a clear sign of the Creator and a path to tawḥīd; the author quotes a poem saying each thing has a sign of God’s oneness.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r3.anchor: وفي كل شيء له آية تدل على أنه واحد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r4.claim: The plural al-ʿālamīn guarantees inclusion of every created kind: a singular definite noun could be heard as the familiar perceptible world, whereas the plural distributes lordship across all named kinds and their individuals.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r4.anchor: فجمع ليفيد الشمول قطعا لأنه حينئذ لا يكون مستعملا في المجموع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r5.claim: The claim that a definite singular is more comprehensive does not undermine this wording; the plural avoids the familiar-world reading and includes all created genera.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r5.anchor: وحديث أن إستغراق المفرد أشمل على ما فيه أمر فرغ عنه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r6.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r6.claim: Some commentators restrict the worlds to beings with knowledge: angels and the two accountable species, humans and jinn.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p78/r6.anchor: وبعضهم خص العالمين بذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r1.speaker: الإمام الأسيوطي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r1.claim: Al-Suyuti derives the term from knowledge when the worlds are understood generally, and from a sign when the term is taken in its broader sense.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r1.anchor: هو مشتق من العلم وعلى القول بالعموم من العلامة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r2.claim: One reported view limits the worlds to jinn and humans, appealing to the description of the Messenger as a warner to all worlds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r2.anchor: وقيل هم الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r3.speaker: جعفر الصادق
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r3.claim: A view transmitted from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq limits the worlds to humans; al-Alusi suggests humans are the central object of religious duties and messengers.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r3.anchor: وهو المنقول عن جعفر الصادق والمأخوذ من بحر أهل البيت ورب البيت أدرى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r4.claim: Humanity is a concentrated summary of created things, and reflection on the self reveals the Creator's greatness; the apt reading here remains universal.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r4.anchor: ولعل الوجه فيه الإشارة إلى أن الإنسان هو المقصود بالذات من التكليف بالحلال والحرام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r5.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r5.claim: An aphorism attributed to the Gate of Knowledge says that the human being contains the greater world and carries both remedy and illness within.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r5.anchor: دواؤك فيك وما تبصر وداؤك منك وما تشعر وتزعم أنك جرم صغير

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r6.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the universal sense because the worlds are innumerable and God's nurturing encompasses every existing thing, both celestial and earthly.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r6.anchor: والمناسب للمقام هنا العموم والعوالم كثيرة لا تحصيها الأرقام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r7.speaker: بعض الأخبار
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r7.claim: A report says God created one hundred thousand lamps suspended from the Throne, with the heavens, earth, Paradise, and Hell in one lamp; only God knows the rest.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r7.anchor: وروى في بعض الأخبار أن الله تعالى خلق مائة ألف قنديل وعلقها بالعرش

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r8.speaker: كعب الأحبار
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r8.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says only God can count the number of worlds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r8.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار لا يحصى عدد العالمين إلا الله تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r9.claim: Every contingent being depends on God's continual nurturing for existence and persistence; sustaining it also means keeping all its possible impediments absent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p79/r9.anchor: وما من ذرة من ذرات العوالم إلا وهي حيطة تربيته سبحانه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r1.claim: A mystic's saying contrasts God's care for the servant with the servant's lax service: God tends him as though no other servant existed, though God owns countless others.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r1.anchor: أحسن قول بعض العارفين أنه تعالى يملك عبادا غيرك وأنت ليس لك رب سواه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r2.claim: The masculine sound plural can denote paucity despite the many worlds, underscoring that all are insignificant beside God's majesty; Arabic usage can also allow either number.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r2.anchor: تنبيها على أن العوالم وإن كثرت قليلة بل أقل من القليل في جنب عظمة الله تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r3.claim: Rabb names the station of divine lordship that calls for the created objects required by attributes such as knowledge, power, will, and hearing.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r3.anchor: إلى حضرة الربوبية التي هي مقام العارفين وهي اسم للمرتبة المقتضية للأسماء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r4.claim: Names beneath Rabb include attributes shared in some respect between Creator and creation and active names exclusive to God; the latter belong under Malik.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r4.anchor: والأسماء التي تحت أسم الرب هي الأسماء المشتركة بين الحق والخلق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r5.claim: Rahman is more comprehensive than Rabb because it gathers every exalted divine attribute, whether exclusive to God or related to creation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r5.anchor: وأما الفرق بين الرب والرحمن فهو أن الرحمن عندهم أسم لمرتبة أختصت بجميع الأوصاف العلية الألهية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r6.claim: Allah signifies the all-encompassing divine essence and highest level; below it are oneness, mercifulness, lordship, and sovereignty, while absolute divine uniqueness has no manifestation of created qualities.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r6.anchor: فهو أسم لمرتبة ذاتية جامعة وفلك محيط بالحقائق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r7.speaker: أرباب الظاهر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r7.claim: Outward scholars explain frequent supplication with Rabb as fitting because a petitioner seeks what seems beneficial for personal nurture and care.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r7.anchor: وقال أرباب الظاهر الداعي لا يطلب إلا ما يظنه صلاحا لحاله وتربية لنفسه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r8.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r8.claim: Sufi masters say the appropriate divine name in prayer changes with the seeker's spiritual state and whether the experience is one of differentiation or union.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p80/r8.anchor: وعند ساداتنا الصوفية قدس الله تعالى أسرارهم يختلف الكلام بإختلاف المقام فرقا وجمعا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r1.claim: The primordial spirits first heard and affirmed God's lordship, so they call on Him by the first name through which they recognized and pledged themselves to Him.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r1.anchor: فهم ينادونه سبحانه بأول أسم قررهم به فأقروا وأخذ به عليهم العهد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r2.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r2.claim: Ibn ʿArabi describes the universal Spirit, initially unaware of its origin, as journeying inward until God showed it its secrets and taught it to recognize Him as Lord, while reserving divinity to Himself.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r2.anchor: مما حاصله أن الله تعالى لما أوجد الكلمة المعبر عنها بالروح الكلي إيجاد إبداع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r3.claim: Opening the Fatiha's descriptions with Lord of the worlds suits the Prophet's mission as a profound act of nurturing humanity and hints at compassion for all people.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r3.anchor: ويعلم منه إشارة سر إفتتاح الأوصاف في الفاتحة برب العالمين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r4.speaker: زيد بن علي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r4.claim: A reading attributed to Zayd ibn ʿAli puts Rabb al-ʿalamin in the accusative; al-Alusi finds the first grammatical explanation, an implied praise or mention verb, most apparent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r4.anchor: وقد قرء رب العالمين بالنصب ونسب ذلك إلى زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r5.claim: One analysis treats the accusative as an adjective cut off from its antecedent, supplying an implied verb such as I praise or I mention; an objection about the following adjective is answered by taking Rahman as apposition.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r5.anchor: فقيل نصب على القطع ويقدر العامل هنا أمدح للمقام أو أذكر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r6.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r6.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects deriving the accusative from the earlier praise merely by attraction, arguing that this mechanism belongs to coordination; al-Alusi disputes that objection using grammatical authorities.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r6.anchor: وليس على التوهم كما توهم أبو حيان فضعفه بزعمه أنه من خصائص العطف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r7.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r7.claim: Another analysis supplies the earlier word al-ḥamd as the governing verb; objections concern the definite verbal noun's government and an intervening predicate, both answered by grammarians.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r7.anchor: وقيل بفعل مقدر دل عليه الحمد وليس على التوهم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r8.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r8.claim: Other proposed parses take Rabb as a vocative or a past-tense verb, but al-Alusi finds the vocative unclear and the verbal reading syntactically remote.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r8.anchor: وقيل بالنداء ولا يخفى ما فيه من اللبس والفصل والإلتفات

ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r9.claim: Al-Alusi considers an accusative absolute construction the strongest and nearly compelled by the apparent wording.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p81/r9.anchor: والمناسب المناسبة وأهون الأمور عندي أولها بل يكاد يقطع الظاهر بالقطع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r5.claim: The descriptions close by pointing to resurrection, just as Lord of the worlds opened with origination; they explain the prior praise and prepare for the prayer that follows.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r5.anchor: وإنما ختم سبحانه هذه الأوصاف بهذا الوصف إشارة إلى الإعادة كما أفتتح بما يشير إلى الإبداء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r6.claim: The five names answer four grounds for praising someone: inherent perfection, past beneficence, hoped-for future kindness, and fear of power; God encompasses them all.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r6.anchor: أن الذي يحمده الناس ويعظمونه إنما يكون حمده وتعظيمه لأحد أمور أربعة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r7.speaker: الإمام
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r7.claim: An argument for rational gratitude before revelation says the verse establishes God's praiseworthiness through creation, mercy, and future judgment; al-Alusi replies that this proof itself is scriptural, not rational.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r7.anchor: ومن الناس من أستدل كما قال الإمام على وجوب اشكر عقلا قبل مجيء الشرع

ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r8.claim: Al-Alusi says deriving the duty of gratitude from God's own revealed declaration only proves it through revelation, so it cannot establish a pre-revelation rational duty.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r8.anchor: فهو سمعي لا عقلي فالمستدل به كناطح صخرة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r9.claim: A Sufi anthropology maps the five divine names to the human's angelic intellect, devilish, predatory, animal, and dense bodily dimensions, with cited verses illustrating the correspondences.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p85/r9.anchor: فالإنسان بدن ونفس شيطانية ونفس سبعية ونفس بهيمية وجوهر ملكي عقلي

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.claim: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.anchor: واتفقوا على أن الفاتحة سبع آيات فالآية الأولى عند من يعدها من الفاتحة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r1.claim: Al-hamd is phrased as a report that God alone deserves praise, while teaching people to say ‘praise belongs to God.’
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r1.anchor: لفظه خبر كأنه يخبر أن المستحق للحمد هو الله عز وجل وفيه تعليم الخلق تقديره قولوا الحمد لله

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r2.claim: Hamd can mean gratitude for a blessing or praise for a praiseworthy quality; it is broader than thanks, since one thanks for blessings but praises knowledge or courage too.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r2.anchor: والحمد يكون بمعنى الشكر على النعمة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r3.claim: Another distinction says praise is spoken verbally while gratitude is enacted bodily.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r3.anchor: وقيل: الحمد باللسان قولا والشكر بالأركان فعلا

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r4.claim: The lām in lillah marks entitlement, as in saying that a house belongs to Zayd.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r4.anchor: اللام فيه للاستحقاق كما يقال الدار لزيد

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r5.claim: Rabb means owner or one who nurtures and sets right; God owns and sustains all worlds, whereas a human may be called rabb only with a qualifier.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r5.anchor: فالله تعالى مالك العالمين ومربيهم، ولا يقال للمخلوق

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r6.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r6.claim: Ibn Abbas defines the worlds as jinn and humans because they are morally addressed beings; the verse calls the Quran a warning to them.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r6.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هم الجن والإنس لأنهم المكلفون بالخطاب

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r7.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد والحسن
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r7.claim: Qatada, Mujahid, and al-Hasan understand the worlds as all created beings, as Pharaoh’s question and Moses’ answer clarify.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r7.anchor: وقال قتادة ومجاهد والحسن: هم جميع المخلوقات

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r8.speaker: أبو عبيدة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r8.claim: Abu Ubayda counts four world communities—angels, humans, jinn, and devils—and excludes beasts because they do not reason.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r8.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: هم أربع أمم: الملائكة والإنس والجن والشياطين

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r9.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r9.claim: Saʿid b. al-Musayyab says God has one thousand worlds: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r9.anchor: قال سعيد بن المسيب لله ألف عالم ستمائة في البحر وأربعمائة في البر

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r10.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r10.claim: Muqatil b. Hayyan says there are eighty thousand worlds, evenly divided between sea and land.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r10.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن حيان: لله ثمانون ألف عالم أربعون ألفا في البحر وأربعون ألفا في البر

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r11.speaker: وهب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r11.claim: Wahb says there are eighteen thousand worlds and this world is only one of them, like a tent in a desert compared with the ruined land.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p52/r11.anchor: وقال وهب لله ثمانية عشر ألف عالم الدنيا عالم منها

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53/r12.speaker: كعب الأحبار
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53/r12.claim: Kaʿb al-Ahbar says no one can count the worlds except God, who alone knows his armies.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p53/r12.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار: لا يحصي عدد العالمين أحد إلا الله

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r1.claim: Ḥamd is praise for chosen excellence, including a blessing, while madḥ is praise for any excellence; one praises knowledge but merely commends beauty.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r1.anchor: هو الثناء على الجميل الاختياري من نعمة أو غيرها

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r2.claim: Some regard ḥamd and madḥ as equivalent; shukr is gratitude for a blessing expressed in speech, action, and belief.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r2.anchor: والشكر: مقابلة النعمة قولا وعملا واعتقادا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r3.claim: Gratitude is broader than praise and commendation in one respect but narrower in another; praise is its chief expression because it displays blessings and makes gratitude audible.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r3.anchor: فهو أعم منهما من وجه، وأخص من آخر ولما كان الحمد من شعب الشكر

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r4.claim: A report calls praise the head of gratitude and says one who does not praise God has not thanked Him.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r4.anchor: الحمد رأس الشكر، وما شكر الله من لم يحمده

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r5.claim: The word is nominative as a subject with لله as predicate, though an accusative reading exists; nominative signals praise as universal and enduring rather than newly arising.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r5.anchor: وإنما عدل عنه إلى الرفع ليدل على عموم الحمد وثباته له

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r6.claim: The definite article can mark the genus or all praise: in reality every good comes from God, directly or through an intermediary, as 16:53 says.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r6.anchor: إذ الحمد في الحقيقة كله له، إذ ما من خير إلا وهو موليه بوسط أو بغير وسط

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r7.claim: The entitlement to praise implies that God is living, powerful, willing, and knowing.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r7.anchor: وفيه إشعار بأنه تعالى حي قادر مريد عالم

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r8.claim: Two recitations assimilate the dāl and lām in either direction, treating them as one word because the terms are used together.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2/r8.anchor: وقرىء الحمد لله بإتباع الدال اللام وبالعكس تنزيلا لهما

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.claim: Rabb originally means gradual nurturing toward completion, then became an intensive description; another derivation treats it as a noun for the owner who preserves and develops what he owns.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r1.anchor: وهي تبليغ الشيء إلى كماله شيئا فشيئا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.claim: Rabb is used of others only in a qualified phrase, whereas al-ʿālam names what makes something known and came to mean everything besides God.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r2.anchor: ولا يطلق على غيره تعالى إلا مقيدا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.claim: The worlds comprise all substances and accidents, whose possibility and need for a necessary cause show God's existence; the plural gathers different genera, with rational beings predominant in its form.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r3.anchor: وهو كل ما سواه من الجواهر والأعراض، فإنها لإمكانها وافتقارها إلى مؤثر واجب لذاته تدل

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.claim: An alternative restricts the term to knowledgeable beings—angels, humans, and jinn—with other creatures included only secondarily.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r4.anchor: اسم وضع لذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.claim: Another view means human beings here: each person contains counterparts of the greater world's substances and accidents, through which the Creator is known, as 51:21 invites people to observe themselves.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r5.anchor: عني به الناس ههنا فإن كل واحد منهم عالم

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.claim: An accusative reading treats رب العالمين as praise, direct address, or an implied action indicated by الحمد.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r6.anchor: وقرىء { رب العلمين } بالنصب على المدح.

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.claim: Possible things need God not only to originate them but also to keep them in existence.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:2#2/r7.anchor: وفيه دليل على أن الممكنات كما هي مفتقرة إلى المحدث حال حدوثها فهي مفتقرة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.speaker: أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.claim: Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.anchor: قال شيخنا الإمام المحقق أبو الفضل محمد بن العلامة القدوة أبي عبد الله محمد ابن العلامة القدوة أبي القاسم محمد المشدالي المغربي

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.claim: A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.anchor: أن اسم كل سورة مترجم عن مقصودها هلأن أسم كل شيء تظهر المناسبة بينه وبين مسماه عنوانه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.claim: The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.anchor: فمدار هذه الأسماء كما ترى على أمر خفي كاف لكل مراد وهو المراقبة التي سأقول إنها مقصودها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.claim: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.anchor: فكل شيء لا يفتتح بها لا اعتداد به ، وهي كنز لكل شيء شافية لكل داء

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.claim: The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.anchor: الغرض الذي سبقت له الفاتحة وه إثبات استحقاق الله تعالى لجميع المحامد وصفا الكمال ، واختصاصه بملك الدنيا والآخرة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.claim: The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.anchor: وأشد منه أنه لما كانت نسبة البسملة من الفاتحة نسبة الفاتحة من القرآن صدرت بها الفاتحة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.claim: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.anchor: ولما كانت البسملة نوعا من الحمد ناسب كل المناسبة تعقيبها باسم الحمد ةالكلي الجامع لجميع أفراده

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r7.claim: Al-hamd lillah establishes that God deserves praise for His essence and perfection; Rabb al-alamin adds His lordship, sovereignty and beneficence, while the worlds point to creation's beginning and the inference to resurrection.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r7.anchor: ولما أثبت بقوله : { الحمد لله } أنه المستحق لجميع المحامد لا لشىء غير ذاته الحائز لجميع الكمالات أشار إلى

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r8.claim: Al-Harali defines al-hamd as complete praise covering all actions and attributes, all from God and free of blame; its definite form signals praise reaching its full extent.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r8.anchor: قال الحرالي : و { الحمد } المدح الكامل الذي يحيط بجميع الأفعال والأوصاف , على أن جميعها إنما هو من الله سبحانه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r9.claim: Lordship does not yield wellbeing without mercy, so Rahman and Rahim follow al-hamd and encourage people to persist in praising God.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r9.anchor: ولما كانت مرتبة الربوبية لا تستجمع الصلاح إل بالرحمة اتبع ذلك بصفتي { الرحمن الرحيم } ترغبيا

BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.claim: Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.anchor: قال الحرالي : وهذه الآيات أى هذه وما بهدها مما جاء كلام الله فيه جارياعلى لسان خلقه فإن القرآن كله كلام الله

BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.claim: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.anchor: وتلك هي صلاتهم المقسمة التى عبر عنها فيما صح عنه علية الصلاة والسلام من قوله تعالى : ( قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين )

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.claim: The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.anchor: قال الأصبهاني : فإن القرآن معجز والركن الأبين الإعجاز يتعلق بالنظم والترتيب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r5.speaker: مسعود التفتازاني
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r5.claim: Al-Taftazani maps the Fatiha's blessings to two creations and two preservations: creation in Rabb al-alamin, preservation in mercy, second creation in judgment, and afterlife preservation in worship onward.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r5.anchor: كما قال العلامة سعد الدين مسعود ابن عمرو التفتازاني الشافعي . إلى جميع النعم فغنها ترجع إلى إيجاد وإبقاء ثانيافي دار الفناء والبقاء

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r6.claim: The root and forms of al-hamd suggest reaching an end, extension, encompassing and circularity; these imply lowering the head and can lead to contentment and gratitude.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r6.anchor: وهذا يرجع إلى أصل مدلول الحمد فإن مادته بكل ترتيب تدور على بلغوغ الغاية ويلزم منه الاتساع

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.claim: Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو الحسن الحرالي في مفتاح الباب القفل لفهم القرآن المنزل في أخر الباب التاسع منه : ولننه هذه الأبواب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.claim: Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.anchor: ووجه فوت أم القرآن مقصود تنزيله التفصيل والجوامع , فيه نجوم مبثوثة غير منتظمة , وحداة إثر واحدة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.claim: A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.anchor: بعثت لأتمم مكارم الأخلاق . أن إلى ربك المنتهى .

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.claim: Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.anchor: ومن مجيده وهو ما حربت أحكامه من بين عاجل ما شهد وآجل ما علم

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.claim: Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.anchor: وما كان منه بتدريج وتقريب للأفهام ففاءت من حال إلى حال

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.claim: The passage names al-Baqara 2:281 as the last revealed verse and says its recitation position between the debt verse and the verse before it shows revelation and recitation order can differ.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.anchor: وجعلوها بين آية الدين والآية قبلها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.claim: Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.anchor: وأما الجمع ففي قلبه نسبة جوامعه السبع في أم القرآن إلى القرآن بمنزلة نسبة جمعه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.claim: Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.anchor: وعلى لسانه في أمد أيام النبوة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.speaker: عائشة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.claim: Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.anchor: قالت عائشة رضى الله عنها : كان خلقه القرآن

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.claim: Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.anchor: فالآيات الثلاث الول قال شاملة لكل معنى تضمنته الأسماء الحسنى والصفات العلى

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.claim: Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.anchor: فقد يتطابق قرآن الأمر وتطور الخلق وقد لا يتابق والله يتولى إقامتها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.claim: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضى الله عنه قال : سمعت زسول الله صلى اله عليه وسلم يقول

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.claim: Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.anchor: مقصودها إقامة الدليل على أن الكتاب هدى ليتبع يفي كل ما قال ، وأعظم ما يهدي إليه الإيمالن بالغيب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.claim: The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.anchor: فلذلك سميت بها السورة وكانت بذلك أحق من قصة إبراهيم عليه الصلاة والسلام لأنها في نوع البشر

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.claim: The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.anchor: ولا سيما وقد اتبعت بوصف القلوب والحجارة بما عم اللمهتدين بالكتاب والضالين فوصفها بالقسوة الموجبة للشقوة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.claim: The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.anchor: وفيها إشارة إلى أن هذا الكتاب فينا كما لو كان فينا خليفة من أولي العزم من الرسل يرشدنا في كل أمر

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.claim: Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.anchor: وسميت الزهراء لإنارتها طريق الهداية والكفاية في الدنيا والآخرة ، ولأيجابها إسفار الوجوه يفي يوم الجزاء

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.claim: Because praise is the seventh inclusive letter, the Fatiha begins with it and gathers the seven universals diffused through the Qur'an, as the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.anchor: ولما كان حرف الحمد هو سابعها الجامع افتتح الله به سبحانه وتعالى الفاتحة أم القرآن وأم الكتاب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.claim: The first verse contains praise's seventh letter; the second contains the lawful and forbidden letters that Rahmaniyyah establishes for worldly life, allowing enjoyment and removing either prohibition's burden or sin.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.anchor: فالآية الأولى تشتمل على حرف الحمد السابع ، والثانية تشتمل على حرفي الحلال والحرام

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r3.claim: Alternatively, and the author says this is likelier, Rahmaniyyah universally grants blessings and removes harms whether for felicity or misery, while Rahimiyyah specifically gives the blessings and protection that lead to felicity.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r3.anchor: وأما الرحيمية فطهرتهم من مضار أبدانهم ورجاسة نفوسهم ومجهلة قلوبهم

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r6.claim: The fifth verse's request returns to praise, the sixth to the grace of lawful and forbidden provisions, and the seventh to the sovereign's command; together these complete all seven letters.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r6.anchor: وعادتت مسألة الآيةى الخاتمسة على حرف الحمد ومسألة الآية السادسة على آية النعمة من حرفي الحلال والحرام

BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3.claim: Baqara answers the Fatiha's plea for guidance by directing worshippers to the Book, describing the guided and denied groups as patterns to follow or avoid; its pious are the straight path and its others the path of ruin.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r3.anchor: وأما منسبة ما بعد ذلك للفاتحة فهو أنه لما أخبلا سبحانه وتعالى أن عباده المخلصين سألوا في الفاتحة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r4.claim: Alternatively, the surah's purpose is solely to describe the Book; it establishes the truth of its meaning, exposes disbelief and hypocrisy to show that inward faith matters, then proves its inimitable form and authority for teaching law.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p31/r4.anchor: وإن شئت قلت : مقصود هذه السورة وصف الكتاب فقط وما عدا ذلك فتوابع ولوازم

DURR-FULL:v1p24/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p24/r2.speaker: الله تعالى
DURR-FULL:v1p24/r2.claim: When the servant says “al-hamd lillah,” God says the servant has thanked and praised Him.
DURR-FULL:v1p24/r2.anchor: فإذا قال {الحمد لله} قال الله: شكرني

DURR-FULL:v1p24/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
