DURR-FULL:v1p24/r3.speaker: الله تعالى
DURR-FULL:v1p24/r3.claim: The report explains “Lord of the worlds” as lord of humans, jinn, angels, devils, all creation, and everything.
DURR-FULL:v1p24/r3.anchor:
فإذا قال {رب العالمين} قال الله شهد عبدي أني رب العالمين
رب الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين

DURR-FULL:v1p29/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r8.claim: A prophetic report calls al-hamd the head of gratitude: a servant has not thanked God until praising Him.
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r8.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قرأ {الحمد} رأس الشكر

DURR-FULL:v1p29/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r9.claim: When a returned camel prompted the Prophet to fulfill a vow of gratitude, he said “al-hamd lillah,” which the Companions accepted as thanks.
DURR-FULL:v1p29/r9.anchor: عن النواس بن سمعان قال: سرقت ناقة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال لئن ردها الله لأشكرن ربي

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r1.speaker: الحكم بن عمير
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r1.claim: In a weak report, saying “al-hamd lillah rabb al-alamin” counts as thanking God, after which He increases the speaker.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r1.anchor: قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا قلت {الحمد لله رب العالمين} فقد شكرت الله

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas says that when the servant says al-hamd, God says the servant has thanked Him.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r2.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال {الحمد لله} كلمة الشكر إذا قال العبد {الحمد لله} قال الله شكرني عبدي

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas defines praise as gratitude, praise of God, and acknowledgment of His blessings, guidance, and originating bounty.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r3.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: {الحمد} هو الشكر والاستحذاء لله والاقرار بنعمه وهدايته وابتدائه

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r4.speaker: علي
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r4.claim: Ali answers Umar that al-hamd is a phrase God approved for Himself and loves to be spoken.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r4.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: قال عمر: قد علمنا سبحان الله

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r5.speaker: كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r5.claim: Kab says “al-hamd lillah” is praise of God.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r5.anchor: عن كعب قال {الحمد لله} ثناء على الله

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r6.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak calls al-hamd the cloak of the Merciful.

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r7.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن الجبائي
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r7.claim: Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Jubba'i says prayer, fasting, and every good deed for God are gratitude, with al-hamd the best form.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r7.anchor: عن أبي عبد الرحمن الجبائي قال: الصلاة شكر والصيام شكر وكل خير تفعله لله شكر

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r8.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r8.claim: The Prophet says the best remembrance is “la ilaha illa Allah” and the best supplication is “al-hamd lillah.”
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r8.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أفضل الذكر لا إله إلا الله وأفضل الدعاء {الحمد لله

DURR-FULL:v1p30/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r9.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r9.claim: A sound report says the praise offered for any divine blessing is better than the blessing received; related reports extend this to every blessing and all the world.
DURR-FULL:v1p30/r9.anchor: بسند صحيح عن أنس قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ما أنعم الله على عبده نعمة فقال {الحمد لله

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r1.claim: The Prophet says purification is half of faith, al-hamd fills the balance, and glorification fills the space between heaven and earth, among other deeds' spiritual benefits.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r1.anchor: عن أبي موسى الأشعري قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الطهور شطر الإيمان {والحمد لله} تملأ الميزان

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r2.claim: Another report says al-hamd fills the balance, while tasbih is half of it and takbir fills the space between heaven and earth.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r2.anchor: عن رجل من بني سليم أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال سبحان الله نصف الميزان والحمد لله تملأ الميزان

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r3.claim: Ibn Umar reports that al-hamd fills the balance and there is no barrier between “la ilaha illa Allah” and God.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r3.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمر قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم التسبيح نصف الميزان والحمد لله تملؤه

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r4.speaker: الأسود بن سريع
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r4.claim: Al-Aswad ibn Sari asked to recite praises he had composed, and the Prophet replied that God loves praise.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r4.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع التميمي قال قلت: يا رسول الله ألا أنشدك محامد حمدت بها ربي

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r5.claim: The Prophet says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, so God praised Himself with “al-hamd lillah.”
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r5.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال ليس شيء أحب إليه الحمد من الله

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r6.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r6.claim: Anas reports that deliberation is from God, haste from Satan, God is most ready to excuse, and praise is most beloved to Him.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r6.anchor: عن أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال التأني من الله والعجلة من الشيطان

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r7.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r7.claim: A report says monotheism is the price of Paradise and al-hamd repays each blessing, while people receive Paradise according to their deeds.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r7.anchor: عن أنس قال: قال رسول الله التوحيد ثمن الجنة

DURR-FULL:v1p31/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r8.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r8.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that every significant matter begun without praise of God is deficient.
DURR-FULL:v1p31/r8.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه بحمد الله فهو أقطع

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r1.claim: When someone sneezes and says al-hamd, an angel responds “Lord of the worlds”; when the sneezer repeats it, the angel says “may God have mercy on you.”
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r1.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال: إذا عطس أحدكم فقال {الحمد لله} قال الملك: رب العالمين فإذا قال رب العالمين

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r2.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r2.claim: A report attributed to Ali says that saying “al-hamd lillah rabb al-alamin” at each heard sneeze prevents toothache and earache.
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r2.anchor: عن علي ابن أبي طالب قال: من قال عند كل عطسة سمعها {الحمد لله رب العالمين} على كل حال

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r3.speaker: واثلة بن الأسقع
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r3.claim: Wathila reports that praising God when greeting a sneezer prevents abdominal illness; another report says God told Solomon to remember Him when someone sneezes even seven seas away.
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r3.anchor: من بادر العاطس بالحمد لم يضره شيء من داء البطن

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r4.claim: After an expedition returned safely, the Prophet fulfilled his pledge to thank God by saying “al-hamd lillah.”
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r4.anchor: عن علي قال بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم سرية من أهله فقال: اللهم لك علي إن رددتهم سالمين

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r5.claim: A report about an Ansar expedition says the Prophet pledged thanks if they returned safe with spoils, then said he had fulfilled that pledge and praised God.
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r5.anchor: سعد بن اسحق بن كعب بن عجرة عن أبيه عن جده قال بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بعثا من الأنصار

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r6.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r6.claim: When Jaafar ibn Muhammad's mule returned, he thanked God with only “al-hamd lillah,” saying this gathered all praise.
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r6.anchor: عن جعفر بن محمد قال: فقد أبي بغلته فقال: لئن ردها الله علي لأحمدنه بمحامد يرضاها

DURR-FULL:v1p32/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r7.speaker: منصور بن إبراهيم
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r7.claim: Mansur ibn Ibrahim reports the saying that al-hamd is the most multiplied speech.
DURR-FULL:v1p32/r7.anchor: منصور بن ابراهيم قال: يقال إن {الحمد لله} أكثر الكلام تضعيفا

DURR-FULL:v1p33/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r1.speaker: سفيان الثوري
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r1.claim: Sufyan al-Thawri says al-hamd is both remembrance and gratitude, a combination found in no other expression.
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r1.anchor: عن محمد بن حرب قال: قال سفيان الثوري: {الحمد لله} ذكر وشكر وليس شيء يكون ذكرا وشكرا غيره

DURR-FULL:v1p33/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r2.claim: Abd Allah ibn Amr assigns distinct meanings to the formulas: tasbih is the creatures' prayer, al-hamd is gratitude, tahlil is sincerity, takbir fills heaven and earth, and “no power” expresses surrender.
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r2.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص قال: إن العبد إذا قال: سبحان الله فهي صلاة الخلائق

DURR-FULL:v1p33/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr interpret “Lord of the worlds” as Lord of jinn and humans.
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r3.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله {رب العالمين} قال: الجن والإنس

DURR-FULL:v1p33/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas also explains the Lord of the worlds as God of all creation, the heavens and their inhabitants, the earths and their inhabitants, and all between them, known or unknown.
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r4.anchor:
عن ابن عباس في قوله {رب العالمين} قال: إله الخلق كله
السموات كلهن ومن فيهن

DURR-FULL:v1p33/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r5.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r5.claim: A weak report says God created a thousand communities, 600 in the sea and 400 on land; locusts are the first to perish, followed by the rest like beads when their string breaks.
DURR-FULL:v1p33/r5.anchor: بسند ضعيف عن جابر بن عبد الله قال: قل الجراد في سنة من سني عمر

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r1.claim: Qatada says “Lord of the worlds” encompasses every class of created beings.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r1.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله {رب العالمين} قال: كل صنف عالم

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r2.speaker: تتبع الجهري
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r2.claim: A report counts the worlds as a thousand communities, 600 in the sea and 400 on land.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r2.anchor:
عن تتبع الجهري قال: العالمون ألف أمة
فستمائة في البحر وأربعمائة في البر

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r3.speaker: أبو العالية
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r3.claim: Abu al-Aliya says humans and jinn are two worlds and there are eighteen thousand other worlds of angels, with 3,500 worshipping worlds at each of the earth's four corners.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r3.anchor: عن أبي العالية في قوله {رب العالمين} قال: الإنس عالم والجن عالم وما سوى ذلك ثمانية عشر ألف عالم

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r4.speaker: أبي كعب
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r4.claim: Ubayy ibn Kab identifies the worlds as angels, numbering eighteen thousand; he describes groups in four regions with countless attendants.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r4.anchor: عن أبي كعب قال: العالمون الملائكة وهم ثمانون ثمانية عشر ألف ملك

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r5.speaker: وهب
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r5.claim: Wahb says God has eighteen thousand worlds, of which this world is only one.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r5.anchor:
عن وهب قال: إن لله عز وجل ثمانية عشر ألف عالم
الدنيا منها عالم واحد

DURR-FULL:v1p34/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r9.speaker: أم سلمة
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r9.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as verse one, al-hamd as two, al-Rahman al-Rahim as three, Malik yawm al-din as four, then indicated five for the next verse.
DURR-FULL:v1p34/r9.anchor: عن أم سلمة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ في الصلاة {بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم} فعدها آية {الحمد لله رب العالمين} آيتين

DURR-FULL:v1p36/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p36/r5.speaker: عائشة
DURR-FULL:v1p36/r5.claim: During a drought prayer, the Prophet invoked God as Lord of the worlds, the Merciful, and Master of Judgment, asking for rain that would sustain them; Abu Dawud calls the report rare with a good chain, and says it supports the Medinan no-alif reading.
DURR-FULL:v1p36/r5.anchor: عن عائشة قالت شكا الناس إلى رسول الله

TABATABAI:10:10#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:10:10#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:10:10#2/r3.claim: Praise is description of God’s beautiful acts; only God’s sincere servants, whom He draws near without intermediary, can properly describe Him, as 37:159 says.
TABATABAI:10:10#2/r3.anchor: أن الحمد توصيف، ولا يسع وصفه تعالى لأحد من خلقه إلا للمخلصين من عباده الذين أخلصهم لنفسه وخصهم بكرامة من القرب

RAZI-FULL:v1p15/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p15/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p15/r2.claim: Praise is due to the one who possesses everything in the heavens.

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r5.claim: Praise is praise for blessing, and praising a blessing presupposes knowing it; God’s blessings cannot be counted, as the cited verse says.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r5.anchor: الحمد إنما يكون حمدا على النعمة والحمد على النعمة لا يمكن إلا بعد معرفة تلك النعمة

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r6.claim: Al-Rāzī illustrates the scale of the inquiry through the human body: anatomists found nearly five thousand benefits, and known examples are only a drop beside the unknown; understanding divine wisdom in human creation entails ten thousand or more questions.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r6.anchor: وجدوا قريبا من خمسة آلاف نوع من المنافع والمصالح التي دبرها الله عز وجل بحكمته في تخليق بدن الإنسان

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r7.claim: Considering divine wisdom in the throne, heavens, luminaries, elements, minerals, plants, and animals adds vast further questions; most of creation is made for human benefit, and al-hamd lillah thus encompasses roughly a million issues.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r7.anchor: علم أن هذا المجموع مشتمل على ألف ألف مسألة أو أكثر أو أقل ثم إنه تعالى نبه على أن أكثرها مخلوق لمنفعة الإنسان

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r8.claim: The construction rabb al-ʿālamīn is an iḍāfa, whose relation cannot be known without first knowing both correlated terms.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r8.anchor: وإضافة الشيء إلى الشيء تمتنع معرفتها إلا بعد حصول العلم بالمتضايفين

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r9.claim: Al-ʿālamīn means every existent other than God; these beings comprise extended bodies, separate entities, and attributes, with bodies divided into simple and composite kinds.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r9.anchor: العالمين عبارة عن كل موجود سوى الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r10.claim: Al-Rāzī says there is no proof that only the familiar kinds of bodies exist: an infinite void lies beyond this world, and God can create innumerable greater worlds containing counterparts of its cosmic features; philosophers’ arguments for one world rely on weak premises.
RAZI-FULL:v1p17/r10.anchor: لم يقم دليل على أنه لا جسم إلا هذه الأقسام الثلاثة وذلك لأنه ثبت بالدليل أنه حصل خارج العالم خلاء لا نهاية له

TAB:1:2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r1.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r1.claim: Al-Tabari defines praise as pure thanks to God alone for countless gifts, including faculties for obedience, worldly provision without entitlement, and guidance to lasting bliss; all praise belongs to Him at first and last.
TAB:1:2/r1.anchor: الشكر خالصا لله جل ثناؤه دون سائر ما يُعْبَد من دونه

TAB:1:2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB:1:2/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Gabriel instructed Muhammad to say “praise be to God”; he glosses it as thanks, submission, and acknowledgment of God's blessing and guidance.
TAB:1:2/r2.anchor: قال ابن عباس :  الحمد لله :  هو الشكر

TAB:1:2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r3.speaker: الحكم بن عمير
TAB:1:2/r3.claim: Al-Hakam ibn ʿUmayr reports the Prophet's statement that saying “praise be to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude to God and brings an increase.
TAB:1:2/r3.anchor: عن الحكم بن عمير وكانت له صحبة

TAB:1:2/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r4.speaker: قيل
TAB:1:2/r4.claim: An unnamed view distinguishes praise of God through His beautiful names and attributes from thanks for His favors and gifts.

TAB:1:2/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r5.speaker: كعب الأحبار
TAB:1:2/r5.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār reports that whoever says “praise be to God” has praised God.
TAB:1:2/r5.anchor: عن كعب قال :  من قال :  «الحمد لله » فذلك ثناء على الله

TAB:1:2/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r6.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r6.claim: Al-Tabari notes that Kaʿb's report does not clarify whether praise means praise through God's names and attributes or praise for His blessings.
TAB:1:2/r6.anchor: ولم يبين في الرواية عنه من أي معنيي الثناء اللذين ذكرنا ذلك

TAB:1:2/r7.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB:1:2/r7.claim: The Prophet says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, and that God praised Himself by saying “praise be to God.”
TAB:1:2/r7.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع ،  أن النبيّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قال :  «ليس شيء أحبّ إليه الحمد من الله تعالى

TAB:1:2/r8.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r8.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r8.claim: Al-Tabari argues that Arabic usage allows praise and thanks to stand for one another, since speakers can say “praise be to God, as thanks.”
TAB:1:2/r8.anchor: من الحكم لقول القائل :  الحَمْدُ لِلّهِ شكرا بالصحة

TAB:1:2/r9.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r9.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r9.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamd signals all praise and complete thanks belong to God; without it, the phrase would denote only this speaker's praise.

TAB:1:2/r10.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r10.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r10.claim: Readers and scholars unanimously vocalize al-ḥamdu in the nominative; al-Tabari says the accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment if knowingly read.
TAB:1:2/r10.anchor: قراءة القراءة وعلماء الأمة على رفع الحمد

TAB:1:2/r11.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r11.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r11.claim: God speaks both clauses: He praises Himself, then teaches and obliges His servants to recite them as a test, with an understood command to say them signaled by “You alone we worship.”
TAB:1:2/r11.anchor: بل ذلك كله كلام الله جل ثناؤه ولكنه جل ذكره حمد نفسه وأثنى عليها

TAB:1:2/r12.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r12.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r12.claim: The command “say” is omitted because Arabic speakers omit words recoverable from context; here the following worship clause reveals that the praise clause is also an instruction to servants.
TAB:1:2/r12.anchor: أغنت دلالة ما ظهر عليه من القول عن إبداء ما حذف

TAB:1:2/r13.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r13.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r13.claim: For rab as obedient master or chief, al-Tabari cites Labīd's “lord of Kinda” and al-Nābigha's “lord of my possessions.”

TAB:1:2/r14.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r14.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r14.claim: Rab can mean one who repairs or tends something: al-Farazdaq calls an unrepaired hide “not tended,” while ʿAlqama describes another king tending his affairs.
TAB:1:2/r14.anchor: يعني بذلك في أديم غير مصلح

TAB:1:2/r15.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r15.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r15.claim: A third Arabic sense is owner: one who possesses a thing is called its rabb.

TAB:1:2/r16.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r16.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r16.claim: God is the incomparable master, the one who sets His creatures' affairs right through His gifts, and the owner of creation and command.
TAB:1:2/r16.anchor: والمصلح أمر خلقه بما أسبغ عليهم من نعمه

TAB:1:2/r17.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r17.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB:1:2/r17.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses “Lord of the worlds” as the one who owns all creation, the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and all between them, known and unknown; nothing resembles Him.
TAB:1:2/r17.anchor: قال ابن عباس :  يقول قل الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

TAB:1:2/r18.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r18.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r18.claim: Al-ʿālamūn is the plural of ʿālam, while ʿālam is a collective noun with no singular form from the same word, like anām, rahṭ, and jaysh.

TAB:1:2/r19.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r19.speaker: author
TAB:1:2/r19.claim: Al-ʿālam names classes of peoples and each generation in its era; humans, jinn, and every other created kind form worlds. Al-ʿAjjāj's poem uses “this world” for his contemporaries.
TAB:1:2/r19.anchor: قول العجاج :  *** *** فخندف هامة هذا العالمِ

TAB:1:2/r20.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r20.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB:1:2/r20.claim: A report through ʿIkrima attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the view that the worlds are jinn and humans.
TAB:1:2/r20.anchor: عن عكرمة ،  عن ابن عباس :  رب العالمين :  الجن والإنس

TAB:1:2/r21.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r21.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB:1:2/r21.claim: A report through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the gloss “Lord of the jinn and humans.”
TAB:1:2/r21.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير ،  عن ابن عباس ،  في قول الله جل وعزّ :  رب العالمين :  قال :  رب الجن والإنس

TAB:1:2/r22.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r22.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
TAB:1:2/r22.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Adam's descendants, jinn, and humans each constitute a distinct world.
TAB:1:2/r22.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير ،  قوله :  رب العالمين قال :  ابن آدم ،  والجن والإنس كل أمة منهم عالم على حِدَته

TAB:1:2/r23.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r23.speaker: مجاهد
TAB:1:2/r23.claim: Mujāhid interprets “Lord of the worlds” as Lord of humans and jinn.
TAB:1:2/r23.anchor: عن مجاهد :  الحمد لله رب العالمين قال :  الإنس والجنّ

TAB:1:2/r24.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r24.speaker: قتادة
TAB:1:2/r24.claim: Qatāda says every kind is a world.
TAB:1:2/r24.anchor: عن قتادة :  رب العالمين قال :  كل صنف :  عالم

TAB:1:2/r25.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r25.speaker: أبو العالية
TAB:1:2/r25.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says humans and jinn are worlds, alongside either eighteen thousand or fourteen thousand other worlds (he is unsure), of angels on earth, 3,500 in each corner, created to worship God.

TAB:1:2/r26.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:2/r26.speaker: ابن جريج
TAB:1:2/r26.claim: Ibn Jurayj interprets the worlds as jinn and humans.
TAB:1:2/r26.anchor: عن ابن جريج ،  في قوله :  رب العالمين قال :  الجن والإنس

TAB:1:7/r54.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r54.speaker: أهل الإلحاد الطاعنون في القرآن
TAB:1:7/r54.claim: Critics ask why al-Fātiḥa has seven verses when, they argue, the meaning of its remaining verses is already contained in “Master of Judgment Day” and “You alone we worship and ask for help.”
TAB:1:7/r54.anchor: فما الوجه إذ كان الأمر على ما وصفت في إطالة الكلام بمثل سورة أم القرآن بسبع آيات

TAB:1:7/r55.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r55.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r55.claim: Earlier scriptures each contain some meanings found together in the Qur'an: the Torah gives admonitions and detail, the Psalms praise and glorify, and the Gospel admonishes and reminds; the Qur'an gathers these and adds more.
TAB:1:7/r55.anchor: كالتوراة التي هي مواعظ وتفصيل ، والزّبور الذي هو تحميد وتمجيد ، والإنجيل الذي هو مواعظ وتذكير

TAB:1:7/r56.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r56.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r56.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says the prior books lack a miracle certifying their recipients, whereas the Qur'an's unmatched composition defeats all attempts to produce even a short surah and proves Muhammad's prophethood.
TAB:1:7/r56.anchor: نظمه العجيب ، ورصفه الغريب ، وتأليفه البديع ، الذي عجزت عن نظم مثل أصغر سورة منه الخطباء

TAB:1:7/r57.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r57.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r57.claim: The Qur'an's varied contents—encouragement, warning, commands, prohibitions, stories, argument, and parables—also make its extended expression purposeful.

TAB:1:7/r58.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r58.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r58.claim: Al-Fātiḥa's inimitable arrangement proves prophethood, while its praise and glorification direct people to recognize God's greatness, sovereignty, power, and dominion and to thank Him for His favors.
TAB:1:7/r58.anchor: ليذكروه بآلائه ويحمدوه على نعمائه ، فيستحقوا به منه المزيد ويستوجبوا عليه الثواب الجزيل

TAB:1:7/r59.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r59.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r59.claim: The account of those favored through knowledge of God and His enabling teaches that every religious and worldly blessing comes from Him, directing requests to God rather than idols or rivals.
TAB:1:7/r59.anchor: تعريف عباده أن كل ما بهم من نعمة في دينهم ودنياهم فمنه ، ليصرفوا رغبتهم إليه

TAB:1:7/r60.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r60.speaker: author
TAB:1:7/r60.claim: Recounting punishments for disobedience warns people away from sin and from incurring God's anger, whose consequences lead to destruction.
TAB:1:7/r60.anchor: ترهيب عباده عن ركوب معاصيه ، والتعرض لما لا قبل لهم به من سخطه

TAB:1:7/r61.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r61.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB:1:7/r61.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said God answers the worshipper's recitation: He calls al-ḥamdu praise, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm commendation, Mālik Yawm al-Dīn glorification, and the rest of the surah the servant's share.
TAB:1:7/r61.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : «إذا قال العبد : الحمد لله رب العالمين ، قال الله : حمدني عبدي

TAB:1:7/r62.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r62.speaker: أبو هريرة
TAB:1:7/r62.claim: A second Abū Hurayra version gives the same recitation exchange but is not attributed to the Prophet.
TAB:1:7/r62.anchor: عن أبي هريرة ، قال : إذا قال العبد : الحمد لله ، فذكر نحوه ، ولم يرفعه

TAB:1:7/r63.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB:1:7/r63.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB:1:7/r63.claim: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh reports the divine saying that the prayer is divided between God and His servant, with the servant receiving what he asks; the first three praises are God's, and what follows is for the servant.
TAB:1:7/r63.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : «قال الله عز وجل : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين وله ما سأل

TABATABAI:2:21-25#11/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:21-25#11/r2.speaker: بعض النصارى
TABATABAI:2:21-25#11/r2.claim: He also quotes a Christian's parody of al-Fatiha as another failed counter-imitation.

THALABI:v1p90/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p90/r1.speaker: بعض العلماء
THALABI:v1p90/r1.claim: Some scholars reconcile reports that the Fatiha is Meccan and Medinan by saying Gabriel revealed it twice, once in each place, to honor its status; this explains its name “Mathani.”
THALABI:v1p90/r1.anchor: قال بعض العلماء وقد لفق بين هذين القولين: أنها مكية ومدنية، نزل بها جبرئيل مرتين مرة بمكة ومرة بالمدينة

THALABI:v1p90/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p90/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p90/r2.claim: Abu Said al-Khudri reports the Prophet saying that the Opening of the Book is a cure for poison.
THALABI:v1p90/r2.anchor: عن أبي سعيد الخدري أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «فاتحة الكتاب شفاء من السم»

THALABI:v1p90/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p90/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p90/r3.claim: Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman reports that recitation of “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” by a child at school can avert a destined punishment for forty years.
THALABI:v1p90/r3.anchor: عن حذيفة بن اليمان قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن القوم ليبعث الله عليهم العذاب حتما مقضيا

THALABI:v1p90/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p90/r4.speaker: الحسن
THALABI:v1p90/r4.claim: Al-Hasan says knowledge of all revealed books is gathered in the Quran, then in its muṣḥaf section, then in the Fatiha; knowing its interpretation is like knowing all revealed books.
THALABI:v1p90/r4.anchor: عن الحسن قال: أنزل الله عز وجل مائة وأربعة كتب من السماء أودع علومها أربعة: التوراة والإنجيل والزبور والفرقان

BURHAN:v3p326/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p326/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v3p326/r1.claim: The successive praises intensify the servant's attention: God's exclusive praise, universal lordship, gifts of mercy, and command of judgment prepare the worshipper to approach and seek help.
BURHAN:v3p326/r1.anchor: فإن العبد إذا افتتح حمد مولاه بقوله الحمد لله الدال على اختصاصه بالحمد وجد من نفسه التحرك للإقبال عليه

BURHAN:v3p326/r2.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v3p326/r2.speaker: قيل
BURHAN:v3p326/r2.claim: One explanation says praise uses third person because it ranks below worship, while direct address elevates the worshipper's encounter; similarly, blessing is explicitly attributed to God but anger is phrased obliquely as a matter of etiquette.
BURHAN:v3p326/r2.anchor: وقيل إنما اختير للحمد لفظ الغيبة وللعبادة الخطاب للإشارة إلى أن الحمد دون العبادة في الرتبة

BURHAN:v4p338/r13.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v4p338/r13.speaker: author
BURHAN:v4p338/r13.claim: These three senses can coincide in praise of God: He deserves praise, has authority over it, and is the one to whom it belongs.
BURHAN:v4p338/r13.anchor: ويجوز إن تجمع هذه الثلاثة كقولك الحمد لله لأنه يستحق الحمد ووليه والمخصوص به

BURHAN:v1p438/r3.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p438/r3.speaker: ابن حبان
BURHAN:v1p438/r3.claim: Ibn Hibban reads the report comparing al-Fatiha with the Torah and Gospel as a difference in reward granted by God’s favor, not as intrinsic superiority within the Quran.
BURHAN:v1p438/r3.anchor: قال ابن حبان فى حديث أبى بن كعب رضى الله عنه ما أنزل الله فى التوارة ولا فى الإنجيل مثل أم القرآن

BURHAN:v1p438/r4.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p438/r4.speaker: ابن حبان
BURHAN:v1p438/r4.claim: Ibn Hibban says calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah means greatest in reward, not that one part of the Quran is intrinsically superior.
BURHAN:v1p438/r4.anchor: قال وقوله أعظم سورة أراد به فى الأجر لا أن بعض القرآن أفضل من بعض

BURHAN:v1p439/r1.author: al-Zarkashī
BURHAN:v1p439/r1.speaker: author
BURHAN:v1p439/r1.claim: Abu Said reports the Prophet calling al-Fatiha the greatest surah in a Bukhari narration; al-Zarkashi says this does not conflict with Ayat al-Kursi’s rank among verses, since the comparisons concern surahs and verses respectively.
BURHAN:v1p439/r1.anchor: وهذا لا يعارض ما قبله بأفضلية الفاتحة لأن تلك باعتبار السور وهذه باعتبار الآيات

ITQAN:v4p420/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p420/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
ITQAN:v4p420/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the Fatiha encompasses praise, worship through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; every Qur’anic verse falls under one of these topics.
ITQAN:v4p420/r1.anchor: وبيان اشتمالها على علوم القرآن قرره الزمخشري باشتمالها على الثناء على الله تعالى بما هو أهله وعلى التعبد بالأمر والنهي وعلى الوعد والوعيد

ITQAN:v4p420/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p420/r2.speaker: الإمام فخر الدين
ITQAN:v4p420/r2.claim: Fakhr al-Din maps the Qur’an’s four aims—God, resurrection, prophethood, and divine decree—onto the Fatiha: praise, Judgment Day, worship and reliance, and guidance through the surah’s end; this supports its name Umm al-Qur’an.
ITQAN:v4p420/r2.anchor: وقال الإمام فخر الدين المقصود من القرآن كله تقرير أمور أربعة الإلهيات والمعاد والنبوات وإثبات القضاء والقدر لله تعالى

ITQAN:v4p420/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p420/r3.speaker: البيضاوي
ITQAN:v4p420/r3.claim: Al-Baydawi says the Fatiha contains theoretical wisdom, practical rulings in walking the straight path, and knowledge of the ranks of the blessed and abodes of the wretched.
ITQAN:v4p420/r3.anchor: وقال البيضاوي هي مشتملة على الحكم النظرية والأحكام العملية التي هي سلوك الطريق المستقيم والاطلاع على مراتب السعداء ومنازل الأشقياء

ITQAN:v4p420/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p420/r4.speaker: الطيبي
ITQAN:v4p420/r4.claim: Al-Tibi divides the Fatiha’s religious knowledge into foundations (God and attributes, prophethood, resurrection), branches (worship), ethical perfection and seeking the path, and accounts of earlier peoples with promise and threat.
ITQAN:v4p420/r4.anchor: وقال الطيبي هي مشتملة على أربعة أنواع من العلوم التي هي مناط الدين

ITQAN:v4p421/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p421/r1.speaker: الغزالي
ITQAN:v4p421/r1.claim: Al-Ghazali lists three essential Qur’anic aims—knowing God, the straight path, and the return in the Hereafter—and three supplementary aims: the obedient, deniers’ speech, and the stations of the path, all signaled by the Fatiha.
ITQAN:v4p421/r1.anchor: وقال الغزالي مقاصد القرآن سنة ثلاثة مهمة وثلاثة متمة الأولى تعريف المدعو إليه كما أشير إليه بصدرها

ITQAN:v4p421/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p421/r2.speaker: الزركشي وناصر الدين بن الميلق
ITQAN:v4p421/r2.claim: They reconcile the hadith calling the Fatiha two-thirds of the Qur’an by saying it indicates all Qur’anic aims through inclusion and implication, but not direct correspondence; those are two of three modes of indication.
ITQAN:v4p421/r2.anchor: ذكره الزركشي في شرح التنبيه وناصر الدين بن الميلق قال وأيضا الحقوق ثلاثة حق الله على عباده

ITQAN:v4p421/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p421/r3.speaker: ناصر الدين بن الميلق
ITQAN:v4p421/r3.claim: A second explanation counts three kinds of rights—God’s claim on servants, servants’ claim on God, and people’s claims on one another—and says the Fatiha explicitly covers the first two, hence two-thirds.
ITQAN:v4p421/r3.anchor: قال وأيضا الحقوق ثلاثة حق الله على عباده وحق العباد على الله وحق بعض العباد على بعض وقد اشتملت الفاتحة صريحا على الحقين الأولين فناسب كونها بصريحها ثلثين

ITQAN:v4p421/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p421/r5.speaker: author
ITQAN:v4p421/r5.claim: There is no conflict between hadiths calling the Fatiha the greatest surah and al-Baqara the greatest: al-Baqara is greatest among surahs other than the Fatiha because of its detailed laws, parables, and arguments.
ITQAN:v4p421/r5.anchor: قلت ولا تنافي أيضا بين كون الفاتحة أعظم السور وبين الحديث الآخر أن البقرة أعظم السور

ITQAN:v4p421/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p421/r6.speaker: ابن العربي
ITQAN:v4p421/r6.claim: Ibn al-Arabi quotes a teacher saying the Fatiha contains a thousand commands, prohibitions, rulings, and reports; Ibn Umar spent eight years teaching it because of its jurisprudential depth.
ITQAN:v4p421/r6.anchor: قال ابن العربي في أحكامه سمعت بعض أشياخي يقول فيها ألف أمر وألف نهي وألف حكم وألف خبر

ITQAN:v4p490/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p490/r1.speaker: علي
ITQAN:v4p490/r1.claim: Ali said, as transmitted by Ibn Abi Jamra, that he could load seventy camels with commentary on the Umm al-Qur’an; the source explains the remark by showing how much each phrase requires.
ITQAN:v4p490/r1.anchor: قال ابن أبي جمرة عن علي رضي الله عنه أنه قال لو شئت أوقر سبعين بعيرا من تفسير أم القرآن لفعلت

ITQAN:v4p490/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v4p490/r2.speaker: ابن أبي جمرة
ITQAN:v4p490/r2.claim: Explaining the scale of commentary, Ibn Abi Jamra says the opening requires explaining praise, the divine name and transcendence, and the worlds, their nature, types, number, and extent.
ITQAN:v4p490/r2.anchor: يحتاج تبيين معنى الحمد وما يتعلق به الاسم الجليل الذي هو الله وما يليق به من التنزيه ثم يحتاج إلى بيان العالم وكيفيته

ITQAN:v3p284/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p284/r1.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p284/r1.claim: The Fatiha points to all major Qur’anic disciplines: knowledge of God and attributes, prophecy, resurrection, worship, ethical conduct and the straight path, and stories teaching the outcomes of obedience and disobedience.
ITQAN:v3p284/r1.anchor: وقد وجه ذلك بأن العلوم التي احتوى عليها القرآن قامت بها الأديان أربعة علم الأصول ومداره على معرفة الله وصفاته

ITQAN:v3p284/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p284/r2.speaker: author
ITQAN:v3p284/r2.claim: By signaling all Qur’anic aims, the Fatiha achieves an exemplary opening and combines beautiful words, pleasing cadence, and rhetorical forms.
ITQAN:v3p284/r2.anchor: فنبه في الفاتحة على جميع مقاصد القرآن وهذا هو الغاية في براعة الاستهلال مع ما اشتملت عليه من الألفاظ الحسنة والمقاطع المستحسنة وأنواع البلاغة

ITQAN:v2p339#7/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses praise to God as thanks to God.
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r4.anchor: عن الضحاك عن ابن عباس في قوله تعالى ﴿ الحمد لله ﴾ قال الشكر لله

ITQAN:v2p339#7/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses Lord of the worlds as the whole of creation.
ITQAN:v2p339#7/r5.anchor: 2105 ﴿ رب العالمين ﴾ قال له الخلق كله

ITQAN:v2p543#2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r1.speaker: author
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r1.claim: Al-ḥamdu li-llāh is read with nominative case as a subject, accusative as a verbal noun, or genitive by vowel assimilation.
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r1.anchor: ﴿ الحمد لله ﴾ قرئ بالرفع على الابتداء والنصب على المصدر والكسر على إتباع الدال اللام في حركتها

ITQAN:v2p543#2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r2.speaker: author
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r2.claim: Rabb al-ʿālamīn is read genitive as an adjective, nominative with an implicit subject, or accusative with an implicit verb or as a vocative.
ITQAN:v2p543#2/r2.anchor: ﴿ رب العالمين ﴾ قرئ بالجر على أنه نعت وبالرفع على القطع بإضمار مبتدأ وبالنصب عليه بإضمار فعل

ITQAN:v1p223/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v1p223/r2.speaker: author
ITQAN:v1p223/r2.claim: A good stop may be made, but starting with the words that follow is not sound; the opening praise is the example.
ITQAN:v1p223/r2.anchor: والحسن هو الذي يحسن الوقف عليه ولا يحسن الابتداء بما بعده نحو ﴿ الحمد لله رب العالمين ﴾

ITQAN:v3p302/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
ITQAN:v3p302/r4.speaker: الخويي
ITQAN:v3p302/r4.claim: Al-Khuyi says al-Fatiha fittingly gives the broadest divine attribute, Lord of all creation, while other surahs open with particular acts or attributes.
ITQAN:v3p302/r4.anchor: في تفسير الخويي ابتدئت الفاتحة بقوله ﴿ الحمد لله رب العالمين ﴾ فوصف بأنه مالك جميع المخلوقين

DAMGHANI:v1p143/r8.author: al-Dāmghānī
DAMGHANI:v1p143/r8.speaker: author
DAMGHANI:v1p143/r8.claim: Ḥamd can mean thanks or gratitude to God.
DAMGHANI:v1p143/r8.anchor: الحمد بمعنى الشكر قوله تعالى في فاتحة الكتاب

DAMGHANI:v1p329/r11.author: al-Dāmghānī
DAMGHANI:v1p329/r11.speaker: author
DAMGHANI:v1p329/r11.claim: Al-ʿālamīn can mean jinn and humans, as in praise of the Lord of all worlds and the Qur’an’s warning to the worlds.
DAMGHANI:v1p329/r11.anchor: العالمين الجن والانس قوله سبحانه في سورة الفاتحة

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās first defines the worlds as all rational beings among humans, jinn, and angels.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس : العالمون كل من يعقل من الإنس والجن والملائكة

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r2.claim: In another report, Ibn ʿAbbās says the worlds are every living being.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r2.anchor: وقال في رواية أخرى : العالمون كل ذي روح

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r3.claim: In ordinary usage, calling someone the best of the worlds can mean the people of his own era; lines by Labīd and al-Ḥuṭayʾa illustrate this usage.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r3.anchor: ويقال فلان خير العالم . ويراد بذلك أهل زمانه ، وأنشدوا للبيد

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r4.speaker: شيخنا
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r4.claim: The speculative theologians use ʿālam for the created universe as a whole: the celestial sphere, heavens, earth, and what lies between; al-Zajjāj is said to hold this meaning.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r4.anchor: قال شيخنا : فأما أهل النظر ، فالعالم عندهم اسم يقع على الكون الكلي المحدث

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r5.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r5.claim: Some derive ʿālam from ʿalāma, a sign pointing to its Creator; that derivation supports taking it for all created existence.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r5.anchor: وقيل : إن العالم مشتق مما هو علامة ، لأنه دال على خالقه

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r6.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r6.claim: Another derivation connects ʿālam to knowledge, supporting Ibn ʿAbbās’s interpretation.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r6.anchor: وقيل : إن اشتقاقه من العلم . وهذا يقوي ما ذكرناه عن ابن عباس

IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r7.speaker: بعض المفسرين
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r7.claim: One of six Qur’anic senses is every living being, as in the opening praise of God.
IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p444/r7.anchor: وذكر بعض المفسرين أن العالم في القرآن على ستة أوجه

NASHR:v1p47/r2.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p47/r2.speaker: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة
NASHR:v1p47/r2.claim: Ibrahim b. Abi Ablah reads the first lām in al-ḥamdulillāh with ḍamma.
NASHR:v1p47/r2.anchor: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة (الحمد لله) بضم اللام الأولى

NASHR:v1p47/r3.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p47/r3.speaker: الحسن البصري
NASHR:v1p47/r3.claim: Al-Hasan reads the dāl of al-ḥamdulillāh with kasra; Ibn al-Jazari says both this and the preceding form are linguistically distant, explained as vowel-following.
NASHR:v1p47/r3.anchor: الحسن البصري بكسر الدال وفيهما بعد في العربية ومجازهما الاتباع

NASHR:v1p47/r12.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p47/r12.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p47/r12.claim: Maki deems these noncanonical-imam readings permissible when reliably transmitted, since each has a sound Arabic analysis and agrees with the codex spelling; Ibn al-Jazari says others also share some forms.
NASHR:v1p47/r12.anchor: القراءة به لمن رواه عن الثقات جائزة لصحة وجهه في العربية وموافقته الخط إذا صح نقله

NASHR:v1p48/r1.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p48/r1.speaker: زيد بن علي بن الحسين، رؤبة بن العجاج، هارون بن موسى العتكي، الحسن
NASHR:v1p48/r1.claim: These readers pronounce the dāl of al-ḥamdu with fatḥa; the accusative is treated as a verbal noun with its commonly understood verb omitted.
NASHR:v1p48/r1.anchor: وهي (الحمد لله) بنصب الدال، (عن) زيد بن علي

NASHR:v1p48/r2.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p48/r2.speaker: الحسن
NASHR:v1p48/r2.claim: Al-Hasan also reads the lām in Allāh with fatḥa, matching the preceding accusative; the source calls this a dialect of some Qays speakers.
NASHR:v1p48/r2.anchor: (وعن) الحسن أيضا، (الحمد لله) بفتح اللام إتباعا لنصب الدال وهي لغة بعض قيس

NASHR:v1p48/r3.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p48/r3.speaker: قتيبة عن الكسائي
NASHR:v1p48/r3.claim: Qutayba transmits imāla of the alif in lillāh from al-Kisa'i, explained by the following kasra.
NASHR:v1p48/r3.anchor: وإمالة الألف من (لله) لقتيبة عن الكسائي ووجهها الكسرة بعد

NASHR:v1p48/r4.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p48/r4.speaker: أبو زيد سعيد بن أوس الأنصاري
NASHR:v1p48/r4.claim: Abu Zayd reports rabb al-ʿālamīn in both nominative and accusative; successive adjectives may differ, with some governed by an implied verb and others by an implied subject, but not revert to genitive.
NASHR:v1p48/r4.anchor: ووجهه أن النعوت إذا تتابعت وكثرت جازت المخالفة بينها فينصب بعضها بإضمار فعل

NASHR:v1p227/r4.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p227/r4.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p227/r4.claim: Stopping after these phrases is good because their sense is understood, but starting with attached phrases such as rabb al-ʿālamīn, ṣirāṭ alladhīna, or ghayr al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim is poor, except at verse ends per the Sunnah.
NASHR:v1p227/r4.anchor: الوقف على ذلك وما أشبهه حسن ; لأن المراد من ذلك يفهم، ولكن الابتداء ب (الرحمن الرحيم

NASHR:v1p49/r7.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p49/r7.speaker: قتيبة عن الكسائي، كردم عن نافع، ورش
NASHR:v1p49/r7.claim: The author adds unlisted transmissions: Qutayba from al-Kisa'i has imāla in al-ʿālamīn and al-raḥmān; Kurram from Nafi and al-Ahwazi from Warsh lengthen vowels in mālik, naʿbudu, and iyyāka.
NASHR:v1p49/r7.anchor: وبقي منها روايات أخرى رويناها منها إمالة (العالمين والرحمن) بخلاف لقتيبة عن الكسائي، ومنها إشباع الكسرة من (ملك يوم الدين)

NASHR:v1p229/r1.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v1p229/r1.speaker: author
NASHR:v1p229/r1.claim: A pause on an incomplete fragment such as “bi-smi,” “al-ḥamdu,” or “rabbi” leaves the utterance unfinished and without an intelligible meaning.
NASHR:v1p229/r1.anchor: نحو الوقف على: بسم، وعلى: الحمد، وعلى: رب، وملك يوم، وإياك

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r1.claim: Ḥamd is verbal praise of beauty, for a blessing or otherwise, and its opposite is blame; it is not a reversal of madḥ, since madḥ can apply to inanimate things.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r1.anchor: { الحمد } الثناء على الجميل من نعمة أو غيرها باللسان وحده

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r2.speaker: ابن الأنباري
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī treats ḥamd as an inversion of madḥ; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because a jewel may be praised but not thanked.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r2.anchor: خلافا لابن الأنباري ،   إذ هما في التصريفات متساويان

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r3.claim: Views say ḥamd and shukr are synonymous, ḥamd is broader, or shukr praises God's acts while ḥamd praises His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān prefers ḥamd as broader.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r3.anchor: والحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد ،   أو الحمد أعم

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r4.claim: The lām can express possession, transfer of ownership, entitlement, relation, cause, communication, exclamation, specification, result, location, endpoint, and superiority; Qur'anic and Arabic examples illustrate these functions.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r4.anchor: اللام : للملك وشبهه ،   وللتمليك وشبهه ،   وللاستحقاق

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r5.claim: Rabb can mean master, owner, constant one, deity, or reformer; some add “companion,” supported by a poem about the master of the dogs.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r5.anchor: { رب العالمين } الرب : السيد ،   والمالك ،   والثابت

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r6.speaker: بعضهم
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r6.claim: Some lexicographers allow rabb to mean “companion,” adducing a poem in which a man approaches as master of the dogs.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r6.anchor: وزاد بعضهم بمعنى الصاحب ،   مستدلا بقوله

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r7.claim: One report from Ibn ʿAbbās defines al-ʿālamīn as every being with a soul.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r7.anchor: ومدلوله كل ذي روح ،   قاله ابن عباس

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r9.claim: Another report from Ibn ʿAbbās specifies humans, jinn, and angels.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r9.anchor: أو الإنس والجن والملائكة ،   قاله أيضا ابن عباس

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r10.speaker: أبو عبيدة والفراء
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r10.claim: Abū ʿUbayda and al-Farrāʾ include humans, jinn, angels, and devils among al-ʿālamīn.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r10.anchor: أو الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين ،   قاله أبو عبيدة والفراء

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r11.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-ʿālamīn means the two classes of moral beings, humans and jinn.

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r12.speaker: أبو معاذ
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r12.claim: Abū Muʿādh restricts al-ʿālamīn to the children of Adam.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r12.anchor: أو بنو آدم ،   قاله أبو معاذ

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r13.speaker: الصادق
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r13.claim: Al-Ṣādiq defines al-ʿālamīn as the people of Paradise and the Fire.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r13.anchor: أو أهل الجنة والنار ،   قاله الصادق

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r14.speaker: عبد الرحمن بن زيد
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r14.claim: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Zayd says al-ʿālamīn means those who receive provision.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r14.anchor: أو المرتزقون ،   قاله عبد الرحمن بن زيد

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r15.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r15.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda define al-ʿālamīn as every created thing.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r15.anchor: أو كل مصنوع ،   قاله الحسن وقتادة

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r16.speaker: بعضهم
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r16.claim: Another reported interpretation restricts al-ʿālamīn to spiritual beings.

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r17.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r17.claim: The majority read al-ḥamdu with ḍamma on the dāl. Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla assimilates its mīm to the following lām; al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's, a stranger assimilation.

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r18.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r18.speaker: الحسن وزيد بن علي
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r18.claim: Al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī assimilate the dāl's kasra to the lām's kasra; the author calls this stranger because a case vowel follows a non-case vowel.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r18.anchor: كما أتبع الحسن وزيد بن علي كسرة الدال لكسرة اللام

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r19.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r19.speaker: هارون العتكي ورؤبة وسفيان بن عيينة
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r19.claim: Hārūn al-ʿAtakī, Ruʾba, and Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna read al-ḥamda in the accusative.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r19.anchor: وقرأ هارون العتكي ،   ورؤبة ،   وسفيان بن عيينة الحمد بالنصب

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r20.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r20.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r20.claim: The article in al-ḥamd may be anaphoric, defining the familiar praise; essential, defining the nature; or generic, encompassing all praises. A verbal noun is ordinarily not pluralized.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r20.anchor: والحمد مصدر معرف بأل ،   إما للعهد ،   أي الحمد المعروف بينكم لله

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r21.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r21.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r21.claim: Ibn al-Aʿrābī records the plural aḥmad for ḥamd, apparently treating its different kinds as distinct, and cites a poem using aḥmadī.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r21.anchor: وحكى ابن الأعرابي : جمعه على أحمد

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r22.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r22.speaker: القراء السبعة
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r22.claim: The nominative reading is stronger and agreed upon by the seven canonical readers: it states that praise is established and enduringly belongs to God, including praise by God and others.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r22.anchor: وقراءة الرفع أمكن في المعنى ،   ولهذا أجمع عليها السبعة

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r23.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r23.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r23.claim: With nominative al-ḥamdu the lām marks entitlement; with accusative al-ḥamda a verb such as “I praise God” must be supplied, conveying renewed action.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r23.anchor: ومعنى اللام في لله الاستحقاق ،   ومن نصب ،   فلا بد من عامل

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r24.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r24.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r24.claim: For the accusative reading, Abū Ḥayyān prefers an omitted verb directly indicated by the wording, such as “I praise God,” over “I say” or “adhere to praise.”
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r24.anchor: والأول هو الصحيح لدلالة اللفظ عليه

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r25.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r25.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r25.claim: In the accusative reading the lām is explanatory, not a strengthening of transitivity, since the verbal noun cannot govern this phrase as its object.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r25.anchor: وفي قراءة النصب ،   اللام للتبيين ،   كما قال أعني لله

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r26.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r26.speaker: زيد بن علي وطائفة
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r26.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī and a group read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative as praise; the reading weakens if the following adjectives remain genitive.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r26.anchor: قرأ زيد بن علي وطائفة { رب العالمين } بالنصب على المدح

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r27.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r27.speaker: الأهوازي
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r27.claim: Al-Ahwāzī reports Zayd ibn ʿAlī reading rabb, raḥmān, and raḥīm all in the accusative, avoiding the mismatch in case.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r27.anchor: على أن الأهوازي حكى في قراءة زيد بن علي أنه قرأ { رب العالمين ،   الرحمن الرحيم } بنصب الثلاثة

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r28.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r28.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r28.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects parsing accusative rabb as an implied verb of praise or as apposition: one rests on imagined syntax, the other is interrupted by raḥmān raḥīm.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r28.anchor: وقول من زعم أنه نصب رب بفعل دل عليه الكلام قبله

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r29.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r29.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r29.claim: Rabb may be a verbal noun used adjectivally or an active participle with deleted alif; as a title it is exclusive to God, while others require a possessive complement.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r29.anchor: ورب مصدر وصف به على أحد وجوه الوصف بالمصدر

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r30.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r30.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r30.claim: The article in al-ʿālamīn is exhaustive; ʿālam is an irregular collective and its sound masculine plural is even more irregular because it violates some conditions of that pattern.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r30.anchor: وأل في العالمين للاستغراق ،   وجمع العالم شاذ لأنه اسم جمع

ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r31.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r31.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r31.claim: Abū Ḥayyān prefers that al-ʿālamīn denote morally responsible beings, supported by the verse about signs for the knowledgeable; Ḥafṣ's kasra on the lām clarifies the sense.
ABUHAYYAN:1:2/r31.anchor: والذي أختاره أنه ينطلق على المكلفين

ALUSI:1:2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r1.claim: The opening of al-Fātiḥa is also the final wording of the supplications in 10:10, giving the sūra a return-to-the-beginning frame.
ALUSI:1:2/r1.anchor: وهو أول الفاتحة وآخر الدعوات الخاتمة كما قال تعالى

ALUSI:1:2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r2.speaker: الجنيد
ALUSI:1:2/r2.claim: Junayd was asked about the spiritual end and answered that it is returning to the beginning, an apt pattern for the sūra’s opening praise.
ALUSI:1:2/r2.anchor: قدس سره ما النهاية ؟ فقال الرجوع إلى البداية

ALUSI:1:2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r3.claim: In its familiar lexical sense, ḥamd is verbal praise of beauty, whether the praised excellence is an inherent virtue or a bestowed favor.
ALUSI:1:2/r3.anchor: والحمد على المشهور هو : الثناء باللسان على الجميل سواء تعلق بالفضائل أم بالفواضل

ALUSI:1:2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r4.claim: The act of ḥamd involves five elements: what is praised by, what is praised for, a praiser, a praised one, and an expression indicating the praised quality.
ALUSI:1:2/r4.anchor: قالوا ولا بد لتحققه من خمسة أمور : محمود به ومحمود عليه وحامد ومحمود

ALUSI:1:2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r5.speaker: الإمام الرازي
ALUSI:1:2/r5.claim: Al-Rāzī allows the praised quality to be positive or privative, transitive or intransitive, and voluntary or involuntary; al-Dawwānī and others endorse this account.
ALUSI:1:2/r5.anchor: لا فرق عند الإمام الرازي قدس سره بين كونه ثبوتيا أو سلبيا متعديا أو غير متعد

ALUSI:1:2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r6.speaker: العلامة في شرح التهذيب
ALUSI:1:2/r6.claim: A view reported and adopted in Sharḥ al-Tahdhīb requires the quality praised and the ground for praise to be voluntary.
ALUSI:1:2/r6.anchor: نقل عن البعض وجوب كونه اختياريا واختاره كما في المحمود عليه

ALUSI:1:2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r7.claim: The fact that people do not praise stature or a bright face, or that a pearl goes unpraised, cannot by itself prove whether the restriction lies in the praised quality or the ground for praise.
ALUSI:1:2/r7.anchor: لم يسمع الحمد على رشاقة القد وصباحة الخد لم يسمع الحمد بهما

ALUSI:1:2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r8.claim: The thing praised for is the cause of the praise: its excellence becomes manifest through the praised person’s possession of it; most scholars include both acts and enduring qualities.
ALUSI:1:2/r8.anchor: ظاهر كلام الجمهور أنه أعم من كونه فعلا صادرا من المحمود أو كيفية قائمة به

ALUSI:1:2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r9.speaker: الإمام الرازي
ALUSI:1:2/r9.claim: Al-Rāzī appears to restrict the ground of praise to an act performed voluntarily by the praised person.
ALUSI:1:2/r9.anchor: ويفهم كلام الإمام اختيار الأول ، واشترط أن يكون حصوله من المحمود باختياره

ALUSI:1:2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r10.claim: One quality can be both what a person is praised by and what they are praised for, as when someone is seen giving generously or praying; the two roles arise under different aspects.
ALUSI:1:2/r10.anchor: قد يكون الشيء الواحد محمودا به وعليه معا كأن رأي من ينعم أو يصلي

ALUSI:1:2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r11.claim: Praising God for essential attributes raises a problem if ḥamd requires voluntary acts, since those attributes may be identical with or additional to the divine essence.
ALUSI:1:2/r11.anchor: واستشكل الحمد على صفاته تعالى الذاتية سواء جعلت عين ذاته أو زائدة عليها

ALUSI:1:2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r12.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r12.claim: One solution treats praise of divine attributes as praise for what is effectively voluntary because God’s essence suffices for those attributes.
ALUSI:1:2/r12.anchor: وأجيب بأن الحمد عليها بتنزيلها منزلة الاختياري لكون ذاته كافية فيها

ALUSI:1:2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r13.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r13.claim: Another solution defines voluntary action as action attributable to a free agent, whether or not that agent chose it in this instance.
ALUSI:1:2/r13.anchor: أو بأن المراد بالفعل الاختياري المنسوب إلى الفاعل المختار

ALUSI:1:2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r14.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r14.claim: A further view says divine attributes issue by choice in the sense that God would bring them about if He willed and would not if He did not, without making them temporally originated.
ALUSI:1:2/r14.anchor: وقيل : إنها صادرة بالاختيار بمعنى إن شاء فعل وإن لم يشأ لم يفعل

ALUSI:1:2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r15.speaker: الفلاسفة
ALUSI:1:2/r15.claim: Philosophers appeal to the distinction between a necessary conditional and the actuality of its antecedent, but al-Ālūsī argues that necessity leaves divine volition nominal or makes the world’s origin incompatible with their account.
ALUSI:1:2/r15.anchor: وقالوا إن صدق الشرطية لا يقتضي وجود مقدمها ولا عدمه

ALUSI:1:2/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r16.claim: Al-Ālūsī concludes that lexical ḥamd is praise for voluntary acts; praise of essential attributes is either figurative through their voluntary effects or conventional praise, both unobjectionable.
ALUSI:1:2/r16.anchor: والحق الحقيق بالاتباع أن الحمد اللغوي لا يكون إلا على الأفعال الاختيارية

ALUSI:1:2/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r17.speaker: الصدر
ALUSI:1:2/r17.claim: The praiser must exalt the praised one through praise both outwardly and inwardly.
ALUSI:1:2/r17.anchor: أن يكون معظما بثنائه للمحمود ظاهرا وباطنا كما حققه الصدر

ALUSI:1:2/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r18.speaker: المحققون
ALUSI:1:2/r18.claim: The discerning scholars do not require the praiser to believe the praised quality actually exists; it suffices that the description not accompany an assertion of contempt.
ALUSI:1:2/r18.anchor: لا يلزم اعتقاد اتصاف المحمود بالجميل عند المحققين ، بل الشرط عدم اقترانه ثبوت تحقير

ALUSI:1:2/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r19.speaker: الدواني
ALUSI:1:2/r19.claim: Al-Dawwānī explains al-Sharīf’s requirement of inward and outward exaltation as intending the performative creation of esteem, not belief in a proposition.
ALUSI:1:2/r19.anchor: أراد بالاعتقاد لازمه ، وهو إنشاء التعظيم لا معناه الحقيقي

ALUSI:1:2/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r20.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r20.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the replies that a praiser must believe the literal description or must intend a metaphorical description; denial of a statement’s content does not prevent its rhetorical use.
ALUSI:1:2/r20.anchor: يرده أن الأول خلاف البديهة والثاني خلاف الواقع

ALUSI:1:2/r21.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r21.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r21.claim: The fifth element is an expression that manifests the praised one’s praiseworthiness; speech is conventionally singled out because the tongue is the usual instrument of speaking.
ALUSI:1:2/r21.anchor: وقد اشتهر تقييده باللسان وأريد به جارحة النطق

ALUSI:1:2/r22.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r22.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r22.claim: A person without a tongue can still praise through lip sounds or speech produced in another organ, as witnessed in a person lacking the whole tongue.
ALUSI:1:2/r22.anchor: فلو فقد إنسان لسانه فأثنى بحروفه الشفوية

ALUSI:1:2/r23.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r23.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r23.claim: The Qurʾānic statement that every thing glorifies God with praise shows that praise is not confined to utterance by a human tongue.
ALUSI:1:2/r23.anchor: وإن من شيء إلا يسبح بحمده

ALUSI:1:2/r24.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r24.speaker: الأكثر
ALUSI:1:2/r24.claim: Most scholars explain God’s self-praise as declaring His entitlement to praise, commanding praise, quoting the words of servants, or figuratively displaying His perfections; al-Sayyid favors the last account.
ALUSI:1:2/r24.anchor: فذهب الأكثر إلى أنه إخبار باستحقاق الحمد وأمر به أو مقول على ألسنة العباد

ALUSI:1:2/r25.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r25.speaker: الدواني
ALUSI:1:2/r25.claim: Al-Dawwānī considers figurative divine praise unnecessary because the people of truth affirm that God truly speaks; al-Ālūsī reads the tongue restriction as relative or customary.
ALUSI:1:2/r25.anchor: كون الحمد في حقه سبحانه مجازا بعيد عن قاعدة أهل الحق من إثبات الكلام له حقيقة

ALUSI:1:2/r26.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r26.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r26.claim: The lexical reality of ḥamd is manifesting perfection; spoken praise is merely its most obvious and familiar form, while manifestation through action is even fuller.
ALUSI:1:2/r26.anchor: فإن حقيقته عندهم إظهار صفات الكمال ، ولما كان الإظهار القولي أظهر أفراده

ALUSI:1:2/r27.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r27.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r27.claim: One distinction is that ḥamd applies to voluntary actions of knowing beings, while madḥ also applies to involuntary qualities and nonrational things.
ALUSI:1:2/r27.anchor: أحدها : أن الحمد يختص بالثناء على الفعل الاختياري لذوي العلم ، والمدح يكون في الاختياري وغيره

ALUSI:1:2/r28.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r28.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r28.claim: Ḥamd presupposes knowledge rather than conjecture and concerns complete qualities; madḥ may rest on conjecture or a pleasing but imperfect trait.
ALUSI:1:2/r28.anchor: وثانيها وثالثها : أن الحمد يشترط صدوره عن علم لا ظن ، وأن تكون الصفات المحمودة صفات كمال

ALUSI:1:2/r29.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r29.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r29.claim: Ḥamd carries greater reverence and grandeur than madḥ, applies more particularly to rational beings and eminent persons, and is more often used of God.
ALUSI:1:2/r29.anchor: أن في الحمد من التعظيم والفخامة ما ليس في المدح

ALUSI:1:2/r30.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r30.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r30.claim: Ḥamd reports another’s virtues with love and reverence, so it combines information with an act of esteem; madḥ is bare information.
ALUSI:1:2/r30.anchor: أن الحمد إخبار عن محاسن الغير مع المحبة والإجلال

ALUSI:1:2/r31.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r31.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r31.claim: Ḥamd is generally commanded, as in the saying that whoever does not thank people does not thank God, whereas madḥ is not universally praised and flatterers are rebuked.
ALUSI:1:2/r31.anchor: وسادسها : أن الحمد مأمور به مطلقا ففي الأثر : «من لم يحمد الناس لم يحمد الله »

ALUSI:1:2/r32.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r32.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:2/r32.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī appears to treat ḥamd and madḥ as synonymous; al-Ālūsī rejects that position and maintains that madḥ can praise what is involuntary.
ALUSI:1:2/r32.anchor: ويشعر كلام الزمخشري في «الكشاف والفائق » بترادفهما

ALUSI:1:2/r33.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r33.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r33.claim: Some distinguish shukr from ḥamd by reserving shukr for bodily action and ḥamd for speech.

ALUSI:1:2/r34.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r34.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r34.claim: Other definitions reserve shukr for apparent blessings or, alternatively, for inward blessings.
ALUSI:1:2/r34.anchor: جعله على النعم الظاهرة ، والآخر على النعم الباطنة

ALUSI:1:2/r35.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r35.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI:1:2/r35.claim: Al-Rāghib points to a definition of shukr as verbal expression for a blessing, while the familiar account includes grateful speech, service by the limbs, and belief and love in the heart.
ALUSI:1:2/r35.anchor: والمعروف أنه ما كان في مقابلتها قولا باللسان وعملا وخدمة بالأركان

ALUSI:1:2/r36.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r36.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI:1:2/r36.claim: Al-Ṭībī says the technical usage of the legal theorists means worship, which is complete only through speech, bodily acts, and the heart.
ALUSI:1:2/r36.anchor: قول الطيبي إن هذا عرف أهل الأصول فإنهم يقولون شكر المنعم واجب

ALUSI:1:2/r37.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r37.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r37.claim: Qurʾān 34:13 uses shukr for action, supporting the broader usage of gratitude beyond speech.

ALUSI:1:2/r38.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r38.speaker: النواس بن سمعان
ALUSI:1:2/r38.claim: Al-Ṭabarānī reports from al-Nawwās b. Samʿān that the Prophet vowed to thank God if his she-camel returned; when it did, he said al-ḥamdu lillāh, and the Companions expected further prayer or fasting.
ALUSI:1:2/r38.anchor: عن النواس بن سمعان : «أن ناقة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الجدعاء سرقت

ALUSI:1:2/r39.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r39.speaker: صاحب التجريد
ALUSI:1:2/r39.claim: The author of al-Tajrīd adds a fourth form of gratitude: thanking God by God, since no one but God can give Him His due thanks.
ALUSI:1:2/r39.anchor: وزاد بعضهم في أقسام الشكر رابعا وهو شكر الله تعالى بالله

ALUSI:1:2/r40.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r40.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r40.claim: People generally recognize three modes of shukr; it overlaps with ḥamd in some respects, but ḥamd is its strongest branch because it openly discloses the blessing.
ALUSI:1:2/r40.anchor: والذي أطبق عليه الناس التثليث وعلى كل حال بينه وبين الحمد عموم وخصوص من وجه

ALUSI:1:2/r41.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r41.speaker: ابن عمر
ALUSI:1:2/r41.claim: A report from Ibn ʿUmar calls ḥamd the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God unless he praises Him; al-Ālūsī notes its chain is interrupted.
ALUSI:1:2/r41.anchor: قال صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما رواه ابن عمر رضي الله تعالى عنهما : " الحمد رأس الشكر ما شكر الله تعالى عبد لا يحمده

ALUSI:1:2/r42.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r42.speaker: أنس
ALUSI:1:2/r42.claim: Al-Ālūsī cites a supporting report from Anas in which God tells Abraham that praise is the key to gratitude and gratitude ascends to the Lord of the Throne.
ALUSI:1:2/r42.anchor: إبراهيم سأل ربه فقال يا رب ما جزاء من حمدك؟ قال الحمد مفتاح الشكر

ALUSI:1:2/r43.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r43.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r43.claim: Calling ḥamd the head of gratitude suits its status as the most visible and principal form; this also explains why the Qurʾān opens with praise and begins the precious sūra with what is most precious.
ALUSI:1:2/r43.anchor: شبهه صلى الله عليه وسلم بالرأس الذي هو أظهر الأعضاء وأعلاها

ALUSI:1:2/r44.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r44.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r44.claim: Hamd is more elevated as worship than shukr because it need not be prompted by a benefit received, unlike gratitude for a gift.
ALUSI:1:2/r44.anchor: لو قال جل شأنه الشكر لله كان ثناء عليه تعالى بسبب إنعام وصل إلى ذلك القائل

ALUSI:1:2/r45.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r45.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r45.claim: An additional rationale is that shukr responds to finite gifts, while ḥamd can praise even for the unbounded benefit of averting harm, which is more urgent than gaining benefit.
ALUSI:1:2/r45.anchor: الشكر على الإعطاء وهو متناه والحمد يكون على المنع وهو غير متناه

ALUSI:1:2/r46.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r46.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r46.claim: In the common account, ḥamd has a limited means but a general object, whereas shukr has a general means but is directed specifically toward blessings.
ALUSI:1:2/r46.anchor: مورد الحمد في المشهور خاص ومتعلقه عام ، والشكر بالعكس موردا ومتعلقا

ALUSI:1:2/r47.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r47.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r47.claim: Although tasbīḥ commonly precedes taḥmīd, the sūra omits it because praise includes declaring God free of defects while the reverse is not always true; tasbīḥ elsewhere serves a different purpose.
ALUSI:1:2/r47.anchor: التسبيح داخل في التحميد دون العكس

ALUSI:1:2/r48.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r48.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r48.claim: Tasbīḥ signals that God is free of defects, while ḥamd also points to His positive beneficence and the knowledge, power, and sufficiency that make it possible.
ALUSI:1:2/r48.anchor: والثاني يشير إلى كونه محسنا إلى العباد ولا يكون محسنا إليهم إلا إذا كان عالما قادرا غنيا

ALUSI:1:2/r49.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r49.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r49.claim: Alternatively, every tasbīḥ is a kind of praise, but ḥamd is broader because it includes both negative and positive attributes while tasbīḥ addresses negative attributes.
ALUSI:1:2/r49.anchor: كل تسبيح حمد وليس كل حمد تسبيحا لأن التسبيح يكون بالصفات السلبية فحسب

ALUSI:1:2/r50.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r50.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r50.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes the article in al-ḥamdu as generic: it points to the familiar notion of praise, as in Labīd’s verse describing the camels.
ALUSI:1:2/r50.anchor: ومعناه الإشارة إلى ما يعرفه كل أحد من أن الحمد ما هو مثله في قول لبيد يصف العير وأتنه

ALUSI:1:2/r51.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r51.speaker: لبيد
ALUSI:1:2/r51.claim: Labīd’s line, cited as linguistic evidence, uses al-ʿirāk for the camels pressing together at the watering place.
ALUSI:1:2/r51.anchor: في قول لبيد يصف العير وأتنه : وأرسلها العراك ولم يذدها

ALUSI:1:2/r52.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r52.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:2/r52.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the exhaustive interpretation of al-ḥamdu a mistaken assumption held by many.
ALUSI:1:2/r52.anchor: حتى قال والاستغراق الذي يتوهمه كثير من الناس وهم

ALUSI:1:2/r53.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r53.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r53.claim: Some tie the generic reading to the Muʿtazilī account that human actions belong to their agents; al-Ālūsī replies that good acts still depend on God’s enabling and empowering.
ALUSI:1:2/r53.anchor: فقيل : إنه مبني على مسألة خلق الأعمال فإن أفعال العباد لما كانت مخلوقة لهم عند المعتزلة

ALUSI:1:2/r54.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r54.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r54.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects arguments that the generic article means only the perfect kind or that a verbal noun cannot convey exhaustive scope; context can make either reading exhaustive.
ALUSI:1:2/r54.anchor: ورد بأن اختصاص الجنس يستلزم اختصاص أفراده أيضا

ALUSI:1:2/r55.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r55.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:2/r55.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī paraphrases the phrase as we praise God with a praise, then treats إياك نعبد as an answer explaining how that praise is performed.
ALUSI:1:2/r55.anchor: لما كان معناه نحمد الله حمدا كان إخبارا عن ثبوت حمد غير معين

ALUSI:1:2/r56.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r56.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r56.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers an exhaustive reading here: the sūra’s encompassing attributes of lordship, mercy, and sovereignty support all praise belonging to God, and the shift to إياك نعبد marks a new address rather than an explanation.
ALUSI:1:2/r56.anchor: لأن الكلام الأول جار على المدح للغائب بسبب استحقاقه كل الحمد والثاني جار على الحكاية عن نفس الحامد

ALUSI:1:2/r57.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r57.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r57.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī’s statement in 64:1 that sovereignty and praise belong exclusively to God supports a comprehensive reading, though the present context gives further reason to include every instance of praise.
ALUSI:1:2/r57.anchor: فقال في قوله تعالى : { له الملك وله الحمد } قدم الظرفان ليدل بتقديمهما على معنى اختصاص الملك والحمد

ALUSI:1:2/r58.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r58.speaker: أبو العباس المرسي
ALUSI:1:2/r58.claim: Al-Mursī says the article is covenantal because God praised Himself eternally on behalf of creatures unable to encompass His praise, supported by the prophetic supplication that He is as He praised Himself.
ALUSI:1:2/r58.anchor: قلت لابن النحاس ما تقول في الألف واللام في الحمد أجنسية هي أم عهدية

ALUSI:1:2/r59.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r59.speaker: بعض ساداتنا الصوفية
ALUSI:1:2/r59.claim: Some Sufis understand the praise as belonging to God Himself, like sovereignty and creation-command: He is both praiser and praised, and all things are His manifestations.
ALUSI:1:2/r59.anchor: أن الحمد لله على حد الكبرياء لله و { أَلاَ لَهُ الخلق والأمر }

ALUSI:1:2/r60.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r60.speaker: الماتريدي
ALUSI:1:2/r60.claim: Al-Māturīdī says God praised Himself in order to teach creatures, and this is fitting because He inherently deserves praise.
ALUSI:1:2/r60.anchor: أنه جعل هذا حمدا من الله تعالى لنفسه قال وإنما حمد نفسه ليعلم الخلق

ALUSI:1:2/r61.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r61.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r61.claim: The transmitted and standard reading has al-ḥamdu in the nominative as a subject with lillāhi as its predicate.
ALUSI:1:2/r61.anchor: ثم إن الحمد : فيما تواتر مرفوع

ALUSI:1:2/r62.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r62.speaker: الحسن البصري وزيد بن علي
ALUSI:1:2/r62.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Zayd b. ʿAlī read with the dāl assimilated toward the following lām; Ibrāhīm b. Abla and Bedouins assimilate the reverse way.
ALUSI:1:2/r62.anchor: وقرأ الحسن البصري وزيد بن علي ( الحمد لله ) باتباع الدال اللام

ALUSI:1:2/r63.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r63.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r63.claim: This cross-word assimilation is permissible because the two frequently paired words are treated as if they were one word.
ALUSI:1:2/r63.anchor: وجاز ذلك استعمالا مع أن الاتباع إنما يكون في كلمة واحدة

ALUSI:1:2/r64.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r64.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r64.claim: Some prefer Ibrāhīm’s reading because following the first sound is easier than the reverse and because the dāl’s inflection is stronger than the lām’s fixed vowel.
ALUSI:1:2/r64.anchor: فقيل قراءة إبراهيم أسهل لأمرين أحدهما : أن اتباع الثاني للأول أيسر

ALUSI:1:2/r65.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r65.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r65.claim: Others prefer al-Ḥasan’s reading because the second sound more commonly follows the first and the uninflected sound should follow the inflected one.
ALUSI:1:2/r65.anchor: وقيل : إن قراءة الحسن أحسن لأن الأكثر جعل الثاني

ALUSI:1:2/r66.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r66.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:2/r66.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls Ibrāhīm’s reading أشف, a word that can indicate either greater clarity or greater obscurity.
ALUSI:1:2/r66.anchor: وكأنه لتعارض الترجيح قال الزمخشري : وأشف القراءتين قراءة إبراهيم

ALUSI:1:2/r67.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r67.speaker: هارون بن موسى
ALUSI:1:2/r67.claim: Hārūn b. Mūsā reads al-ḥamda in the accusative, a construction common among Arabs for a definite verbal noun with an implied verb such as نحمد.
ALUSI:1:2/r67.anchor: وقرأ هارون بن موسى ( الحمد لله ) بالنصب وعامة بني تميم وكثير من العرب ينصبون المصادر بالألف واللام

ALUSI:1:2/r68.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r68.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r68.claim: The implied verb for the accusative is in the first-person plural, matching naʿbudu and nastaʿīn and the humility of worship, rather than a majestic first-person singular.
ALUSI:1:2/r68.anchor: قدروه نحمد بنون الجماعة لأنه مقول على ألسنة العباد ومناسب لنعبد ونستعين

ALUSI:1:2/r69.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r69.speaker: الغزالي
ALUSI:1:2/r69.claim: Al-Ghazālī interprets the congregational prayer report as the worshippers speaking collectively in the first-person plural.
ALUSI:1:2/r69.anchor: صلاة الجماعة تفضل صلاة الفذ بسبع وعشرين درجة

ALUSI:1:2/r70.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r70.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r70.claim: The nominative reading is strongest because the nominal sentence, in this context, conveys settled and enduring praise rather than a renewed act of praising.
ALUSI:1:2/r70.anchor: وأرفع القراءات قراءة الرفع لدلالة الجملة الاسمية على الثبوت والدوام

ALUSI:1:2/r71.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r71.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r71.claim: Grammarians may treat an underlying verbal form as the source construction for verbal nouns, but here the nominative form answers the rhetorical need for an established state.
ALUSI:1:2/r71.anchor: إن أصل هذا المصدر النصب لأن المصادر أحداث متعلقة بمحالها

ALUSI:1:2/r72.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r72.speaker: معظم العلماء
ALUSI:1:2/r72.claim: Most scholars consider الحمد لله informative: otherwise God’s possession of the praised qualities would begin only when the speaker utters the praise.
ALUSI:1:2/r72.anchor: اختلف في جملة الحمد هل هي إخبارية أم إنشائية ؟ فالذي عليه معظم العلماء أنها إخبارية

ALUSI:1:2/r73.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r73.speaker: ابن الهمام
ALUSI:1:2/r73.claim: Ibn al-Humām argues that ḥamd is performative because it manifests qualities rather than establishing them, so praise need not be informative.
ALUSI:1:2/r73.anchor: وذكر أن ما ذكر باطل لأن اللازم من المقارنة انتفاء وصف الواصف لا الاتصاف

ALUSI:1:2/r74.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r74.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r74.claim: Al-Ālūsī sides with the majority: the sentence informs that God deserves praise, while a believer who says it intending reverent description is rightly called a praiser.
ALUSI:1:2/r74.anchor: والذي ارتضيه أنها إخبارية كما عليه المعظم ويد الله تعالى مع الجماعة والمراد الإخبار بأن الله تعالى مستحق الحمد

ALUSI:1:2/r75.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r75.speaker: داود
ALUSI:1:2/r75.claim: In a report, David asks how to thank God when gratitude itself is among His gifts; God answers that recognizing inability to thank Him is itself gratitude.
ALUSI:1:2/r75.anchor: وقد نقل أن داود عليه السلام قال : يا رب كيف أشكرك والشكر من آلائك ؟

ALUSI:1:2/r76.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r76.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r76.claim: The servants’ contingent praise relates to God without inhering in Him, just as knowledge relates to its objects without becoming part of them.
ALUSI:1:2/r76.anchor: المراد تعلق الحمد به تعالى ولا يلزم من التعلق القيام كتعلق العلم بالمعلومات

ALUSI:1:2/r77.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r77.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r77.claim: Some take the verbal noun in a passive sense, meaning that God is the one praised; because its form allows several construals, early commentators counted forty-two possibilities.
ALUSI:1:2/r77.anchor: وقيل إن الحمد مصدر بناء المجهول فيكون الثابت له عز شأنه هو المحمودية

ALUSI:1:2/r78.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r78.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r78.claim: A particularly unusual parsing makes the lām causal, so that praise is established for God’s sake.
ALUSI:1:2/r78.anchor: وقيل وهو من الغرابة بمكان أن اللام للتعليل

ALUSI:1:2/r79.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r79.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r79.claim: Naming God by His essential name avoids suggesting that He deserves praise only through one particular attribute; entitlement by essence still means entitlement for divine excellence.
ALUSI:1:2/r79.anchor: أتى باسم الذات في الحمدلة لئلا يتوهم لو اقتصر على الصفة اختصاص استحقاقه الحمد بوصف دون وصف

ALUSI:1:2/r80.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r80.speaker: بعض ساداتنا
ALUSI:1:2/r80.claim: A Sufi account divides praise from God into praise of His essence, unity, manifestations, qualities, effects, and acts, while creaturely praise varies with knowledge and capacity.
ALUSI:1:2/r80.anchor: فإن وجد من الحق وصدر من الوجود المطلق فتارة يكون على الذات بانفرادها ووحدتها

ALUSI:1:2/r81.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r81.speaker: author
