ALUSI:1:2/r81.claim: When the distinction between Creator and creation is considered together, all praise comes from God and returns to Him; there is no praiser or praised one apart from Him.
ALUSI:1:2/r81.anchor: وإذا اعتبر الجمع كان الكل منه وإليه

ALUSI:1:2/r82.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r82.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r82.claim: Praise precedes the divine name because the speaker is about to perform the act of praise; in 30:18 the order is reversed for a different purpose.
ALUSI:1:2/r82.anchor: وإنما قدم الحمد على الاسم الكريم لاقتضاء المقام مزيد اهتمام به

ALUSI:1:2/r83.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r83.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r83.claim: Rabb originally denotes tarbiya: gradually bringing a thing to the fullness suited to its primordial capacity, from the growth of a young child.
ALUSI:1:2/r83.anchor: والرب في الأصل مصدر بمعنى التربية

ALUSI:1:2/r84.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r84.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r84.claim: Rabb is explained as an intensive verbal noun, a form of exaggerated agent noun, or—according to Abū Ḥayyān—an agent noun with a deleted alif; one grammatical account is disputed.
ALUSI:1:2/r84.anchor: والظاهر أنه من مبالغة اسم الفاعل أو هو اسم فاعل وأصله رأب

ALUSI:1:2/r85.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r85.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r85.claim: Rabb is also used for creator, master, king, benefactor, reformer, worshipped one, and companion; tarbiya is the primary sense, with the others best treated as figurative extensions.
ALUSI:1:2/r85.anchor: ويطلق أيضا على الخالق والسيد والملك والمنعم والمصلح والمعبود والصاحب

ALUSI:1:2/r86.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r86.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:2/r86.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī interprets rabb here as owner; al-Ālūsī prefers tarbiya because owner would repeat the sense of Mālik yawm al-dīn and gives no clear reason for placing al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm between them.
ALUSI:1:2/r86.anchor: وحمله الزمخشري هنا على معنى المالك ولعل ما اخترناه خير منه

ALUSI:1:2/r87.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r87.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI:1:2/r87.claim: Al-Ṭībī finds it preferable to intend both meanings of rabb and their shared sense, as a figure of speech can preserve the direct and implied meaning together.
ALUSI:1:2/r87.anchor: ما اختاره الطيبي من وجوب حمل الرب على كلا مفهوميه

ALUSI:1:2/r88.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r88.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r88.claim: In ordinary usage rabb is not freely applied to anyone but God unless restricted by an addition or other qualifier; Ibn Ḥilaza’s unqualified poetic usage is rare.
ALUSI:1:2/r88.anchor: لا يطلق لغة على غيره تعالى إطلاقا مستفيضا إلا مقيدا بإضافة

ALUSI:1:2/r89.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r89.speaker: ابن حلزة
ALUSI:1:2/r89.claim: Ibn Ḥilaza’s poem calls al-Mundhir rabb, an unusual unqualified application of the title to a human being.
ALUSI:1:2/r89.anchor: وقول ابن حلزة في المنذر بن ماء السماء : وهو الرب والشهيد

ALUSI:1:2/r90.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r90.speaker: النابغة
ALUSI:1:2/r90.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse uses rabb without a qualifier, illustrating a disputed poetic license.
ALUSI:1:2/r90.anchor: وجوز بعضهم إطلاقه منكرا كما في قوله النابغة : نحث إلى النعمان حتى نناله

ALUSI:1:2/r91.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r91.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:2/r91.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet forbidding a person to say feed or perform ablution for your rabb and instructing him to say master or patron; a note in the source calls this report abrogated.
ALUSI:1:2/r91.anchor: وروى الشيخان عن أبي هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه : «لا يقل أحدكم أطعم ربك وضئ ربك

ALUSI:1:2/r92.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r92.speaker: السيوطي
ALUSI:1:2/r92.claim: Al-Suyūṭī interprets the restriction as a legal rather than purely linguistic ban on calling someone other than God rabb.
ALUSI:1:2/r92.anchor: واستظهر الإمام السيوطي أن المراد نفي إطلاقه على غيره تعالى شرعا

ALUSI:1:2/r93.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r93.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r93.claim: Joseph’s use of rabb for his master, and the prostration before Joseph, are explained as permissions specific to that earlier time.
ALUSI:1:2/r93.anchor: وأجابوا عن قول يوسف عليه السلام

ALUSI:1:2/r94.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r94.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r94.claim: Although ʿālamīn is a sound masculine plural, it can cover nonrational beings if the word is restricted to rational creatures, if rational beings predominate, or if the others are treated as signs of knowledge.
ALUSI:1:2/r94.anchor: واعترض بأنه يعم العقلاء وغيرهم وعالمون خاص بالعقلاء

ALUSI:1:2/r95.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r95.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r95.claim: The suggestion that ʿālamīn is a unique collective noun on the pattern of sound plurals does not settle its form; the author distinguishes ordinary plurals, collective generics, and collective nouns.
ALUSI:1:2/r95.anchor: وقيل : هو اسم جمع على وزن السلامة ولا نظير له

ALUSI:1:2/r96.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r96.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r96.claim: ʿĀlam means what makes something known and is commonly used for all that God created, including substances and accidents, or for a whole class of beings.
ALUSI:1:2/r96.anchor: والعالم كالخاتم اسم لما يعلم به وغلب فيما يعلم به الخالق تعالى شأنه

ALUSI:1:2/r97.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r97.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r97.claim: The term can denote the aggregate or one or more kinds, but it is not normally applied to a single person; in its basic sense every dependent individual is a sign of its Maker.
ALUSI:1:2/r97.anchor: ويطلق على مجموع الأجناس وهو الشائع كما يطلق على واحد منها فصاعدا

ALUSI:1:2/r98.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r98.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r98.claim: Each possible thing, great or small, points to the Creator because all depend on the Necessary Being for existence.
ALUSI:1:2/r98.anchor: لإمكانه وافتقاره دليل لائح على الصانع المجيد

ALUSI:1:2/r99.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r99.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r99.claim: The definite plural makes the scope of divine lordship explicit across every created kind; singular al-ʿālam might be mistaken for the familiar perceptible world alone.
ALUSI:1:2/r99.anchor: وإنما أتى الرب سبحانه بالجمع المعرف لأنه لو أفرد وعرف بلام الاستغراق لم يكن نصا فيه

ALUSI:1:2/r100.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r100.speaker: الطيبي
ALUSI:1:2/r100.claim: Al-Ṭībī answers that singular exhaustive scope could cover individuals yet fail to make the multiplicity of kinds explicit, so the plural is clearer here.
ALUSI:1:2/r100.anchor: لكن الغرض استغراق الأجناس المختلفة فلو أفرد وقيل رب العالم

ALUSI:1:2/r101.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r101.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r101.claim: Some restrict the worlds to rational beings among angels, humans, and jinn; al-Suyūṭī associates this reading with ʿilm, while universal scope fits ʿalāma, sign.
ALUSI:1:2/r101.anchor: وبعضهم خص { العالمين } بذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

ALUSI:1:2/r102.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r102.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r102.claim: Other reported views limit the worlds to jinn and humans, or to humans alone, citing the Qurʾānic uses in 25:1 and 26:165.
ALUSI:1:2/r102.anchor: وقيل هم الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى : { لِيَكُونَ للعالمين نذيرا }

ALUSI:1:2/r103.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r103.speaker: جعفر الصادق
ALUSI:1:2/r103.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq is reported to identify the worlds as humans; al-Ālūsī says the broader reading suits the context, while human beings are the focal recipients of law and prophecy.
ALUSI:1:2/r103.anchor: وهو المنقول عن جعفر الصادق والمأخوذ من بحر أهل البيت

ALUSI:1:2/r104.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r104.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r104.claim: Human beings are described as a synthesis and miniature of the cosmos; reflection on oneself and the earth reveals signs of the Creator.
ALUSI:1:2/r104.anchor: ومن تأمل في ذاته وتفكر في صفاته ظهرت له عظمة باريه

ALUSI:1:2/r105.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r105.speaker: بعض الأخبار
ALUSI:1:2/r105.claim: A report says God created one hundred thousand lamps hung from the Throne, with the heavens, earth, and all they contain in a single lamp; only God knows the rest.
ALUSI:1:2/r105.anchor: وروي في بعض الأخبار «أن الله تعالى خلق مائة ألف قنديل وعلقها بالعرش

ALUSI:1:2/r106.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r106.speaker: كعب الأحبار
ALUSI:1:2/r106.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says no one can enumerate the worlds except God, who creates things people do not know and alone knows His hosts.
ALUSI:1:2/r106.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار : لا يحصي عدد العالمين إلا الله تعالى

ALUSI:1:2/r107.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r107.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r107.claim: Every possible being remains under God’s nurture: without the continuing influx of divine support and the removal of every impediment, it would return to nonexistence.
ALUSI:1:2/r107.anchor: وما من ذرة من ذرات العوالم إلا وهي في حيطة تربيته سبحانه

ALUSI:1:2/r108.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r108.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r108.claim: Because contingent beings need a cause both to begin and to persist, continual divine preservation is itself tarbiya; keeping even indefinitely many possible obstacles absent sustains a thing.
ALUSI:1:2/r108.anchor: كما لا يستحق شيء من الممكنات بذاته الوجود ابتداء لا يستحقه بقاء

ALUSI:1:2/r109.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r109.speaker: بعض العارفين
ALUSI:1:2/r109.claim: A mystic observes that God has other servants, but each person has no lord but Him, while God nurtures each as though He had no servant but that person.
ALUSI:1:2/r109.anchor: أنه تعالى يملك عبادا غيرك وأنت ليس لك رب سواه

ALUSI:1:2/r110.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r110.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r110.claim: Although the sound masculine plural often denotes a small number, the form here hints that all created worlds remain few beside God’s greatness; the plural can also denote many.
ALUSI:1:2/r110.anchor: وإنما كان الجمع بالواو والنون مع أنه في المشهور جمع قلة

ALUSI:1:2/r111.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r111.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r111.claim: For the gnostics, the station of lordship comprises names that call for objects, such as knowing and power, including shared names and creative names directed toward creatures.
ALUSI:1:2/r111.anchor: وقد أشار سبحانه وتعالى بقوله : { رب العالمين } إلى حضرة الربوبية التي هي مقام العارفين

ALUSI:1:2/r112.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r112.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r112.claim: The Sufi hierarchy distinguishes Rabb, Rahmān, and Allāh: Rahmān encompasses more divine attributes, while Allāh names the highest, all-encompassing station of divinity.
ALUSI:1:2/r112.anchor: وأما الفرق بين الرب والرحمن فهو أن الرحمن عندهم اسم لمرتبة اختصت بجميع الأوصاف العلية الإلهية

ALUSI:1:2/r113.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r113.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r113.claim: In this hierarchy, the essence-only manifestation of aḥadiyya is not disclosed to creatures, whereas ulūhiyya manifests the divine in relation to others.
ALUSI:1:2/r113.anchor: ومن ثم منع أهل الله تعالى تجلي الأحدية ولم يمنعوا تجلي الألوهية

ALUSI:1:2/r114.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r114.speaker: أرباب الظاهر
ALUSI:1:2/r114.claim: The outward scholars explain why petitioners say yā Rabb: a petitioner seeks what benefits and nurtures him, so calling on the nurturer is especially apt.
ALUSI:1:2/r114.anchor: الداعي لا يطلب إلا ما يظنه صلاحا لحاله وتربية لنفسه

ALUSI:1:2/r115.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r115.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r115.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s own Sufi reading is that souls invoke God by the first name through which they acknowledged Him in the primordial covenant.
ALUSI:1:2/r115.anchor: أن الأرواح أول ما شنفت آذانها وعطرت أردانها بسماع وصف الربوبية

ALUSI:1:2/r116.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r116.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
ALUSI:1:2/r116.claim: Ibn ʿArabī’s account says the universal spirit sought its source without knowing that the sought reality was already within it, then recognized God in the station of lordship.
ALUSI:1:2/r116.anchor: مما حاصله : أن الله تعالى لما أوجد الكلمة المعبر عنها بالروح الكلي إيجاد إبداع

ALUSI:1:2/r117.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r117.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
ALUSI:1:2/r117.claim: In Ibn ʿArabī’s account the spirit names God its Rabb; God gives it divine names and attributes to know through existence, while veiling the manner of that gift because the creature cannot bear it.
ALUSI:1:2/r117.anchor: فقال : أنت ربي فلم يعرفه إلا في حضرة الربوبية

ALUSI:1:2/r118.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r118.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r118.claim: Opening the sūra’s descriptions with Rabb al-ʿālamīn suits the Prophet’s mission and asks for compassion toward all creatures, since God is their Lord.
ALUSI:1:2/r118.anchor: ويعلم منه إشارة سر افتتاح الأوصاف في الفاتحة برب العالمين

ALUSI:1:2/r119.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r119.speaker: زيد بن علي
ALUSI:1:2/r119.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī is reported to read rabb al-ʿālamīn in the accusative; the author’s preferred parse is an accusative of detachment with an implied verb such as أمدح.
ALUSI:1:2/r119.anchor: وقد قرئ ( رب العالمين ) بالنصب ونسب ذلك إلى زيد بن علي

ALUSI:1:2/r120.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r120.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r120.claim: One analysis treats the accusative as detachment from the preceding construction, supplying a verb of praise or mention; another says the prior الحمد licenses the construction.
ALUSI:1:2/r120.anchor: فقيل نصب على القطع ويقدر العامل هنا أمدح للمقام أو أذكر

ALUSI:1:2/r121.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r121.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI:1:2/r121.claim: Other proposed governors are the expressed الحمد, a vocative, or a past-tense reading of rabb; al-Ālūsī objects to the first for its syntax and to the latter parses as awkward.
ALUSI:1:2/r121.anchor: وقيل بفعل مقدر دل عليه الحمد وليس على التوهم

ALUSI:1:2/r122.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:2/r122.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:2/r122.claim: Al-Ālūsī considers accusative detachment the strongest analysis, especially if al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm is read in the accusative as a substitute rather than an adjective.
ALUSI:1:2/r122.anchor: وأهون الأمور عندي أولها بل يكاد يقطع الظاهر بالقطع

BAGHAWI:1:2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r1.claim: “Praise be to God” is grammatically a report about the one truly deserving praise, while instructing people to say it.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r1.anchor: لفظه خبر كأنه ، يخبر عن المستحق للحمد هو الله عز وجل ، وفيه تعليم الخلق تقديره قولوا الحمد لله .

BAGHAWI:1:2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r2.claim: Hamd can mean gratitude for a favor or praise for a praiseworthy quality; shukr is only for a favor, so hamd is broader and every praiser is grateful, but not every grateful person is a praiser.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r2.anchor: والحمد يكون بمعنى الشكر على النعمة ، ويكون بمعنى الثناء عليه بما فيه من الخصال الحميدة ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r3.claim: Another distinction assigns hamd to spoken praise and shukr to bodily action, illustrated by praise to God and the command to David's family to work in gratitude.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r3.anchor: وقيل الحمد باللسان قولاً والشكر بالأركان فعلاً قال الله تعالى ( وقل الحمد لله الذي لم يتخذ ولداً )

BAGHAWI:1:2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r4.claim: The lām in “for God” marks entitlement, as in saying that a house belongs to Zayd.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r4.anchor: اللام فيه للاستحقاق كما يقال الدار لزيد .

BAGHAWI:1:2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r5.claim: Rabb can mean owner: God owns the worlds, just as one speaks of the owner of a house as its lord.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r5.anchor: فالرب يكون بمعنى المالك ، كما يقول لمالك الدار رب الدار ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r6.claim: Rabb can also mean one who cultivates and repairs; God nurtures and sets the worlds right.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r6.anchor: ويكون بمعنى التربية والإصلاح ، يقال : رب فلان الضيعة يربها إذا أتمها وأصلحها فهو رب ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r7.claim: Only God may be called al-Rabb with the definite article, since it universalizes ownership and no creature owns everything; a creature is called lord only in a possessive construction.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r7.anchor: ولا يقال للمخلوق وهو الرب معرفاً ، إنما يقال رب كذا مضافاً لأن الألف واللام للتعميم ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:2/r8.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam, a plural noun with no singular of the same form.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r8.anchor: والعالمين جمع عالم والعالم ، جمع لا واحد له من لفظه ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI:1:2/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas identifies the worlds as jinn and humans, since they are morally addressed; the cited verse calls the Messenger a warner to the worlds.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r9.anchor: قال ابن عباس : هم الجن والإنس لأنهم المكلفون بالخطاب ، قال الله تعالى : { ليكون للعالمين نذيراً }

BAGHAWI:1:2/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r10.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد والحسن
BAGHAWI:1:2/r10.claim: Qatada, Mujahid, and al-Hasan say the worlds are all created beings, citing the Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r10.anchor: وقال قتادة و مجاهد و الحسن : جميع المخلوقين . قال الله تعالى : ( قال فرعون وما رب العالمين ؟ قال رب السماوات والأرض وما بينهما )

BAGHAWI:1:2/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r11.speaker: أبو عبيد
BAGHAWI:1:2/r11.claim: Abu ʿUbayd counts four communities as the worlds: angels, humans, jinn, and devils; beasts are excluded because they do not reason, and the term derives from knowledge.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r11.anchor: قال أبو عبيد : أربع أمم الملائكة ، والإنس ، والجن ، والشياطين ، مشتق من العلم ولا يقال للبهائم عالم ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r12.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
BAGHAWI:1:2/r12.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib estimates a thousand worlds: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r12.anchor: قال سعيد بن المسيب : لله ألف عالم ستمائة في البحر وأربعمائة في البر ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r13.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r13.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
BAGHAWI:1:2/r13.claim: Muqatil ibn Hayyan estimates eighty thousand worlds, half in the sea and half on land.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r13.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن حيان : لله ثمانون ألف عالم ، أربعون ألفاً في البحر ، وأربعون ألفاً في البر ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r14.speaker: وهب
BAGHAWI:1:2/r14.claim: Wahb estimates eighteen thousand worlds, with our world only one; inhabited land beside desolation is like a tent in a desert.
BAGHAWI:1:2/r14.anchor: وقال وهب : لله ثمانية عشر ألف عالم ، الدنيا عالم منها ، وما العمران في الخراب إلا كفسطاط في صحراء ،

BAGHAWI:1:2/r15.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:2/r15.speaker: كعب الأحبار
BAGHAWI:1:2/r15.claim: Kaʿb al-Ahbar says no one can count the worlds except God, citing “none knows your Lord's hosts except He.”
BAGHAWI:1:2/r15.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار لا يحصى عدد العالمين أحد إلا الله قال ( وما يعلم جنود ربك إلا هو )

BAGHAWI:1:7/r36.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:7/r36.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAGHAWI:1:7/r36.claim: In a qudsi report, God divides prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each part of al-Fatiha; Baghawi grades it sahih.
BAGHAWI:1:7/r36.anchor: قال الله عز وجل : قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين ، نصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي ولعبدي ما سأل ،

BAYDAWI:1:2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r1.claim: Ḥamd praises chosen goodness, whether a blessing or otherwise; madh praises goodness without qualification, so one praises knowledge and generosity but only commends beauty.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد هو الثناء على الجميل الاختياري من نعمة أو غيرها

BAYDAWI:1:2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r2.claim: Some consider ḥamd and madh synonymous or close companions.

BAYDAWI:1:2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r3.claim: Shukr responds to a blessing through speech, action, and belief; a poem names hand, tongue, and hidden heart as the three responses.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r3.anchor: والشكر : مقابلة النعمة قولا وعملا واعتقادا

BAYDAWI:1:2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r4.claim: Shukr is broader than ḥamd and madh in one respect and narrower in another; praise is a branch of gratitude and better signals blessings than hidden belief or ambiguous bodily acts, so it is gratitude's chief element.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r4.anchor: ولما كان الحمد من شعب الشكر أشيع للنعمة ،   وأدل على مكانها

BAYDAWI:1:2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r5.speaker: النبي
BAYDAWI:1:2/r5.claim: The Prophet is quoted saying praise is the head of gratitude and that whoever does not praise God has not thanked Him.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r5.anchor: فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام :  " الحمد رأس الشكر ،   وما شكر الله من لم يحمده "

BAYDAWI:1:2/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r6.claim: Blame is the opposite of praise, and ingratitude the opposite of shukr.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r6.anchor: والذم نقيض الحمد والكفران نقيض الشكر

BAYDAWI:1:2/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r7.claim: Al-ḥamdu is nominative as subject with “to God” as predicate, though an accusative reading is also reported.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r7.anchor: ورفعه بالابتداء وخبره لله وأصله النصب وقد قرئ به

BAYDAWI:1:2/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r8.claim: The nominative conveys universal and permanent praise belonging to God rather than newly arising praise.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r8.anchor: وإنما عدل عنه إلى الرفع ليدل على عموم الحمد وثباته له

BAYDAWI:1:2/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r9.claim: Ḥamd is a verbal noun normally governed by an implicit, rarely used verb; its article may denote the genus or point to the familiar idea of praise.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r9.anchor: وهو من المصادر التي تنصب بأفعال مضمرة لا تكاد تستعمل معها

BAYDAWI:1:2/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r10.claim: If the article is exhaustive, all praise belongs to God because He bestows every good directly or indirectly; this implies He is living, powerful, willing, and knowing.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r10.anchor: إذ الحمد في الحقيقة كله له ،   إذ ما من خير إلا وهو موليه بوسط أو بغير وسط

BAYDAWI:1:2/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r11.claim: Readings assimilate dāl and lām in opposite directions, treating the letters as one word because they are used together.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r11.anchor: وقرئ الحمد لله بإتباع الدال اللام وبالعكس

BAYDAWI:1:2/r12.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r12.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r12.claim: Rabb originally means tarbiya, bringing something to perfection little by little, then became an intensive description like ṣawm and ʿadl.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r12.anchor: الرب في الأصل مصدر بمعنى التربية : وهي تبليغ الشيء إلى كماله شيئا فشيئا

BAYDAWI:1:2/r13.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r13.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r13.claim: Another derivation makes rabb a descriptive form from rabba-yarubbuhu; it then means owner because an owner preserves and nurtures what is owned.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r13.anchor: وقيل هو نعت من ربه يربه فهو رب

BAYDAWI:1:2/r14.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r14.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r14.claim: Rabb is unqualified for God alone, though it can be qualified for others, as in “return to your lord.”
BAYDAWI:1:2/r14.anchor: ولا يطلق على غيره تعالى إلا مقيدا كقوله { ارجع إلى ربك }

BAYDAWI:1:2/r15.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r15.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r15.claim: ʿĀlam means what makes something known, like a signet or mold; it came to denote all besides God, substances and accidents, whose contingency indicates the necessary Creator.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r15.anchor: والعالم اسم لما يعلم به ،   كالخاتم والقالب ،   غلب فيما يعلم به الصانع تعالى

BAYDAWI:1:2/r16.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r16.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r16.claim: The plural encompasses diverse classes and uses the masculine rational plural because rational beings predominate among them.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r16.anchor: وإنما جمعه ليشمل ما تحته من الأجناس المختلفة ،   وغلب العقلاء منهم

BAYDAWI:1:2/r17.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r17.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r17.claim: Another view restricts al-ʿālamīn to rational beings—angels and the human and jinn races—with others included secondarily.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r17.anchor: وقيل اسم وضع لذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

BAYDAWI:1:2/r18.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r18.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r18.claim: A further view takes it here to mean people: each person contains counterparts of the cosmos that reveal the Creator, as in the verse about looking within oneself.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r18.anchor: وقيل عني به الناس ههنا فإن كل واحد منهم عالم

BAYDAWI:1:2/r19.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r19.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r19.claim: The accusative rabb al-ʿālamīn is analyzed as praise, a vocative, or an implied verb indicated by “praise.”
BAYDAWI:1:2/r19.anchor: وقرئ { رب العالمين } بالنصب على المدح

BAYDAWI:1:2/r20.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI:1:2/r20.speaker: author
BAYDAWI:1:2/r20.claim: Contingent things need an originator at coming-to-be and a sustainer for as long as they exist.
BAYDAWI:1:2/r20.anchor: وفيه دليل على أن الممكنات كما هي مفتقرة إلى المحدث حال حدوثها

BIQAI:1:2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI:1:2/r1.claim: Because the basmala is a kind of praise, it is naturally followed by the comprehensive name al-ḥamd; this implicitly calls people to praise God as the one deserving every praise.
BIQAI:1:2/r1.anchor: من الحمد ناسب كل المناسبة تعقيبها باسم الحمد الكلي الجامع

BIQAI:1:2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI:1:2/r2.claim: People should make this form of praise open their affairs, since it awakens hope and fear of God and leads to steadfastness on guidance.
BIQAI:1:2/r2.anchor: وخصوا هذا النوع من الحمد في افتتاح أموركم لما ذكر من استشعار الرغبة إليه والرهبة منه المؤدى إلى لزوم طريق الهدى

BIQAI:1:2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI:1:2/r3.claim: Al-ḥamd lillāh establishes that God deserves every praise by His essence and all perfections; Rabb adds that He deserves praise as Lord, Owner, and Benefactor.
BIQAI:1:2/r3.anchor: أنه المستحق لجميع المحامد لا لشيء غير ذاته الحائز لجميع الكمالات

BIQAI:1:2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI:1:2/r4.claim: Al-ʿālamīn points to creation's beginning, inviting inference from the made thing to its Maker and from the beginning to resurrection, as the Torah also begins with creation for this reason.

BIQAI:1:2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r5.speaker: أبو الحسن الحرالي
BIQAI:1:2/r5.claim: Al-Ḥarālī defines ḥamd as complete praise encompassing every action and attribute: all are from God and all are praise untouched by blame.
BIQAI:1:2/r5.anchor: قال الحرالي{[92]} : و { الحمد }{[93]} المدح الكامل

BIQAI:1:2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:2/r6.speaker: أبو الحسن الحرالي
BIQAI:1:2/r6.claim: Al-Ḥarālī says that when praise is understood to pervade everything, the definite form al-ḥamd signals its completion; al- marks the endpoint and perfection of what it qualifies.
BIQAI:1:2/r6.anchor: قال الحرالي{[92]} : و { الحمد }{[93]} المدح الكامل

BIQAI:1:7/r27.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI:1:7/r27.speaker: العلامة سعد الدين مسعود ابن عمرو التفتازاني الشافعي
BIQAI:1:7/r27.claim: The first preservation is signaled by the Merciful, the Compassionate, whose great and subtle gifts sustain life.
BIQAI:1:7/r27.anchor: وأما الإبقاء الأول فبقوله : { الرحمن الرحيم } أي المنعم بجلائل النعم

DURR:1:1/r112.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:1/r112.speaker: الله
DURR:1:1/r112.claim: The report glosses al-Hamd as gratitude and praise to God.
DURR:1:1/r112.anchor: فإذا قال { الحمد لله } قال الله : شكرني عبدني وحمدني .

DURR:1:1/r113.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:1/r113.speaker: الله
DURR:1:1/r113.claim: The Lord of the worlds is Lord of humans, jinn, angels, devils, all creation, and everything.
DURR:1:1/r113.anchor: قال الله شهد عبدي أني رب العالمين . رب الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين ورب الخلق ، ورب كل شيء

DURR:1:2/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r1.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r1.claim: The Prophet calls al-hamd the head of gratitude: a servant has not thanked God unless he praises Him.
DURR:1:2/r1.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قرأ { الحمد } رأس الشكر ، فما شكر الله عبد لا يحمده

DURR:1:2/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r2.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r2.claim: In a weakly chained report, the Prophet treats saying al-hamdulillah after his stolen camel returned as fulfilling his vow to thank God.
DURR:1:2/r2.anchor: عن النواس بن سمعان قال : سرقت ناقة رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم فقال

DURR:1:2/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r3.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r3.claim: A weak report from the Companion al-Hakam ibn Umayr says that saying Lord of the worlds is gratitude to God, bringing an increase.
DURR:1:2/r3.anchor: عن الحكم بن عمير وكانت له صحبة قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:1:2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas calls al-hamd the word of gratitude; when a servant says it, God says that His servant has thanked Him.
DURR:1:2/r4.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال { الحمد لله } كلمة الشكر إذا قال العبد { الحمد لله } قال الله شكرني عبدي

DURR:1:2/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:1:2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas explains al-hamd as gratitude, humble submission to God, and acknowledgment of His blessings, guidance, creation, and other favors.
DURR:1:2/r5.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : { الحمد } هو الشكر والاستحذاء لله ، والإقرار بنعمه ، وهدايته

DURR:1:2/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r6.speaker: علي
DURR:1:2/r6.claim: When Umar asks what al-hamd is, Ali answers that it is a phrase God chose for Himself and loves people to say.
DURR:1:2/r6.anchor: قال علي : كلمة رضيها الله لنفسه ، وأحب أن تقال

DURR:1:2/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r7.speaker: كعب
DURR:1:2/r7.claim: Kaʿb defines al-hamd as praise of God.
DURR:1:2/r7.anchor: عن كعب قال { الحمد لله } ثناء على الله

DURR:1:2/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r8.speaker: الضحاك
DURR:1:2/r8.claim: Al-Dahhak metaphorically calls al-hamd the mantle of the All-Merciful.
DURR:1:2/r8.anchor: عن الضحاك قال { الحمد } رداء الرحمن

DURR:1:2/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r9.speaker: أبو عبد الرحمن الجبائي
DURR:1:2/r9.claim: Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Jubbaʾi says prayer, fasting, and every good deed done for God count as gratitude, with al-hamd the best gratitude.
DURR:1:2/r9.anchor: عن أبي عبد الرحمن الجبائي قال : الصلاة شكر ، والصيام شكر ، وكل خير تفعله لله شكر ، وأفضل الشكر { الحمد }

DURR:1:2/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r10.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r10.claim: The Prophet says the best remembrance is there is no god but God, while the best supplication is al-hamdulillah; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
DURR:1:2/r10.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r11.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r11.claim: In a hasan report, the Prophet says praise after a blessing is better than the blessing received.
DURR:1:2/r11.anchor: بسند حسن عن أنس قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r12.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r12.claim: The Prophet says al-hamd is better than any blessing bestowed on a servant.
DURR:1:2/r12.anchor: عن جابر قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r13.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r13.claim: Al-Hasan transmits that every blessing praised by the servant is surpassed by praise of God, whatever the blessing may be.
DURR:1:2/r13.anchor: عن الحسن قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r14.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r14.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r14.claim: The Prophet says that if someone possessed the entire world and then said al-hamdulillah, the praise would be better than it all.
DURR:1:2/r14.anchor: عن أنس قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r15.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r15.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r15.claim: The Prophet says purification is half of faith and al-hamd fills the balance; other phrases fill the space between heaven and earth, while prayer, charity, patience, and the Quran serve as signs or testimony.
DURR:1:2/r15.anchor: عن أبي موسى الأشعري قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r16.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r16.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r16.claim: A man of Banu Sulaym reports that the Prophet said al-hamd fills the balance, while other remembrances fill the space between heaven and earth; purification and fasting are each half of a measure.
DURR:1:2/r16.anchor: عن رجل من بني سليم أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

DURR:1:2/r17.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r17.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r17.claim: The Prophet says glorification is half the balance and al-hamd fills it; there is no barrier between God and the declaration of divine unity.
DURR:1:2/r17.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمر قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r18.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r18.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r18.claim: When al-Aswad ibn Sariʿ offers the Prophet praises he composed for God, the Prophet replies that his Lord loves praise; al-Hakim authenticates the report.
DURR:1:2/r18.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع التميمي قال " قلت : يا رسول الله ألا أنشدك محامد حمدت بها ربي تبارك وتعالى قال : أما أن ربك يحب الحمد

DURR:1:2/r19.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r19.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r19.claim: The Prophet says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, so God praised Himself by saying al-hamdulillah.
DURR:1:2/r19.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال " ليس شيء أحب إليه الحمد من الله ، ولذلك أثنى على نفسه فقال { الحمد لله }

DURR:1:2/r20.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r20.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r20.claim: The Prophet contrasts divine forbearance with satanic haste and says nothing is more beloved to God than praise.
DURR:1:2/r20.anchor: عن أنس عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال " التأني من الله ، والعجلة من الشيطان

DURR:1:2/r21.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r21.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r21.claim: A report from Anas says tawhid is the price of Paradise and al-hamdulillah the price of every blessing; people share Paradise according to their deeds.
DURR:1:2/r21.anchor: من طريق أبان عن أنس قال : قال رسول الله " التوحيد ثمن الجنة ، و{ الحمد لله } ثمن كل نعمة ، ويتقاسمون الجنة بأعمالهم

DURR:1:2/r22.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r22.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r22.claim: Anas reports that tawhid is the price of Paradise and praise repays gratitude for every blessing.
DURR:1:2/r22.anchor: من طريق ثابت عن أنس مرفوعا " التوحيد ثمن الجنة ، والحمد وفاء شكر كل نعمة

DURR:1:2/r23.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r23.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r23.claim: The Prophet says every important matter begun without praise of God is deficient.
DURR:1:2/r23.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r24.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r24.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:1:2/r24.claim: Ibn Abbas describes an exchange at sneezing: the sneezer says al-hamdulillah, an angel answers Lord of the worlds, and after the sneezer repeats it the angel asks God to show mercy.
DURR:1:2/r24.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال : إذا عطس أحدكم فقال { الحمد لله } قال الملك : رب العالمين فإذا قال رب العالمين

DURR:1:2/r25.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r25.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
DURR:1:2/r25.claim: Ali says that whoever says the full praise at every sneeze heard, in any circumstance, will never suffer toothache or earache.
DURR:1:2/r25.anchor: عن علي ابن أبي طالب قال : من قال عند كل عطسة سمعها { الحمد لله رب العالمين } على كل حال ما كان

DURR:1:2/r26.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r26.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r26.claim: The Prophet says whoever anticipates a sneezer with praise will be spared abdominal illness.
DURR:1:2/r26.anchor: عن واثلة بن الأسقع قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

DURR:1:2/r27.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r27.speaker: موسى بن طلحة
DURR:1:2/r27.claim: Musa ibn Talha reports God's instruction to Solomon to remember Him if anyone sneezes, even beyond seven seas.
DURR:1:2/r27.anchor: عن موسى بن طلحة قال : أوحى الله إلى سليمان : إن عطس عاطس من وراء سبعة أبحر فاذكرني

DURR:1:2/r28.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r28.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r28.claim: Ali reports that the Prophet vowed to thank God properly if his family expedition returned safely; on their return he said al-hamdulillah for God's abundant favors and counted that as fulfilling the vow.
DURR:1:2/r28.anchor: عن علي قال " بعث رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم سرية من أهله فقال : اللهم لك علي إن رددتهم سالمين أن أشكرك حق شكرك

DURR:1:2/r29.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r29.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r29.claim: In a report from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra, the Prophet promises gratitude if an Ansar force returns safe with booty; when reminded, he says he has fulfilled it with thanks and abundant praise.
DURR:1:2/r29.anchor: من طريق سعد بن اسحق بن كعب بن عجرة عن أبيه عن جده

DURR:1:2/r30.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r30.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
DURR:1:2/r30.claim: Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad tells how he vowed to praise God with approved praises if his mule returned, then said al-hamdulillah alone because it encompasses all praise.
DURR:1:2/r30.anchor: عن جعفر بن محمد قال : فقد أبي بغلته فقال : لئن ردها الله علي لأحمدنه بمحامد يرضاها

DURR:1:2/r31.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r31.speaker: منصور بن إبراهيم
DURR:1:2/r31.claim: Mansur ibn Ibrahim transmits the saying that al-hamdulillah is the expression whose reward is multiplied most.
DURR:1:2/r31.anchor: من طريق منصور بن إبراهيم قال : يقال إن { الحمد لله } أكثر الكلام تضعيفا

DURR:1:2/r32.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r32.speaker: سفيان الثوري
DURR:1:2/r32.claim: Sufyan al-Thawri says al-hamdulillah is both remembrance and gratitude, a combination found in no other expression.
DURR:1:2/r32.anchor: عن محمد بن حرب قال : قال سفيان الثوري : { الحمد لله } ذكر وشكر ، وليس شيء يكون ذكرا وشكرا غيره

DURR:1:2/r33.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r33.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص
DURR:1:2/r33.claim: Ibn ʿAmr assigns distinct functions to remembrances: glorification is creation's prayer, al-hamd gratitude, tawhid sincerity, takbir fills heaven and earth, and the declaration of God's powerlessness-to-act-without-help brings God's command to submit.
DURR:1:2/r33.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عمرو بن العاص قال : إن العبد إذا قال : سبحان الله فهي صلاة الخلائق ، وإذا قال { الحمد لله } فهي كلمة الشكر

DURR:1:2/r34.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r34.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:1:2/r34.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the worlds as jinn and humans.
DURR:1:2/r34.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله { رب العالمين } قال : الجن والإنس

DURR:1:2/r35.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r35.speaker: مجاهد
DURR:1:2/r35.claim: Mujahid likewise identifies the worlds as jinn and humans.
DURR:1:2/r35.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله { رب العالمين } قال : الجن والإنس

DURR:1:2/r36.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r36.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR:1:2/r36.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr gives the same identification of the worlds as jinn and humans.

DURR:1:2/r37.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r37.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR:1:2/r37.claim: Ibn Abbas also explains the Lord of the worlds as Lord of all creation: all the heavens and their inhabitants, all earths and their inhabitants, and everything between them, known or unknown.
DURR:1:2/r37.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله { رب العالمين } قال : إله الخلق كله

DURR:1:2/r38.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r38.speaker: رسول الله
DURR:1:2/r38.claim: A weak report from Jabir recounts Umar's search for locusts and a prophetic saying that God made a thousand communities, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land; locusts are the first to perish, after which the others follow like a broken necklace.
DURR:1:2/r38.anchor: بسند ضعيف عن جابر بن عبد الله قال : قل الجراد في سنة من سني عمر التي ولي فيها

DURR:1:2/r39.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r39.speaker: قتادة
DURR:1:2/r39.claim: Qatada says each kind or class is a world.
DURR:1:2/r39.anchor: ابن جريج عن قتادة في قوله { رب العالمين } قال : كل صنف عالم

DURR:1:2/r40.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r40.speaker: تتبع الجهري
DURR:1:2/r40.claim: Al-Tatabbuʿ al-Jahri says the worlds are a thousand communities, six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
DURR:1:2/r40.anchor: عن تتبع الجهري قال : العالمون ألف أمة . فستمائة في البحر ، وأربعمائة في البر

DURR:1:2/r41.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r41.speaker: أبو العالية
DURR:1:2/r41.claim: Abu al-ʿAliya counts humans and jinn as two worlds and says there are another eighteen thousand worlds of angels; each of earth's four corners has 3,500 worlds created to worship God.
DURR:1:2/r41.anchor: عن أبي العالية في قوله { رب العالمين } قال : الإنس عالم ، والجن عالم ، وما سوى ذلك ثمانية عشر ألف عالم من الملائكة

DURR:1:2/r42.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r42.speaker: أبي بن كعب
DURR:1:2/r42.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb identifies the worlds as angels, numbering eighteen thousand; four regions each have four or five hundred angels, each with innumerable helpers.
DURR:1:2/r42.anchor: من طريق شهر بن حوشب عن أبي كعب قال : العالمون الملائكة وهم ثمانون ثمانية عشر ألف ملك

DURR:1:2/r43.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:2/r43.speaker: وهب
DURR:1:2/r43.claim: Wahb says God has eighteen thousand worlds, of which this world is only one.
DURR:1:2/r43.anchor: عن وهب قال : إن لله عز وجل ثمانية عشر ألف عالم . الدنيا منها عالم واحد

DURR:1:3/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR:1:3/r1.speaker: قتادة
DURR:1:3/r1.claim: Qatada says the Lord of the worlds describes what God has made.
DURR:1:3/r1.anchor: عن قتادة في قول الله { الحمد لله رب العالمين } قال : ما وصف من خلقه

ABUDAWUD:821/r2.author: ABUDAWUD
ABUDAWUD:821/r2.speaker: الله تعالى
ABUDAWUD:821/r2.claim: In a hadith qudsi transmitted by Abu Hurayra, God divides al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise and glorification receive divine responses, worship is mutual, and the guidance petition belongs to the servant.
ABUDAWUD:821/r2.anchor: قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى قَسَمْتُ الصَّلاَةَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ عَبْدِي

DURR-FULL:v1p16/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r5.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r5.claim: Mujāhid says the revelation of al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn greatly distressed Iblīs, who groaned and snorted; those who groan or snort are accursed.
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r5.anchor: ابن الضريس عن مجاهد قال: لما نزلت {الحمد لله رب العالمين} شق على إبليس مشقة شديدة

DURR-FULL:v1p16/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r9.speaker: رجاء الغنوي
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r9.claim: Rajāʾ al-Ghanawī attributes to the Prophet a healing practice using God's own praise of Himself, naming al-ḥamdu lillāh and al-Ikhlāṣ; whoever is not healed by the Qur'an is not healed by God.
DURR-FULL:v1p16/r9.anchor: عن رجاء الغنوي قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم استشفوا بما حمد الله به نفسه قبل أن يحمده خلقه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r1.claim: Important unfamiliar teaching should be preceded by preparation that removes resistance and mental obstacles, so hearers can benefit from guidance.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r1.anchor: الشأن في الخطاب بأمر مهم لم يسِبق للمخاطب به خطابٌ من نوعه أنْ يُستأنَس له قبل إلقاء المقصود

IBNASHUR:1:2/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r8.claim: The many requirements for successful guidance and reception gather around these six foundations of spiritual preparation.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r8.anchor: وجدتها عاكفة حول هذه الأركان الستة فكن في استقصائها لبيباً

IBNASHUR:1:2/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r9.claim: The prayer teaches believers to value blessings properly by thanking their giver, praising the giver of reason and success.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r9.anchor: أن يقدروا النعمة حق قدرها بشكر المنعم بها فأراهم كيف يُتَوِّجُون مناجاتَهم بحمد واهب العقل ومانح التوفيق

IBNASHUR:1:2/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r10.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r10.claim: Al-Fatiha serves as the Quran's proem or a sermon introduction; this literary arrangement aids understanding and attentive reception.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r10.anchor: فسورة الفاتحة بما تقرر مُنَزَّلَةٌ من القرآن مَنْزلَة الديباجة للكتاب أو المقدمة للخطبة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r11.claim: A preface should be concise so listeners are not tired by waiting; the shortness of Al-Fatiha explains its placement before the longer surahs.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r11.anchor: القاعدة الأولى إيجاز المقدمة لئلا تمل نفوس السامعين بطول انتظار المقصود وهو ظاهر في الفاتحة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r12.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r12.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r12.claim: A good opening hints at its subject, preparing receptive hearers and allowing advanced hearers to assess or complete the argument; this displays the speaker's command of it.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r12.anchor: الثانية أن تشير إلى الغرض المقصود وهو ما يسمى براعة الاستهلال لأن ذلك يهيىء السامعين لسماع تفصيل ما سيرد عليهم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r13.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r13.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r13.claim: A preface should use concise, comprehensive expression, a principle discussed by rhetoricians for places requiring careful composition.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r13.anchor: الثالثة أن تكون المقدمة من جوامع الكلم وقد بين ذلك علماء البيان عند ذكرهم المواضع

IBNASHUR:1:2/r14.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r14.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r14.claim: A fourth rule for a preface is to begin with praise of God.

IBNASHUR:1:2/r15.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r15.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r15.claim: The surah's preparation rejects atheism and materialism, polytheism, stubbornness, and errors corrupting sound knowledge or true law; this is why it is called the Mother of the Quran.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r15.anchor: فالفاتحة تضمنت مناجاة للخالق جامعة التنزه عن التعطيل والإلحاد والدهرية بما تضمنه قوله : { ملك يوم الدين }

IBNASHUR:1:2/r16.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r16.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r16.claim: Arabic dignitary address begins with praise before a request; Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt says that praise of the addressee can itself satisfy the petitioner.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r16.anchor: أَأَذْكُرُ حاجتي أَم قَدْ كفاني *** حَيَاؤُكَ إِنَّ شيمتَك الحَياء

IBNASHUR:1:2/r17.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r17.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNASHUR:1:2/r17.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra, attributed to the Prophet, says an important matter not begun with praise of God is cut off; Ibn Ashur gives no grading.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r17.anchor: حديث أبي هريرة عن النبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم « كلُّ أمرٍ ذي بال لا يُبدأ فيه بالحمدُ لله أو بالحمد فهو أقطع »

IBNASHUR:1:2/r18.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r18.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r18.claim: Muslims consequently called valuable speech lacking opening praise abtar; Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan's Basran sermon was nicknamed al-Batra for this omission.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r18.anchor: فلم يزل المسلمون من يومئذٍ يُلقِّبُون كل كلام نفيس لم يشتمل في طالعه على الحمد بالأبتر

IBNASHUR:1:2/r19.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r19.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r19.claim: Hamd is praise of a beautiful quality, whether an intentional action such as generosity or aiding the distressed, or another quality such as courage.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r19.anchor: و ( الحمد ) هو الثناء على الجميل أي الوصف الجميل الاختياري فعلاً كان كالكرم وإغاثة الملهوف أم غيره كالشجاعة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r20.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r20.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r20.claim: Thanā is the broader category of favorable mention and is not the opposite of hamd; some anomalously use it for mention regardless of praise or blame.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r20.anchor: فالثناء الذكر بخير مطلقاً وشذ من قال يستعمل الثناء في الذكر مطلقاً

IBNASHUR:1:2/r21.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r21.speaker: ابن القطاع
IBNASHUR:1:2/r21.claim: Ibn al-Qatta is associated with the anomalous view that thanā can mean mention generally, including neutral mention; Ibn Ashur says a hadith wording misled him.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r21.anchor: ونسبا إلى ابن القطاع وغرَّه في ذلك ما ورد في الحديث

IBNASHUR:1:2/r22.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r22.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r22.claim: Calling blameworthy mention thanā in a hadith is figurative word matching that indirectly urges people either to speak well of Muslims or refrain.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r22.anchor: وإنما هو مجاز دعت إليه المشاكلة اللفظية والتعريض بأن من كان متكلماً في مسلم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r23.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r23.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r23.claim: Nithā, with initial n, applies to praise or blame and is more commonly used for blame.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r23.anchor: وأما الذي يستعمل في الخير والشر فهو النثاء بتقديم النون وهو في الشر أكثر كما قيل

IBNASHUR:1:2/r24.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r24.speaker: الجمهور
IBNASHUR:1:2/r24.claim: The majority distinguish madh from hamd by making madh broader: it can praise voluntary or nonvoluntary qualities.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r24.anchor: وأما المدح فقد اختلف فيه فذهب الجمهور إلى أن المدح أعم من الحمد فإنه يكون على الوصف الاختياري وغيره

IBNASHUR:1:2/r25.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r25.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r25.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls hamd and madh equivalent; a proposed reading takes his word 'brothers' to mean derivational relatives like jazb and jadhb.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r25.anchor: وقال صاحب « الكشاف » الحمد والمدح أخوان فقيل أراد أخوان في الاشتقاق الكبير

IBNASHUR:1:2/r26.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r26.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r26.claim: Ibn Ashur rejects the derivational-sibling reading: the commentators' synonym reading fits al-Zamakhshari's gloss in al-Fa'iq and his treating blame as hamd's opposite.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r26.anchor: والذي عليه المحققون من شراح « الكشاف » أنه أراد من الأخوة هنا الترادف لأنه ظاهر كلامه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r27.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r27.speaker: السيد الشريف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r27.claim: Al-Sayyid al-Sharif, apparently also Sa'd al-Din, reads the synonyms as retaining the voluntary-quality restriction, citing al-Zamakhshari on 49:7.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r27.anchor: وعلى الأول حمله السيد الشريف وهو ظاهر كلام سعد الدين

IBNASHUR:1:2/r28.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r28.speaker: عبد الحكيم السلكوتي
IBNASHUR:1:2/r28.claim: Abd al-Hakim al-Salkuti takes synonymy to cancel the voluntary-quality restriction for both words, presenting this as a possible or transmitted reading rather than a preference.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r28.anchor: وعلى المحمل الثاني وهو أن يكون قُصد من الترادف إلغاء قيد الاختياري في كليهما حمله المحقق عبد الحكيم السلكوتي

IBNASHUR:1:2/r29.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r29.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r29.claim: To allow praise of God's essential attributes under the majority's definition, scholars offer three replies: the attributes count as voluntary by their perfection, by their effects, or because God acts freely even when the praised attribute is not voluntary.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r29.anchor: على اختيار الجمهور أيضاً ظاهراً ؛ فإن ما ورد عليهم من أن مذهبهم يستلزم أن لا يحمد الله تعالى

IBNASHUR:1:2/r30.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r30.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r30.claim: Ibn Ashur answers that nonvoluntariness is a defect in human qualities but perfection in God's eternal, necessary attributes; no analogy to human choice is needed, as with God's having no child.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r30.anchor: أما عدم الاختيار المختص بالصفات الذاتية الإلهية فإنه ليس عبارة عن نقص في صفاته ولكنه كمال نشأ من وجوب الصفة للذات

IBNASHUR:1:2/r31.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r31.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r31.claim: Hamd is the strongest language available to people for praising God, though it cannot fully convey realities beyond ordinary human experience.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r31.anchor: على أن توجيه الثناء إلى الله تعالى بمادة ( حمد ) هو أقصى ما تسمى به اللغة الموضوعة لأداء المعاني المتعارفة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r32.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r32.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r32.claim: Al-hamdu is nominative as the subject in every transmitted reading, and li-llah is its predicate, related to the general existential predicate.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r32.anchor: ( الحمد ) مرفوع بالابتداء في جميع القراءات المروية وقوله ( لله ) خبره فلام ( لله ) متعلق بالكون والاستقرار العام

IBNASHUR:1:2/r33.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r33.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR:1:2/r33.claim: Sibawayhi explains that praise expressions originally use an omitted verb in the absolute accusative, as in 'we praise God with praise'; the verbal noun replaces the verb.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r33.anchor: قال سيبويه هذا باب ما ينصب من المصادر على إضمار الفعل غير المستعمل إظهاره

IBNASHUR:1:2/r34.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r34.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r34.claim: Sibawayhi distinguishes supplicatory accusative sources from declarative ones such as hamdan and shukran, whose omitted verbs mean 'I praise' or 'I thank'.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r34.anchor: ثم قال بعد أبواب : هذا باب ما ينتصب على إضمار الفعل المتروك إظهاره من المصادر

IBNASHUR:1:2/r35.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r35.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r35.claim: The cited grammar says a definite source such as al-hamdu can be raised as a subject because it is declarative and definite; the sense of the omitted verb remains.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r35.anchor: ثم قال بعد باب آخر : هذا باب يختار فيه أن تكون المصادر مبتدأة مبنياً عليها ما بعدَها

IBNASHUR:1:2/r36.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r36.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r36.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also describes hamd's original accusative with an omitted verb and its shift to nominative as a means of indicating stability.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r36.anchor: وأصله النصب بإضمار فعله على أنه من المصادر التي ينصبها العرب بأفعال مضمرة في معنى الإخبار

IBNASHUR:1:2/r37.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r37.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r37.claim: The nominative makes a nominal sentence for permanence, the generic article broadens it, and fronting highlights it; the accusative construction cannot convey all three effects.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r37.anchor: والعدول عن النصب هنا إلى الرفع ليتأتى لهم الدلالةُ على الدوام والثبات بمصير الجملة اسمية

IBNASHUR:1:2/r38.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r38.speaker: سيبويه
IBNASHUR:1:2/r38.claim: A reading with al-hamda in the accusative and definite article is a Tamimi dialect form attested by Sibawayhi; its implied verb limits praise to the speaker or intended group.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r38.anchor: وهي لغة تميم كما قال سيبويه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r39.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r39.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r39.claim: Raising hamd announces praise from the speaker and all creation, whereas the accusative announces only the speaker's praise.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r39.anchor: الذي يَرْفع الحمدَ يُخبرُ أنَّ الحمدَ منه ومن جميع الخلق

IBNASHUR:1:2/r40.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r40.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r40.claim: Although anomalous, the accusative reading documents an Arabic stage in this familiar construction, showing that some speakers retained its absolute-object origin even with the article.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r40.anchor: واعلم أن قراءة النصب وإن كانت شاذة إلا أنها مجدية هنا لأنها دلت على اعتبار عربي في تطور هذا التركيب المشهور

IBNASHUR:1:2/r41.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r41.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r41.claim: The nominative is more eloquent than the accusative, and definite accusative is more expressive than indefinite accusative; raising marks permanence and stability.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r41.anchor: فقد بان أن قوله { الحمدُ لله } أبلغ من { الحمدَ لله } بالنصب

IBNASHUR:1:2/r42.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r42.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r42.claim: Al-Zamakhshari compares the nominative 'peace' in 51:25 with the earlier accusative greeting: Abraham answers with a more enduring, better greeting.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r42.anchor: قال في « الكشاف » : « إن العدول عن النصب إلى الرفع للدلالة على ثبات المعنى

IBNASHUR:1:2/r43.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r43.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r43.claim: Praise is foregrounded because revelation of the Quran is the immediate great blessing being acknowledged; its contextual importance can take precedence over God's name's intrinsic importance.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r43.anchor: قدم الحمد لأن المقام هنا مقام الحمد إذ هو ابتداء أَوْلى النعم بالحمد وهي نعمة تنزيل القرآن

IBNASHUR:1:2/r44.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r44.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r44.claim: The subject is deliberately fronted because another familiar formula could place the predicate first; the choice itself signals emphasis.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r44.anchor: لأن للبلغاء صيغتين متعارفتين في حمد الله تعالى إحداهما { الحمدُ لله } كما في الفاتحة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r45.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r45.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r45.claim: The article in al-hamd marks a known genus: its referent is recognizable to speaker and hearer, making the expression emphatic rather than singling out one instance.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r45.anchor: والتعريف فيه بالألف واللام تعريف الجنس لأن المصدر هنا في الأصل عوض عن الفعل

IBNASHUR:1:2/r46.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r46.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r46.claim: Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating the article as grammatically exhaustive; Ibn Ashur agrees that it marks genus, while the construction's combined effect entails all praise.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r46.anchor: صاحب « الكشاف » : « والاستغراق الذي توهمه كثير من الناس وهم منهم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r47.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r47.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r47.claim: The genus article with the possessive lam implies all praise belongs to God: if any instance belonged to another, exclusive possession of the genus would fail; this is hyperbolic restriction.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r47.anchor: إذ لو تحقق فرد من أفراد الحمد لغير الله تعالى لتحقق الجنس في ضمنه فلا يتم معنى اختصاص الجنس

IBNASHUR:1:2/r48.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r48.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r48.claim: The lam in li-llah may mean figurative exclusive possession or strengthen the verbal noun's relation as a weak, derived construction; exclusivity is also conveyed by the two definite parts.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r48.anchor: واللام في قوله تعالى : { للَّه } يجوز أن يكون للاختصاص على أنه اختصاص ادعائي كما مر

IBNASHUR:1:2/r49.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r49.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r49.claim: One group treats the sentence as a plain report that praise belongs to God, objecting that this leaves the speaker not actually praising Him.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r49.anchor: هذا وقد اختلف في أن جملة ( الحمد ) هل هي خبر أو إنشاء

IBNASHUR:1:2/r50.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r50.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r50.claim: Defenders of a purely declarative analysis answer that reporting praise recognizes God's beautiful attributes, that the speaker is included in the general report, or that inherited practice entails following it.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r50.anchor: وأجيب بأن الخبر بثبوت الحمد له تعالى اعتراف بأنه موصوف بالجميل إذ الحمد هو عين الوصف بالجميل

IBNASHUR:1:2/r51.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r51.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r51.claim: A response says literal report may serve its implied praise, as saying 'long sword-strap' to imply tall stature.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r51.anchor: وأجيب بأن المعنى المطابقي قد يؤتى به لأجل المعنى الالتزامي لأنه وسيلة له

IBNASHUR:1:2/r52.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r52.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r52.claim: Another group says the wording remains a report but its intended purpose is performative praise, like declarative wording for grief in 3:36; report form permits permanence, universality, exclusivity, and emphasis.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r52.anchor: وذهب فريق ثان إلى أن جملة { الحمد لله } هي خبر لا محالة إلا أنه أريد منه الإنشاء

IBNASHUR:1:2/r53.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r53.speaker: فريق ثان
IBNASHUR:1:2/r53.claim: A contrasting position calls the sentence a pure performative, shifted from reporting into praise like contracts and verbs of praise or blame.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r53.anchor: المذهب الثاني أن جملة { الحمد لله } إنشاء محض لا إشعار له بالخبرية

IBNASHUR:1:2/r54.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r54.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r54.claim: Ibn Ashur's preferred account is a report used to perform praise: the intention is performative, while report form supplies duration, universality, exclusivity, and emphasis unavailable to direct performative wording.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r54.anchor: والحق الذي لا محيد عنه أن الحمد لله خبر مستعمل في الإنشاء فالقصد هو الإنشائية لا محالة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r55.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r55.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r55.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's phrase 'we brought into being thanks for its Creator' confirms that Arabs described praise or thanks as something they create, treating it as performative expression.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r55.anchor: قول ذي الرمة : ولما جرت في الجزل جرياً

IBNASHUR:1:2/r56.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r56.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r56.claim: Allah is the proper name of the necessarily existent essence, worthy of every praise.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r56.anchor: والله هو اسم الذاتِ الواجبِ الوجود المستحق لجميع المحامد

IBNASHUR:1:2/r57.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r57.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r57.claim: The name derives from al-ilah, definite form of ilah, a generic word for deity; ilah is linked to worship or states entailing humble reverence and follows a passive fa'al pattern like kitab.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r57.anchor: وأصل هذا الاسم الإله بالتعريف وهو تعريف إلاه الذي هو اسم جنس للمعبود مشتق من أله بفتح اللام بمعنى عبد

IBNASHUR:1:2/r58.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r58.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r58.claim: Ibn Ashur thinks the name was established before Arab idolatry and originally signified the unique deity; it became a proper name through exclusive reference, not common usage.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r58.anchor: وأحسب أن اسمه تعالى تقرر في لغة العرب قبل دخول الإشراك فيهم فكان أصل وضعه دالاً على انفراده بالألوهية

IBNASHUR:1:2/r59.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r59.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r59.claim: Arabs do not appear to have used definite singular al-ilah for an idol: they used a possessive construction, another title, or the plural alihah.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r59.anchor: وإننا لم نقف على أن العرب أطلقوا الإله معرفاً باللام مفرداً على أحد أصنامهم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r60.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r60.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r60.claim: The name's origin recalls God specifically as deity and signals that He alone deserves worship because He created all.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r60.anchor: وأراهم أبدعوا وأعجبوا إذ جعلوا علم ذاته تعالى مشتقاً من اسم الجنس المؤذن بمفهوم الألوهية

IBNASHUR:1:2/r61.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r61.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r61.claim: Frequent use led speakers to drop the hamza from al-ilah, as in al-nas from al-unas; Ba'ith ibn Hurayth preserves al-ilah and Ubayd ibn al-Abras preserves al-unas with hamza.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r61.anchor: فحذفوا الهمزة من الإله لكثرة استعمال هذا اللفظ عند الدلالة عليه تعالى

IBNASHUR:1:2/r62.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r62.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r62.claim: Proper-name formation can alter a word: Ibn Jinni's example Shums ibn Malik changes the usual vowel, and Zamakhshari cites fixed-case Abdullah; Allah's naming has no parallel among personal names.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r62.anchor: شمس بضم الشين وأصله شَمس بفتحها كما قالوا حجر وسلمى فيكون مما غير عن نظائره لأجل العلمية

IBNASHUR:1:2/r63.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r63.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r63.claim: Calling Allah with ya while retaining the definite article shows that speakers treat the article as part of the name, unlike ordinary nouns entered by al.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r63.anchor: وقد دلوا على تناسيهم ما في الألف واللام من التعريف وأنهم جعلوهما جزءاً من الكلمة بتجويزهم نداء اسم الجلالة

IBNASHUR:1:2/r64.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r64.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r64.claim: Al-Zamakhshari uses al-Ba'ith's 'ma'adh al-ilah' as evidence that Allah originated from al-ilah; Ibn Ashur says this is persuasive because ma'adh conventionally takes Allah as its complement.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r64.anchor: وقد احتج صاحب « الكشاف » على كون أصله الإله ببيت البعيث المتقدم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r65.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r65.speaker: الجوهري عن سيبويه
IBNASHUR:1:2/r65.claim: Another proposed derivation takes Allah from laah, a verbal noun meaning to be hidden; the article was added to suggest the original sense, as in fadl and majd used as names.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r65.anchor: وهذا الوجه ذكر الجوهري عن سيبويه أنه جوزه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r66.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r66.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r66.claim: A second proposal derives the name from wilah, 'overwhelmed and bewildered'; initial waw became hamza after kasra, then the article was added and hamza dropped.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r66.anchor: ومنها أن أصله وِلاَهٌ بالواو فِعال بمعنى مفعول من وله

IBNASHUR:1:2/r67.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r67.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r67.claim: A further etymology borrows Syriac laaha as a divine name, Arabized by removing its final alif and adding the article.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r67.anchor: ومنها أن أصله ( لاَها ) بالسريانية علم له تعالى فعرب بحذف الألف وإدخال اللام عليه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r68.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r68.speaker: الزجاج ونسب إلى الخليل وسيبويه
IBNASHUR:1:2/r68.claim: Another group says the name was coined directly for God without derivation from alaha; one rationale is that Arabs named everything and would not leave God unnamed.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r68.anchor: ومنها أنه علم وضع لاسم الجلالة بالقصد الأولي من غير أخذ من أله وتصييره الإله

IBNASHUR:1:2/r69.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r69.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r69.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Arabs pronounce Allah's lam emphatically except where the preceding sound requires kasra, treating inherited consensus as evidence against speculative explanations.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r69.anchor: ولذلك أبَى صاحب « الكشاف » التعريج عليه فقال : « وعلى ذلك ( أي التفخيم ) العرب كلهم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r70.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r70.speaker: جمع من العلماء
IBNASHUR:1:2/r70.claim: A group of scholars, cited by al-Tilimsani, says discussion of Allah's name should be avoided out of reverence and because it requires scriptural permission.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r70.anchor: ومن أعجب الآراء ما ذكره صاحب « المنهل الأصفى في شرح الشفاء » التلمساني عن جمع من العلماء

IBNASHUR:1:2/r71.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r71.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r71.claim: Rabb is an attribute of Allah: after praise is attached to His essence to show inherent entitlement, the attribute adds entitlement through His qualities; this is clearer than saying 'praise belongs to Lord of the worlds.'
IBNASHUR:1:2/r71.anchor: وصف لاسم الجلالة فإنه بعد أن أسند الحمد لاسم ذاته تعالى تنبيهاً على الاستحقاق الذاتي

IBNASHUR:1:2/r72.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r72.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r72.claim: The four descriptions—Lord of the worlds, Merciful, Compassionate, King of Judgment Day—show each divine name's meaning merits praise and distinguishes God from alleged deities.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r72.anchor: وقد أجرى عليه أربعة أوصاف هي : رب العالمين ، الرحمن ، الرحيم ، ملك يوم الدين

IBNASHUR:1:2/r73.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r73.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r73.claim: Rabb may be a verbal noun or adjective on fa'l from rabba-yarubbu, 'to nurture and govern,' or from 'to own'; a verbal noun is intensive.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r73.anchor: والرب إما مصدر وإما صفة مشبهة على وزن فَعْل مِنْ رَبَّه يَرُبُّه بمعنى رباه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r74.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r74.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r74.claim: Tarbiya means gradually bringing something to completion; the adjective pattern fa'l from fa'ala yaf'ulu is rare, as in namma-yunimmu, nammun.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r74.anchor: والتربية تبليغ الشيء إلى كماله تدريجاً

IBNASHUR:1:2/r75.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r75.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r75.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers 'nurturer and governor' over 'owner' because it fits God's management of creation toward perfection and avoids redundancy with 'King of Judgment Day'; the latter can specify the afterlife.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r75.anchor: والأظهر أنه مشتق من ربه بمعنى رباه وساسه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r76.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r76.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
IBNASHUR:1:2/r76.claim: Al-Zamakhshari limits rabb to 'master and owner,' its frequent Arabic sense, while allowing verbal-noun or adjective analysis; Ibn Ashur says context can select a less frequent established sense.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r76.anchor: وإن كان الأكثر في كلام العرب ورود الرب بمعنى الملك والسيد وذلك الذي دعا صاحب « الكشاف »

IBNASHUR:1:2/r77.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r77.speaker: الحارث بن حلزة
IBNASHUR:1:2/r77.claim: Al-Harith ibn Hilliza calls Amr ibn Hind al-rabb in a poem, evidence that Arabs applied the title to a human ruler.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r77.anchor:
قال الحرث بن حلزة :
وهو الرب والشهيد

IBNASHUR:1:2/r78.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r78.speaker: النابغة
IBNASHUR:1:2/r78.claim: Al-Nabigha calls al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith rabb and uses rabb again of al-Nu'man when describing God's favor to him.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r78.anchor: وقال النابغة في النعمان بن الحارث : تخب إلى النعمان حتى تناله *** فدى لك من رب طريفي وتالدي

IBNASHUR:1:2/r79.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r79.speaker: غاوي بن ظالم أو عباس بن مرداس
IBNASHUR:1:2/r79.claim: A pre-Islamic poet applies rabb to an idol, ridiculing a deity with a fox urinating on its head; al-Uzza was also called al-Rabba and the plural is ارباب.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r79.anchor: كما قال غاوي بن ظالم أو عباس بن مرداس : أَرَبٌّ يبول الثعلبان برأسه

IBNASHUR:1:2/r80.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r80.speaker: صاحب الكشاف ومن تابعه
IBNASHUR:1:2/r80.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and followers claim rabb was used for others only with a qualifier; Ibn Ashur rejects this on unqualified poetic usage and the plural أرباب.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r80.anchor: وقال صاحب « الكشاف » ومن تابعه : إنه لم يطلق على غيره تعالى إلا مقيداً

IBNASHUR:1:2/r81.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r81.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r81.claim: The Quran uses rabb for the Egyptian official in 12:23 and for multiple false gods in 12:39, confirming that Arabic applies the term to beings other than God.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r81.anchor: وقد ورد الإطلاق في الإسلام أيضاً حين حكى عن يوسف عليه السلام قوله : { إنه ربي أحسن مثواي }

IBNASHUR:1:2/r82.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r82.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r82.claim: A hadith discourages calling a human master 'my rabb' as etiquette to prevent implication of worship; 'master' is preferred, compounds for a house or animal are allowed, and unrestricted use for a king is more disliked.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r82.anchor: إنما ورد في الحديث النهي عن أن يقول أحد لسيده ربي وليقل سيدي

IBNASHUR:1:2/r83.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r83.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r83.claim: Al-alamin is the plural of alam; few nouns on fa'il take this plural, with yasm (jasmine) the other example, whose plurals occur in al-A'sha's verse.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r83.anchor: و ( العالمين ) جمع عالم قالوا ولم يجمع فاعَلٌ هذا الجمع إلا في لفظين عالم وياسم

IBNASHUR:1:2/r84.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r84.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r84.claim: An alam is a genus among existing things; the word may derive from knowledge or sign because each genus is distinguishable and serves as a sign by which it is known.

IBNASHUR:1:2/r85.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r85.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r85.claim: The fa'il pattern usually marks an instrument; worlds are thus imaginatively instruments for knowing the Maker or truths, a subtle coinage by the Arabs.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r85.anchor: وهذا البناء مختص بالدلالة على الآلة غالباً كخاتم وقالب وطابع فجعلوا العوالم لكونها كالآلة للعلم بالصانع

IBNASHUR:1:2/r86.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r86.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r86.claim: The plural uses the rational masculine form even though some worlds are nonrational, by giving precedence to rational beings.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r86.anchor: ولقد أبدعوا إذ جمعوه جمع العقلاء مع أن منه ما ليس بعاقل تغليباً للعاقل

IBNASHUR:1:2/r87.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r87.speaker: التفتزاني
IBNASHUR:1:2/r87.claim: Al-Taftazani says alam names knowledgeable beings or each genus through which the Creator is known; singular alam normally needs a qualifying genitive, while 'the entire cosmos' is later theological terminology.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r87.anchor: قال التفتزاني في « شرح الكشاف » : « العالم اسم لذوي العلم ولكل جنس يعلم به الخالق

IBNASHUR:1:2/r88.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r88.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r88.claim: In this rhetorical context the definite article is exhaustive: there is no external or mental antecedent and no suitable literal or generic reading, so all genera are included.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r88.anchor: والتعرف فيه للاستغراق بقرينة المقام الخطابي فإنه إذا لم يكن عهد خارجي

IBNASHUR:1:2/r89.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r89.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r89.claim: Exhausting all genera entails their individuals, since lordship over abstract essences makes no sense; the plural with the definite article explicitly signals comprehensive scope.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r89.anchor: إلا أن استغراق الأجناس يستلزم استغراق أفرادها استلزاماً واضحاً إذ الأجناس لا تقصد لذاتها

IBNASHUR:1:2/r90.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:2/r90.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:2/r90.claim: The plural prevents an antecedent or generic reading and explicitly indicates exhaustive scope; Ibn Ashur rejects the Sakaki school's claim that singular is more comprehensive, referring to 2:31 for discussion.
IBNASHUR:1:2/r90.anchor: ولما صارت الجمعية قرينة على الاستغراق بطل منها معنى الجماعات فكان استغراق الجموع مساوياً لاستغراق المفردات أو أشمل منه

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r1.claim: Al-ḥamd is complete praise, and its definite article encompasses the entire genus of praises.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r1.anchor: { الحمد } معناه الثناء الكامل ،   والألف واللام فيه لاستغراق الجنس من المحامد

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r2.claim: Praise is broader than gratitude: gratitude responds to a favor done to the grateful person, and is one kind of praise.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r2.anchor: وهو أعم من الشكر ،   لأن الشكر إنما يكون على فعل جميل يسدى إلى الشاكر

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r3.claim: People who praise divide into those who give thanks for a favor and those who praise the praised one's attributes.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r3.anchor: فالحامد من الناس قسمان : الشاكر والمثني بالصفات

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r4.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r4.claim: Al-Ṭabarī treats ḥamd and shukr as synonyms; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as unsatisfactory.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r4.anchor: وذهب الطبري إلى أن الحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد ،   وذلك غير مرضي

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r5.speaker: بعض الناس
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r5.claim: An unnamed view distinguishes gratitude as praise for God's acts and blessings from praise for His attributes; Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds this distinction sounder than synonymy.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r5.anchor: حكي عن بعض الناس أنه قال : «الشكر ثناء على الله بأفعاله وأنعامه ،   والحمدُ ثناء بأوصافِه

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r6.claim: Al-Ṭabarī cites “praise to God, in gratitude” as proof of synonymy, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says “in gratitude” specifies praise for a blessing and therefore proves distinction.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r6.anchor: لأن قولك شكراً إنما خصصت به الحمد أنه على نعمة من النعم

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r7.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r7.claim: The seven canonical readers and most people pronounce the final dāl of al-ḥamdu with ḍamma.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r7.anchor: وأجمع السبعة وجمهور الناس على رفع الدال من «الحمدُ لله »

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r8.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r8.claim: Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj read al-ḥamda with fatḥa, on an understood omitted verb.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r8.anchor: وروي عن سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج «الحمدَ لله » بفتح الدال وهذا على إضمار فعل

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r9.speaker: الحسن بن الحسن وزيد بن علي
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r9.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read al-ḥamdi with kasra, assimilating its ending to the following word.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r9.anchor: وروي عن الحسن بن الحسن وزيد بن علي : «الحمدِ لله » ،   بكسر الدال على إتباع الأول الثاني

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r10.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r10.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads al-ḥamdu li-llahi with both dāl and lām rounded, assimilating the first to the second.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r10.anchor: وروي عن ابن أبي عبلة( {[15]} ) : «الحمدُ لُله » ،   بضم الدال واللام ،   على اتباع الثاني الأول

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r11.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r11.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reads the phrase as God's praise of Himself, implicitly commanding people to say “praise be to God”; he compares the implicit command in 1:5.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r11.anchor: قال الطبري : { الحمد لله } ثناء أثنى به على نفسه ،   وفي ضمنه أمر عباده أن يثنوا به عليه ،   فكأنه قال : «قولوا الحمد لله »

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r12.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r12.claim: Arabic can omit a referent recoverable from context, as in the cited poem where the answer identifies the person being dug for as a vizier.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r12.anchor: فقالَ السائلونَ لِمَنْ حفرْتُمْ .   .   .   فقال القائلونَ لهمْ وزيرُ

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r13.speaker: طائفة
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r13.claim: A group reads rabb with fatḥa, rather than the standard genitive form.

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r14.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r14.claim: One explanation of the accusative rabb is that it is an accusative of praise.

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r15.speaker: بعضهم
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r15.claim: Another explanation takes rabb as a vocative; on this analysis the following “You alone” also fits as a vocative.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r15.anchor: وقال بعضهم : «هو على النداء ،   وعليه يجيء { إياك } »

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r16.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r16.claim: Rabb can mean the worshipped one; Ghāwī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā's verse applies the word to an idol.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r16.anchor: والرب في اللغة : المعبود ،   والسيد المالك

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r17.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r17.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r17.claim: Rabb also means a master or owner, as in the expression “lord of slaves and servants.”
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r17.anchor: ومما جاء بمعنى السيد المالك قولهم : رب العبيد والمماليك

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r18.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r18.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r18.claim: Rabb may denote the person in charge who manages affairs; Labīd uses it of the lord of Kinda and Maʿadd.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r18.anchor: ومما جاء بمعنى القائم بالأمور الرئيس فيها قول لبيد :

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r19.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r19.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r19.claim: Rabb can mean king, as in al-Nābigha's line about traveling to al-Nuʿmān.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r19.anchor:
ومما جاء بمعنى الملك قوله النابغة :
تخبُّ إلى النعمان حتّى تنالَهُ

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r20.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r20.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r20.claim: The verb rabb may mean to repair or put right: al-Farazdaq describes leather as marbūb when properly treated.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r20.anchor: ومن معنى الإصلاح قولهم : أديم مربوب ،   أي مصلح ،   قال الشاعر( {[20]} ) الفرزدق

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r21.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r21.speaker: صفوان بن أمية
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r21.claim: At Ḥunayn, while still a polytheist, Ṣafwān said he preferred to be ruled by a Qurashī rather than a Hawāzin man.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r21.anchor: قول صفوان بن أمية لأخيه يوم حنين : «لأن يربني رجل من قريش خير من أن يربني رجل من هوازن »

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r22.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r22.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r22.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās said he would rather be ruled by a man from his own clan than by someone outside it; al-Bukhārī cites the report in his commentary on Sūrat al-Tawba.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r22.anchor: ومنه قول ابن عباس في شأن عبد الله بن الزبير ،   وعبد الملك بن مروان : «وإن كان لا بد لأن يربني رجل من بني عمي

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r23.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r23.speaker: علقمة بن عبدة
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r23.claim: ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbda uses rabb for the ruler who takes charge of and sets right his affairs.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r23.anchor: قول الشاعر علقمة بن عبدة : [ الطويل ] .

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r24.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r24.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r24.claim: These senses can overlap, but God alone is Rabb in the unrestricted sense, the Lord of lords in every respect.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r24.anchor: وهذه الاستعمالات قد تتداخل ،   فالرب على الإطلاق الذي هو رب الأرباب على كل جهة هو الله تعالى

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r25.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r25.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r25.claim: Al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam and comprises every existent apart from God; humanity, jinn, and other groups can each be called an ʿālam.
