IBNATIYYA:1:2/r25.anchor: جمع عالم ،   وهو كل موجود سوى الله تعالى

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r26.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r26.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r26.claim: Each successive generation or age can be called an ʿālam, which makes the plural appropriate for the world's changing times.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r26.anchor: ومن حيث عالم الزمان متبدل في زمان آخر حسن جمعها

IBNATIYYA:1:2/r27.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r27.speaker: الزجاج
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r27.claim: Al-Zajjāj says ʿālam has no singular of the same form and derives from knowledge or a sign because the world points to its maker.
IBNATIYYA:1:2/r27.anchor: ولفظة العالم جمع لا واحد له من لفظه وهو مأخوذ من العلم والعلامة لأنه يدل على موجده ،   كذا قال الزجاج

KASHSHAF:1:2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r1.claim: Hamd and madh are synonymous: praise for something beautiful, whether a blessing, good lineage, or courage.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد والمدح أخوان ، وهو الثناء والنداء على الجميل

KASHSHAF:1:2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r2.claim: Gratitude is for blessings and occurs by heart, tongue, and limbs; the poet names hand, tongue, and hidden conscience.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r2.anchor: أفادتكم النعماء مني ثلاثة *** يدي ولساني والضمير المحجبا

KASHSHAF:1:2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r3.claim: Hamd is performed by the tongue alone and is one branch of gratitude.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r3.anchor: والحمد باللسان وحده ، فهو إحدى شعب الشكر

KASHSHAF:1:2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r4.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:1:2/r4.claim: A Prophetic report calls praise the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God without praising Him.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r4.anchor: الحمد رأس الشكر ، ما شكر الله عبد لم يحمده

KASHSHAF:1:2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r5.claim: Verbal praise publicizes a blessing and reveals awareness more clearly than hidden inward belief or ambiguous bodily acts.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r5.anchor: لأن ذكر النعمة باللسان والثناء على موليها

KASHSHAF:1:2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r6.claim: Praise is opposite blame; gratitude is opposite ingratitude.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r6.anchor: والحمد نقيضه الذمّ ، والشكر نقيضه الكفران

KASHSHAF:1:2/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r7.claim: Al-hamdu is the subject and the prepositional phrase li-llah its predicate.

KASHSHAF:1:2/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r8.speaker: بعضهم
KASHSHAF:1:2/r8.claim: Some readers use the accusative al-hamda, understood with an omitted verb.

KASHSHAF:1:2/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r9.claim: The accusative treats hamd as a verbal noun with an omitted verb, as in shukran, kufran, and ajaban.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r9.anchor: المصادر التي تنصبها العرب بأفعال مضمرة في معنى الإخبار

KASHSHAF:1:2/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r10.claim: Subhanaka and maʿadha Allah stand in for their verbs, which speakers do not normally use alongside them.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r10.anchor: ينزلونها منزلة أفعالها ويسدون بها مسدها

KASHSHAF:1:2/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r11.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r11.claim: The nominative instead of the accusative presents praise as established and lasting.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r11.anchor: والعدل بها عن النصب إلى الرفع على الابتداء

KASHSHAF:1:2/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r12.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r12.claim: In 11:69 Abraham's nominative greeting signals more lasting peace than the visitors' accusative greeting.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r12.anchor: رفع السلام الثاني للدلالة على أن إبراهيم عليه السلام حياهم بتحية أحسن من تحيتهم

KASHSHAF:1:2/r13.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r13.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r13.claim: The sense is we praise God with praise; 1:5 explains the manner as worshipping and seeking help from Him.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r13.anchor: نحمد الله حمدا ، ولذلك قيل : { إياك نعبد وإياك نستعين }

KASHSHAF:1:2/r14.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r14.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r14.claim: The definite article marks generic praise, what everyone recognizes among kinds of acts; it does not signal exhaustive totality.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r14.anchor: هو تعريف الجنس ، ومعناه الإشارة إلى ما يعرفه كل أحد

KASHSHAF:1:2/r15.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r15.speaker: الحسن البصري
KASHSHAF:1:2/r15.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri reads the dāl with kasra by assimilation to the lām.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r15.anchor: وقرأ الحسن البصري : { الحمد لله } بكسر الدال

KASHSHAF:1:2/r16.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r16.speaker: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة
KASHSHAF:1:2/r16.claim: Ibrahim ibn Abi Abla reads the lām with damma by assimilation to the dāl.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r16.anchor: وقرأ إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة : { الحمد لله } بضم اللام

KASHSHAF:1:2/r17.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r17.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r17.claim: Al-Zamakhshari prefers Ibrahim's reading because the stronger inflectional vowel controls the lexical vowel.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r17.anchor: حيث جعل الحركة البنائية تابعة للإعرابية التي هي أقوى

KASHSHAF:1:2/r18.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r18.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r18.claim: Rabb means owner; Safwan tells Abu Sufyan he prefers being owned by a Qurayshi to a Hawazini.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r18.anchor: قول صفوان لأبي سفيان : لأن يربني رجل من قريش أحب إلي

KASHSHAF:1:2/r19.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r19.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r19.claim: Rabb may be an adjective formed from a verbal noun, expressing intensity like ʿadl.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r19.anchor: وصفا بالمصدر للمبالغة كما وصف بالعدل

KASHSHAF:1:2/r20.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r20.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r20.claim: Unqualified rabb is only used of God; for others it is qualified, such as owner of a house or camel.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r20.anchor: ولم يطلقوا الرب إلا في الله وحده

KASHSHAF:1:2/r21.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r21.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r21.claim: Quran examples use rabb relationally in 12:50 and 12:23.

KASHSHAF:1:2/r22.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r22.speaker: زيد بن علي
KASHSHAF:1:2/r22.claim: Zayd ibn Ali reads rabb al-alamin in the accusative as praise or an understood gloss of al-hamdu lillah.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r22.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي رضي الله عنهما : { رب العالمين } بالنصب على المدح

KASHSHAF:1:2/r23.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r23.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r23.claim: Al-alam may mean beings with knowledge, angels and the two rational classes, humans and jinn.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r23.anchor: العالم : اسم لذوي العلم من الملائكة والثقلين

KASHSHAF:1:2/r24.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r24.speaker: قيل
KASHSHAF:1:2/r24.claim: Another view takes al-alamin to mean everything the Creator knows, including bodies and accidents.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r24.anchor: وقيل : كل ما علم به الخالق من الأجسام والأعراض

KASHSHAF:1:2/r25.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r25.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r25.claim: The plural includes every genus covered by the word.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r25.anchor: ليشمل كل جنس مما سمي به

KASHSHAF:1:2/r26.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:2/r26.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:2/r26.claim: Though alam is a noun, it can take the rational plural because it carries a descriptive sense of knowledge.
KASHSHAF:1:2/r26.anchor: ساغ ذلك لمعنى الوصفية فيه وهي الدلالة على معنى العلم

MAWARDI:1:2/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r1.claim: Hamd is praise of the praised one’s beautiful attributes and actions, while shukr is praise for a favor; every shukr is hamd but not every hamd is shukr, so God may praise Himself but not thank Himself.
MAWARDI:1:2/r1.anchor: فهو الثناء على المحمود بجميل صفاته وأفعاله ،   والشكرُ الثناء عليه بإنعامه ،   فكلُّ شكرٍ حمدٌ ،   وليسَ كلُّ حمدٍ شكراً

MAWARDI:1:2/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r2.claim: Hamd differs from madh: hamd is deserved only for a good act, while madh may praise an act or a non-action; all hamd is madh, but not vice versa.
MAWARDI:1:2/r2.anchor: أن الحمد لا يستحق إلا على فعلٍ حسن ،   والمدح قد يكون على فعل وغير فعل ،   فكلُّ حمدٍ مدحٌ وليْسَ كل مدحٍ حمداً

MAWARDI:1:2/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r3.claim: God may be praised for knowledge and power but not hamd for them, since they are attributes of essence; He may be praised and hamd for creating and providing, attributes of action.
MAWARDI:1:2/r3.anchor: جاز أن يمدح الله تعالى على صفته ،   بأنه عالم قادر ،   ولم يجز أن يحمد به ،   لأن العلم والقدرة من صفات ذاته

MAWARDI:1:2/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r4.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r4.claim: One derivation of rabb is owner, as in the owner of a house.
MAWARDI:1:2/r4.anchor: أنه مشتق من المالك ،   كما يقال رب الدار أي مالكها

MAWARDI:1:2/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r5.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r5.claim: Another derivation is master; 12:41 calls a human master rabb.
MAWARDI:1:2/r5.anchor:
أنه مشتق من السيد ،   لأن السيد يسمى ربّاً ،   قال تعالى :
{ أَمَّا أَحَدُكُمَا فَيَسْقِي رَبَّهُ خَمْراً

MAWARDI:1:2/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r6.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r6.claim: A third meaning is manager; rabbani scholars are so called for managing people through knowledge, and a housewife is called rabbat al-bayt for managing the home.
MAWARDI:1:2/r6.anchor: أن الرب المدَبِّر ،   ومنه قول الله عزَّ وجلَّ : { وَالرَّبَّانِيُّونَ وَالأحْبَارُ }{[10]} وهم العلماء ،   سموا ربَّانيِّين ،   لقيامهم بتدبير الناس بعلمهم

MAWARDI:1:2/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r7.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r7.claim: A fourth derivation connects rabb to nurturing; stepchildren are named rabائب because the husband raises them, as in 4:23.
MAWARDI:1:2/r7.anchor: الرب مشتق من التربية ،   ومنه قوله تعالى

MAWARDI:1:2/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r8.claim: If rabb means owner or master, it describes God’s essence; if it means manager or nurturer, it describes His action.
MAWARDI:1:2/r8.anchor: فعلى هذا ،   أن صفة الله تعالى بأنه رب ،   لأنه مالك أو سيد ،   فذلك صفة من صفات ذاته ،   وإن قيل لأنه مدبِّر لخلقه ،   أو مُربِّيهم

MAWARDI:1:2/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r9.claim: With the definite article, rabb is exclusive to God; without it, the word is shared by God and His servants.
MAWARDI:1:2/r9.anchor: ومتى أدْخَلت عليه الألف واللام .   اختص الله تعالى به دون عباده ،   وإن حذفتا منه ،   صار مشتركاً بين الله وبين عباده

MAWARDI:1:2/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI:1:2/r10.claim: Al-alamin is the plural of alam, with no singular of the same form, like raht and qawm; each age or community is an alam, as the cited al-A‘raj verse illustrates.
MAWARDI:1:2/r10.anchor: فهو جمع عَالم ،   لا واحد له من لفظه ،   مثل : رهط وقوم ،   وأهلُ كلِّ زمانٍ{[13]} عَالَمٌ ،   قال العجاج

MAWARDI:1:2/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI:1:2/r11.claim: Ibn Abbas takes the worlds to mean rational beings: angels, humans, and jinn.
MAWARDI:1:2/r11.anchor: أنّه ما يعقِل : من الملائكة ،   والإنس والجنِّ ،   وهذا قول ابن عباس

MAWARDI:1:2/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r12.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r12.claim: Another view takes the worlds to mean the present world and all it contains.

MAWARDI:1:2/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r13.speaker: أبو إسحاق الزجاج
MAWARDI:1:2/r13.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes the worlds to include everything God created in this world and the afterlife.
MAWARDI:1:2/r13.anchor: أن العالم كل ما خلقه الله تعالى في الدنيا والآخرة ،   وهذا قول أبي إسحاق الزجَّاج

MAWARDI:1:2/r14.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r14.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r14.claim: The derivation from knowledge fits the interpretation that alam means rational beings.
MAWARDI:1:2/r14.anchor: أنه مشتق من العلم ،   وهذا تأويل مَنْ جعل العالم اسماً لما يعقل

MAWARDI:1:2/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI:1:2/r15.speaker: unattributed
MAWARDI:1:2/r15.claim: The alternative derivation is from sign, since the worlds are signs pointing to their creator; this fits the interpretation that alam means all created things.
MAWARDI:1:2/r15.anchor: أنه مشتق من العلامة ،   لأنه دلالة على خالقه ،   وهذا تأويل مَنْ جعل العالم اسماً لكُلِّ مخلوقٍ

NASAFI:1:1/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:1/r12.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
NASAFI:1:1/r12.claim: Abu Hurayra reports God’s dialogue dividing the Fatiha between Himself and the servant: praise, glorification, and exaltation belong to God; the worshipper’s request for guidance and the response to it belong to the servant, while worship and aid are shared.
NASAFI:1:1/r12.anchor: قال الله تعالى قسمت الصلاة أي الفاتحة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين ولعبدي ما سأل

NASAFI:1:2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r1.claim: Hamd is describing someone with praise and excellence, giving preference to the praiseworthy quality.
NASAFI:1:2/r1.anchor: { الحمد } الوصف بالجميل على جهة التفضيل ، وهو رفع بالابتداء

NASAFI:1:2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r2.claim: Al-hamdu is nominative as a subject, though it can be read accusative with an implied verb as an explanatory verbal noun, like ‘thanks’ or ‘ingratitude’; nominative wording conveys a settled, enduring meaning.
NASAFI:1:2/r2.anchor: وقد قرئ بإضمار فعله على أنه من المصادر المنصوبة بأفعال مضمرة في معنى الإخبار

NASAFI:1:2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r3.claim: The lām in lillah attaches to an omitted predicate, understood as ‘due’ or ‘established.’
NASAFI:1:2/r3.anchor: واللام متعلق بمحذوف أي واجب أو ثابت

NASAFI:1:2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r4.speaker: قيل
NASAFI:1:2/r4.claim: One view treats hamd and madh as near-synonyms: both are praise and notice of beauty, whether for a blessing, courage, or noble lineage.
NASAFI:1:2/r4.anchor: وقيل : الحمد والمدح أخوان وهو الثناء والنداء على الجميل من نعمة وغيرها

NASAFI:1:2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r5.claim: Unlike hamd, shukr is only for a blessing and can be expressed by heart, tongue, and limbs; the cited poet names hand, tongue, and the veiled heart as its three forms.
NASAFI:1:2/r5.anchor: وأما الشكر فعلى النعمة خاصة وهو بالقلب واللسان والجوارح قال

NASAFI:1:2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r6.speaker: النبي
NASAFI:1:2/r6.claim: A Prophetic report calls praise the head of gratitude and says a servant has not thanked God without praising Him; praise leads because the tongue makes gratitude more public than the hidden heart or ambiguous bodily acts.
NASAFI:1:2/r6.anchor: الحمد رأس الشكر ما شكر الله عبد لم يحمده

NASAFI:1:2/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r7.speaker: قيل
NASAFI:1:2/r7.claim: Another distinction makes madh praise inherent perfections, shukr praise for beneficence, and hamd broad enough to cover both.
NASAFI:1:2/r7.anchor: وقيل : المدح ثناء على ما هو له من أوصاف الكمال ككونه باقيا قادرا

NASAFI:1:2/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r8.claim: For Nasafi, the definite article in al-hamd is comprehensive, against the Mu‘tazila; its attachment to Allah, the name of the divine essence, gathers all perfections and reflects the doctrine of created acts.
NASAFI:1:2/r8.anchor: والألف واللام فيه للاستغراق عندنا خلافاً للمعتزلة

NASAFI:1:2/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r9.claim: Rabb means owner; the cited exchange has Safwan tell Abu Sufyan that being owned by a Qurayshi is preferable to being owned by a Hawazini. Rabb can also be a verbal noun used intensively as an adjective.
NASAFI:1:2/r9.anchor: { رَبّ العالمين } الرب المالك ومنه قول صفوان لأبي سفيان : لأن يربني رجل من قريش

NASAFI:1:2/r10.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r10.claim: Rabb is used absolutely only of God, while for human masters it is restricted by a possessive phrase, as in Joseph’s story; al-Wasiti explains God as creator at the beginning, sustainer, and forgiver at the end.
NASAFI:1:2/r10.anchor: ولم يطلقوا الرب إلا في الله وحده وهو في العبيد مع التقييد

NASAFI:1:2/r11.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r11.speaker: الواسطي
NASAFI:1:2/r11.claim: Al-Wasiti describes God as creator at the beginning, nourisher through provision, and forgiver at the end.
NASAFI:1:2/r11.anchor: وقال الواسطي : هو الخالق ابتداء ، والمربي غذاء ، والغافر انتهاء

NASAFI:1:2/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r12.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r12.claim: Rabb is one of God’s greatest names.
NASAFI:1:2/r12.anchor: وهو اسم الله الأعظم والعالم كل ما علم به الخالق

NASAFI:1:2/r13.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r13.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r13.claim: Al-‘alamin may mean everything the Creator knows of bodies, substances, and accidents, or every existing thing besides God, named for being evidence of His existence.
NASAFI:1:2/r13.anchor: والعالم كل ما علم به الخالق من الأجسام والجواهر والأعراض

NASAFI:1:2/r14.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI:1:2/r14.speaker: author
NASAFI:1:2/r14.claim: The plural ending -in is used although normally associated with rational beings or their equivalent because ‘alamin has an adjectival sense, indicating knowledge.
NASAFI:1:2/r14.anchor: وإنما جمع بالواو والنون مع أنه يختص بصفات العقلاء أو ما في حكمها

QURTUBI:1:2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r1.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra and Abu Saʿid says that when a servant praises God, God affirms that the servant has spoken truly and that praise belongs to Him.
QURTUBI:1:2/r1.anchor: عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : ( إذا قال العبد الحمد لله قال صدق عبدي الحمد لي )

QURTUBI:1:2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r2.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r2.claim: Anas reports that God is pleased when a servant eats or drinks and praises Him for it; Qurtubi cites this from Muslim.
QURTUBI:1:2/r2.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( إن الله ليرضى عن العبد

QURTUBI:1:2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r3.speaker: الحسن
QURTUBI:1:2/r3.claim: Al-Hasan says that no blessing exists for which praise of God is not better than the blessing itself.
QURTUBI:1:2/r3.anchor: وقال الحسن : ما من نعمة إلا والحمد لله أفضل منها

QURTUBI:1:2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r4.claim: Anas reports from the Prophet that when God gives a servant a blessing and the servant praises Him, the praise is better than what was received.
QURTUBI:1:2/r4.anchor: وروى ابن ماجه عن أنس بن مالك قال : قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( ما أنعم الله على عبد نعمة

QURTUBI:1:2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r5.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r5.claim: A report in Nawādir al-uṣūl from Anas says that if someone possessed the whole world and then praised God, the praise would be better than it.
QURTUBI:1:2/r5.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( لو أن الدنيا كلها بحذافيرها بيد رجل من أمتي ثم قال : الحمد لله

QURTUBI:1:2/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r6.claim: Abu ʿAbd Allah explains that the person first receives the world and then the enduring word of praise, which is better because the world perishes while the word remains among the righteous deeds.
QURTUBI:1:2/r6.anchor: قال أبو عبد الله : معناه عندنا أنه قد أعطي الدنيا ثم أعطي على أثرها هذه الكلمة

QURTUBI:1:2/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r7.claim: Another wording says that what the servant gave was more than what he received; this frames praise as the servant’s gift and the world as God’s gift, though both ultimately come from God.
QURTUBI:1:2/r7.anchor: وقيل في بعض الروايات : لكان ما أعطى أكثر مما أخذ

QURTUBI:1:2/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r8.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r8.claim: Ibn ʿUmar reports that angels could not record a servant’s praise fitting God’s majesty, so God told them to write it as the servant had said until He rewards him.
QURTUBI:1:2/r8.anchor: عن ابن عمر أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حدثهم : ( أن عبدا من عباد الله قال : يا رب لك الحمد

QURTUBI:1:2/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r9.claim: The language note explains that aʿḍala means a matter became difficult and intractable; muʿaḍḍalāt are hardships, and the verb also describes obstructed childbirth.
QURTUBI:1:2/r9.anchor: قال أهل اللغة : أعضل الأمر : اشتد واستغلق

QURTUBI:1:2/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r10.claim: Given that usage, the report’s wording may be read as aʿḍalat al-malakayn or ʿaḍḍalat al-malakayn without a preposition.
QURTUBI:1:2/r10.anchor: فعلى هذا يكون : أعضلت الملكين أو عضلت الملكين بغير باء

QURTUBI:1:2/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r11.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r11.claim: Abu Malik al-Ashʿari reports from the Prophet that purification is half of faith, praise fills the balance, and glorification with praise fills or fills the space between heaven and earth; Qurtubi cites Muslim.
QURTUBI:1:2/r11.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم : [ الطهور شطر الإيمان والحمد لله تملأ الميزان

QURTUBI:1:2/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r12.speaker: طائفة
QURTUBI:1:2/r12.claim: One group considers praise of God better than the declaration of unity because praise includes both tawhid and praise, while the declaration includes tawhid alone.
QURTUBI:1:2/r12.anchor: فقالت طائفة : قوله الحمد لله رب العالمين أفضل لأن في ضمنه التوحيد

QURTUBI:1:2/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r13.speaker: طائفة
QURTUBI:1:2/r13.claim: Another group considers la ilaha illa Allah better because it repels unbelief and associating partners, and people fight on its basis; they cite the Prophet’s command to fight until people say it.
QURTUBI:1:2/r13.anchor: وقالت طائفة : لا إله إلا الله أفضل لأنها تدفع الكفر والإشراك وعليها يقاتل الخلق

QURTUBI:1:2/r14.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r14.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI:1:2/r14.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya chooses la ilaha illa Allah as superior, citing the report that it is the best thing the Prophet and earlier prophets said.
QURTUBI:1:2/r14.anchor: واختار هذا القول ابن عطية قال : والحاكم بذلك قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( أفضل ما قلت أنا والنبيون

QURTUBI:1:2/r15.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r15.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r15.claim: Muslims agree that God is praised for all blessings, including faith; since faith belongs to the created worlds, Qurtubi infers that faith is God’s act and creation, contrary to the Qadari claim that humans create it.
QURTUBI:1:2/r15.anchor: أجمع المسلمون على أن الله محمود على سائر نعمه وأن مما أنعم الله به الإيمان

QURTUBI:1:2/r16.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r16.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r16.claim: In Arabic, al-ḥamd is complete praise; the definite article encompasses every kind of praise, all of which God deserves because He has the most beautiful names and highest attributes.
QURTUBI:1:2/r16.anchor: الحمد في كلام العرب معناه الثناء الكامل ، والألف واللام لاستغراق الجنس

QURTUBI:1:2/r17.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r17.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r17.claim: The cited verse uses the word aḥmadī as a plural of ḥamd, supporting the linguistic discussion of the word’s forms.
QURTUBI:1:2/r17.anchor: في قول الشاعر : وأبلج محمود الثناء خَصَّصْتُه

QURTUBI:1:2/r18.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r18.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r18.claim: Ḥamd is the opposite of blame; ḥamīd and maḥmūd describe one praised, and taḥmīd is more emphatic than ḥamd.
QURTUBI:1:2/r18.anchor: فالحمد نقيض الذم ، تقول : حمدت الرجل أحمده حمدا فهو حميد ومحمود والتحميد أبلغ من الحمد

QURTUBI:1:2/r19.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r19.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r19.claim: The poet’s use of muḥammad for a person rich in praiseworthy qualities explains the name Muhammad; another verse says the Throne’s Lord is Maḥmūd and the Prophet is Muhammad.

QURTUBI:1:2/r20.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r20.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r20.claim: Maḥmada means the opposite of blame; aḥmada can mean one’s affairs turned praiseworthy or that one found a place pleasing, while a ḥamada is someone who overpraises things and ḥamadat al-nār is the sound of its flames.
QURTUBI:1:2/r20.anchor: والمحمدة : خلاف المذمة . وأحمد الرجل : صار أمره إلى الحمد . وأحمدته : وجدته محمودا

QURTUBI:1:2/r21.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r21.speaker: الطبري والمبرد
QURTUBI:1:2/r21.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Mubarrad hold that ḥamd and shukr have the same meaning; Qurtubi says this view is not sound.
QURTUBI:1:2/r21.anchor: ذهب أبو جعفر الطبري وأبو العباس المبرد إلى أن الحمد والشكر بمعنى واحد سواء وليس بمرضي

QURTUBI:1:2/r22.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r22.speaker: ابن عطاء
QURTUBI:1:2/r22.claim: Al-Sulami transmits from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ the synonymy view; Ibn ʿAṭāʾ explains praise as gratitude for God enabling people to learn and praise Him.
QURTUBI:1:2/r22.anchor: قال ابن عطاء : معناه الشكر لله إذ كان منه الامتنان على تعليمنا إياه

QURTUBI:1:2/r23.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r23.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI:1:2/r23.claim: Al-Ṭabarī argues the terms are synonymous because Arabic permits the phrase al-ḥamdu lillāhi shukran, praise to God in gratitude.
QURTUBI:1:2/r23.anchor: واستدل الطبري على أنهما بمعنى بصحة قولك : الحمد لله شكرا

QURTUBI:1:2/r24.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r24.speaker: ابن عطية
QURTUBI:1:2/r24.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya counters that adding shukran narrows the praise to gratitude for a particular blessing, which shows the words are not identical.
QURTUBI:1:2/r24.anchor: قال ابن عطية : وهو في الحقيقة دليل على خلاف ما ذهب إليه

QURTUBI:1:2/r25.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r25.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI:1:2/r25.claim: Some scholars say gratitude is broader because it can be expressed by tongue, limbs, and heart, while praise is verbal alone.
QURTUBI:1:2/r25.anchor: وقال بعض العلماء : إن الشكر أعم من الحمد ؛ لأنه باللسان وبالجوارح والقلب

QURTUBI:1:2/r26.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r26.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI:1:2/r26.claim: Another view makes praise broader because it includes both gratitude and commendation, can stand in place of gratitude, and is not itself replaced by gratitude.
QURTUBI:1:2/r26.anchor: وقيل : الحمد أعم لأن فيه معنى الشكر ومعنى المدح ، وهو أعم من الشكر

QURTUBI:1:2/r27.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r27.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI:1:2/r27.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls praise the word of every grateful person and illustrates its use by Adam, Noah, Abraham, David and Solomon, Muhammad, and the people of Paradise.
QURTUBI:1:2/r27.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال : الحمد لله كلمة كل شاكر

QURTUBI:1:2/r28.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r28.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r28.claim: Qurtubi’s preferred distinction is that praise commends attributes without requiring prior kindness, whereas gratitude praises a benefactor for a favor; praise is broader because it includes commendation as well as thanks.
QURTUBI:1:2/r28.anchor: قلت : الصحيح أن الحمد ثناء على الممدوح بصفاته من غير سبق إحسان

QURTUBI:1:2/r29.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r29.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r29.claim: Ḥamd can also mean satisfaction: one says I tested him and praised him to mean I was pleased with him; Qurtubi links this usage to maqāman maḥmūdan and a prophetic phrase about approving washing the urethra.
QURTUBI:1:2/r29.anchor: ويذكر الحمد بمعنى الرضا يقال : بلوته فحمدته ، أي رضيته . ومنه قوله تعالى :

QURTUBI:1:2/r30.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r30.speaker: جعفر الصادق
QURTUBI:1:2/r30.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq gives a symbolic reading of the letters: ḥāʾ signifies unity, mīm dominion, and dāl permanence; knowing these is knowing God.
QURTUBI:1:2/r30.anchor: ويذكر عن جعفر الصادق في قوله " الحمد لله " : من حمده بصفاته كما وصف نفسه

QURTUBI:1:2/r31.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r31.speaker: شقيق بن إبراهيم
QURTUBI:1:2/r31.claim: Shafīq ibn Ibrāhīm says gratitude has three conditions: recognizing the giver, being content with what was given, and not disobeying God while one retains strength.
QURTUBI:1:2/r31.anchor: وقال شقيق بن إبراهيم في تفسير " الحمد لله " قال : هو على ثلاثة أوجه : أولها

QURTUBI:1:2/r32.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r32.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r32.claim: God praises Himself and opens His Book with praise, while people are forbidden to claim purity for themselves; Qurtubi cites the command not to praise yourselves and the report to throw dust in flatterers’ faces.
QURTUBI:1:2/r32.anchor: أثنى الله سبحانه بالحمد على نفسه وافتتح كتابه بحمده ، ولم يأذن في ذلك لغيره

QURTUBI:1:2/r33.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r33.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r33.claim: God’s self-praise precedes any creature’s praise and is without cause, while created praise is mixed with ulterior causes.
QURTUBI:1:2/r33.anchor: أي سبق الحمد مني لنفسي أن يحمد نفسه أحد من العالمين ، وحمدي نفسي لنفسي في الأزل

QURTUBI:1:2/r34.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r34.speaker: علماؤنا
QURTUBI:1:2/r34.claim: Qurtubi’s scholars say an imperfect creature should not praise himself to attract benefits or repel harm.
QURTUBI:1:2/r34.anchor: قال علماؤنا : فيستقبح من المخلوق الذي لم يعط الكمال أن يحمد نفسه ليستجلب لها المنافع

QURTUBI:1:2/r35.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r35.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI:1:2/r35.claim: One explanation says God praised Himself eternally because His servants cannot fulfill the duty of praising Him; even the Messenger declared that he could not enumerate praise to God.
QURTUBI:1:2/r35.anchor: وقيل : لما علم سبحانه عجز عباده عن حمده حمد نفسه بنفسه لنفسه في الأزل

QURTUBI:1:2/r36.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r36.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r36.claim: The Prophet’s confession that he cannot enumerate praise to God illustrates the limits of human praise.
QURTUBI:1:2/r36.anchor: ألا ترى سيد المرسلين كيف أظهر العجز بقوله : ( لا أحصي ثناء عليك )

QURTUBI:1:2/r37.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r37.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r37.claim: A poet says that when people praise God rightly, He is as they praise Him and greater than their praise can express.
QURTUBI:1:2/r37.anchor: وأنشدوا : إذا نحن أثنينا عليك بصَالح *** فأنت كما نُثْنِي وفوق الذي نُثْنِي

QURTUBI:1:2/r38.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r38.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI:1:2/r38.claim: Another explanation says God praised Himself eternally because He knew His blessings would overwhelm servants’ ability to repay them, thereby easing the burden of indebtedness and making the blessing more enjoyable.
QURTUBI:1:2/r38.anchor: وقيل : حمد نفسه في الأزل لما علم من كثرة نعمه على عباده وعجزهم على القيام بواجب حمده

QURTUBI:1:2/r39.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r39.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة ورؤبة بن العجاج
QURTUBI:1:2/r39.claim: The seven readers and most people read the dāl in al-ḥamdu with nominative ḍamma; Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj are reported to read it accusative, with an implied verb.
QURTUBI:1:2/r39.anchor: وأجمع القراء السبعة وجمهور الناس على رفع الدال من " الحمد لله "

QURTUBI:1:2/r40.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r40.speaker: سيبويه
QURTUBI:1:2/r40.claim: Sībawayh says nominative al-ḥamdu lillāh conveys that praise from the speaker and all creatures belongs to God, while the accusative reports only the speaker’s own praise.
QURTUBI:1:2/r40.anchor: سيبويه قال : إذا قال الرجل الحمد لله بالرفع ففيه من المعنى مثل ما في قولك : حمدت الله حمدا

QURTUBI:1:2/r41.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r41.speaker: غير سيبويه
QURTUBI:1:2/r41.claim: Another explanation takes the nominative as an appeal for pardon and as exaltation and glorification, so it functions as supplication rather than a plain report.
QURTUBI:1:2/r41.anchor: وقال غير سيبويه . إنما يتكلم بهذا تعرضا لعفو الله ومغفرته وتعظيما له وتمجيدا

QURTUBI:1:2/r42.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r42.speaker: الطبري
QURTUBI:1:2/r42.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says God’s praise of Himself implicitly commands His servants to praise Him, as though the wording said, Say praise belongs to God.
QURTUBI:1:2/r42.anchor: قال الطبري : " الحمد لله " ثناء أثنى به على نفسه وفي ضمنه أمر عباده أن يثنوا عليه

QURTUBI:1:2/r43.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r43.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r43.claim: Qurtubi treats the implied command to say as a common Arabic ellipsis whose context supplies the omitted words, and says the same construction applies to the later address, as though it said, Say, You alone we worship.
QURTUBI:1:2/r43.anchor: وعلى هذا يجيء قولوا إياك . وهذا من حذف العرب ما يدل ظاهر الكلام عليه

QURTUBI:1:2/r44.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r44.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة
QURTUBI:1:2/r44.claim: Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads the dāl and lām with ḍamma by vowel assimilation for phonetic harmony, a common pattern illustrated by other words and a poetic line.
QURTUBI:1:2/r44.anchor: وروي عن ابن أبي عبلة : " الحمد لله " بضم الدال واللام على إتباع الثاني الأول

QURTUBI:1:2/r45.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r45.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي
QURTUBI:1:2/r45.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan and Zayd ibn ʿAlī read the dāl of al-ḥamd with kasra by assimilation of the first vowel to the second.
QURTUBI:1:2/r45.anchor: وروي عن الحسن بن أبي الحسن وزيد بن علي : " الحمد لله " بكسر الدال على اتباع الأول الثاني

QURTUBI:1:2/r46.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r46.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r46.claim: Rabb means owner; al-Ṣiḥāḥ says it is a divine name used of others only in an annexed construction, though pre-Islamic Arabs also used it for a king.
QURTUBI:1:2/r46.anchor: قوله تعالى : " رب العالمين " أي مالكهم ، وكل من ملك شيئا فهو ربه

QURTUBI:1:2/r47.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r47.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r47.claim: Rabb also means master: Qurtubi cites the command to remember Joseph with his master and the report that a slave woman gives birth to her mistress.
QURTUBI:1:2/r47.anchor: والرب : السيد : ومن قوله تعالى : " اذكرني{[66]} عند ربك "

QURTUBI:1:2/r48.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r48.speaker: الهروي وغيره
QURTUBI:1:2/r48.claim: Al-Harawī and others say rabb can mean one who rectifies, manages, mends, or tends something to completion; they connect rabbāniyyūn with tending the books.
QURTUBI:1:2/r48.anchor: والرب : المصلح والمدبر والجابر والقائم . قال الهروي وغيره : يقال لمن قام بإصلاح شيء

QURTUBI:1:2/r49.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r49.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r49.claim: A prophetic question about a blessing one tends means taking responsibility for it and putting it right.
QURTUBI:1:2/r49.anchor: وفي الحديث : ( هل لك من نعمة تربها عليه ) أي تقوم بها وتصلحها

QURTUBI:1:2/r50.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r50.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r50.claim: Rabb can also mean the deity, as shown by a poet’s line about a lord upon whose head a fox urinates.
QURTUBI:1:2/r50.anchor: والرب : المعبود ومنه قول الشاعر : أرب يبول الثعلبان برأسه

QURTUBI:1:2/r51.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r51.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI:1:2/r51.claim: Al-Naḥḥās records the intensive forms rabbāhu, rabbabahu, and rabbatahu; al-Ṣiḥāḥ says rabbahu, rabbabahu, and tarabbabahu all mean he raised him, and marbūb means the one raised.
QURTUBI:1:2/r51.anchor: ويقال على التكثير{[67]} : رباه ورببه وربته ، حكاه النحاس

QURTUBI:1:2/r52.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r52.speaker: بعض العلماء
QURTUBI:1:2/r52.claim: Some scholars call Rabb the greatest name of God because callers frequently invoke Him by it and it conveys the bond of care, mercy, and need between Lord and servant.
QURTUBI:1:2/r52.anchor: قال بعض العلماء : إن هذا الاسم هو اسم الله الأعظم لكثرة دعوة الداعين به

QURTUBI:1:2/r53.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r53.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r53.claim: One derivation traces Rabb to tarbiya, since God manages and nurtures creation; the stepdaughter is called rabība because her mother’s husband raises her. In this sense it is an attribute of action, while owner or master denotes an attribute of essence.
QURTUBI:1:2/r53.anchor: واختلف في اشتقاقه فقيل : إنه مشتق من التربية ، فالله سبحانه وتعالى مدبر لخلقه ومربيهم

QURTUBI:1:2/r54.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r54.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r54.claim: With the definite article, Rabb is specific to God; without it, the term can apply to God or a servant, but God alone owns owners and owned things, creates and provides, and cannot lose His dominion as human owners can.
QURTUBI:1:2/r54.anchor: متى أدخلت الألف واللام على " رب " اختص الله تعالى به ، لأنها للعهد وإن حذفنا منه صار مشتركا

QURTUBI:1:2/r55.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r55.speaker: قتادة
QURTUBI:1:2/r55.claim: Qatāda says al-ʿālamīn is the plural of ʿālam and means every existing thing other than God, with no singular on this pattern, like rahṭ or qawm.
QURTUBI:1:2/r55.anchor: فقال قتادة : العالمون جمع عالم وهو كل موجود سوى الله تعالى ولا واحد له من لفظه

QURTUBI:1:2/r56.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r56.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
QURTUBI:1:2/r56.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says the worlds are the people of each era, citing the address about men among the worlds; al-ʿAjjāj and Jarīr also use ʿālam for human communities.
QURTUBI:1:2/r56.anchor: قاله الحسين بن الفضل ، لقوله تعالى : " أتأتون الذكران{[71]} من العالمين "

QURTUBI:1:2/r57.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r57.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI:1:2/r57.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the worlds are jinn and humans, citing the Qur’an’s description of the Prophet as a warner to all worlds, since he was not sent as a warner to animals.
QURTUBI:1:2/r57.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : العالمون الجن والإنس ، دليله قوله تعالى : " ليكون للعالمين{[73]} نذيرا "

QURTUBI:1:2/r58.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r58.speaker: الفراء وأبو عبيدة
QURTUBI:1:2/r58.claim: Al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda restrict the term to rational beings: humans, jinn, angels, and devils, excluding animals because the plural form is for rational beings; al-Aʿshā’s verse is cited.
QURTUBI:1:2/r58.anchor: وقال الفراء وأبو عبيدة : العالم عبارة عمن يعقل ، وهم أربعة أمم : الإنس والجن والملائكة والشياطين

QURTUBI:1:2/r59.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r59.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
QURTUBI:1:2/r59.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam says the worlds are the beings who receive sustenance.
QURTUBI:1:2/r59.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم : هم المرتزقون

QURTUBI:1:2/r60.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r60.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
QURTUBI:1:2/r60.claim: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ says the worlds are spiritual beings; a similar Ibn ʿAbbās gloss includes every living creature moving on earth.
QURTUBI:1:2/r60.anchor: ونحوه قول أبي عمرو بن العلاء : هم الروحانيون . وهو معنى قول ابن عباس أيضا : كل ذي روح دب على وجه الأرض

QURTUBI:1:2/r61.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r61.speaker: وهب بن منبه
QURTUBI:1:2/r61.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih says God has eighteen thousand worlds, of which this world is one.
QURTUBI:1:2/r61.anchor: وقال وهب بن منبه : إن لله عز وجل ثمانية عشر ألف عالم ، الدنيا عالم منها

QURTUBI:1:2/r62.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r62.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
QURTUBI:1:2/r62.claim: Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī says God has forty thousand worlds, with the inhabited world from east to west counting as one.
QURTUBI:1:2/r62.anchor: وقال أبو سعيد الخدري : إن لله أربعين ألف عالم ، الدنيا من شرقها إلى غربها عالم واحد

QURTUBI:1:2/r63.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r63.speaker: مقاتل
QURTUBI:1:2/r63.claim: Muqātil says there are eighty thousand worlds, forty thousand on land and forty thousand at sea.
QURTUBI:1:2/r63.anchor: وقال مقاتل : العالمون ثمانون ألف عالم ، أربعون ألف عالم في البر وأربعون ألف عالم في البحر

QURTUBI:1:2/r64.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r64.speaker: الربيع بن أنس عن أبي العالية
QURTUBI:1:2/r64.claim: Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas transmits from Abū al-ʿĀliya that jinn and humans are worlds and that each of earth’s four corners contains 1,500 worlds created to worship God.
QURTUBI:1:2/r64.anchor: وروى الربيع بن أنس عن أبي العالية قال : الجن عالم والإنس عالم وسوى ذلك للأرض أربع زوايا

QURTUBI:1:2/r65.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r65.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r65.claim: Qurtubi prefers the first view, that the worlds include every creature and existent thing, supported by Pharaoh asking about the Lord of the worlds and Moses answering that He is Lord of the heavens, earth, and all between them.
QURTUBI:1:2/r65.anchor: قلت : والقول الأول أصح هذه الأقوال ؛ لأنه شامل لكل مخلوق وموجود

QURTUBI:1:2/r66.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r66.speaker: الزجاج والخليل
QURTUBI:1:2/r66.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives ʿālam from knowledge or a sign: it is everything God created in this life and the next and it points to its maker and planner; al-Khalīl likewise says a sign or marker indicates a thing.
QURTUBI:1:2/r66.anchor: ثم هو مأخوذ من العلم والعلامة لأنه يدل على موجده . كذا قال الزجاج قال : العالم كل ما خلقه الله

QURTUBI:1:2/r67.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r67.speaker: الجنيد
QURTUBI:1:2/r67.claim: A man praised God before al-Junayd but stopped before saying Lord of the worlds; al-Junayd urged him to complete the verse, explaining that created things vanish when paired with the Eternal.
QURTUBI:1:2/r67.anchor: وقد ذكر أن رجلا قال بين يدي الجنيد : الحمد لله فقال له : أتمها كما قال الله قل رب العالمين

QURTUBI:1:2/r68.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI:1:2/r68.speaker: author
QURTUBI:1:2/r68.claim: Rabb may be read in the nominative by syntactic disconnection, meaning He is Lord of the worlds, or in the accusative as a word of praise.
QURTUBI:1:2/r68.anchor: يجوز الرفع والنصب في " رب " فالنصب على المدح والرفع على القطع ، أي هو رب العالمين

RAZI:1:1/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:1/r1.speaker: author
RAZI:1:1/r1.claim: Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.
RAZI:1:1/r1.anchor: بسم الله الرحمان الرحيم } نشرع في أداء كل الخيرات والمأمورات

RAZI:1:2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r1.claim: Praise is praise for a blessing, and praise for a blessing requires knowing it; God’s blessings cannot be counted, as the Qur’an says.
RAZI:1:2/r1.anchor: الحمد إنما يكون حمدا على النعمة

RAZI:1:2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r2.claim: A rational person should examine the self, composed of soul and body; the body is the less excellent and less beneficial of the two parts.
RAZI:1:2/r2.anchor: العاقل يجب أن يعتبر ذاته ،   وذلك لأنه مؤلف من نفس وبدن

RAZI:1:2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r3.claim: Anatomists have identified nearly five thousand benefits and interests that God wisely arranged in the creation of the human body.
RAZI:1:2/r3.anchor: أصحاب التشريح وجدوا قريبا من خمسة آلاف نوع من المنافع والمصالح

RAZI:1:2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r4.claim: Known bodily benefits are only a drop in the ocean of the unknown; understanding divine wisdom in creating the human being involves ten thousand questions or more.
RAZI:1:2/r4.anchor: نسبة هذا القدر المعلوم المذكور إلى ما لم يعلم وما لم يذكر كالقطرة في البحر المحيط

RAZI:1:2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r5.claim: Adding the wisdom evident in the Throne, Footstool, heavens, fixed and moving stars, and the varied measures and colors of created things expands the inquiry to roughly a million questions.
RAZI:1:2/r5.anchor: إلى هذه الجملة آثار حكم الله تعالى في تخليق العرش والكرسي وأطباق السماوات ،   وأجرام النيرات

RAZI:1:2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r6.claim: The same inquiry includes the wisdom in minerals, plants, animals, their kinds and states; God has made most of creation serve human benefit.
RAZI:1:2/r6.anchor: تخليق الأمهات والمولدات من الجمادات والنباتات والحيوانات وأصناف أقسامها وأحوالها

RAZI:1:2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r7.claim: Razi links the statement that God subjected what is in the heavens and earth for people to the vast created benefits contained in praise.
RAZI:1:2/r7.anchor: كما قال تعالى : { وسخر لكم ما في السماوات وما في الأرض }

RAZI:1:2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r8.claim: Because all these innumerable blessings and their wisdom fall under praise to God, the phrase “Praise belongs to God” encompasses about a million questions, more or less.
RAZI:1:2/r8.anchor: أن قوله جل جلاله : { الحمد لله } مشتمل على ألف ألف مسألة

RAZI:1:2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r9.claim: “Lord” is in a genitive construction with “the worlds” as its genitive complement; understanding this relation requires knowing both terms.
RAZI:1:2/r9.anchor: أن قوله : { رب } مضاف وقوله : { العالمين } مضاف إليه

RAZI:1:2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r10.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r10.claim: One cannot know God as Lord of the worlds without first understanding what “Lord” and “the worlds” mean.
RAZI:1:2/r10.anchor: فمن المحال حصول العلم بكونه تعالى ربا للعالمين إلا بعد معرفة رب والعالمين

RAZI:1:2/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r11.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r11.claim: The worlds comprise every existent other than God: spatial bodies, incorporeal entities, and attributes; bodies divide into simple entities and composites.
RAZI:1:2/r11.anchor: العالمين عبارة عن كل موجود سوى الله تعالى ،   وهي على ثلاثة أقسام : المتحيزات

RAZI:1:2/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r12.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r12.claim: Razi lists spheres, stars and elemental “mothers” among simple bodies, and the three generated kinds—minerals, plants and animals—among composites.
RAZI:1:2/r12.anchor: فهي الأفلاك والكواكب والأمهات ،   وأما المركبات فهي المواليد الثلاثة

RAZI:1:2/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r13.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r13.claim: Razi says there is no proof that bodies are limited to the familiar cosmic categories: since an infinite void lies beyond the world and God can do all possible things, He can create countless external worlds, each larger than this one and containing analogous heavens, earths and celestial bodies.
RAZI:1:2/r13.anchor: ثبت بالدليل أنه حصل خارج العالم خلاء لا نهاية له ،   وثبت بالدليل أنه تعالى قادر

RAZI:1:2/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r14.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r14.claim: Razi rejects philosophers’ arguments that there is only one world as weak and based on unsound premises; he cites Abū al-ʿAlāʾ al-Maʿarrī’s verses about God’s many heavens and the smallness of our past and future.
RAZI:1:2/r14.anchor: ودلائل الفلاسفة في إثبات أن العالم واحد دلائل ضعيفة ركيكة مبنية على مقدمات واهية

RAZI:1:2/r15.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r15.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r15.claim: Even a lifetime devoted to mineral wonders, plants’ flowers and fruits, or the varieties of beasts, wild animals, birds and insects would not reach the depths of these topics.
RAZI:1:2/r15.anchor: لنفد عمره في أقل القليل من هذه المطالب

RAZI:1:2/r16.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:2/r16.speaker: author
RAZI:1:2/r16.claim: Razi links the inexhaustibility of created wonders and divine wisdom to the Qur’anic image of earthly trees as pens and seas as ink, which would not exhaust God’s words.
RAZI:1:2/r16.anchor: ولو أن ما في الأرض من شجرة أقلام والبحر يمده من بعده سبعة أبحر ما نفدت كلمات الله

ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r5.claim: In non-Qur'anic speech, ‘rabb al-ʿālamīn’ may be genitive as a continuation or accusative as praise, with an implied ‘I mention the Lord of the worlds.’
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r5.anchor: فمن نصب رب العالمين فإنما ينصب لأنه ثناء على الله

ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r6.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r6.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r6.claim: The accusative construction means ‘I mention the Lord of the worlds’; the nominative construction means ‘He is the Lord of the worlds.’
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r6.anchor: فقوله: رب العالمين - كأنه قال أذكر رب العالمين، وإذا قال رب العالمين فهو على قولك: هو رب العالمين

ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r7.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r7.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r7.claim: An unnamed poet's line illustrates that accusative participles may follow a preceding noun or be accusatives of praise, while nominative forms can state ‘they are the ones’; the grammarians accept the listed case combinations.
ZAJJAJ:v1p43/r7.anchor: الطاعنين ولما يظعنوا أحدا. . . والقائلين لمن دار نخليها

ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r1.claim: Although nominative and accusative forms are possible in ordinary speech, the Qur'an uses the best and most eloquent wording, ‘rabb al-ʿālamīn al-raḥmān al-raḥīm.’
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r1.anchor: قد فسرنا أنه لا يجوز في القرآن إلا (رب العالمين الرحمن الرحيم)

ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r2.claim: ‘Al-ʿālamīn’ means everything God created, as in ‘He is Lord of everything.’
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r2.anchor: معناه كل ما خلق الله، كما قال؛

ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r3.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r3.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r3.claim: ‘Al-ʿālamīn’ is the plural of ‘ʿālam’; the word has no singular from its own form because it gathers different kinds, while a singular ‘ʿālam’ would gather members of one kind.
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r3.anchor: وهو جمع عالم، تقول: هؤلاء عالمون، ورأيت عالمين، ولا واحد لعالم من لفظه لأن عالما جمع لأشياء مختلفة

ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r4.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r4.speaker: سيبويه
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r4.claim: Sibawayh says the plural nūn is opened to distinguish it from the dual nūn, which is kasra.
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r4.anchor: وزعم سيبويه أنها فتحت ليفرق بينها وبين نون الإثنين، تقول: هذان عالمان

ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r5.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r5.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r5.claim: The plural nūn is also opened at a meeting of two still letters; kasra is avoided as heavy after wāw or yāʾ, as in the cited forms ‘sawfa’ and ‘ayna Zayd.’
ZAJJAJ:v1p46/r5.anchor: وكذلك نون الجماعة فتحت لالتقاء الساكنين، ولم تكسر لثقل الكسرة بعد الواو والياء

NASHR:v2p410/r6.author: Ibn al-Jazarī
NASHR:v2p410/r6.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
NASHR:v2p410/r6.claim: For Ibn Kathīr, takbīr begins after al-Ḍuḥā at each sūra through al-Nās; after its final takbīr he recites al-Fātiḥa and five opening verses of al-Baqara through وأولئك هم المفلحون, then the completion supplication. Al-Dānī calls this al-ḥāl al-murtaḥil.
NASHR:v2p410/r6.anchor: من آخر سورة والضحى مع فراغه من كل سورة إلى آخر

BIQAI-FULL:v2p706#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v2p706#2/r3.speaker: الغزالي
BIQAI-FULL:v2p706#2/r3.claim: Al-Ghazālī reads the Fātiḥa’s repeated mention of mercy as signaling both perfect creation and provision for each world and mercy in the afterlife.
BIQAI-FULL:v2p706#2/r3.anchor: قال الغزالي في أوائل كتاب الجواهر

DURR-FULL:v1p11/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r3.claim: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet calling “Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds” the Mother of the Qurʾan, the Mother of the Book, and the seven oft-repeated.
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r3.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم {الحمد لله رب العالمين} أم القرآن وأم الكتاب والسبع المثاني

DURR-FULL:v1p11/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r8.speaker: علي
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r8.claim: ʿAli identifies the seven oft-repeated as al-Hamd; when told it has only six verses, he counts the basmala as a verse.
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r8.anchor: عن عبد خير قال: سئل علي رضي الله عنه عن السبع المثاني فقال {الحمد لله رب العالمين}

DURR-FULL:v1p11/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r9.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r9.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that al-Fatiha has seven verses, including the basmala, and is the seven oft-repeated, the Magnificent Qurʾan, the Mother of the Qurʾan, and the Fatiha of the Book.
DURR-FULL:v1p11/r9.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم {الحمد لله رب العالمين} سبع آيات {بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم} إحداهن
